[Prop 13 of arXiv:2605.31568, 'Lipschitz continuity of the time constant for continuum percolation'] Given $d \ge 2$, there exists $C_d < \infty$ such that the following holds.
    If $G$ is an induced subgraph of $G_\lam$, for any $W \subset \R^d$ 
    and any path $\gamma$ in $G$, 
    there exists a self-avoiding path $\gamma'$ in $G$
    with the same endpoints as $\gamma$
    such that all vertices of $\gamma'$ lie in $\gamma$, and
    \[
        |\gamma' \cap W| \le C_d \mathrm{vol}(W + B(1/2)).
    \]
    Moreover,
    we can either take $\gamma = \gamma'$
    or $|\gamma'| < |\gamma|$.

[Proposition P:airy1-alpha-mixing of arXiv:2607.17113, 'Two-time spatial decorrelation for the flat KPZ fixed point'] For each fixed $s>0$, there are constants $C_s,c_s>0$ such that the process
  $\{\mathfrak{h}(s,y): y\in \mathbb{R}\}$ has the $\alpha$-mixing coefficient
  \begin{align}
    \alpha_s(d)& \coloneqq 
    \sup_a
    \sup_{\substack{
    E_-\in\sigma(\mathfrak{h}(s,y):y\le a)\\
    E_+\in\sigma(\mathfrak{h}(s,y):y\ge a+d)}}
    |\mathbb{P}(E_-\cap E_+)-\mathbb{P}(E_-)\mathbb{P}(E_+)| \nonumber \\
    &
    \le
    C_s \,\mathrm{e}^{-c_s d^3/s^2},
    \qquad d\ge0.
    
  \end{align}
title: Proposition P:airy1-alpha-mixing of arXiv:2607.17113

body: FIRES WHEN a proof about a constrained operator bounds the constrained part and then treats the UNCONSTRAINED part as if it were also bounded. WHAT HAPPENED: the definition of a xi-QSO constrains only same-block pairs; cross-block pairs may have arbitrary coefficients P_{ij,k}. The first pass bounded the new empty-body mass by x_0' >= x_0^2 + (1/q)(1 - x_0)^2 and concluded convergence, but that last inequality quietly assumes the cross-block coefficients sum to at most one - which the definition permits but does not force - so the mass produced at states other than 0 is uncontrolled and can be recycled into cross-block pairs at the next step. Whether that recycling can sustain a nontrivial fixed point is exactly what the Cauchy-Schwarz bound does NOT decide. CONDITION OF FAILURE: any unconstrained coefficient block that the bound silently constrains. THE FIX that closed it: lower-bound x_0' by the contributions that MUST land on 0 under the definition - the pair (0,0), the pairs containing 0, and the same-block pairs - which gives 1 - x_0' <= (1 - 1/q)(1 - x_0)^2 with no assumption on the cross-block coefficients at all.

body: Let M be a block matrix [[A, B], [C, D]] with A a p by p invertible matrix, D a q by q matrix, B a p by q matrix, and C a q by p matrix. Then M is invertible if and only if the Schur complement S = D - C A^{-1} B is invertible, and in that case det(M) = det(A) det(S). If in addition M is Hermitian (C = B*, A and D Hermitian) and A is positive definite, then M is positive semidefinite (respectively positive definite) if and only if S is positive semidefinite (respectively positive definite). [standard, e.g. Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, Appendix A]

[Theorem rosenthal of arXiv:2604.24914, 'SPDEs with time-independent\\ L\'evy colored noise'] Let $\{M_t\}_{t \geq 0}$ be a c\`adl\`ag square-integrable martingale with $M_0=0$ and $\langle M \rangle$ be its predictable quadratic variation. We denote by $(\Delta M)_t$ the jump size of $M$ at time $t$. Then for any $p \geq 2$, there exists a constant $\mathcal{B}_p>0$ depending on $p$ such that for any $t>0$,
$$\|\sup_{s \leq t}|M_s|\|_p \leq \mathcal{B}_p \Big(\| \langle M \rangle_t^{1/2}\|_p +\|\sup_{s \leq t}|(\Delta M)_s| \|_p\Big).$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Rosenthal's inequality

[Definition1 weak_Markovian_halfplane of arXiv:2603.05491, '\textbf{Local limits of uniform triangulations with boundaries in high genus}'] A random triangulation of the half-plane $H$ is said to satisfy a weak spatial Markov property if there exists a function $a$ such that, for any $t$, we have
\[
\mathbb{P}(t \subset H) = a(|\partial^{*}t| - |\partial t|, |t_{\mathrm{in}}|).
\]
We say that $H$ is strongly Markovian if there exist constants $\beta,\lambda > 0$ such that, for any $t$, we have 
\[
\mathbb{P}(t \subset H) = \beta^{|\partial^{*}t| - |\partial t|}\lambda^{|t_{\mathrm{in}}|}.
\]
title: Definition1 weak_Markovian_halfplane of arXiv:2603.05491

body: [Corollary 8 (FIID sparse unique infinite clusters) of arXiv:2504.02435, 'Poisson-Voronoi percolation in higher rank'] Let $G$ be a connected higher rank semisimple real Lie group with property (T). Let~$\Pi$ be the Poisson point process on $G$ of intensity $1$ equipped with iid ${\rm Unif}[0,1]$ marks. Then, for every $\eps>0$, there is a $G$-equivariant factor graph $\mathcal H$ of $\Pi$ with a unique infinite cluster and $\mathbb E\big[ {\rm deg}_{\mathcal H(\Pi_0)}(1_G) \big]\le\eps$ for $\Pi_0=\Pi\cup\{1_G\}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: FIID sparse unique infinite clusters

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Check both implications through the ergodic theorem for the environment process. Result: One direction is standard: if an invariant absolutely continuous probability measure Q exists and is ergodic, the ergodic theorem for the environment chain gives X_n/n -> E_Q[local drift] a.s., and transience in direction l plus Kozlov's theorem (Q equivalent to P, unique) makes the limit velocity well defined; it is nonzero in direction l provided E_Q[d(0,omega) . l] > 0, which follows from transience in direction l ONLY IF one also knows the velocity cannot vanish under transience, which is itself the ballisticity question, so this direction reduces to: invariant a.c. measure + transient in l implies v . l > 0. Under (E) the Kalikow-type argument gives v . l >= 0 but not strict positivity. The converse (ballistic implies invariant a.c. measure) is known under (UE) and (IID) from the renewal structure with finite expected regeneration time; under (ERG) only, regenerations are unavailable and the construction of Q fails. Both directions therefore reduce to statements known under (IID)+(UE) and unproved under (ERG)+(E). Obstruction: Without i.i.d. renewal structure neither the construction of the invariant measure nor strict positivity of the velocity is available.

Let X and Y be finite sets and let F = Y^X be the set of all objective functions f : X -> Y. A search algorithm a is a deterministic rule that, given the sequence of points sampled so far and their values, picks a new point of X not yet sampled; d_m(f, a) denotes the sequence of m sampled values it produces on f. For any two algorithms a and b, any m, and any sequence d of m values, the number of functions f in F with d_m(f, a) = d equals the number with d_m(f, b) = d. Hence every performance measure that depends only on the sampled value sequence has the same average over all of F for every algorithm.
finite search and value spaces
0 <= m <= |X|, since an algorithm that never revisits a point can sample at most |X| points
the average is uniform over ALL functions in Y^X; for a non-uniform prior, or a structured class of functions, algorithms can and do differ
algorithms never resample a point

body: A non-degenerate probability distribution \mu is said to be stable (or strictly stable if d_n = 0) if for every n \ge 2 and independent random variables X_1, \dots, X_n \sim \mu, there exist constants c_n > 0 and d_n \in \mathbb{R}$ such that \sum_{k=1}^n X_k \stackrel{d}{=} c_n X_1 + d_n. The scaling constant necessarily takes the form c_n = n^{1/\alpha} for a unique parameter \alpha \in (0, 2], called the characteristic exponent (or index of stability).

body: Let H(q,p,t) be a Hamiltonian on phase space with canonical coordinates (q,p), whose flow is generated by Hamilton's equations dq/dt = dH/dp, dp/dt = -dH/dq. Liouville's theorem states that the time-t flow map preserves phase-space (Lebesgue) volume: for every measurable region D, the volume of the image of D under the flow equals the volume of D, for all t; equivalently the flow's Jacobian determinant is identically 1. If rho(q,p,t) is the phase-space density of an ensemble evolving under H, this is equivalent to partial rho/partial t + {rho, H} = 0, where {.,.} is the Poisson bracket, so density is constant along trajectories.
title: Liouville's theorem (Hamiltonian mechanics)

  \[e^{-\lambda_0t}\mathbb{E}[S_j(t)]=(av+\mu)\int_0^t e^{-\lambda_0 s}P_j(s)\,ds=(av+\mu)\frac{\Gamma(j)\Gamma(\lambda_0/\lambda_1+1)}{\Gamma(j+\lambda_0/\lambda_1+1)}\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(\lambda_0/\lambda_1)_n(j)_n}{(j+1+\lambda_0/\lambda_1)_nn!}p_1^n\]

  And, the following frequency asymptotic:

  \[\lim_{t\to\infty}e^{-\lambda_0t}\mathbb{E}[S_j(t)]=(av+\mu)\frac{q_1\Gamma(\lambda_0/\lambda_1+1)}{\lambda_1j^{\lambda_0/\lambda_1+1}}(1-p_1)^{-\lambda_0/\lambda_1}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{j^{\lambda_0/\lambda_1+2}}\right)\]

[Lemma 19 (\citet{ejp2021,sambale2023some}) of arXiv:2608.26618, 'A Unified Descriptive-Complexity Framework for Model Selection under Correlated Designs'] Let $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_n)^\top$ be independent, mean-zero
sub-Weibull $(\alpha,\zeta)$ random variables for all $i$ and some $\alpha\in(0,2]$.
Let $A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be a symmetric matrix. Then, for every $t\ge 0$,
\begin{equation*}
\Pr\!\Big(
\big|\varepsilon^\top A\varepsilon-\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon^\top A\varepsilon)\big|
\ge t
\Big)
\ \le\
2\exp\!\left\{
-c_{\alpha,\zeta}
\min\!\left(
\frac{t^2}{\sigma^4\|A\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2},\
\Big(\frac{t}{\sigma^2\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}}\Big)^{\alpha/2}
\right)
\right\},
\end{equation*}
where $\|A\|_F$ is the Frobenius norm and
$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is the operator norm. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \citet{ejp2021,sambale2023some}

[Lem lem1 of arXiv:2412.05521, 'Random attractors for the stochastic Nernst-Planck-Navier-Stokes system with multiplicativ'] Let $t_0$ be a real number and $\varphi(t)\in L_{loc}^{1}(t_{0},\infty )$ be a function satisfying $\varphi'(t)\in L_{loc}^{1}(t_{0},\infty )$. Let $h(t)\in L_{loc}^{1}(t_{0},\infty)$ and $k(t)\in L_{loc}^{1}([t_{0},\infty ))$.  Let $\varphi(t)$ satisfy the differential inequality
		$$\displaystyle{ \varphi'(t) \leq \varphi(t)k(t) + h(t)\quad \mathrm{for\ a.e.}\quad t \in (t_{0},\infty ), }$$
		then
		$$\displaystyle{\varphi(t) \leq \varphi(t_{0})e^{\int_{t_{0}}^{t}k(\xi)\,d\xi } +\int_{t_{0}}^{t}h(\xi)e^{\int_{\xi}^{t}k(s)\,ds }\,d\xi\quad \mathrm{for\ all}\quad t \in [t_{0},\infty ). }$$
		In particular, if $k(t) = C$ for all $t\geq t_0$ is a real constant, then
		$$\displaystyle{ \varphi(t)\leq \varphi(t_{0})e^{-C(t_{0}-t) } + \int_{t_{0}}^{t}h(\xi)e^{-C(\xi-t)}\,d\xi\quad \mathrm{for\ all}\quad t \in [t_{ 0},\infty ). }$$
		Furthermore, if $h(t) = D$ for all $t\geq t_0$ is a real constant, then
		$$\displaystyle{ \varphi(t)\leq \varphi(t_{0})e^{-C(t_{0}-t) } + \frac{D}{C}(e^{-C(t_{0}-t) } - 1)\quad \mathrm{for\ all}\quad t \in [t_{ 0},\infty ). }$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \textbf{Gronwall's inequality}

[Theorem thm:TASEPexo of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take $f_1, \ldots, f_k \in\operatorname{UC}_+$.
            For each $\epsilon>0$, we take $d_\epsilon>0$, such that $d_\epsilon\epsilon^{1/2}|\log(\epsilon)|\to 0$ as $\epsilon\to 0$.
            Take half-space TASEPs $(h_t^{\epsilon, i}, t\ge 0)$ for $i\in\llbracket 1, k\rrbracket$ under the $d_\epsilon$-coupling, with each $\mathbf{A}_\epsilon h_0^{\epsilon, i}\to f_i$ in $\operatorname{UC}_+$ as $\epsilon\to 0$.
            The boundary parameter is taken either (1) fixed $\alpha> \frac{1}{2}$ and $\rho=-\infty$, or (2) $\alpha = \frac{1}{2}-\rho\epsilon^{1/2}/2$ for some $\rho\in\mathbb{R}$.
            Then 
                            \[
                \big\{ \mathbf{A}_\epsilon h^{\epsilon,i}_{2\epsilon^{-3/2}t} (x) + \epsilon^{-1}t \big\}_{(i,x,t)\in\llbracket 1, k\rrbracket\times \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\times \mathbb{R}_+} \stackrel{d}{\to} \{f_i\diamond \mathcal{L}^\rho(\cdot, 0; x, t)\}_{(i,x,t)\in\llbracket 1, k\rrbracket\times \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\times \mathbb{R}_+},
                \]
            in the following senses:
            \begin{itemize}
                \item[(i)] if there is a constant $C>0$, such that $\mathbf{A}_\epsilon h^{\epsilon,i}_0(x)+2\epsilon^{-1/2}x$ is constant for $x\ge C, \epsilon > 0, i \in \llbracket1, k \rrbracket$, then the convergence is in the uniform-on-compact topology;
                \item[(ii)] if there is a constant $C>0$, such that $\mathbf{A}_\epsilon h^{\epsilon,i}_0(x) \le C(1+x)$ for each $i\in\llbracket 1,k\rrbracket$ and $x\ge 0$, then the convergence is in the sense of finite dimensional distributions.
            \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:AR_pos_signs of arXiv:2604.22453, 'Adapted Wasserstein Barycenters of Gaussian Processes'] Let \(\mathbb{X}^1,\ldots,\mathbb{X}^K\) be the univariate \(AR(1)\) processes defined by
(equation eq:AR_def of the paper), with \(\sigma_t^k>0\) and \(\alpha_t^k\ge 0\) for every
\(k\in[K]\) and \(t=2,\ldots,T\). Then, for every \(t\in[T]\), we have
\[
\mathbf P_t^\star:=\mathbf 1_K\mathbf 1_K^\intercal
\]
where $\mathbf{1}_K:=[1,1,\dots,1]^\intercal\in\mathbb{R}^K$
is the unique minimizer of \(\Phi_t\) over \(\mathscr{P}_+(K)\).

Consequently, the common-noise input condition holds, the restricted and
unrestricted barycenter values coincide, and the barycenter admits the ordinary
filtered Gaussian representative
\[

\accentset{\overline{\hphantom{\mathbb{X}}}}{\mathbb{X}}
=\mathbb{G}^{0,
\accentset{\overline{\hphantom{L}}}{L}
}\in\mathcal{FG}(T,1),
\qquad

\accentset{\overline{\hphantom{L}}}{L}
_{\cdot,t}
=
\mathbf L_{\cdot,t}\Lambda\mathbf 1_K
=
\sum_{k=1}^K\lambda_k L_{\cdot,t}^k,
\qquad t\in[T].
\]
Equivalently, under the common innovation convention,
\[

\accentset{\overline{\hphantom{X}}}{X}
_u=\sum_{k=1}^K\lambda_kX_u^k,
\qquad u\in[T].
\]
Thus, the adapted barycenter, both unrestricted in \(\mathrm{FP}_2\) and restricted to
\(\mathcal{FG}(T,1)\), coincides with the Knothe--Rosenblatt barycenter.

[Lemma 18 of arXiv:2609.03185, 'Uniqueness of tangent flows in free boundary flow'] Let $\delta_1, \delta_2$ be the constants from Lemma ~\ref{lemma 3.4} and $C_0$ be the constant from Corollary \ref{cor 3.3}. Then there exist $\epsilon_0 > 0$ and a large $L >0$ such that the following holds. Suppose that 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\tau + 2L \le T_\alpha,$
    \item $\tilde{\delta_1},\tilde{\delta_2} \in (\delta_1, \delta_2)$ with $\tilde{\delta_1} < \tilde{\delta_2},$
    \item $|\alpha| \leq \epsilon_0,$
    \item $\mathcal{D}_{\mathscr {T}^{\alpha, \mathscr C_+}_\tau}(M_{\tau_0}) \leq \epsilon_0.$
    \item $\mathcal{D}_{\mathscr {T}^{\alpha, \mathscr C_+}_{\tau+L}}(M_{\tau_0+L}) > \max\Big\{e^{-\frac {\tau_0} {8}}, C_0  e^{- \frac{(R_\alpha-1)^2}{8p_0}}\Big\}.$
\end{enumerate}
If 
$$\mathcal{D}_{\mathscr {T}^{\alpha, \mathscr C_+}_{\tau+L}}(M_{\tau_0 + L}) \geq e^{\tilde{\delta_1}L} \mathcal{D}_{\mathscr {T}^{\alpha, \mathscr C_+}_\tau} (M_{\tau_0}),$$

body: [Definition def:irreducible-comp of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] An animal $\Gamma \in \ensuremath{\mathcal P}_V({\ensuremath{\mathsf u}}, \mathsf v)$ is called left-irreducible if it has no cone-points, and $\Gamma \subset \ensuremath{\mathcal Y}^\blacktriangleright(\mathsf v)$. Similarly, $\Gamma$ is right-irreducible if it has no cone-points and $\Gamma \subset \ensuremath{\mathcal Y}^\blacktriangleleft({\ensuremath{\mathsf u}})$. We say $\Gamma$ is irreducible if it is both right and left irreducible. The set of all left-irreducible, right-irreducible, and irreducible animals with starting point at ${\mathsf{o}^*}$ is denoted ${\ensuremath{\mathsf A}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf L}}, {\ensuremath{\mathsf A}}_{\ensuremath{\mathsf R}}, {\ensuremath{\mathsf A}}$ respectively. (So each of these sets consist of $\Gamma$ in $\bigcup_B \ensuremath{\mathcal P}_V({\mathsf{o}^*}, B)$.)
title: Irreducible components

body:
[Proposition 51 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let $X$ be a smooth proper $k$-scheme of dimension $d$.
We assume $\omega_X$ is anti-ample.
Then the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $X$ is HT-split.
\item We have
\[
H^{i}(X,\Omega_X^j \otimes \omega_X)=0 \quad (i+j=d-1,j>0).
\]
\item Akizuki--Nakano-type vanishing holds on $X$.
\end{enumerate}

[Lem planarclassification of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Suppose that $M$ admits a minimal lamination $\Lambda$ with simply connected leaves. Then either $\Lambda$ is a homologically trivial sphere, or $M$ is homeomorphic to a connected sum
    $$M \cong M'\#K_1\#\dots \#K_m,$$
    where the $K_i$'s are compact 3-manifolds, $M'$ is one of $S^1\times S^2$, $S^1 \times D^2$, $\mathbb{T}^3$, or $\mathbb{T}^2 \times I$, and $\Lambda$ is contained in $M'$ and is semi-conjugate to a linear foliation on $M'$. In particular, $\Lambda$ is measured.

[Theorem s of arXiv:2411.05204, '\Large\bf Sample Path Properties of the Fractional Wiener--Weierstrass Bridge'] Consider a centered Gaussian process $(X(t))_{t\in[0,1]}$ with
\begin{align}
\frac{1}{L}\sigma(|h|)\leq \left\lVertX(t+h)-X(t)\right\rVert_2\leq L\sigma(|h|)
\end{align}
for all $t,t+h\in[0,1]$, where $\sigma$ is concave and regularly varying at $0$ with index $H\in(0,1)$. Suppose $\Psi(x):=\sigma(x)(\log\log(1/x))^{1/2}$ is strictly increasing and denote by $\Phi$ its inverse, then
\[
{\mathbb P}\left(\frac{1}{L}<v_\Phi( X )<\infty\right)=1
\]for this choice of $\Phi$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 23 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] Assume that $\mu$ is finitely supported. More precisely, assume that there exist

\[
    \mu(dx)

\[
    \operatorname{Supp}(\mu)=\{x_1,\dots,x_N\}.

Then under Assumption~\ref{ass:Laws existence} and Assumption~\ref{ass:a-existence-solution} (i), equation \eqreftag{eq:MV-a} admits a weak solution with initial law
$\pi_0$.

body:
[Lemma 12 of arXiv:2608.29427, '\small Positive mass and rigidity \\ for asymptotically flat tangent bundles'] Suppose that \(\widetilde g\) is an interpolating metric and that
	\[
	\xi(x,\y)=o(|\y|^{-1})
	\qquad\text{as }|\y|\to\infty
	\]
	for every \(x\in U_\infty\). Then the connecting metric \(\mathdutchcal g\) is constant in the preferred coordinates on \(U_\infty\), equivalently,
	\[
	{}^{\mathdutchcal g}\Gamma_{ib}^{\,j}=0
	\qquad\text{on }U_\infty.
	\]
	Consequently, on \(TU_\infty\),
	\begin{align}
		\widetilde g_{ij}
		&=
		\psi g_{ij}+(1-\psi)\delta_{ij},\notag\\
		\widetilde g_{i\dot j}
		&=
		a^c_{ij}, \\

[Proposition 9 (Minimality of the effective support) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] One has
\[
 P(x)=P\bigl(\operatorname{proj}_{E(P)}x\bigr).
\]
The subspace \(E(P)\) is the smallest linear subspace with this property.
If \(Q=P\circ U\), then \(U\) maps \(E(Q)\) isometrically onto \(E(P)\).
Consequently the finite Torelli theorem remains valid for different
ambient dimensions after adjoining and then discarding silent Gaussian
coordinates.

[Defn 3 of arXiv:2608.13208, 'Universality in dimension $1$ of kinetically constrained lattice gases'] A KCLG is said to be \emph{ergodic} at $q$ if $\mu_{q}$-almost
surely $\eta\connected{}{}\eta^{0,1}$. Note that due to the monotonicity
of $c$ adding vacancies helps ergodicity, and we may define the critical
parameter
\begin{eqnarray*}
q_{c} & = & \inf\{q\in(0,1):\text{the process is ergodic for }q\}\\
 & = & \sup\{q\in(0,1):\text{ the process is not ergodic for }q\}.
\end{eqnarray*}
By the same argument as \cite{BertiniToninelli}, this notion of ergodicity
implies that $0$ is a simple eigenvalue of the generator in $L^{2}(\mu_{q})$.

body:
For fixed integers C>=0, M>=1 and d>=2, the priors dmu_+/dgamma_d=1+(1/2)sin(omega*x_1), dmu_-/dgamma_d=1-(1/2)sin(omega*x_1), omega=d^(C+M+2), have LSI constant <=3 and covariance <=I. With A*x=x_2 and sigma=1 their observation laws coincide and their posterior TV separation exceeds 3/16 at every observation. Nevertheless the same Gaussian forward scores q_u=-x/(1+u^2) have squared L2 score error <=d^-2M/u^2 under both convolved priors for every u>=d^-C. A sampler supplied only this common approximate-score interface cannot have posterior TV error <=1/16 for both priors on more than half their observations. This is an information/interface obstruction, not computational hardness for identifying prior descriptions or prior samplers.
Fixed finite smoothing-cutoff and inverse-polynomial accuracy budgets C,M
Only approximate forward scores, A, sigma and y are supplied
No prior sample oracle, identifying prior description, exact scores or scores below d^-C

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:286871452285642712315214181d32476eed2b0cbb76e151766bff65fda0c9eb","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/28/286871452285642712315214181d32476eed2b0cbb76e151766bff65fda0c9eb.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:d3865bf78eafb27c44900ef791fa73baebcb34d6684cac19d277c9fde301b55c","bundle_entry_key":"draft-finite-forward-score-tv-obstruction","bundle_id":"population.t411-finite-score-tv-boundary-004","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"posterior sampling; approximate score information; total variation","draft":"w740/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.sampling:draft-finite-forward-score-tv-obstruction","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C009: a finite-forward-score boundary for TV sampling

Version 2, 20 October 2026. Kind: moved; target: T411 Target 1.
Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty or independent verification claim.

## 1. Statement and computational scope

Fix integers C>=0, M>=1 and dimension d>=2. Set omega=d^(C+M+2), a=1/2. Let gamma_d be standard Gaussian measure and define

    d mu_+ / d gamma_d (x) = 1+a sin(omega x_1),
    d mu_- / d gamma_d (x) = 1-a sin(omega x_1).

Both are positive smooth probability laws, have covariance operator at most one, and satisfy

    Ent_mu(f^2) <= 2 C_LS E_mu ||grad f||^2,  C_LS <= 3.

For the nonzero observation A x=x_2 and noise sigma=1, the two observation laws are identical. At every observation y their posterior laws have TV distance strictly greater than 3/16. In particular their ratio ||A||^2 C_LS/sigma^2 is at most 3, and hence satisfies any fixed bound c log d for sufficiently large d.

Nevertheless the SAME score functions q_u(x)=-x/(1+u^2), simultaneously for every u>=d^-C, satisfy

    E_{mu_+ * N(0,u^2 I)} ||q_u-score_+,u||^2 <= d^-2M/u^2,
    E_{mu_- * N(0,u^2 I)} ||q_u-score_-,u||^2 <= d^-2M/u^2.

Therefore an algorithm given only these approximate forward scores, the shared observation model and observation y cannot guarantee posterior TV error <=1/16 for both priors on more than half their observations. This holds irrespective of running time, under this nonidentifying input interface.

This is NOT computational hardness for explicit priors. It excludes access to a prior sampler, an identifying prior description, exact scores, or scores below the stated cutoff. The priors themselves are easily sampled by rejection from gamma_d with acceptance (1 +/- a sin(omega x_1))/(1+a). No conclusion is drawn about those stronger interfaces. C and M are fixed precision/cutoff budgets, not universal bounds on every possible accuracy request. The result gives no inverse problem hardness when a generative oracle is supplied.

## 2. LSI and covariance

The density integrates to one since sin is odd. It lies in [m,B]=[1/2,3/2]. The elementary bounded perturbation argument is as follows. For any nonnegative g,

    Ent_nu(g) = inf_{t>0} E_nu [g log(g/t)-g+t].

The integrand is nonnegative, including its continuous value at g=0. Taking the infimum after bounding the density by B gives Ent_mu(g)<=B Ent_gamma(g). Standard Gaussian LSI gives Ent_gamma(f^2)<=2 E_gamma ||grad f||^2; the lower density bound gives E_gamma ||grad f||^2<=m^-1 E_mu ||grad f||^2. Thus C_LS<=B/m=3. This proof also works directly in dimension d, without a separate tensorization assertion. Use smooth tests of finite energy and then the usual closure.

The first-coordinate raw second moment is one: its perturbation integrates x^2 sin(omega x) against an even Gaussian and vanishes. Its mean is +/- a omega exp(-omega^2/2). The remaining coordinates are independent standard Gaussians with zero means. Thus the covariance is diagonal with first entry 1-a^2 omega^2 exp(-omega^2)<=1 and all other entries one.

## 3. TV separation survives every observation

By the half-L1 convention,

    TV(mu_+,mu_-) = a E |sin(omega Z)|
                 >= a E sin^2(omega Z)
                 = (1-exp(-2 omega^2))/4 > 3/16.

The last inequality uses omega>=1 and exp(2)>4. Observation Y=X_2+G is independent of X_1, and has law N(0,2) under either prior. Given Y=y, X_2 is N(y/2,1/2); all other Gaussian coordinates retain their original independent laws. The first coordinate retains its respective oscillatory law. Tensoring with the common remaining-coordinate posterior leaves TV unchanged, by direct integration of the product densities. This proves the separation for every y.

Let K_y be the output law of a sampler on the common scores and the common y, integrating its internal random coins. It is the same law for both input instances. The sets of observations on which TV(K_y,mu_+(.|y))<=1/16 and TV(K_y,mu_-(.|y))<=1/16 are disjoint: their intersection would contradict the triangle inequality and 2/16<3/16. Under the common Y law the two success probabilities sum to at most one. At least one prior has success probability at most one half. This statement concerns output distributions, not TV distance of individual output points.

## 4. Exact convolved density and score

Write v=1+u^2. Under the Gaussian reference model X~N(0,1), Y=X+uG, the conditional law X|Y=y is N(y/v,u^2/v). The Gaussian characteristic function therefore gives

    p_+,u(y)=phi_v(y)[1+a rho sin(omega y/v)],
    p_-,u(y)=phi_v(y)[1-a rho sin(omega y/v)],
    rho=exp(-omega^2 u^2/(2v)).

The remaining d-1 coordinates are independent N(0,v). Differentiating the positive densities, only the first score coordinate differs from q_u. Pointwise its absolute difference is bounded by

    a rho omega / [v(1-a rho)] <= rho omega/v.

Consequently, under either convolved law,

    u^2 E||q_u-score||^2 <= (omega^2 u^2/v^2) exp(-omega^2 u^2/v)
                         <= z exp(-z),  z=omega^2 u^2/(1+u^2).

This is a pointwise bound followed by integration, and requires no comparison of the two expectation measures.

## 5. Explicit uniform polynomial precision

For u>=d^-C, monotonicity of u^2/(1+u^2) implies

    z >= omega^2 d^-2C/(1+d^-2C) >= z0=d^(2M+4)/2 >= 1.

Since z exp(-z) decreases for z>=1, it is enough to prove log(z0)+2M log d <= z0. Indeed

    log(z0)+2M log d <= (4M+4)log d
                       <= (2M+2)d
                       <= d^(2M+4)/2=z0.

The middle bound uses log d<=d/2 for d>=2. The last reduces to d^(2M+3)>=4M+4, which follows from d>=2, M>=1: 2^5>=8 at M=1 and each increment multiplies the left side by four while increasing the right side by four. Thus z exp(-z)<=d^-2M. This proves the asserted error for all u>=d^-C, without an upper cutoff.

For rational u the common q_u is an exactly rational linear function. On polynomial-size dyadic schedules its coefficient description and network size are polynomial. If a rational-coefficient ReLU realization is wanted, represent each coordinate as -(ReLU(x_i)-ReLU(-x_i))/v. No microscopic feature of the prior has to be encoded in the supplied scores. No exact-real coefficient oracle is needed on those schedules.

## 6. Relation to T411 and prior work

The frontier dossier specifies L2-accurate forward scores and asks for TV in Target 1. The primary GPX paper arXiv:2402.12727v2, Definition 1.1 (PDF page 4), imposes a positive polynomial lower smoothing cutoff; Definition 1.2 on the same page instead uses coupling closeness, not TV. This elementary example explains why an LSI hypothesis alone does not convert such finite-cutoff approximate-score information into a TV guarantee.

The bounded perturbation LSI argument is standard (often called Holley-Stroock); Gaussian LSI was recalled earlier as card claim_4bdeb13cc86ab526b0013e02b6024d3dede00f91d34eca4a10273fa64375e52c. The Gaussian transform and the remaining calculations are given above in full. This is an explicit interface boundary, with no assertion that the example or method is new. It does not settle Target 1 when its oracle is strengthened. It also does not weaken or replace the separate OWF-based Target 2 candidate.

Least trusted issue for review: whether the intended Target 1 input model actually permits arbitrary approximate-score realizations above a fixed positive cutoff. [Lemma L-Lip-d of arXiv:2507.01406, '{\Large On Iterated Lorenz Curves with Applications: The Multivariate Case }'] \noindent  For each $n\geq 1$, the map $L_{n}:[0,1]^{d}
\rightarrow \lbrack 0,1]$ is uniformly Lipschitz with respect to the $\ell
^{1}$--norm. More precisely, 
\begin{equation}
|L_{n}(x)-L_{n}(y)|\leq \frac{1}{c_{d}}\Vert x-y\Vert _{1},\qquad x,y\in
\lbrack 0,1]^{d}.  
\end{equation}

Consequently, the family $(L_{n})_{n\geq 1}$ is $\sqrt{d}/c_{d}$-Lipschitz
with respect to the Euclidean norm. Moreover, since under the standing
density assumptions $L_{0}\in C([0,1]^{d})$, the full family $(L_{n})_{n\geq
0}$ is relatively compact in $C([0,1]^{d})$ with the uniform topology.

\noindent In particular, for any sequence $n_{k}\rightarrow \infty $ there
exists a subsequence $n_{k_{\ell }}$ and a continuous distribution function $
L^{\ast }$ on $[0,1]^{d}$ such that 
\begin{equation}
\sup_{x\in \lbrack 0,1]^{d}}|L_{n_{k_{\ell }}}(x)-L^{\ast }(x)|\rightarrow
0\qquad \text{as }\ell \rightarrow \infty .  
\end{equation}
The marginals $L_{i}^{n_{k_{\ell }}}$ converge uniformly on $[0,1]$ to the
marginals $L_{i}^{\ast }$ of $L^{\ast }$. Each $L_{i}^{\ast }$ is a
continuous distribution function on $[0,1]$.

body:
Own-work method draft supporting T342-C001: when an isotropically oriented single ReLU teacher does not meet an independent-harmonic-coefficient theorem, average its quadratic population projection error over teacher direction. Only its harmonic covariance is used; no independence of the actual neuron coefficients is asserted. Couple that covariance to an independent Gaussian harmonic surrogate after checking convergence of total mass as well as each fixed degree. Adding missing lower odd polynomial terms to the student activation changes feature-span projections by rank at most twice the polynomial-space dimension. Apply the trace-rank bound only to the teacher HIGH-degree covariance; its order-d^(-k) eigenvalues can make that perturbation negligible. Separately fit low degrees with the explicit Monte Carlo estimator, then recover a fixed teacher through conditional sphere Poincare and rotation invariance. Finite-sample ridge error is not an orthogonal population projection and needs additional bounds. This method is part of the v2 reviewer-passed proof, with v3 explanatory additions awaiting separate audit.

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2608.30733, 'An Operator-Theoretic Characterization of Gaussian Measure Singularity under Mean Shifts'] Fix $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and let $\rho=\alpha(1-\alpha)$. Let $P_1=\mathbb G(m_1,\mathsf K)$ and $P_2=\mathbb G(m_2,\mathsf K)$ be Gaussian measures on a separable Hilbert space $H$ with common covariance
operator $\mathsf K$, whose eigenvalues satisfy $\lambda_j>0$ for every $j$,
and let $m_\Delta=m_2-m_1$.
Then the following statements are equivalent:
\[
P_1\perp P_2,
\qquad
\Delta_q\longrightarrow\infty,
\qquad
\frac{\mathcal A_q^{(4)}}{\mathcal A_q^{(F)}}\longrightarrow1.
\]
Equivalently, $P_1\perp P_2\iff\mathcal A_q^{(4)}\sim\mathcal A_q^{(F)}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Defn def.stabilizing_marking of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] \ 
   \begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt] 
\item   We say that   $\xi$  {\em is  stabilizing on the marked
   point process $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$} if 
there 
is an increasing-decreasing family of   
functions $\varphi_p: (0, \infty) \to [0,1], p \in \mathbb{N}$   
   such that
\begin{equation} 
 \sup_{x_1,\ldots,x_p \in \mathbb{R}^d} \mathbb{P}_{\bk x1p}
\bigl(R^\xi( \tilde{x}_1,\tilde{\mathcal{P}}) > r \bigr) \leq \varphi_p(r), \ r > 0. 
\end{equation}

\item   We say that   $\xi$  {\em is stabilizing on finite windows of $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$} if for all $p \in \mathbb{N}$ there 
is an increasing-decreasing family of   
functions $\varphi_p: (0, \infty) \to [0,1], p \in \mathbb{N}$,
such that
\begin{equation} 
 \sup_{1 \leq n < \infty} \sup_{x_1,\ldots,x_p \in W_n} \mathbb{P}_{\bk x1p}
\bigl(R_{W_n}^\xi( \tilde{x}_1,\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n) > r \bigr) \leq \varphi_p(r), \ r > 0.
\end{equation}
 \item   We say that $\xi$ is {\em fast stabilizing} on $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$, or on finite windows of $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$, if 
  $(\varphi_p)_{p \in \mathbb{N}}$ are  fast decreasing.
 Without loss of generality we always assume that $\varphi_p\le\varphi_{p+1}$ for all $p\in \mathbb{N}$.
\end{enumerate}

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, A homogeneous space with no nonconstant quasiharmonic functions (October 2026), answers Problem 2 of Appendix II of M. Bjorklund, Five remarks about random walks on groups (arXiv:1406.0763), which asks for a countable measured group (G, mu) and a subgroup H of infinite index such that G/H admits no nonconstant left mu-harmonic or mu-quasiharmonic functions. G is the group of finitely supported permutations of {0, 1, 2, ...}, H the stabiliser of 0, and mu gives mass p_n > 0 to each transposition (0 n), the p_n summing to 1. The induced walk on G/H is a walk on an infinite star; at a leaf k the quasiharmonic equation forces u(k) = u(0) - c/p_k with c the defect, and the equation at the centre is a series whose terms tend to -c, so c = 0 and u is constant. G is not finitely generated and mu has infinite support; the finitely generated case is not treated. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/bjorklund-star-quotient (commit 02c95296756a). Not refereed.
title: A homogeneous space G/H of infinite index with no nonconstant quasiharmonic functions, answering Bjorklund's Problem 2 (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/bjorklund-star-quotient)

body: In mathematics, the prime number theorem (PNT) describes the asymptotic distribution of prime numbers among the positive integers. It formalizes the intuitive idea that primes become less common as they become larger by precisely quantifying the rate at which this occurs. The theorem was proved independently by Jacques Hadamard and Charles Jean de la Vallée Poussin in 1896 using ideas introduced by Bernhard Riemann.

[Thm 11 (Convergence from resultant distributions) of arXiv:2608.06576, 'The Resultant Distribution Method: Universality for $p$-adic Random Matrices and Polynomia'] Let $P^S_1,P^S_2,\ldots$ be random elements of $\mathscr{P}^S$. Assume that the
following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every fixed polynomial $Z\in\mathscr{P}^S$, the sequence of random
variables
$$
\val\bigl(\Res(P^S_n,Z)\bigr),\qquad n\geq 1,
$$
converges weakly in $\Z_{\geq 0}\cup\{\infty\}$ as $n\to\infty$. 

\item The sequence $\{\deg P^S_n\}_{n\geq 1}$ is tight; namely, 
$$
\lim_{D\to\infty}\sup_{n\geq 1}
\mathbf{P}(\deg P^S_n>D)=0.
$$ 
\end{enumerate}
Then there exists a random element $P^S_\infty$ of $\mathscr{P}^S$, unique in
distribution, such that
$$
P^S_n
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
P^S_\infty,
\qquad n\to\infty.
$$
Furthermore, for every fixed polynomial $Z\in\mathscr{P}^S$, we have
$$
\val\bigl(\Res(P^S_n,Z)\bigr)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
\val\bigl(\Res(P^S_\infty,Z)\bigr),
\qquad n\to\infty.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Definition 1 of arXiv:2607.26254, 'A Simple Model of Sea Spray'] Let $\mathcal{F}(dr)$ be a finite measure on $(0,\infty)$ and for each fixed $r>0,$ let $(z_t(r), r_t) $ be a pair of nonnegative functions of $t\geq 0.$ Let
$$
\zeta=\inf\{\, t>0\mid z_t=0\quad\text{or}\quad r_t=0\,\}.
$$
be the duration of the droplet. We assume, 
\begin{itemize}
\item{$r_t, \,z_t(r)$ are continuous  on the interval $[0,\zeta]$}
\item{if $r_t=0$ for some $t>0$ then $r_s=0$ and $z_s=0$ for all $s\geq t$}
\item{if $z_t(r)=0$ for some $t>0$ then $z_s(r)=0$ and $r_s=0$ for all $s\geq t$}
\end{itemize}

\mpar
Let $\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}\times (0,\infty)$ and let $\Lambda(dr\, dt)=\mathcal{F}(dr) dt.$ Let $\mathcal{N}$ be the Poisson point process whose intensity measure is $\Lambda.$ Let $\mathcal{M}$ be the space of positive measures on $[0,\infty)$ and let $C([0,\infty),\mathcal{M})$ be the space of continuous functions from $[0,\infty)$ to $\mathcal{M}.$

\mpar
Let $\phi\colon (0,\infty)\to C([0,\infty), \mathcal{M})$ be defined by the rule,
$$
\phi(r,t) = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r_t^3\rho\, \delta_{z_t(r)}
$$
Then the sea spray process is defined by the formula,

$$
\mathcal{S}_t =\int_{-\infty}^t\int_0^\infty \phi(t-s,r)\, \mathcal{N}(dr\, ds).
$$

body: In numerical analysis and linear algebra, lower–upper (LU) decomposition or factorization factors a matrix as the product of a lower triangular matrix and an upper triangular matrix. The product sometimes includes a permutation matrix as well. LU decomposition can be viewed as the matrix form of Gaussian elimination. Computers usually solve square systems of linear equations using LU decomposition, and it is also a key step when inverting a matrix or computing the determinant of a matrix. It is also sometimes referred to as LR decomposition. The LU decomposition algorithm for general matrices was introduced by the Polish astronomer Tadeusz Banachiewicz in 1938.
title: LU decomposition

body: A statistic T(X) is sufficient for a parameter theta if the conditional distribution of the data X given T(X) does not depend on theta: T captures everything the sample says about theta. Fisher-Neyman factorization characterizes sufficiency: T is sufficient exactly when the likelihood factors as p_theta(x) = g_theta(T(x)) h(x) with h free of theta.
title: Sufficient Statistic and Factorization

[Definition def:tree-cylinder-square-sums-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] For \(n\ge0\), define 
\[
\Sigma_n
=
\sum_{\lvert u \rvert=n}C_u^2.
\]

More generally, for a vertex 
\(
u\in\mathcal T
\),
define the descendant tree-cylinder square sum by 
\[
\Sigma^{(u)}_n
=
\sum_{\lvert v \rvert=n}\left(C^{(u)}_v\right)^2,
\qquad
C^{(u)}_v=L_v^{(u)}M^{(uv)}.
\]

Thus
\[
\Sigma_n=\Sigma^{(\varnothing)}_n
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\Sigma_0=M^2.
\]

body:
[Proposition 2.5 of arXiv:2512.19517v1, 'Spiking and Resetting' (Cédric Bernardin and Vsevolod Vladimirovich Tarsamaev); numbered Proposition 6 in the earlier card; corrected to the increment form]

## Proposition 2.5 (increment form)

Assume the standing hypotheses of Section 1: (f,h\in C^2([0,1])), (f(1)<0<f(0)), (h(1)=0), (h'(1)\ne0), and (h(x)>0) on ([0,1)). Let

\[
e_1^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t^\varepsilon>y_*^\varepsilon\},\qquad
e_2^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge e_1^\varepsilon:X_t^\varepsilon=0\},
\]

and define the post-(e_1^\varepsilon) holding time

\[
d_2^\varepsilon:=e_2^\varepsilon-e_1^\varepsilon.
\]

Then, for every (t\ge0),

\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathbb P(d_2^\varepsilon>t)=e^{f(1)t},
\]

so (d_2^\varepsilon\Rightarrow \operatorname{Exp}(-f(1))).

The proof in the paper restarts the deterministic flow at (e_1^\varepsilon) with local time (s=0); its displayed survival integral is therefore for (d_2^\varepsilon), not the absolute epoch (e_2^\varepsilon). The source says that after the stopping time “the process evolves deterministically until the next reset” (v1 HTML lines 252-257), which is precisely an increment statement.

## Later alternating holding-time sentence

For the recursively defined epochs (e_k^\varepsilon), the strong Markov property applies to the increments

\[
e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon-e_{2k}^\varepsilon,
\qquad
e_{2k+2}^\varepsilon-e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon,
\]

not to the increasing absolute epochs themselves. The alternating increments are the quantities that can be independent and have the two respective holding-time laws. Any downstream card should preserve this distinction.

## Why the absolute-time statement cannot hold as written

For every (\varepsilon), (e_2^\varepsilon\ge e_1^\varepsilon), hence

\[
\mathbb P(e_2^\varepsilon>t)\ge\mathbb P(e_1^\varepsilon>t).
\]

This stochastic order must persist at continuity points of any weak limits. Yet the paper permits (f(x)=1-3x) and (h(x)=1-x), for which (f(0)=1) and (f(1)=-2). Its two displayed absolute-time limits would require (e^{-2t}\ge e^{-t}) for (t>0), an immediate contradiction. No additional relation between (f(0)) and (f(1)) is present in the standing hypotheses.

Vanishing entropy per volume alone cannot imply equality of states. On n binary sites take P_n=delta_(0,...,0) and Q_n=(delta_(0,...,0)+delta_(1,...,1))/2. Then D(P_n||Q_n)=log2 for every n, hence D/n tends to0, while the limiting cylinder event X_1=1 has probabilities0 and1/2. Check: The density dP_n/dQ_n is2 on its only supported configuration, so the relative entropy is exactly log2. The two consistent infinite-volume measures are visibly different. Obstruction: A successful variational argument needs a uniqueness mechanism beyond zero specific entropy, plus a theorem placing every DLR state in the admissible stationary finite-energy class. The diagnostic does not construct a second sine-beta Gibbs measure.

[Theorem T_pc of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] Fix $r\geqslant5$. Let $\gamma>0$ be the unique positive root of
\begin{equation}
(r-2)!\gamma^{r-2} = \alpha_{{r\choose2}-2}\,.
\end{equation}
Then, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
\[
\mathbb P(\langle \mathcal G_{n,p}\rangle_{K_r}=K_n) \to \left\{
\begin{matrix}
0,&\text{if }\gamma np^\lambda =1 -\varepsilon;\\
1,&\text{if }\gamma np^\lambda =1+\varepsilon, 
\end{matrix}
\right.
\]
as $n\to\infty$. In particular,
\[
p_c(n,K_r)\sim (\gamma n)^{-1/\lambda}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Heuristic derivation of the three scalings and identification of the rigorous gaps. Result: Free/zero boundary: the largest cluster among about n^d / n^4 ... the box contains clusters whose sizes have tail P(|C| >= k) ~ k^{-1/2} in mean field, cut off at the box scale where the cluster diameter ~ k^{1/4} reaches n, i.e. k ~ n^4; the number of clusters of size about n^4 in the box is n^d P(|C(0)| ~ n^4)/n^4 ~ n^{d-6} which is large for d > 6, and the maximum of n^{d-6} clusters with tail k^{-1/2} cut off at n^4 gives the log n factor through the extreme-value count, hence n^4 log n. Rigorous status: the upper bound n^4 log n follows from the cluster-size tail and a union bound; the matching lower bound needs the tail near the cutoff to be exactly of the mean-field form k^{-1/2} up to constants for k up to c n^4 inside a box with boundary, which is a boundary-condition-sensitive statement (the two-point function near the boundary decays faster). Wired boundary: the boundary is one cluster of size n^{d-1} plus the vertices connected to it, the latter of order n^{d-1} times the expected number of vertices connected to the boundary per boundary vertex (~ sum over distance r of r^{d-1} r^{-(d-2)} ... the two-point function summed over a half-space gives order n^2, so the wired giant should be n^{d-1} times a constant only if the connection density to the boundary is summable, which it is in d > 6 only after the one-arm exponent: P(0 <-> boundary at distance r) ~ r^{-2}, and the sum over the box of r^{-2} is n^{d-2}, dominated by the boundary itself... so the constant a_w exists iff the total number of vertices connected to the boundary from distance >= 1 is O(n^{d-1}), which follows from the extrinsic one-arm exponent 2 (Kozma-Nachmias) by summing r^{-2} over the layers r <= n: sum_r n^{d-1} r^{-2} = O(n^{d-1}). So the wired scaling n^{d-1} up to constants is rigorous from the known one-arm exponent; the existence of the limit constant a_w needs the sharp one-arm asymptotics (C0066). Bulk and zero cases remain open at the level of the lower bound. Key identity: Wired: |C_max^{(w)}| = n^{d-1}(1 + sum_r P(one-arm to distance r)) = Theta(n^{d-1}) by the extrinsic one-arm exponent 2; the limit constant requires C0066. Obstruction: Boundary-sensitive cluster-size tails for bulk/zero conditions; sharp one-arm constant for the wired constant.

DEFINITION. The Cesaro means of a sequence (s_n)_{n >= 0} are sigma_n = (s_0 + s_1 + ... + s_n) / (n + 1). A series sum a_n with partial sums s_n is Cesaro summable (C,1) to L if sigma_n -> L. THEOREM (Cauchy; Cesaro). If s_n -> L then sigma_n -> L: convergence implies Cesaro convergence to the same limit (the method is regular). The converse fails: the series 1 - 1 + 1 - 1 + ... has partial sums 1, 0, 1, 0, ... and Cesaro means (m+1)/(2m+1) or 1/2 tending to 1/2, so it is (C,1)-summable to 1/2 without converging. Two further facts, cited: a (C,1)-summable series has a_n / n -> 0, so a series whose terms do not satisfy a_n = o(n) is not Cesaro summable at all; and Hardy's Tauberian theorem says that a (C,1)-summable series with a_n = O(1/n) converges. Cesaro means of Fourier series are the Fejer means, and Fejer's theorem is exactly this regularity turned into a positive summability kernel.
real or complex sequences
the Cesaro means are the (C,1) means; higher-order (C,k) means and Abel summation are stronger methods, also regular

body:
[Theorem 10 (Ogg's Formula) of arXiv:2609.01485, 'On the Ramification of Quadratic Fields where the Torsion of a Rational Elliptic Curve Gro'] Let $E/K$ be an elliptic curve defined over a local field $K$, with ring of integers $R$ and residual field $k$. Consider 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $v_K(\Delta)$.  The valuation of the minimal discriminant of $E/K$.
        \item $f(E/K)$. The exponent of the conductor of $E/K$.
        \item $m(E/K)$. The number of components, defined over $\overline{k}$ and counted without multiplicity, on the special fiber of a minimal proper regular model of $E$ over $R$.
    \end{itemize}
    Then
    $$
    v_K(\Delta) = f(E/K) + m(E/K) -1
    $$
title: Ogg's Formula

[Cor B-Sig_surface of arXiv:2609.01751, 'Orthogonal polynomials which are eigenfunctions of a partial differential operator'] For $\mu > -\frac12$ and ${\boldsymbol{\kappa}} \in {\mathbb R}^{d_2-1}$ with ${\kappa}_i > -1$, $1 \le i \le d_2-1$,
\begin{align*} 
   & - \int_{{\mathbb B}^{d_1} \rtimes \Sigma^{d_2}}{\mathfrak D}_{\mu, {\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb B}\rtimes\Sigma}
     f (\bm x,\bm y) \cdot g(\bm x, \bm y) \bm W_{\mu, {\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}(\bm x, \bm y)^{{\mathbb B}\rtimes\Sigma} \mathrm{d} \bm x \mathrm{d} \bm y  \\
  &  = \int_{{\mathbb B}^{d_1} \rtimes \Sigma^{d_2}}  \frac{1}{|\bm y|} \sum_{i=1}^{d_1} \partial_{x_i} f(\bm x,\bm y)\cdot \partial_{x_i} g(\bm x,\bm y) 
  \bm W_{\mu+1,{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb B}\rtimes \Sigma}(\bm x,\bm y)  \mathrm{d} \bm x \mathrm{d} \bm y  \notag \\ 
  & +  \int_{{\mathbb B}^{d_1} \rtimes \Sigma^{d_2}}  \frac{1}{|\bm y|} \sum_{1 \le i< j \le d_1}  D_{i,j}^{(\bm x)} f(\bm x, \bm y) \cdot D_{i,j}^{(\bm x)} g(\bm x, \bm y) 
  \bm W_{\mu,{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb B}\rtimes \Sigma}(\bm x,\bm y)  \mathrm{d} \bm x \mathrm{d} \bm y  \notag \\ 
  & + \int_{{\mathbb B}^{d_1} \rtimes \Sigma^{d_2}}   \sum_{1\le i< j \le d_2} (\partial_{y_j} - \partial_{y_j}) f(\bm x,\bm y) \cdot 
    (\partial_{y_i} - \partial_{y_j})g(\bm x,\bm y)
  \bm W_{\mu,{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb B}\rtimes \Sigma}(\bm x,\bm y) \mathrm{d} \bm x \mathrm{d} \bm y  \notag \\
  &  +  \int_{{\mathbb B}^{d_1} \rtimes \Sigma^{d_2}} \frac{1}{|\bm y|} (|{\bm y}| \partial_{d_2} - {\langle} {\bm x},\nabla_{\bm x}{\rangle}) f(\bm x,\bm y) 
  \cdot (|{\bm y}| \partial_{d_2} - {\langle} {\bm x},\nabla_{\bm x}{\rangle})g(\bm x,\bm y) 
  \bm W_{\mu,{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}}^{{\mathbb B}\rtimes \Sigma}(\bm x,\bm y)  \mathrm{d} \bm x \mathrm{d} \bm y.  \notag
 \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
For a unit $i$, the individual treatment effect $\tau_i$ is the difference between its potential outcomes under treatment and control: $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. Because at most one potential outcome is observed for any individual, $\tau_i$ is fundamentally unobservable (the Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference).
Potential outcomes Y_i(1) and Y_i(0) are well-defined
title: Individual Treatment Effect (ITE)

body:
[Definition def:escape of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix a send sequence~$\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$, a $\lambda \in (0,1)$, and a high-level state $\Psi= (g,\tau,j,\overline{z},\mathcal{S},\textup{type})$.
 

Fix a (possibly random) tuple $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^E(\tau)$ of
disjoint sets
$\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^E(\tau) = (\mathbf{arr}_1^E(\tau),\mathbf{arr}_2^E(\tau),\ldots)$
where each $ \mathbf{arr}^E_{i}(\tau)\subseteq \mathcal{B}(\tau)$ and, 
for $i>j$, $\mathbf{arr}_i^E(\tau) = \emptyset$. 

An escape process \newsym{E}{Escape process}{E} with 
high-level state $\Psi$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$, birth rate~$\lambda$, and
initial population $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^E(\tau)$
is the generalised backoff process with 
send sequence~$\overline{p}$, start time~$\tau$, the birth distribution~$\mathcal{D}$ that always returns~$0$,  initial population~$\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^E(\tau)$, and which satisfies the following constraints.

For all $t\geq \tau$, define 
$\mathbb{S}^E(t) := \{S \in \mathcal{S}\colon \mathcal{N}^E_S(t+1) \le \lambda |S|/80\}$.
Let
$\hat{S}^E(t) := 
\cup_{S \in \mathbb{S}^E(t)} S$. Finally,
define
\[
\Xi^E(t) := \begin{cases}
\lambda |\hat{S}^E(t)|/80 & \mbox{ if }|\hat{S}^E(t)| \ge 100/\lambda^2,\\
0 & \mbox{ otherwise,}
\end{cases}
\]
and $\newsym{nu-E}{end-of-step arrival rate of escape process}{\nu^E(t)} := \exp(-\Xi^E(t)/192)$.
For $t>\tau$, $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^E(t)$ and $\overline{\mathbf{e}}^E(t)$ are defined as follows. 
\begin{itemize}
\item  For each $i\in [j]$, 
$\mathrm{arr}_i^E(t)$ is a Bernoulli r.v.~with parameter~$\nu^E(t-1)$. These are independent for different~$i$ and for different~$t$. For all $i>j$,  $\mathrm{arr}^E_i(t) = 0$.
\item For all $i \in [j-1]$,   $\mathbf{e}_i^E(t) = \emptyset$. For all $i \ge j$, $\mathbf{e}^E_i(t) = \mathbf{s}^E_i(t)$.
\end{itemize}

Note that we have not specified the name of the ball in $\mathbf{arr}_i^E(t)$, in the event that $\mathrm{arr}_i^E(t)=1$.
title: Definition def:escape of arXiv:2602.21315

body:
Own-work draft: proof (unaudited); independent mathematical and novelty review pending. Balanced four-point frozen precursor only; not a general absence theorem.

For completeness, the full kernel here is H_nu(x,z)=E_W[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2*1{W.x>0,W.z>0}*(x.z)], W~N(0,I_3). Its normalized training matrix is H_nu(x_i,x_j)/4.

# C016 v1: why fixed iid heads do not inherit the paired construction
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: route-failure. Target: 1.
This is an obstruction to the existing witness route, not absence of epochwise
double descent in iid-initialized networks. Novelty is unestablished.

## 1. Precisely the precursor model considered
Let 0<e<1/4, D0=1+e^2+e^4, x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2t)/sqrt(D0), s,t in {+1,-1}.
The population is uniform on these four points. Set
u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2), c_e=e^2/sqrt(D0(1+e^2)), alpha=c_e/2.
The teacher g(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2 has Walsh coefficients
(theta_0,theta_s,theta_t,theta_st)=(0,alpha,alpha,alpha).
Here the name u_e denotes the teacher direction; nu below is a different,
fixed readout magnitude in (0,1]. Initialize m independent neurons with
W_j~N(0,I_3), a_j independently uniform on {+nu,-nu}, independently of W_j.
Let z_h^(m) be the Walsh coefficients of the random initial output.
Consider the deterministic FULL initial kernel H_nu from C009/C014,
including both trained layers, and real-time-interpolated kernel GD
with step gamma=1/2. If lambda_h are its normalized four-point eigenvalues,
put b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2), q_h(t)=exp(-b_h t).
The phrase interpolation only means allowing real t in this exact spectral
formula; at integer t it is precisely discrete GD, not gradient flow.
Use centered independent effective label errors of Walsh variance alpha^2.
For instance, four independent errors +/-2alpha have exactly this property.
Balanced replication with fixed sigma and n chosen so sigma^2/n~alpha^2
also gives the same conclusions with rho_e= sigma^2/(n alpha^2)->1.

The noise-averaged clean risk, conditional on initialization, is exactly
 Q_e(t;z)=sum_h [q_h(t)^2(z_h-theta_h)^2
                         +alpha^2(1-q_h(t))^2].           (1)
No independence between noise Walsh modes is needed: Parseval removes
cross-mode terms. The derivative below refers to this interpolated FROZEN
risk, not derivatives of finite-width ReLU iterates.
We use the already recorded full-kernel clocks
 b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), b_t~b_st~nu^2 e^2/(8pi),
 b_0 -> a positive constant, eta=(b_t+b_st)/b_s~e.
This is the four-point balanced precursor of C015, NOT its continuous,
iid-input-count, actual-network model. No automatic transfer of the negative
result to that stronger model is asserted.

## 2. Initial covariance on the correct signal scale
Let phi_h(W)=one-quarter sum_(s,t) h(s,t) ReLU(W.x_(s,t)).
For each fixed e, ordinary finite-dimensional iid CLT gives
 z^(m) => Z_e as m->infinity, a centered Gaussian four-vector with
 Var(Z_(e,h))=nu^2 lambda_h^RF, lambda_h^RF=E phi_h(W)^2.
The covariance is diagonal by invariance of W under coordinate sign flips.
One can get the vector CLT by applying the scalar finite-variance CLT to
every linear combination. Width is deterministic, not a stopped random list.
All moments used are finite since |phi_h|<=||W|| on the unit inputs.

For almost every W with W_0 !=0,
 phi_s(W)/e -> W_1 1{W_0>0}.
Group the two s values for each t and use ReLU's Lipschitz property to get
 |phi_s(W)|<=e |W_1|/sqrt(D0).
Dominated convergence therefore proves
 lambda_s^RF/e^2 -> E[W_1^2 1{W_0>0}]=1/2.              (2)
Grouping instead by the t coordinate similarly gives
 |phi_t(W)|, |phi_st(W)|<=e^2 |W_2|/sqrt(D0),
so their variances are O(e^4). The constant-mode variance is O(1).
Since alpha~e^2/2, the fast standardized initial output satisfies
 Var(Z_(e,s)/alpha)~2nu^2/e^2.                            (3)
Thus the initial fast prediction error is not negligible on the teacher's
scale. Let A_e=(Z_(e,s)/alpha-1)^2. For any fixed C>0, the Gaussian maximum
density bound gives
 P(eta A_e<=C) <= 2 sqrt(C/eta)/sqrt(2pi Var(Z_(e,s)/alpha))
                    =O(sqrt(Ce)/nu) ->0.                 (4)
Hence eta A_e diverges to infinity in probability. This uses no independence
between A_e and the other modes.

## 3. The old fast-minimum witness diverges on its normalized scale
Let k_1=floor(log(2)/b_s), the C010/C015 precursor's fast witness.
Then q_s(k_1)->1/2. From the single nonnegative term in (1), for any fixed C,
 P(Q_e(k_1;Z_e)/alpha^2<=C)
 <= P(|Z_(e,s)/alpha-1|<=sqrt(C)/q_s(k_1))=O(sqrt(C)e/nu)->0. (5)
Thus Q_e(k_1;Z_e)/alpha^2 ->infinity in probability, rather than 7/2.
This is an iterated width-then-e statement for the iid initialization;
finite-width convergence in distribution follows from the preceding CLT.
For an upper bound at a distributional event boundary one may enlarge C
arbitrarily and use Portmanteau; no uniform-in-e CLT rate is claimed.
The paired-initialization witness statement itself is unaffected.

## 4. The old central peak window is decreasing in the frozen model
Put B_e=log(1/eta), t_e(s)=(B_e+s)/b_s. For any fixed L<infinity,
q_s(t_e(s))=eta exp(-s). Differentiate (1), divide by
2 alpha^2(b_t+b_st), and separate the fast mode. Its contribution is exactly
 exp(-s)-eta(A_e+1)exp(-2s).                              (6)
For the two slow modes, (Z_h/alpha-1)^2 is tight by the O(e^4) covariance
bound. Their rate ratios b_h/(b_t+b_st) are bounded and q_h<=1, hence their
combined contribution is uniformly O_P(1) over |s|<=L.
The constant-mode contribution is o_P(1): b_0 is bounded away from zero,
Z_0=O_P(1), alpha^2~e^4/4, and q_0(t_e(s)) decays faster than every power
of e uniformly on this fixed s interval. Consequently

 sup_|s|<=L Q'_e(t_e(s);Z_e)/(2alpha^2(b_t+b_st))
 <= exp(L)-eta A_e exp(-2L)+O_P(1) -> -infinity
                                                        (7)
by (4). With probability tending to one this entire old peak window is
strictly decreasing in the frozen-risk interpolation. In particular, its
interval maximum lies at the left endpoint, not at the paired model's
interior peak. Tightness plus (4), rather than independence, is sufficient.
The same proof works when the effective noise factor rho_e tends to1:
replace exp(-s) in (6) by rho_e exp(-s) and1 by rho_e.

## 5. What this settles and what remains open
Merely replacing paired heads by fixed-variance iid heads while retaining
the unit-teacher scaling, noise scaling and peak witnesses does NOT preserve
C010/C015's precursor argument: the witness risk diverges and the old
central peak interval has the wrong derivative sign in the limiting frozen
model. This is the exact failure point, not a theorem of global monotonicity.
Other times, other teachers/noise scales, non-lazy learning, the continuous
iid-input model and the actual finite-width derivative pattern remain open.
In particular, C015's positive paired-initialization result is not retracted.
Next route: choose teacher/noise scales jointly with initial GP covariance
before proposing iid-head witnesses. Shrinking readout variance changes the
full-kernel clocks, so one cannot keep fixed-nu clock asymptotics silently.

Sources: own C009 full-kernel clocks, C010/C013/C015 teacher and witnesses;
self-contained Lipschitz/dominated-convergence calculation (2). Scalar iid
CLT from Donsker's invariance principle evaluated at time1, recalled card
claim_ce0cd7266679161a8821c7246e4dad6e99fad5e929f3b7da95ca24c19e76a7e9
(source locator: Billingsley, Convergence of Probability Measures, Theorem8.2;
the book is not newly consulted). No independent review or novelty assertion.
All explicit definitions and fixed-nu spectral clock premises in the statement
Deterministic width tends to infinity before e tends to zero; Gaussian hidden weights and independent heads +/-nu, fixed0<nu<=1
Unit-norm single-index ReLU teacher on the four near-collinear points; effective Walsh label-noise variance alpha^2 or rho_e alpha^2 with rho_e->1
Noise-averaged frozen full-kernel risk; negative conclusion not automatically transferred to continuous iid-input nonlinear GD

body:
AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. All-aspect averaged MMSE comparison, proof unaudited. Let X,B be finite-second-moment real N by P signals with B biorthogonally invariant, delta^2=E sum_j(sigma_j(X)-sigma_j(B))^2/(NP) for any coupling of decreasing singular-value profiles, and v=max(E||X||_F^2,E||B||_F^2)/(NP). With independent standard Gaussian channel noise and per-entry Bayes errors m_X,m_B, for every S,h>0 the integral from 0 to S of [m_X(s)-m_B(s)]_+ ds is at most v*h+4*S*sqrt(S+h)*delta/h. If 0<delta<=1 this is at most [v+4*S*sqrt(S+1)]*sqrt(delta); delta=0 gives pointwise domination. Haar mixing increases Bayes error while the mixed MI is within sqrt(s)*delta of the reference. A quantitative L1 derivative inequality for concave Lipschitz functions supplies the bound without assuming a reference MI or MMSE limit. Consequently claim 008 gives integral_0^S [m_X_N-m_B_N]_+ ds->0 for every finite S, for independent fixed centered iid unit-variance finite-fourth-moment factors at every positive finite aspect ratio. The positive gap tends to zero in SNR measure; an appropriate subsequence has a nonpositive limsup almost everywhere. This does not prove fixed-SNR domination for the full sequence. Raw product loss gaps are divided by N. Novelty of the application remains unestablished.
Real signals; standard independent Gaussian observation noise; finite second moments for the finite-dimensional statement.
Biorthogonally invariant reference and a finite expected squared ordered singular-value coupling.
For the product consequence: independent arrays of fixed centered iid unit-variance real laws with finite fourth moments and positive finite limits P/N,M/N.
The spectral-coupling and Gaussian-smoothed entropy dependencies in claims 008 and 006 are themselves unaudited.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:2e44d59280b1916040573540efa7f0ec8c320e62ea1f3c29364ad93b0f123195","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/2e/2e44d59280b1916040573540efa7f0ec8c320e62ea1f3c29364ad93b0f123195.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:8ad30b8a1104b62c5be3d02bfaebfa86767727f95afa1eb266ce776a93917169","bundle_entry_key":"integrated-mmse-haar-wasserstein-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-integrated-mmse-all-aspects-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:integrated-mmse-haar-wasserstein-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# All-aspect integrated positive MMSE comparison

Target 2. Proof draft, unaudited. This does not prove the full pointwise
all-SNR target. Novelty of the application is unestablished.

## 1. Finite-dimensional statement

Let X,B be random real N by P matrices with finite second moments, and let
B be biorthogonally invariant. Put d=NP and r=min(N,P). Choose any coupling
of their decreasing singular-value vectors a,b, and write

    delta^2=E sum_(j=1)^r (a_j-b_j)^2/d,
    v=max(E||X||_F^2/d, E||B||_F^2/d).

For each Q, let m_Q(s) denote its normalized Bayes squared error in the
independent standard Gaussian channel sqrt(s)Q+W. For every S,h>0,

    integral_0^S [m_X(s)-m_B(s)]_+ ds
      <= v*h + 4*S*sqrt(S+h)*delta/h.                 (1)

Here [x]_+=max(x,0). No log-concavity of either signal law and no limiting
mutual-information formula or differentiability assumption is imposed.

## 2. Haar symmetrization and two-sided information closeness

Let H(X)=LXR^T with independent Haar orthogonal matrices, independent of X.
Revealing L,R can only reduce the Bayes squared error. Conditional on the
rotations, rotate the independent Gaussian observation and the estimate
back to the original coordinates. The conditional Bayes risk equals that
of X, so, exactly at each finite dimension,

    m_X(s) <= m_H(X)(s).                              (2)

Equivalently this is concavity of Bayes risk in the prior law; it is not
obtained by differentiating a one-sided information inequality.

Couple H(X) and B by giving their coupled profiles a,b the same independent
Haar frames. Their laws are correct (B is biorthogonally invariant) and
their mean squared Frobenius distance is d*delta^2. The Gaussian-smoothed
entropy comparison already proved in orbit_comparison.md, Section 1,
therefore gives, for normalized mutual informations f,g,

    f(s)=I(H(X);sqrt(s)H(X)+W)/d,
    g(s)=I(B;sqrt(s)B+W)/d,
    |f(s)-g(s)| <= sqrt(s)*delta.                     (3)

For clarity, that finite-second-moment bound follows by interpolating a
coupled input pair, using the continuity equation for the convolved
density, and applying Cauchy-Schwarz. The conditional transport velocity
has L2 norm no larger than the coupled input distance, and the output
Fisher information is at most d by its Gaussian score identity. Thus
|I(A;sqrt(s)A+W)-I(C;sqrt(s)C+W)|<=sqrt(sd)*W2(A,C).
L2 truncation extends the bounded-input calculation to finite second
moments; the earlier proof supplies the entropy-tail justification.

I-MMSE gives f'=m_H(X)/2 and g'=m_B/2. Both f,g are concave and Lipschitz
on every finite nonnegative SNR interval, and 0<=f',g'<=v/2 almost
everywhere. The bound follows from the zero estimator; monotonicity of
MMSE follows by Gaussian-channel degradation. These facts require only
finite second moments, not the higher moments used in the product
application below.

## 3. Quantitative derivative argument

On [0,S+h], (3) gives epsilon=sqrt(S+h)*delta. Apply the lemma in
concave_derivative_l1.md with L=v/2. Then

    integral_0^S |m_H(X)(s)-m_B(s)| ds
      =2 integral_0^S |f'(s)-g'(s)| ds
      <= v*h+4*S*sqrt(S+h)*delta/h.

By (2), [m_X-m_B]_+<=|m_H(X)-m_B| pointwise, proving (1).
All smoothing here is over SNR, not over the singular-value density.
In particular it does not use the divergent fixed-Poisson-smoothing
weighted spectral integral discussed in the numerical diagnostics.

If 0<delta<=1, choose h=sqrt(delta). Equation (1) yields

    integral_0^S [m_X-m_B]_+ ds
      <= [v+4*S*sqrt(S+1)]*sqrt(delta).               (4)

If delta=0, the shared-Haar coupling has identical profiles almost surely,
H(X) has the law of B and (2) proves m_X<=m_B at every SNR directly.

## 4. Consequence for every positive finite matrix aspect ratio

Let X_N=U_N V_N^T/sqrt(N), with independent arrays of fixed centered iid
real unit-variance entry laws, each with finite fourth moment. Let B_N use
independent standard Gaussian factors with the same dimensions. Assume
P/N->alpha and M/N->beta, both positive and finite. Claim 008, Section 3,
equation (10), supplies the expected squared singular-value W2 convergence
and hence couplings with delta_N->0. This spectral dependency remains
unaudited. Here v_N=M/N, since each signal entry has variance M/N.
Applying (4) proves for every finite S>0,

    integral_0^S [m_X_N(s)-m_B_N(s)]_+ ds -> 0.       (5)

Thus the positive MMSE excess tends to zero in Lebesgue measure on every
bounded SNR interval. For any eta>0 the measure where the excess exceeds
eta is bounded by the right side of (4) divided by eta. A subsequence with
summable right sides gives limsup(m_X_N-m_B_N)<=0 almost everywhere along
that subsequence (Tonelli, or the elementary measure bound and
Borel-Cantelli on the SNR interval). A diagonal subsequence covers all
finite intervals. Neither conclusion is pointwise convergence for the
full sequence. No Gaussian-reference MMSE or MI limit is asserted.

The result covers all positive finite aspect ratios, including N=P=M,
but averages over SNR. It complements the uniform-in-SNR pointwise wedge
M>=N+P+1 of claim 013 rather than extending that stronger conclusion.
For raw R=UV^T, the quantity compared in (5) is
[(L_R-L_R^G)/N]_+, since L_R=N*m_X exactly. Fixed positive factor variances
reduce to this statement by scaling the signal and SNR.

## 5. Sources, status, and the hardest open piece

This uses the finite Gaussian-channel facts in Guo-Shamai-Verdu,
arXiv:cs/0412108, Theorem 2, equation (22), and the common-Haar and entropy
comparison in our unaudited claim 006. Its expected spectral coupling is
the specific conclusion of our unaudited claim 008. The calculus lemma
is written out in full rather than taken from a convergence slogan.
No novelty is claimed for that elementary lemma or the standard channel
identities; novelty of this application has not been independently
assessed.

The hardest remaining Target 2 piece is a pointwise all-SNR comparison
outside the log-concavity wedge. Averaged control permits narrow moving
positive excesses and does not settle a specified fixed SNR. The Target 1
dimension-uniform remainder also remains open. This document is a partial
result with explicit dependencies, not a full solution to T287.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:e2d584034903b62a4f133b71ffd771d57b52602eb08aed7f370a42f9d7996a4f","revision_digest":"sha256:9049a16615b6c881f56428e4fa30374de18c37838eb59c8f2c1388516a193ffa","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:integrated-mmse-haar-wasserstein-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-20 claim w718-T287-015 version 1, proof unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: In mathematics, a real-valued function is called convex if the line segment between any two distinct points on the graph of the function lies above or on the graph of the function between the two points. Equivalently, a function is convex if its epigraph is a convex set. In simple terms, a convex function graph is shaped like a cup , while a concave function's graph is shaped like a cap .

body:
[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2607.16954, 'Repeated differentiation of deterministic polynomials with asymptotically radial root dist'] Suppose $P_n$ is a sequence of polynomials of the form $P_n(z)=p_n(z^{m_n})$ with $\deg(p_n)=n$ and $p_n$ having real, non-negative roots. Assume that
\[
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{m_n}{\log(n)}=\infty
\]
and suppose the empirical root measure of $P_n$ converges as $n\rightarrow\infty$ to a compactly supported probability measure $\mu_0$ with radial quantile function $\quant{\mu_0}$. Let $a$ and $b$ be non-negative integers with $b>0$. Then for $0\le t<1,$ define
\[
Q_{n,t}(z)=z^{(b-a)m_n\lfloor nt\rfloor}\left(z^a\left(\frac{d}{dz}\right)^b\right)^{m_n\lfloor nt\rfloor}P_n(z).
\]
Let 
\[
\alpha_{\min}=\max(0,t(b-a)).
\]

Then as $n$ tends to infinity, the empirical root measure of $Q_{n,t}(z)$ tends to a measure $\sigma_t$ whose radial quantile function $\quant{\sigma_t}$ is given by 
\begin{equation}
\quant{\sigma_t}(\alpha)=\left\{\begin{matrix}0 & \text{if }0\le\alpha\le \alpha_{\min},\\ \quant{\mu_0}(\alpha)\left(1-\frac{t(b-a)}{\alpha}\right)^{\frac{b}{b-a}} & \text{if }\alpha_{\min}<\alpha\le 1,\end{matrix}\right.
\end{equation}
in the case $b\ne a$ and 
\[
\quant{\sigma_t}(\alpha)=\quant{\mu_0}(\alpha)e^{-at/\alpha}
\]
when $b=a$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2607.16954

body:
[Theorem 11 of arXiv:2604.13819, 'Convolution, cumulants and infinitesimal generators in the formal power series ring'] The following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}[\rm (1)]
\item If a real-valued random variable $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $M_{X+Y} = M_{X} \boxplus^{-1} M_{Y}$. 
\item $\displaystyle C^{-1}[M_X]({\rm i} z) =  z\frac{d}{dz}C_X^\ast(z)$.
\item If $X$ has all finite moments, then $nr_n(X) = {\rm i}^n \kappa_n^{-1}(M_X)$ for all $n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}$.
\end{enumerate}

body: In mathematics, a real function $f$ of real numbers is said to be uniformly continuous if there is a positive real number $\delta$ such that function values over any function domain interval of the size $\delta$ are as close to each other as we want. In other words, for a uniformly continuous real function of real numbers, if we want function value differences to be less than any positive real number $\varepsilon$, then there is a positive real number $\delta$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon$ for any $x$ and $y$ in any interval of length $\delta$ within the domain of $f$.

[Theorem Sharp small-hole eigenvalue asymptotic, \(d \geq 3\) of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] Let \(d \geq 3\), \(\partial M\)
uniformly \(C^{1,1}\), and \(x_{\varepsilon} \in M\)
with
\(\operatorname{dist}\left( x_{\varepsilon},\partial M \right)/\varepsilon \rightarrow a \in \lbrack 0,\infty\rbrack\).
Then

\[\lambda\left( B_{M}\left( x_{\varepsilon},\varepsilon \right) \right) = \frac{\beta(a)\,\gamma_{d}}{|M|}\,\kappa_{d}(\varepsilon)\,\left( 1 + o(1) \right) = \beta(a)\,\frac{(d - 2)\,\omega_{d - 1}}{2|M|}\,\varepsilon^{d - 2}\left( 1 + o(1) \right).\]

Interior sequences \((a = \infty)\) give \(\beta = 1\)
and boundary sequences
\(\left( a = 0,\ x_{\varepsilon} \in \partial M \right)\) give
\(\beta = \frac{1}{2}\), a factor of two between the two.

[Definition 21 of arXiv:2609.00183, '2609.00183'] Let $\{x_0,...,x_k\} \in B_1(0) \subset \RR^n.$ We say that this set {\bf $\rho$-effectively spans} a $k$-dimensional affine subspace if for all $i=1,...,k,$
   \[
   x_i \notin B_{\rho}(x_0+\text{span}(x_1-x_0,...,x_{i-1}-x_0)).
   \]
   Given a set $F \subset B_1(0),$ we say that {\bf $F \ \rho$-effectively spans} a $k$-dimensional affine subspace if there exists a set $\{x_0,...,x_k\} \subset F$ that $\rho$-effectively spans a $k$-dimensional affine subspace.

[Lemma lem:detect_bad_large_loop of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] For any $b>0$ there exist $M>0$, $p > 0$ such that the following is true. There exists an event $F$ for $h$ (equivalently $\Gamma$) with $\mathbf{P}[F^c] = O(\delta^b)$ and the following holds. 

Sample $z \in \mathcal {D}_{\delta^{1+4a_3}}$ and $J \in \{ \lceil\log_2(\delta^{-1-a_3})\rceil,\ldots,\lfloor\log_2(\delta^{-1-2a_3})\rfloor \}$ uniformly at random, and let $R = 2^{-J}$. Then on the event $F$, for every $e \in \mathcal {E}^{\delta,{\mathrm{bad}}}_i(\mathcal {L})$, $\mathcal {L} \in \widehat{\Gamma}_i^\delta$, $i=0,2$, the following occurs with conditional probability at least $\delta^{8a_3}$:
\begin{itemize}
\item The scale $(z,R)$ is $M$-good for $h$.
\item The number of points in $\partial A(z,R/4,3R/4) \cap X^{\theta_0}_{z,R}$, $\partial A(z,R/8,R/4) \cap X^{\theta_0;*}_{z,R}$, $\partial A(z,R/4,3R/4) \cap X^{\theta_2}_{z,R}$, $\partial A(z,R/4,3R/4) \cap X^{-\pi/2}_{z,R}$, $\partial A(z,R/4,3R/4) \cap X^{+\pi/2}_{z,R}$ is at most $M$.
\item $U_e \subseteq B(z,R^{1+a_3})$ and $E^{i;p}_{z,R}$ occurs with $U_e$ for some $z_1,z_2,w_1$, supposing the internal metrics in $U_e$ are coupled so that they agree with the ones for $\Gamma$.
\end{itemize}

Let G be infinite, connected and locally finite, let o be a vertex, and suppose 0<p_c(G)<1. Let A_n be the event that o connects inside B(o,n) to its distance-n sphere, f_n(p)=P_p(A_n), and mu_n(dp)=f_n'(p)dp on [0,p_c]. Then mu_n converges weakly to theta_o(p_c) times the point mass at p_c. In particular, pointwise control of individual pivotal edges below p_c cannot by itself rule out a critical jump.

body:
Load-bearing hypothesis: self-adjointness requires the equality of domains D(T) = D(T*), not merely ⟨Tx, y⟩ = ⟨x, Ty⟩ on D(T). Everything that makes an operator usable - the spectral theorem, the Borel functional calculus, real spectrum, the unitary group e^{itT}, the resolvent bound 1/|Im z| - fails for a merely symmetric operator. What fails: a closed symmetric operator T that is not self-adjoint never has spectrum inside ℝ; its spectrum is all of ℂ when both n_+ ≥ 1 and n_- ≥ 1 (in particular whenever n_+ = n_- ≥ 1), and a closed half plane when exactly one of n_+, n_- is 0, so 'eigenvalue' and 'spectral decomposition' statements are void. Counterexample: on H = L²(0,1) let T = −i d/dx with D(T) = {f ∈ H¹(0,1) : f(0) = f(1) = 0}. T is densely defined, closed and symmetric, and T* = −i d/dx on all of H¹(0,1). Deficiency: ker(T* − i) = span{e^{−x}} and ker(T* + i) = span{e^{x}}, so n_+ = n_- = 1 and T is not self-adjoint. For every λ ∈ ℂ, Ran(T − λ)^⊥ = ker(T* − λ̄) = span{e^{iλ̄x}} ≠ {0}, so σ(T) = ℂ. Its self-adjoint extensions are the operators T_θ = −i d/dx on {f ∈ H¹(0,1) : f(1) = e^{iθ}f(0)}, θ ∈ [0, 2π), with spectrum {θ + 2πk : k ∈ ℤ} - a different physical momentum operator for each θ. Second counterexample, where no self-adjoint extension exists at all: S = −i d/dx on D(S) = {f ∈ H¹(0, ∞) : f(0) = 0} in L²(0, ∞) is closed and symmetric with ker(S* − i) = span{e^{−x}} and ker(S* + i) = {0}, so n_+ = 1, n_- = 0; S is maximal symmetric and has no self-adjoint extension in L²(0, ∞), so there is no unitary group it generates. Audit rule: whenever a proof invokes the spectral theorem, functional calculus, Stone's theorem, Kato-Rellich or 'the eigenvalues of T', check that self-adjointness (or essential self-adjointness plus passing to the closure) has actually been established, typically via Ran(T ± i) dense or a semibounded range condition.
H is a complex Hilbert space
the operator in question is densely defined and symmetric but its adjoint has a strictly larger domain
title: Pitfall: Symmetric Is Not Self-Adjoint - the Spectral Theorem and Stone's Theorem Need D(T) = D(T*)

body:
In Hilbert space every compact operator is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank operators, and many arguments quietly reuse this in a Banach setting, where it can be false. A Banach space Y has the approximation property (AP) if the identity of Y is a limit of finite-rank operators uniformly on compact subsets of Y; Grothendieck proved that Y has AP if and only if, for every Banach space X, the finite-rank operators are norm dense in K(X,Y). Enflo (1973) produced a separable reflexive Banach space without AP, and Davie and Szankowski showed that l^p for p not equal to 2, and c_0, have closed subspaces without AP; consequently there are Banach spaces X, Y and a compact operator X -> Y that is not a norm limit of finite-rank operators. Szankowski further showed that B(l^2) itself fails AP. What breaks without AP: (a) proofs of Fredholm-type results that first replace a compact K by a finite-rank F with ||K - F|| small; (b) attempts to define a trace on nuclear operators (the trace is well defined on the nuclear operators of X exactly when X has AP; without it the same nuclear operator has representations with different 'traces'); (c) approximation-number arguments imported from Hilbert space. Safe hypotheses to state instead: the space is a Hilbert space, or has a Schauder basis, or has the (bounded) approximation property; classical spaces such as C(K), L^p(mu) for 1 <= p <= infinity, and c_0 all have AP, so the pitfall bites only in exotic settings - but the hypothesis must be present, not assumed silently.
the target space has the approximation property (automatic in Hilbert spaces and in spaces with a Schauder basis)
in a general Banach space compactness alone does not give norm approximation by finite-rank operators
title: Pitfall: 'Compact = Limit of Finite Rank' Needs the Approximation Property

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2608.27433, 'Scalar curvature on K\"ahler blow-ups and systolic inequalities'] Let $(X,\omega)$ be a compact K\"ahler manifold, and let \(X_J\xrightarrow{\mu_J}X_{J-1}\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow X_1\xrightarrow{\mu_1}X_0=X\) be a finite sequence of nontrivial blow-ups along smooth complex submanifolds of codimension at least two. Denote by \(\mu:=\mu_1\circ\cdots\circ\mu_J:X_J\rightarrow X\). For $1\le j\le J$, let $E_j\subset X_j$ be the exceptional divisor of $\mu_j$, and let $\widetilde E_j$ denote its total transform on $X_J$.
Then there are parameter vectors \(\boldsymbol\eps_\ell=(\eps_{1,\ell},\ldots,\eps_{J,\ell})\rightarrow0\) and K\"ahler metrics $\omega_\ell$ on $X_J$ such that
\[
 [\omega_\ell]
 =\mu^*[\omega]-\sum_{j=1}^J\eps_{j,\ell}^2[\widetilde E_j],
\]
satisfying
\begin{equation}
 \norm{S(\omega_\ell)-\mu^*S(\omega)}_{C^0(X_J)}
 \longrightarrow0 \qquad
 \omega_\ell\longrightarrow\mu^*\omega
\text{ in }C^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}
 \bigl(X_J\setminus\operatorname{Exc}(\mu)\bigr).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 2 of arXiv:2608.27433
