[Lem 61 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $q_0 \in [0,1)$, we have $\sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0)$. 

\begin{proof}
    This is a consequence of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered}.
    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$. Then, there exists
    \[
        (q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)
    \]
    such that $\mu(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta) = \mu$.
    Let $\tilde p$ denote the restriction of $p$ to $[q_*,1] \subseteq [q_0,1]$.
    We will argue that $(b,\sigma,w,\tilde p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered} with $q_*$ in place of $q_0$.
    Indeed, conditions~\ref{it:1.1}, \ref{it:2.1}, \ref{it:3.1}, \ref{it:4.2}, \ref{it:5.1}, and \ref{it:6.1} exactly correspond to assumptions~(\ref{i:IAMP-main-coefs}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-diffusivity}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-p}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-budget}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-endpt}), and (\ref{i:IAMP-main-init}) of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}, while condition~\ref{it:1.1} also provides the additional assumption in Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered} that $w(t,\cdot)$ is even and $\zeta^\Ising$ is symmetric. By Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered}, there exists $\iota = \iota(\epsilon)$ with $\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0} \iota(\epsilon) = 0$ such that for all (sufficiently large) $N$, there exists a $C(L,\epsilon)$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$ with
    \[
        \max\Big(
            \bbW_2(\mu(\cA_N), \mu),
            \bbW_2(\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_N), \cP(\{\pm 1\}))
        \Big) \le \iota
    \]
and
    $\bbE[\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)] = \bzero$.
    This implies $\chi_{\cA_N}(0) = 0$.
    Recalling the definition \eqref{e:cM.Lip.q0}, we have $\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;C(L,\epsilon),\iota(\epsilon))$.
    We have thus shown
    \[
        \cM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;C(L,\epsilon),\iota(\epsilon))\,.
    \]
    Thus, for $\cB_\epsilon$ as defined in \eqref{e:W2.ball.notation},
    \[
        \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\Big)
        \subseteq \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;C(L,\epsilon),\iota(\epsilon))\Big)\,.
    \]
    Taking a union over $L>0$ shows
    \[
        \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\Big)
        \subseteq \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;L,\iota(\epsilon))\Big)
        \subseteq \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\tilde\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;L,\tilde\epsilon)\Big)\,,
    \]
    where $\tilde\epsilon = \tilde\epsilon(\epsilon) = \max(\epsilon,\iota(\epsilon))$.
    Since $\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0} \tilde\epsilon(\epsilon) = 0$, taking an intersection over $\epsilon$ yields
    \begin{align*}
        \sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0)
        &\stackrel{\eqref{e:measure.classes.simplification.without.L0}}{=}
        \adjustlimits
        \bigcap_{\epsilon>0} \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\Big) \\
        &\,\,\subseteq
        \adjustlimits \bigcap_{\epsilon>0} \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)\Big)
        \stackrel{\eqref{e:sM.Lip.q0}}{=} \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0)\,. \qedhere
    \end{align*}
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 61 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Prop lim of arXiv:2411.06571, 'Moment-based approach for two erratic KPZ scaling limits'] Let $\phi: \Bbb R\to \Bbb R$ be bounded and continuous. For all $n\in\Bbb N,$ and all $(x_1,...,x_n)\in\Bbb R^n$, we have $$\lim_{\epsilon\to 0} \int_{\Bbb R^n } \Bbb E \bigg[ \prod_{j=1}^n Z_{0,t}^\epsilon (x_j, y_j) \bigg] \prod_{j=1}^n \phi(y_j) dy\cdots dy_n = \mathbf E_{\mathrm{BM}^{\otimes n}}^{(x_1,...,x_n)} \bigg[ e^{\sigma_p^2  \sum_{1\le i<j\le n} L_0^{W^i-W^j}(t) } \prod_{j=1}^n \phi(W^j_t)\bigg] .$$
    Here $\sigma_p^2 = \int_\Bbb R (\varphi * \varphi^{(2p-1)}(x))^2dx,$ with $\varphi$ as in Theorem (mr2 of the paper). The above convergence is uniform on compact subsets of $(x_1,...,x_n)$.

[Thm 4 of arXiv:2605.29469, 'Multiscale Asymptotic Analysis of Kernel-Smoothed Solutions to Fractional Riesz-Bessel Equ'] Assume that the kernel function $g(\cdot,\cdot)$ has a finite Sobolev norm of order~$-\alpha$ with respect to the first variable, and assume that this norm is H\"older continuous of order $\theta \in (0,1]$ with respect to the second variable, that is,
      \[
      \left\|
      g(z,x)-g(z,y)
      \right\|_{H_z^{-\alpha}}
      \le
      C |x-y|^\theta.
      \] Then, the limit random field $U_0^g(t,x)$ in Theorem~\ref{ThmP2.1} is mean-square H\"older continuous in $x$ of any order  $\gamma_x\in (0,\theta).$ It has a continuous modification with sample paths that are almost surely H\"older continuous in $x$ of order $\gamma_x.$

If the following assumption holds true
\[
\left\|
(-\Delta)_z^{(\kappa_0-1)/4}(g(z,x)-g(z,y))
\right\|_{H_z^{-\alpha}}
\le
C |x-y|^{\theta^*},
\]
then, the limit random field $\tilde U_0^g(t,x)$ in Theorem~\ref{ThmP2.2} is mean-square H\"older continuous, and it admits a modification with almost surely continuous sample paths in $x$ of the H\"older order $\gamma_x\in (0,\theta^*)$.

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2608.26692, 'Many Facets in Random Polytopes from Product and Log-Concave Measures'] Let $\nu$ be a full-dimensional log-concave probability measure on $\R^d$ with
density $g$, and let $Z_0,\ldots,Z_d$ be independent random vectors with distribution $\nu$.
Then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{c^d}{\sqrt{d!}\,\norm{g}_\infty} \leq\E\,\vol_d\bigl(\conv\{Z_0,\ldots,Z_d\}\bigr)
 \leq\frac{C^d}{\sqrt{d!}\,\norm{g}_\infty},
\end{equation}
where $c,C>0$ are absolute constants.

[Lemma 5 (Lemma 3.2 in \cite{Isotropic_local}) of arXiv:2608.29872, 'Local Laws and Outlier Eigenvalues for Spiked Separable Covariance Matrices'] Let $\xi$ and $\zeta$ be families of nonnegative random variables.
\begin{itemize}
  \item[(i)] Suppose that $\xi (u,v)\prec \zeta(u,v)$ uniformly in $u\in U$ and $v\in V$. If $|V|\le n^C$ for some constant $C$, then $\sum_{v\in V} \xi(u,v) \prec \sum_{v\in V} \zeta(u,v)$ uniformly in $u$.

\item[(ii)] If $\xi_1 (u)\prec \zeta_1(u)$ and $\xi_2 (u)\prec \zeta_2(u)$ uniformly in $u\in U$, then $\xi_1(u)\xi_2(u) \prec \zeta_1(u)\zeta_2(u)$ uniformly in $u$.

\item[(iii)] Suppose that $\psi(u)\ge n^{-C}$ is deterministic and $\xi(u)$ satisfies $\mathbb E[\xi(u)^2] \le n^C$ for all $u$. Then if $\xi(u)\prec \psi(u)$ uniformly in $u$, we have $\mathbb E\xi(u) \prec \psi(u)$ uniformly in $u$.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition of arXiv:2505.02685, 'On the Spectral Expansion of Monotone Subsets of the Hypercube'] Fix a monotone set $A\subseteq \{0,1\}^{n}$. For all $f:A\rightarrow\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$, we define\footnote{
The energy functional $\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}_{A}(\cdot)$ defined here differs from the standard Dirichlet form of the censored random walk on $A$ by a factor of $n$. This normalization is chosen to better align with the notion of total influence in the analysis of Boolean functions.
}
\[
\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}_{A}(f)\vcentcolon= \frac{1}{4}\cdot \Exu{x\in A}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(f(x)-f(x^{\oplus i})\right)^{2}\cdot\ind{x^{\oplus i}\in A}}.
\]
Here $x^{\oplus i}$ denotes the binary string obtained by flipping the $i$-th bit of $x$.

body:
[Proposition stream of arXiv:2506.20932, 'Thinning to improve two-sample discrepancy'] Let \(m\) be an integer with \(m \le 2n\).
    Let $x_1, \dots, x_{m}$ be i.i.d. samples from a Borel probability distribution in $\mathbb{R}^d$, let $\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_{m}$ be independent Rademacher random variables, and let $T>0$. There is an online algorithm that discards, on average, at most $2n/T$ of the \( x_i \)'s, and achieves 
    $$
    \E \sup_{B, 1 \leq k \leq m} \disc_k(B) 
    \le T \log_2^{2d} n + d \ln(dn) + C_1 d,
    $$
    where the supremum is over all axis-aligned,  half-infinite boxes $B$ and all $k=1,\ldots,m$, and where $C_1$ is an absolute constant. The ``online'' means that, at time $i$, the algorithm decides whether to discard the term $x_i$ based on this and previously retained terms; the decision is never reversed in the future. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem cvPM of arXiv:2605.06488, 'Continuous-state branching processes with L\'evy-Khintchine drift-interaction: Laplace dua'] Let $(X^n)_{n\geq 1}$ be a sequence of $\mathrm{CBDI}$ processes converging $\mathbb{P}_x$-a.s. pointwise towards a process $X$ for every $x\in[0,\infty]$. Let $\mathcal{X}^n$ denote the generator of $X^n$ and $\mathcal{X}$ be an operator such that for every $f\in \mathrm{C}_c^2((0,\infty))$, $\mathcal{X}f$ is continuous and
\[
\|\mathcal{X}^n f-\mathcal{X}f\|_\infty \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} 0.
\]
Then, $X$ solves the martingale problem 
\[\forall x\in(0,\infty), \ f\in \mathrm{C}^2_c((0,\infty)), \quad \left(f(X_t)-\int_0^t\mathcal{X}f(X_s)\mathrm{d} s, \ t\geq 0\right) \ \text{is a } \mathbb{P}_x\text{- martingale}.\]

body:
[Lemma 6 (Conditional two-entry reduction) of arXiv:2604.26298, 'The Expiring Coupon Collector\\ Sliding-Window Surjection Flux and Rare-Entry Laws'] Condition on \(E_0=1\), and let \(a=X_0\) be the color appended at the entry time.  Then the middle block
\[
        U=(X_{-M+1},\ldots,X_{-1})
\]
is a uniform onto word of length \(m=M-1\) over the alphabet \([n]\setminus\{a\}\).  For \(1\le u\le m\), define
\[
        R_u:=\#\bigl\{c\in[n]\setminus\{a\}:
        \text{all occurrences of }c\text{ in }U\text{ lie among }U_1,\ldots,U_u\bigr\}.
\]
Then, conditional on \(U\) and \(E_0\),
\begin{equation}
        \Pbb(E_u=1\mid U,E_0)
        \le
        \frac{R_u}{n}\left(1-\frac1n\right)^{u-1}
        \exp\left\{-(R_u-1)_+\left(1-\frac1{n-1}\right)^{u-1}\right\}.
\end{equation}
Also
\begin{equation}
        \Pbb(E_M=1\mid E_0)=\mu_{n,M}.
\end{equation}

body:
[Corollary c:markov-holonomy-elementary of arXiv:2607.24640, 'The Yang-Mills measure on surfaces via Morse theory'] Let $\gamma,\tilde{\gamma}$ be two elementary curves which are both of type $\operatorname{I}$ or $\operatorname{II}_\pm$ such that $\tilde{\gamma}\preccurlyeq\gamma$.
Then, for any bounded and measurable functions $\Psi_1,\Psi_2$ on $G$, one has
$$
\mathbb{E}\left(\Psi_1(\mathrm{g}_{\tilde{\gamma}}(1))\Psi_2(\mathrm{g}_{\gamma}(1))\right)=e^{\frac{\mathscr{A}_{\tilde{\gamma}}(1)\Delta_G}{2}}\left(\Psi_1e^{\frac{\left(\mathscr{A}_\gamma(1)-\mathscr{A}_{\tilde{\gamma}}(1)\right)\Delta_G}{2}}(\Psi_2)\right)(\operatorname{Id}).
$$ 
Equivalently, for every $\mathrm{g}_1,\mathrm{g}_2$ in $G$, one has
$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\mathrm{g}_{\tilde{\gamma}}(1)\in d\mathrm{g}_1,\mathrm{g}_{\gamma}(1)\in d\mathrm{g}_2\right)=p_{\mathscr{A}_{\tilde{\gamma}}(1)}(\mathrm{g}_1)p_{\mathscr{A}_\gamma(1)-\mathscr{A}_{\tilde{\gamma}}(1)}(\mathrm{g}_2\mathrm{g}_1^{-1})\mu_G^{\otimes 2}(d\mathrm{g}_1,d\mathrm{g}_2).
$$
More generally, for every $m\geqslant1$ elementary curves $\gamma_i,$, $i= 1, \ldots, m$, all of type $\operatorname{I}$ or $\operatorname{II}_\pm$,  with $\gamma_1\preccurlyeq\gamma_2\preccurlyeq\ldots \preccurlyeq\gamma_m$, one has
\begin{align*}
   &\mathbb{P}\left(\mathrm{g}_{\gamma_1}(1)\in d\mathrm{g}_1, \ldots, \gamma_m(1)\in d\mathrm{g}_m\right)\\
   & \quad =p_{\mathscr{A}_{1}(1)}(\mathrm{g}_1)p_{\mathscr{A}_2(1)-\mathscr{A}_1(1)}(\mathrm{g}_2\mathrm{g}_1^{-1}) \ldots p_{\mathscr{A}_{m}(1)-\mathscr{A}_{m-1}(1)}(\mathrm{g}_m\mathrm{g}_{m-1}^{-1}) \mu_G^{\otimes m}(d\mathrm{g}_1,\ldots,d\mathrm{g}_m),
\end{align*}
where $\mathscr{A}_i(1):=\mathscr{A}_{\gamma_i}(1)$

\begin{align}
 P_1K_{\ell,N}P_1

 (\mathcal J_N+\mathcal B_N)+O_\ell(N^{\ell-2}),

 P_1K_{\ell,N}Q_1

 P_{11}K_{\ell,N}P_{11}

 \norm{P_{11}K_{\ell,N}Z_3}

\end{align}
All remainders are operator-norm bounds.  Moreover,
$C_NC_N^*=\mathcal B_N$ and $\left\lVert C_N\right\rVert=2\sqrt{N-1}$.

[Definition 6 of arXiv:2609.02283, 'The game chromatic number of generalized Mycielski graphs of paths and cycles'] A \emph{Type~1 configuration} after Alice's first move consists of a $4$-cycle
\[
 u_1u_2u_3u_4u_1
\]
and two vertices $x_1,x_3$ such that $u_4$ is the only colored vertex, $u_1,u_2,u_3,x_1,x_3$ are uncolored,
\[
 x_1\in N(u_1)\setminus\{u_2,u_4\},\qquad
 x_3\in N(u_3)\setminus\{u_2,u_4\},
\]
and, after Bob colors $u_2$ with a color different from $\varphi(u_4)$,
\[
 \bigl(N[x_1]\cap U\bigr)\cap
 \bigl(N[x_3]\cap U\bigr)=\varnothing.
\]
Here $U$ denotes the set of vertices that remain uncolored after Bob's move.

body:
[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2609.02225, '\textbf{The direct moving plane method for weak solutions of the fractional $p$-Laplacian}'] Let \(q>0\), and set
\[
c_q:=\max\{1,q\}, \qquad \vartheta_q:=\min\{1,q\}.
\]
For every \(0\le b<a\),
\begin{equation}
        0<a^q-b^q
        \le c_q a^{q-1}(a-b).
\end{equation}
Moreover, for every \(M>0\) and \(0\le b<a\le M\),
\begin{equation}
        a^q-b^q
        \le L_{q,M}(a-b)^{\vartheta_q},
\end{equation}
where
\[
L_{q,M}:=
        \begin{cases}
        1, & 0<q\le1,\\
        qM^{q-1}, & q>1.
        \end{cases}
\]

Let A_1, ..., A_n be pairwise independent events with p_i = P(A_i), S = sum_i p_i > 0 and Q = sum_i p_i^2. Then P(A_1 or ... or A_n) >= S^2/(S^2 + S - Q). The right side is at most 1, because Q <= S, and strictly greater than S/(1 + S), because Q > 0. Mutually independent events have union probability exactly 1 - prod_i (1 - p_i), but pairwise independence does not give that formula: for the three even-parity events on the uniform law on {000, 011, 101, 110} the union has probability 3/4, which equals this bound, while 1 - prod_i (1 - p_i) = 7/8.
A_1, ..., A_n pairwise independent
S = sum P(A_i) > 0

[Lemma lem:dict-diffusion of arXiv:2603.14906, 'Four Levels of Thermodynamic Convergence of Singularly Perturbed Markov Semigroups'] Let $\mathcal L$ be given by Eq.~(equation eq:backward-eps1 of the paper) and let $\mathcal L^\dagger$ denote its $L^2(\pi)$-adjoint.
Define the symmetric and antisymmetric parts
\[
\mathcal L^{s}:=\tfrac12(\mathcal L+\mathcal L^\dagger),\qquad
\mathcal L^{a}:=\tfrac12(\mathcal L-\mathcal L^\dagger).
\]
Then for all $f,g\in C_c^\infty(X)$,
\[
\Gamma(f,g)(\zeta)=\langle \nabla f(\zeta),A(\zeta)\nabla g(\zeta)\rangle,
\qquad
\mathcal L^{a} f(\zeta)=-\langle \gamma(\zeta),\nabla f(\zeta)\rangle.
\]
Moreover, writing $\mathrm{id}:X\to\mathbb{R}^d$ for the coordinate map, we have
\[
\Gamma(\mathrm{id}_i,\mathrm{id}_j)=A_{ij},
\qquad
\mathcal L^{a}\mathrm{id}=-\gamma,
\]
in the sense of componentwise identities on $X$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Dictionary between $\mathcal L$, $\Gamma$ and $(A,\gamma)$

body:
[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2608.11071, 'Scaling Laws for Majority-based Opinion Dynamics in the Presence of Stubborn Agents'] Suppose that the polynomial $\Delta_k$ has a  simple root $r\in \mc{S}$ that is stable, i.e., there exists an  interval (region of attraction) $[a,b]\subseteq \mc S$ containing the root such that $\Delta_k(x) >0$ for $x\in [a,r)$ and $\Delta_k(x) < 0$ for $x\in (r,b]$. Then the following properties hold.
    \begin{enumerate}

        \item There exist constants $\eta,C_1>0$ such that for all $x\in B_{\eta}(r)$ we have $\Delta_k'(x)<-C_1$.
        Furthermore, there exists a constant $C_2>0$ such that for all $x \in [a,b]$, we have $\Delta_k(x) (x-r)\leq -C_2 (x-r)^2$.
        
        
        
        

        \item For any $\delta>0$ satisfying $B_\delta(r)\subseteq [a,b]$, there exists $\kappa_\delta>0$  such that $\PP_{x}(T_{\text{exit}}^n(B_{\delta}(r))\leq\exp(\kappa_\delta n))\leq C_4n\exp(-\kappa_\delta n/4)$ for all sufficiently large $n$ and for any $x \in B_{\delta/2}(r)$ where $C_4>0$ is a constant independent of $n$.
        
        \item For any $\delta>0,\epsilon>0$, there exists $n_0(\delta,\epsilon)>0$ such that whenever $n\geq n_0(\delta,\epsilon)$ we have $\EE_{x}[T^n_{\text{enter}}(B_{\delta}(r))\wedge T^n_{\text{exit}}([a,b])]\leq C\log n$ and $\PP_x(T^n_{\text{enter}}(B_\delta(r))>C'\log n/\epsilon)\leq \epsilon$ for all initial state $x\in [a,b]$ where $C$ and $C'$ are positive constants independent of $n$. 
        
        
        \item  If $X^n$ and $\bar X^n$ are chains evolved independently until their first meeting time and synchronously thereafter, started at $x$ and $\bar x$, respectively, and each following the transition rates~\eqref{eq:uprate}-\eqref{eq:downrate}, then for any $\epsilon>0$ and all $n$ sufficiently large, we have $\PP_{x,\bar x}(X^n(t)\neq \bar X^n(t))\leq \epsilon$ whenever $t> \frac{C_3\log n}{\epsilon}$ for some positive constant $C_3$ and  $x,\bar x\in B_{\eta}(r)$ for sufficiently small $\eta>0$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For integers a,b and a positive integer n, a is congruent to b modulo n, written a congruent to b (mod n), if n divides a-b. Congruence modulo n is preserved by addition and multiplication, so the residue classes form the quotient ring Z/nZ with operations induced from the integers.

n is a positive integer

[Lem MV-Seq of arXiv:2608.29013, 'Weighted Homology and Cohomology of Weighted Polyhedra'] Let $(K,\mu)$ be a divisibly weighted triangulation of $(X,\lambda)$. Then there is an exact sequence of chain complex
$$
0 \leftarrow \mathcal{W}_q^{\mathcal{U}}(X,\lambda) \stackrel{\varepsilon}{\longleftarrow} \underset{\mathrm{dim}(\sigma)=0}{\bigoplus} \mathcal{W}_q\left( \mathrm{St}(\sigma,K),\lambda\right) \stackrel{d}{\longleftarrow} \underset{\mathrm{dim}(\sigma)=1}{\bigoplus} \mathcal{W}_q\left(\mathrm{St}(\sigma,K),\lambda\right) \stackrel{d}{\longleftarrow} \cdots$$
where $\varepsilon$ is summing up the chains from all
the open stars via inclusions into $X$.

[Lem 9 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] If $(\mu_{F,n})_{n\ge 1}$ obeys the LDP with rate function $I_F:\cal{Y}_F\to [0,\infty]$ for every $F\in \cal{F}$, then
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[a.] these rate functions are related by
		\[I_F(x) = \inf\{I_G(y):\ y \in \cal{Y}_G,\ \pi_F(y) = x\}\]
		whenever $F,G \in \cal{F}$, $F\subset G$, and $x \in \cal{Y}_F$, and
		\item[b.] the original sequence $(\mu_n)_{n \ge 1}$ obeys the LDP with rate function
		\[I(y) := \sup\{I_F(\pi_F(y)):\ F\in \cal{F}\} \qquad (y \in \Y).\] \qed
	\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem 20 of arXiv:2607.06745, 'Regularization and asymptotic behaviour of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck evolution operators in infin'] Every eigenfunction of $P_{0}$ relative
to a non-zero eigenvalue is twice differentiable. Further, for every
$\omega\in\left(\omega_{0},0\right)$, there exists $C_{\omega}>0$
such that, for every $N\geq2$, $\lambda\in\sigma\left(P_{0}\right)\setminus\left\{ 0\right\} $
and $g\in Ker\left(\lambda I-P_{0}\right)\setminus\left\{ 0\right\} $:
\begin{equation}
\left|\lambda\right|^{N}\left\Vert \nabla^{2}g\right\Vert _{L^{p}\left(X;\mu_{0};\mathcal{L}\left(X\right)\right)}\leq C_{\omega}e^{2\omega NT}\left\Vert g\right\Vert _{L^{p}\left(X,\mu_{0}\right)}.
\end{equation}

Consequently, if $\lambda_{0}\in\sigma\left(P_{0}\right)$ with $\left|\lambda_{0}\right|=e^{\omega_{0}T}$
and $g$ is any eigenfunction of $P_{0}$ relative to $\lambda_{0}$,
then
\[
\left\Vert \nabla^{2}g\right\Vert _{L^{p}\left(X;\mu_{0};\mathcal{L}\left(X\right)\right)}=0.
\]
Thus, by Lemma $\text{\ref{cor: nabla2 uguale 0}}$, $g$ can be considered
a linear functional, up to a $\mu_{0}$-negligible subset of $X$.

[Lemma 3 of arXiv:2603.25615, 'Fourier dimension of Mandelbrot cascades on planar curves'] For $1 \leq p,q\leq \infty$ and $1\le j\le n$, we let
$$
S(p,q,j,n) = \left( \sum_{I \in \Q_j} \left( \sum_{J \in \Q_n , J \subset I} \nu_n(J)^q \right)^{p/q} \right)^{1/p}.
$$
Then, we have
\begin{equation}
\E (S(p,q,j,n)) \lesssim b^{-j\widetilde{\tau}(p) / p  - (n-j) \widetilde{\tau}(q)/q}. 
\end{equation}
Note that $\lim_{p \rightarrow \infty} \widetilde{\tau}(p)/p =\alpha_{\min}$. Thus, in \eqref{eq:E(S(p,q,j,n))}, we adopt the convention $\widetilde{\tau}(\infty) / \infty =\alpha_{\min}  $ if $p=\infty$ or $q=\infty$.

[Definition 24 of arXiv:2603.24616, 'Pinning in non-critical half-space geometric last passage percolation'] Fix a set $\Sigma = \llbracket 1, N \rrbracket$ with $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, $T_1 \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, $q \in (0,1)$, and $c \in [0, q^{-1})$. A $\Sigma$-indexed geometric line ensemble $\mathfrak{L}$ on $\llbracket 0, T_1 \rrbracket$ satisfies the {\em interacting pair Gibbs property} if it is interlacing, meaning that $L_i \succeq L_{i+1}$ for all $i \in \llbracket 1, N - 1 \rrbracket$, and for any $T \in \llbracket 1, T_1\rrbracket$ and any $k\in\llbracket 1,\lfloor(N-1)/2\rfloor\rrbracket$ the following holds. Suppose that $g$ is an increasing path on $\llbracket 0, T\rrbracket$, and $\vec{y} \in \mathfrak{W}_{2k}$ are such that $\mathbb{P}(A) > 0$, where $A$ denotes the event 
$$A =\{  \vec{y} = ({L}_{1}(T), \dots, {L}_{2k}(T)), L_{2k+1} \llbracket 0,T \rrbracket = g \}.$$
Then, we have for any $\{ B_i \in \Omega(T,y_i) \}_{i = 1}^{2k}$ that 
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}\left( L_{i}\llbracket 0,T \rrbracket = B_{i} \mbox{ for $i \in \llbracket 1, 2k \rrbracket$} \, \vert  A \, \right) = \mathbb{P}^{T, \vec{y}, g}_{\ice; q,c} \left( \cap_{i = 1}^{2k} \{Q_i = B_i\} \right),
\end{equation}
where $\mathfrak{Q} = \{Q_i\}_{i = 1}^{2k}$ has law $\mathbb{P}^{T, \vec{y}, g}_{\ice; q,c}$.

body:
[Proposition 11 (Three-point representation of four centered moments) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Let \(X\) be a real random variable satisfying
\begin{equation}
 \E X=0,
 \qquad
 \E X^2=v>0,
 \qquad
 \E X^4<\infty.
\end{equation}
Put
\begin{equation}
 a:=\frac{\E X^3}{v^{3/2}},
 \qquad
 b:=\frac{\E X^4}{v^2},
 \qquad
 c:=b-a^2.
\end{equation}
Then \(c\ge1\).  Define
\begin{equation}
 \alpha:=\frac{\sqrt{a^2+4c}-a}{2},
 \qquad
 \beta:=\frac{\sqrt{a^2+4c}+a}{2},
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 p_-:=\frac{1}{\alpha(\alpha+\beta)},
 \qquad
 p_+:=\frac{1}{\beta(\alpha+\beta)},
 \qquad
 p_0:=1-\frac1c.
\end{equation}
These numbers are nonnegative and sum to one.  If \(Q\) has the three-point
law
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P(Q=-\alpha)=p_-,
 \qquad
 \mathbb P(Q=0)=p_0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb P(Q=\beta)=p_+,
\end{equation}
then \(\widehat X:=\sqrt v\,Q\) satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \E\widehat X^q=\E X^q,
 \qquad q=1,2,3,4.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 |\widehat X|
 \le2\sqrt{\frac{\E X^4}{v}}.
\end{equation}

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Asymptotic uniformity of the final discovered vertex structural calculation Result: Let K(x,y) be the probability that y is last when the walk starts at x. Automorphism equivariance and transitivity imply every row sums to1 and every column has the same sum, hence K is doubly stochastic and pi*K=pi. This proves exact uniformity after a uniform start. However K can be far from the constant matrix: on the complete graph, K(x,x)=0 and K(x,y)=1/(n-1) for y different from x, giving total-variation distance exactly1/n. Check: The complete-graph value follows by permutation symmetry of all vertices other than the start. For a generic doubly stochastic equivariant kernel, the identity kernel is a counterexample to uniform row convergence, so double stochasticity alone cannot solve the walk-specific question. Obstruction: A useful proof must exploit discovery dynamics or show decorrelation from the initial vertex. The symmetry calculation does not do this, and randomizing the initial vertex would erase the actual question.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0247-asymptotic-uniformity-of-the-final-discovered-vertex

Own-work draft, independently checked proof, T326-w697-C02 v3; reviewer urn:mb-agent:d6ca7a10ae76247b PASS on this exact version recorded in AUDITS_FROM_REVIEWER.tsv. In exactly infinite-context population training, fix d>=1, M>=1 task vectors w_i in R^d and rho>=0. Let z(w)=(w,||w||^2/d+rho), J=[I_d,0], C=(1/M)sum_i z(w_i)z(w_i)^T, and P the orthogonal projector onto range C, Q=I-P. Direct Euclidean/Frobenius gradient flow of L(G)=(1/2M)sum_i||G z(w_i)-w_i||^2, with arbitrary initial d by (d+1) matrix G_0 and no ridge, selects G_infinity=JP+G_0Q. Its right-nullspace action remains G(t)Q=G_0Q at all times. For G_0=aJ, a fixed real scalar, and a fresh standard Gaussian task independent of the pool with query covariates N(0,I_d/d), the normalized excess prediction risk is (1-a)^2[d+1-r-q+(eta-1)q(1-q)]/d, where r=rank C, q=Q_(d+1,d+1), eta=(1+rho)^2+2/d. For iid Gaussian task vectors r=min(M,d+1) almost surely. For M<=d, the bracket divided by d differs from (d-M)/d by a number in [0,(1+(eta-1)/4)/d]; for M>=d+1 it is zero. At fixed rho,a, M/d->kappa therefore gives risk ->(1-a)^2(1-kappa)_+, including kappa=1. In the square audit proxy z=w, J=I_d, the exact selector is P+G_0(I-P), with new-task risk ||(G_0-I)(I-P)||_F^2; for G_0=aI it is (1-a)^2(d-r) before division by d. This is a direct effective-matrix statement with its coordinates specified, and applies classical least-squares implicit bias. General attention-factor dynamics are not inferred from it. The written argument uses the finite-dimensional spectral limit exp(-tC)->Q and the uncentered second moment E[zz^T]=diag(I_d,eta); 1540 exact-rational checks support those calculations. Two Lean attempts timed out, so no Lean certification is asserted.

Direct Euclidean gradient flow of the effective matrix; no explicit regularizer
Fresh Gaussian task independent of the pool for the risk formula

body:
[Lemma 11 (Subgaussian Kahane--Khintchine inequality) of arXiv:2608.13687, 'Multiplicative chaos from random multiplicative functions'] Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and fix $(f_i)_{i\in\N}\subset H$.
If $H$ is a real Hilbert space, let $(A_i)_{i\in\N}$ satisfy Case \caseR, and if $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, let $(A_i)_{i\in\N}$ satisfy \caseS.
For any $m\in\N$, 
define  
\[
S_m\coloneqq\sum_{k=1}^m A_k f_k \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sigma_m^2\coloneqq\E\|S_m\|_H^2 =  \sum_{k=1}^m \|f_k\|_H^2 \,.
\]
There exist $c,C>0$ such that for all $m \in \N$ such that  $\sigma_m >0$,
and for all $u\geq 0$,
\begin{align}
        \P(\|S_m\|_H>u)
        \le
        Ce^{-cu^2/\sigma_m^2}\,.
\end{align}
\begin{proof}
A version of the Kahane--Khintchine inequality stated explicitly for Rademacher, Steinhaus, and Gaussian coefficients can be found in \cite[Proposition~6.2.7]{kahane-khintchine-source}\footnote{They call Steinhaus random variables ``complex Rademacher'' random variables.}, which states the bound $\E e^{\delta\|S_m\|_H^2} \leq (1- 2e \delta \E\|S_m\|_H^2)^{-1}$ for all $\delta \in (0, (2e\sigma_m^2)^{-1})$. Equation~\eqref{eq:subgaussian-kahane-khintchine-tail} now follows from taking $\delta = 1/4e\sigma_m^2$ and the Markov inequality.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Subgaussian Kahane--Khintchine inequality

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Controlled generators, exact finite-state diagnostic, coupling, renewal reward or capacity comparison Result: A deadline-success value must carry remaining slack as well as remaining work. For a job arriving at a with size x, slack at t is a+D-t-x_remaining. Two equal-work jobs can have opposite feasibility depending on arrival age. Moreover an admission rule using only current feasibility ignores the opportunity cost of accepted work: a size close to D may be feasible now but block many later short jobs. In a finite-horizon control equation the immediate reward is a unit success at completion before the deadline, rather than the running holding cost used for mean response. Check: Check two residual-size 0.2 jobs with slacks 0.1 and -0.1: the latter cannot succeed even with immediate exclusive service. This separates a feasibility state from a workload-only state without assuming an optimal policy. Obstruction: The stationary success-maximizing policy, admissible preemption/drop rules and its verification remain unresolved.

    \end{equation*}

[Proposition 12 of arXiv:2607.23640, '{\sl Non-equilibrium fluctuations of a two-species exclusion process with slow boundary }'] There exists a unique random element \(\bm Y\) taking values in
	\(\mathcal D([0,T], (\mathscr S^\dagger )')\) such that, for every test function \(\bm f\in \mathscr S^\dagger \),
	\[
	W_t(\bm f)
	=
	\left\langle \bm Y_t,\bm f\right\rangle
	-
	\left\langle \bm Y_0,\bm f\right\rangle
	-
	\int_0^t
	\left\langle \bm Y_s,\mathcal A^\dagger\bm f\right\rangle
	\,\mathrm d s
	\]
	  and
	\[
	N_t(\bm f)
	=
	W_t(\bm f)^2
	-
	\int_0^t
	\mathcal Q_s(\bm f,\bm f)
	\,\mathrm d s
	\]
	are martingales with respect to the natural filtration. Moreover, the initial field
	\(\bm Y_0\) is a centered Gaussian field with covariance
	\[
	\mathbb E\left[
	\bm Y_0(\bm f)\bm Y_0(\bm g)
	\right]
	=
	\sigma(\bm f,\bm g),
	\qquad
	\bm f,\bm g\in\mathscr S^\dagger,
	\]
	where \(\sigma\) is the initial covariance form defined in Theorem \ref{th2.3}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 12 of arXiv:2607.23640

[Proposition 21 (Tree-graph inequality; Aizenman and Newman
\cite{AN84}) of arXiv:2607.24561, 'Range convergence and sharp one-arm asymptotics\\for the critical percolation cluster in h'] For all $m\ge1$ and \emph{all} $x_1,\dots,x_m\in\Z^d$ (not necessarily
distinct, and not necessarily distinct from $0$),
\begin{equation}
\tau_{m+1}(0,x_1,\dots,x_m)\;\le\;
\sum_{T\in\T_m}\ \sum_{(z_v)_{v\in V_{\mathrm{int}}(T)}\in(\Z^d)^{V_{\mathrm{int}}(T)}}
\ \prod_{\{a,b\}\in E(T)}\tau_2(w_a,w_b),
\end{equation}
where $w_0:=0$, $w_i:=x_i$ for leaves and $w_v:=z_v$ for internal vertices.
The bound holds verbatim when some of the points coincide: with the
convention that a repeated point is not repeated in the connection event,
$\tau_{m+1}(0,x_1,\dots,x_m)$ is then a connection function of the distinct
points among $0,x_1,\dots,x_m$, which is still dominated by the displayed
sum (the right-hand side only grows when leaves are placed at coinciding
positions). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Proposition 3.1 of arXiv:2512.19517, 'Spiking and Resetting'] The process $({\bar{X}}^{\varepsilon}_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ with state space $\{0,1\}$ and càdlàg trajectories defined by $\forall t\geq 0,\quad{\bar{X}}^{\varepsilon}_{t}=\sum_{k\geq 0}{\mathbf{1}}_{t\in[e_{2k+1}^{\varepsilon},e_{2k+2}^{\varepsilon})}$ converges in law to the jump Markov process $({\bar{X}}_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ defined in Section 1. Notation from the paper: $X^{\varepsilon}$ is the resetting process on $[0,1)$ that follows the flow $\varepsilon\dot{x}_{t}=\varepsilon f(x_{t})+x_{t}h(x_{t})$, $x_{0}=0$, and is reset to $0$ at rate $\varepsilon^{-1}h(x_{t})$, where $f,h$ are $C^{2}$ on $[0,1]$ with $f(1)<0<f(0)$, $h(1)=0$, $h'(1)\neq 0$ and $h>0$ on $[0,1)$; $y_{*}^{\varepsilon}=1-\varepsilon^{\beta}$ with $\beta\in(0,1/2)$; $e_{0}^{\varepsilon}=0$, $e_{2k+1}^{\varepsilon}=\inf\{t\geq e_{2k}^{\varepsilon}:X_{t}^{\varepsilon}>y_{*}^{\varepsilon}\}$ and $e_{2k+2}^{\varepsilon}=\inf\{t\geq e_{2k+1}^{\varepsilon}:X_{t}^{\varepsilon}=0\}$; and $(\bar{X}_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ (Section 1) is the pure jump Markov process on $\{0,1\}$ with rate $f(0)$ to jump from $0$ to $1$ and rate $-f(1)=|f(1)|$ to jump from $1$ to $0$ (Section 1 of the paper prints this rate as $f(1)$; since $f(1)<0$, the rate is $-f(1)$, the parameter of the exponential limit of the holding time $e_{2}^{\varepsilon}-e_{1}^{\varepsilon}$ in Proposition 2.5).

[Definition 1 of arXiv:2606.06193, 'Peng's Maximum Principle for McKean-Vlasov Stochastic Differential Equations with Common N'] We say that $\varphi \in C_b^{1,1}(\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d),\R^m)$,
    if there exists for all $\vartheta \in L^2(\Omega, \mathbb{R}^d)$ an $\cL(\vartheta)$-modification of $\partial_\mu \varphi(\cL(\vartheta))$, again denoted by $\partial_\mu \varphi(\cL(\vartheta))$, such that $\partial_\mu \varphi: \mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d) \times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ is bounded and Lipschitz continuous, i.e. there is some $C>0$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
        \item $|\partial_\mu \varphi(\mu)(y)| \leq C$, for all $ \mu \in \mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and $ y \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and
        \item $|\partial_\mu \varphi(\mu)(y)-\partial_\mu \varphi(\mu^{\prime})(y^{\prime})| \leq C(W_2(\mu, \mu^{\prime})+|y-y^{\prime}|)$, for all $ \mu, \mu^{\prime} \in \mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and $ y,y^{\prime} \in \mathbb{R}^d$.
    \end{enumerate}

body:
[Proposition 9 of arXiv:2609.03238, 'Representation Defects and Cassels Pairings for Congruent Number Curves'] Assume \eqref{eq:layer}.  Then
\[
16\mid h(-pq),\qquad 16\mid h(-2pq).
\]
In particular,
\[
h(-2pq)\equiv h(-pq)\pmod{16}.
\]
Thus the class number conditions modulo $16$ in
\cite[Thm.~4.9(ii), Thm.~5.4(1)]{Qin22} do not separate the layer
\eqref{eq:layer}.

body:
[Thm Zk of arXiv:2604.10602, 'Fractional Navier-Stokes Equations with Caputo Derivative Driven by Hermite Noise'] Assume $0<\alpha<1$, $H\in(1/2,1)$, $0\le\nu<1$, and $\alpha(1-\nu)+2H>2$. Then for any $p\ge2$ and $t\in[0,T]$,
\[
\|Z_k(t)\|_{L^p(\Omega;\dot{H}^\nu)} \le C_{p,k} \, t^{\frac{\alpha(1-\nu)+2H-2}{2}},
\]
with $C_{p,k}=(p-1)^{k/2}C_0$. Moreover, for $0\le t_1<t_2\le T$,
\[
\|Z_k(t_2)-Z_k(t_1)\|_{L^p(\Omega;\dot{H}^\nu)} \le C_{p,k} (t_2-t_1)^{\gamma},
\]
where $\gamma = \min\bigl\{\frac{2-(2-\nu)\alpha}{2},\ \frac{\alpha(1-\nu)+2H-2}{2}\bigr\}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Lemma cond_prod of arXiv:2412.06701, 'Matsumoto-Yor processes on Jordan algebras'] Let $\left( k_t \ ; \ t \ge 0 \right)$ be a left Brownian motion on $K$. Then for $t>0$, the conditional law of $k_t^*\left( \widetilde\ell_t \right)$ given $\left( k^*_t\left( \widetilde\lambda_s \right) \ ; \ s\le t \right)$ is given by the distribution $\mathrm{GIG}_{E_+}\left( p ; a^{-1}, e \right)$, where $a=k_t\widetilde\lambda_t$.

[Theorem thm:neighbourhood of arXiv:2603.16824, 'Age-dependent random connection models with arc reciprocity: clustering and connectivity'] Let \(\beta>0\), \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), \(\delta>1\), and \(\Gamma\geq 0\). Almost surely, the root \(\0\) in \(\mathscr{D}_o\) has finite degree. More precisely, for \(k\in\mathbb{N}_0\), we have 
    \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
        \item 
    	   for the indegree
    	   \begin{equation*}
    		  \begin{aligned}
    		      & \mathbb{P}_o\big(\sharp\mathscr{N}^{\text{in}}=k\big)\asymp k^{-1-\nicefrac{1}{\gamma}}. 
    		  \end{aligned}	
    		\end{equation*}
    	\item 
            For the outdegree, we have, 
            \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
            	\item
            		if \(\Gamma>\gamma\), then \(\sharp\mathscr{N}^{\text{out}}\) is Poisson distributed with parameter \(\lambda\asymp \tfrac{\omega_d \delta \beta}{\delta-1}(\tfrac{1}{(\Gamma-\gamma)}+\tfrac{1}{\gamma})\), where \(\omega_d\) denotes the volume of the \(d\)-dimensional unit ball.
            	\item 
            		If \(\Gamma=\gamma\), then
            			\[
            		        \mathbb{P}_o\big(\sharp\mathscr{N}^{\text{out}}=k\big) \asymp \int_0^1 \frac{u \log(1/u)^k}{k!} \,\mathrm{d} u = 2^{-(k+1)}.
            			\]
            	\item 
            		If \(\Gamma<\gamma\), then 
            		\[
                		\begin{aligned}
               	    			& \mathbb{P}_o\big(\sharp\mathscr{N}^{\text{out}}=k\big)\asymp k^{-1-\nicefrac{1}{(\gamma-\Gamma)}}.
               	 		\end{aligned}
            		\]
            \end{enumerate} 		
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:distance-ordering of arXiv:2609.03264, 'Certified Spherical MUSIC for 3D Localization under Adversarial Subspace Perturbations'] Fix $j\in\{1,\ldots,s\}$ and order the remaining points by increasing distance from $\bm x_j$:
		\[
		r_1\le r_2\le\cdots\le r_{s-1},
		\qquad
		r_n=\abs{\bm x_j-\bm x_{k_n}}.
		\]
		Then 
		\begin{equation}
			r_n\ge \frac13\delta_X n^{1/3},
			\qquad n=1,\ldots,s-1.

body: [Lemma lem:cle_sle_markov of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] Suppose that $\eta$ is an ${\rm SLE}_\kappa$ in $\mathbf{H}$ from $0$ to $\infty$ and (given $\eta$) $\Gamma$ is a ${\rm CLE}_{\kappa'}$ in the component of $\mathbf{H} \setminus \eta$ to the left of $\eta$. Let $-\infty \le a < b \le 0$, and let $\eta'$ be the branch of the exploration tree of $\Gamma$ from $a$ to $b$ that discovers the loops of $\Gamma$ intersecting $[a,b]$, and let $\widetilde{\eta}$ be the outer boundary of $\eta'$ (we see $\widetilde{\eta}$ as a path from $0$ to $\infty$, allowed to trace parts of $\mathbf{R}_-$ in case $(a,b)\neq(-\infty,0)$). Given $\widetilde\eta$ and the set $\widetilde\eta \cap \eta$, pick two points $\eta(\tau), \eta(\sigma) \in \widetilde\eta \cap \eta$ such that $\eta((\tau,\sigma))$ is a connected component of $\eta \setminus \widetilde{\eta}$. Let $U$ be the component of $\mathbf{H} \setminus (\widetilde{\eta} \cup \eta)$ with $\eta((\tau,\sigma))$ on its right boundary, let $\widetilde{U}$ the component of $\mathbf{H} \setminus (\widetilde{\eta} \cup \eta([0,\tau]) \cup \eta([\sigma,\infty)))$ containing $\eta((\tau,\sigma))$, and let $\Gamma_U$ be the loops of $\Gamma$ that are contained in $\overline{U}$. Then the conditional law of $\eta|_{[\tau,\sigma]}$ given $\Gamma \setminus \Gamma_U$ and $\eta|_{[0,\tau]}$, $\eta|_{[\sigma,\infty)}$ is that of an ${\rm SLE}_\kappa$ in $\widetilde{U}$ from $\eta(\tau)$ to $\eta(\sigma)$ and the conditional law of $\Gamma_U$ given $\Gamma \setminus \Gamma_U$ and $\eta$ is that of a ${\rm CLE}_{\kappa'}$ in $U$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Shmalo, Fourier entropy of threshold functions and their compositions (arXiv:2610.16069, October 2026) proves the Fourier entropy-influence inequality of Friedgut and Kalai (the spectral entropy of f is at most a constant times its total influence) for every linear threshold function f, with arbitrary real weights and arbitrary threshold; the arXiv abstract gives a constant below 8.937. body:
Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system and $A: X \to M_d(\mathbb{R})$ a measurable matrix-valued function. The linear cocycle generated by $A$ over $T$ is $A^n(x) = A(T^{n-1}x) \cdots A(Tx)\,A(x)$ for $n \ge 1$, $A^0 = I$; it satisfies the cocycle identity $A^{n+m}(x) = A^m(T^n x) A^n(x)$. (If $T$ is invertible and $A(x) \in GL_d$, one also sets $A^{-n}(x) = A^n(T^{-n}x)^{-1}$.) The cocycle is (forward) integrable if $\log^+ \|A\| \in L^1(\mu)$, where $\log^+ t = \max(\log t, 0)$ and $\|\cdot\|$ is any matrix norm; it is two-sidedly integrable if also $A(x)$ is invertible a.e. and $\log^+\|A^{-1}\| \in L^1$. For $v \in \mathbb{R}^d \setminus \{0\}$ the (forward) Lyapunov exponent of $v$ at $x$ is $\lambda(x, v) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\|$ when the limit exists (in $[-\infty, \infty)$); more generally $\bar\lambda(x, v) = \limsup$. The function $v \mapsto \bar\lambda(x, v)$ takes finitely many values and satisfies $\bar\lambda(x, u + v) \le \max(\bar\lambda(x,u), \bar\lambda(x,v))$, so for each $x$ the sets $\{v : \bar\lambda(x, v) \le c\} \cup \{0\}$ are linear subspaces and form a filtration of $\mathbb{R}^d$. The prototype is the derivative cocycle $A(x) = Df_x$ of a smooth map $f$ on a manifold (trivialised bundle), whose exponents measure exponential rates of divergence of nearby orbits. Warning: $\|A^n(x)\|^{1/n}$ and $|\text{eigenvalues of } A^n(x)|^{1/n}$ are different things; Lyapunov exponents are the growth rates of SINGULAR values of $A^n(x)$, not eigenvalues, and for non-commuting products the two can differ.
T is measure-preserving on a probability space
A is measurable
integrability of log^+ ||A|| is the standing hypothesis for the multiplicative ergodic theorem

[Definition def:tau of arXiv:2505.02685, 'On the Spectral Expansion of Monotone Subsets of the Hypercube'] For functions $f,g:A\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$, we define
\[
\tau(f,g)\vcentcolon= \min_{a\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}, b\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}}\left\|f-(ag+b)\right\|_{2},
\]
where the $L^{2}$-norm is the norm in the inner product space $L^{2}(A)$.
title: Definition def:tau of arXiv:2505.02685

[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2607.18104, '2607.18104'] Consider two full-space directed landscapes $\mathcal{L}^{1}$, $\mathcal{L}^{2}$.

For any $\mathcal{O} \subseteq \R^2$ and $k\in \lbr 2 \rbr$, write 
$\mathcal{L}^{k}_{\mathcal{O}} := (\mathcal{L}^{k}(x,s;y,t))_{(x,s;y,t) \in (\mathcal{O})^2_{\uparrow}}$ for the restriction of $\mathcal{L}^{k}$ to $(\mathcal{O})^{2}_{\uparrow}$.
There exists $c,C>0$ such that for all $i\in \Z$ and $n\in N$ there exist a coupling $\mathbf{P}^i_n$ of $\mathcal{L}^{1}$ and $\mathcal{L}^{2}$ under which
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{P}^i_n\left( \mathcal{L}^{1}_{\mathcal{O}^{i,1}_n} =   \mathcal{L}^{2}_{\mathcal{O}^{i,3}_n} \text{ and } \mathcal{L}^{1}_{\mathcal{O}^{i,2}_n} =   \mathcal{L}^{2}_{\mathcal{O}^{i,2}_n} \right) \geq 1 - C\exp(-cn^{2}). 
\end{equation}

body: In Vapnik–Chervonenkis theory, the Vapnik–Chervonenkis (VC) dimension is a measure of the size of a class of sets. The notion can be extended to classes of binary functions. It is defined as the cardinality of the largest set of points that the function class can shatter—that is, for which all possible binary labelings can be realized by some function in the class. It was originally defined by Vladimir Vapnik and Alexey Chervonenkis.
title: Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension

Let N>=0 be an integer and nu a real signed Borel measure on R with all absolute polynomial moments finite. Suppose integral f(t)^2 dnu(t)>0 for every nonzero real polynomial f of degree<=N. There are unique monic polynomials q_0,...,q_(N+1) with deg(q_i)=i which are pairwise orthogonal under nu. For each 1<=i<=N+1, q_i has i distinct real roots. For 2<=i<=N+1, the roots of q_i and q_(i-1) strictly interlace, with a root of q_i on either side of the roots of q_(i-1). Squared norms of q_0,...,q_N are positive. No positivity assertion is made for the squared norm of q_(N+1). This is Cohn-Kumar Lemma3.5.

strict squared-norm positivity for every nonzero polynomial of degree<=N
the family extends through degree N+1, while guaranteed positive norms extend only through degree N

[Lem extensiontoadistribution of arXiv:2412.00593, 'A new approach to strong convergence II.\\The classical ensembles'] Let $\nu$ be a linear functional on $\mathcal{P}$. If there exist
$C,K,m \geq 0$ so that
$$
	|\nu(h)| \leq C q^m \sobnorm{h}{0}{[-K, K]}
	\quad\text{for all } h \in \mathcal{P}_q,~q\in\mathbb{N},
$$
then $\nu$ extends to a compactly supported distribution
with $|\nu(h)| \lesssim \|h\|_{C^{m+1}[-K,K]}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Openproblem Quenched complexity of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] The present paper concerns annealed complexity.  In energy regimes where
the Gaussian first- and second-moment exponents coincide, typical
critical-point counts are known to concentrate
[Subag,SubagZeitouni].  A second-moment/Kac--Rice route to a
non-Gaussian quenched theorem would require a comparison of two-point
functionals.  Already the non-Gaussian energy and covariance structures
depend not only on the overlap \(N^{-1}\ip\sigma\tau\) but on the joint
empirical coordinate profile
\[
 \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{(\sigma_i,\tau_i)}.
\]
The full derivative jet additionally requires corresponding joint frame
profiles.  Such a variational comparison and localization analysis
remain open.  In a window with exponentially many typical points, the
natural target is a probability limit of
\(N^{-1}\log\operatorname{Crt}_N^J(B)\); the bounded observable
\(Q_N^J(B)\) in (equation eq:sample-log-count of the paper) instead also covers empty
windows.  By (prop:quenched-cutoff of the paper), convergence in probability of
the latter is equivalent before and after the entrywise cutoff.  This
removes quadratic-scale entries from that auxiliary problem but does not
supply the missing two-point comparison. (Stated as a problem by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Quenched complexity

[Theorem 1 (Ellipsoidal solution for quadratic forcing) of arXiv:2609.00703, 'Ellipsoidal Positivity Sets for Fractional Obstacle Problems with Quadratic Forcing'] Let \(n\ge1\), \(0<s<1\), \(c>0\), and let \(A\) be a positive definite symmetric \(n\times n\) matrix.
Then there exist \(K>0\) and a positive definite symmetric matrix \(B\) such that
\[
u(x)=K\bigl(1-\langle Bx,x\rangle\bigr)_+^{1+s}
\]
is the unique decaying viscosity solution of \eqref{eq:obstacle}--\eqref{eq:forcing}.
Moreover, \(B\) satisfies
\[
\frac{A_B}{c_B}=\frac{A}{c},
\]
where \(c_B\) and \(A_B\) are given by \eqref{eq:cB} and \eqref{eq:AB}, respectively. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Ellipsoidal solution for quadratic forcing

[Definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a real probability measure $\mu$, its $R$-transform is:
$$G_\mu(\xi)=\int_\mathbb R\frac{d\mu(t)}{\xi-t}\implies 
G_\mu\left(R_\mu(\xi)+\frac{1}{\xi}\right)=\xi$$
That is, the $R$-transform is the inverse of the Cauchy transform, up to a $\xi^{-1}$ factor.

Draft author claim, independent review pending. On a finite simple graph G=(V,E), let u be uniform independent integer-q spins and gamma_beta its free zero-field unit-bond Potts Gibbs law. For q>=2 and beta>=0, D(u||gamma_beta)>=|E|*c_q(beta), where c_q(beta)=log((exp(beta)+q-1)/q)-beta/q. Equality holds on forests, and the bound is strict when beta>0 and G has a cycle. On Z^d boxes the limiting deficit per vertex is at least d*c_q(beta)>0 for beta>0. For any fixed full-support product law pi, an induced matching gives the alternative positive lower bound 2*(min pi)^4*tanh(beta/2)^2/(3*2^(d-1)) per vertex. Thus neither uniform nor full-support fixed product trials satisfy a vanishing-deficit hypothesis at positive beta.

[Lemma 23 (Continuity of coercive half-line resolvents) of arXiv:2608.30211, '2608.30211'] Let $\varrho_n\to\varrho$ in $[0,1]$, let $V_n,V\in L^\infty(\R_+)$ be real
with $V_n\to V$ in $L^\infty$, and let $g_n\to g$ in $L^2(\R_+)$.  Denote by
$\mathfrak a_n$ and $\mathfrak a$ the forms of
$-\partial_y^2+V_n$ and $-\partial_y^2+V$, respectively, with the indicated
$\varrho_n$ and $\varrho$ boundary conditions.  Suppose that, for some
$m>0$,
\[
 \mathfrak a_n[h]\geq m\|h\|_2^2,
 \qquad \mathfrak a[h]\geq m\|h\|_2^2
\]
on the corresponding form domains.  If
\[
 z_n=(-\partial_y^2+V_n)^{-1}g_n,
 \qquad z=(-\partial_y^2+V)^{-1}g,
\]
then $z_n\to z$ in $H^1(\R_+)$.  In fact the convergence is in $H^2$ and
hence in $C_b^1$.

[Proposition 12 of arXiv:2606.15432, 'A Concavity Theorem for the Parisi PDE'] Define the map $\Residual:\Opendenseset_\alpha\times \mathcal{X}_1\rightarrow \ParaHoelderzero{\alpha}([0,1]\times\R)$
by
\begin{equation}

  \Residual(\gamma,u)
  \coloneqq
  -\partial_su
  -
  \frac12\gamma(s)\mathfrak A(u),
  \qquad 
  \mathfrak A(u)
  \coloneqq
  \partial_{xx}u+g''+s(\partial_xu+g')^2.
\end{equation}
Then, $\Residual$ satisfies the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The map $\Residual$ is well-defined and 
$\Residual\in  C^2
  \bigl(
  \Opendenseset_\alpha\times\mathcal X_1
  ;\, \ParaHoelderzero{\alpha}([0,1]\times\R)
  \bigr)$.
\item For every \(\gamma\in\Opendenseset_\alpha\),
\[
  \Residual(\gamma,\Psi^\gamma-\log\cosh)=0.
\]

\item Let $\mathfrak L_s^u\coloneqq \frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}+s(\partial_x u + g')\partial_x$.
Then,
\begin{align}
  D_\gamma\Residual(\gamma,u)[h]
  &=
  -\frac12 h(s)
  \mathfrak A(u), 
   \\
  D_u\Residual(\gamma,u)[v]
  &=
  -\partial_sv
  -
  \gamma(s)
  \mathfrak L_s^u v,
   \\
  D^2\Residual(\gamma,u)[(h_1,v_1),(h_2,v_2)]
  &=
-
h_1(s)
\mathfrak L_s^u v_2
-
h_2(s)
\mathfrak L_s^u v_1
-
\gamma(s)s\,\partial_xv_1\,\partial_xv_2.

\end{align}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let $\hat{\bQ}_k$ be the output of Algorithm~\ref{alg:causal order client}, and define
\[
\hat Z_k=\hat{\bQ}_kX_k.
\]
For each true block $C\in\cC_k$, let $\hat C=\psi^{-1}(C)$ denote the corresponding estimated block. Then, for every $i\in\hat C$, the estimated latent variable $\hat Z_{k,(i)}$ lies in the span of the true latent variables indexed by the block ancestors of $C$, namely
\[
\hat Z_{k,(i)}\in \mathrm{span}\{Z_{(j)}:j\in C', C'\in Anc_k^\rblk(C)\}.
\]
Thus, up to the relabeling induced by $\psi$, each estimated latent variable is identified up to block-level ancestor mixing.

\begin{equation}
 \Nrm(\mathcal A_\alpha)\in\RV.
\end{equation}
Consequently, $\Supp(\mathcal A_\alpha)$ is $M$-convex and
\[
 \Supp(\mathcal A_\alpha)
 =\Newt(\mathcal A_\alpha)\cap\ZZ^n.
\]
Thus Conjecture~3.14 of Monical--Tokcan--Yong holds.

body: In mathematics, Choquet theory, named after Gustave Choquet, is an area of functional analysis and convex analysis concerned with measures which have support on the extreme points of a convex set C. Roughly speaking, every vector of C should appear as a weighted average of extreme points, a concept made more precise by generalizing the notion of weighted average from a convex combination to an integral taken over the set E of extreme points. Here C is a subset of a real vector space V, and the main thrust of the theory is to treat the cases where V is an infinite-dimensional topological vector space along lines similar to the finite-dimensional case. The main concerns of Gustave Choquet were in potential theory. Choquet theory has become a general paradigm, particularly for treating convex cones as determined by their extreme rays, and so for many different notions of positivity in mathematics.

[Def ass of arXiv:2601.10568, 'Hydrodynamic Limit with a Weierstrass-type result'] Let $ \{\mu_N\}_{N\geq 1} $ be a sequence of probability measures on $ \Omega_N $, and let $g:\mathbb{T}\to[0,1] $ be a measurable function. If, for any continuous function $ G:\mathbb{T}\to\mathbb{R} $ and every $ \delta>0 $, it holds
	\begin{align*}
		\lim_{N\to+\infty}\mu_N
		\left(
		\eta\in\Omega_N
		:\big|\pi^N(\eta,G)-\langle g,G\rangle\big|>\delta
		\right)
		=0,
	\end{align*}
	we say that the sequence $ \{\mu_N\}_{N\geq 1} $ is a local equilibrium measure associated with the profile $ g $.
title: Local equilibrium distribution

[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2608.30178, '2608.30178'] Let \(\alpha\in(1,2)\) and $\mu_\alpha(\dd z):=\frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(2-\alpha)}z^{-1-\alpha}\1_{\{z>0\}}\dd z$.  For every \(q<\alpha\),  
\[
 \frac1q\int_0^\infty
 \bigl[(1+z)^q-1-qz\bigr]\mu_\alpha(\dd z)
 =j_\alpha(q),
 \qquad q\ne0,
\]
whereas
\[
 \int_0^\infty
 \bigl[\log(1+z)-z\bigr]\mu_\alpha(\dd z)
 =j_\alpha(0)=-1.
\]
Consequently, 
\beqnn
	\int_0^\infty
	\bigl[\Phi_q(u+z)-\Phi_q(u)-z\Phi_q'(u)\bigr]\mu_\alpha(\dd z)
	=j_\alpha(q)u^{q-\alpha} 
	\eeqnn
holds for every \(q<\alpha\) and \(u>0\).
title: Lemma 20 of arXiv:2608.30178

[Theorem th:basic of arXiv:2511.05223, 'Kac's Program and Relative Entropy Decay for Nonlinear Spin-Exchange Dynamics'] Fix a symmetric matrix $J\in{\ensuremath{\mathbb R}} ^{n\times n}$ and a symmetric stochastic $n\times n$ matrix $\ensuremath{\mathcal K}$. Let $\ensuremath{\mathcal A}$ denote the partition of $[n]$ induced by the irreducible components of $\ensuremath{\mathcal K}$. 
 A probability $p \in \mathcal{P}_\ensuremath{\mathcal A}(\Omega)$ is a stationary state if and only if $p=\mu_{J,h}$ for some $h\in\G_\ensuremath{\mathcal A}$.
 
 Moreover, 
 the expected values
$m(p_t,A)$, $A\in \ensuremath{\mathcal A}$,
are independent of $t\ge 0$. Finally, for any initial state $p\in \mathcal{P}_\ensuremath{\mathcal A}(\Omega)$, one has the convergence 
\begin{equation}

\|p_t - \mu_{J,h}\|_{\rm TV}\; \longrightarrow \;0\,,\qquad t\to\infty\,,
\end{equation}
where $\|\cdot\|_{\rm TV}$ denotes the total variation distance and 
$h$ is the unique vector $h\in\G_\ensuremath{\mathcal A}$ such that 
$m_\ensuremath{\mathcal A}(p) = m_\ensuremath{\mathcal A}(\mu_{J,h})$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem th:basic of arXiv:2511.05223

body: In computer science and optimization theory, the max-flow min-cut theorem states that in a flow network, the maximum amount of flow passing from the source to the sink is equal to the total weight of the edges in a minimum cut, i.e., the smallest total weight of the edges which if removed would disconnect the source from the sink.

body:
[Theorem 12 (Spectral Collapse Under Aligned Jumps) of arXiv:2606.25810, 'Spectral Collapse Under Geometric Alignment of Extreme Events'] Let

\[
Q_n = B_n + J_n, \quad J_n = \sum_{k=1}^{m_n} \theta_{n,k} v_{n,k} v_{n,k}^\top,
\]

where:
\begin{itemize}
\item \(B_n\) is symmetric positive semidefinite
\item \(\|v_{n,k}\| = 1\), \(\theta_{n,k} \ge 0\)
\end{itemize}

Assume the following asymptotic conditions as \(n \to \infty\):

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Geometric alignment of jumps:} There exists a unit vector \(u_n\) such that
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{m_n} \theta_{n,k} \left(1 - \langle v_{n,k}, u_n \rangle^2 \right) = o\left(\sum_{k=1}^{m_n} \theta_{n,k}\right).
\]

\item \textbf{Trace dominance:} \(\operatorname{tr}(B_n) = o(\operatorname{tr}(J_n))\)

\item \textbf{Second moment dominance:} \(\operatorname{tr}(B_n^2) = o(\lambda_1(J_n)^2)\)
\end{enumerate}

Then:

\[
\frac{\lambda_1(Q_n)}{\operatorname{tr}(Q_n)} \to 1,
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{erank}(Q_n) \to 1.

[Proposition sp of arXiv:2410.23509, 'Dynkin Games for L\'evy Processes'] Consider a function of the form
\begin{equation}
W(x)=\operatorname{\mathbf{E}}_xQ(S).
\end{equation}
Assume that the three following conditions hold:
\vskip1mm\par\noindent
{\rm(i)}
$Q(x)=0$, for $x\leq x_0$ and $Q(x)$ is non-decreasing and in class $C^2[x_0,\infty)$,
\vskip1mm\par\noindent
{\rm(ii)} there exist $A>0$ and $\alpha>0$ s.t. 
$|Q''(x)|\leq A e^{\alpha x}$,
\vskip1mm\par\noindent
{\rm(iii)} for $\alpha>0$ above, it holds
$
\operatorname{\mathbf{E}} e^{\alpha X_1}<e^r.
$
\vskip1mm\par\noindent
Then
\begin{align}

W'(x_0+)-W'(x_0-)&=Q'(x_0+)\operatorname{\mathbf{P}}(S=0),\\
W'(x+)-W'(x-)&=0,\text{ for $x>x_0$}. 
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 5 (Path and signature conjugacy) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] A continuous path $\gamma:[0,T]\to V$ is \emph{path-conjugate to the line $\lambda_v$} if $v=\gamma_T-\gamma_0$ and there is a based bounded-variation path $\alpha$ such that
\[
\gamma-\gamma_0
 \sim_{\mathrm{rep}}
\alpha*\lambda_v*\overleftarrow{\alpha}.
\]
Its signature is \emph{conjugate to the line signature} if
\[
S(\gamma)=a\e^v a^{-1}
\]
for some bounded-variation signature $a$.
title: Path and signature conjugacy

[Lemma lem:RW1 of arXiv:2411.10829, 'Airy$_\beta$ line ensemble and its Laplace transform'] For any $C_1, C_2>0$, there is a constant $C_3=C_3(C_1,C_2)>0$, such that for any $C_1N^{-2/3}<x<C_2$ and $0\le h, g <C_2$, and $X, H, G\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}$, such that $|X-xN^{2/3}|, |H-hN^{1/3}|, |G-gN^{1/3}|<C_2$, the following estimates hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(1)] When $X+H+G$ is even and $h,g>C_1N^{-1/3}$, we have
\begin{multline*}
\left|N^{1/3}I(X;H,G)-\mathbf I(x;h,g)\right| \\ <C_3\mathbf F(x;h,g)\left(1\wedge (N^{-3/5}x^{-3} + N^{-1/40} + N^{-1/3}/h+N^{-1/3}/g)\right).
\end{multline*}
    \item[(2)] When $X+H$ is even and $h>C_1N^{-1/3}$, we have
\[
\left|N^{2/3}I(X;H,0)-\mathbf I_0(x;h)\right| < C_3\mathbf F_0(x;h)\left(1\wedge (N^{-3/5}x^{-3} + N^{-1/40} +N^{-1/3}/g )\right).
\]
    \item[(3)] When $X+H+G$ is even, $H\le G$, and $g-h>C_1N^{-1/3}$, we have
\begin{multline*}
\left|N^{2/3}I^+(X;H,G)-\exp(-\beta^{-1} xh )\mathbf I_0(x;g-h)\right| \\ <C\mathbf F_0(x;g-h)\left(1\wedge (N^{-3/5}x^{-3} + N^{-1/40} +N^{-1/3}/g)\right).
\end{multline*}
    \item[(4)] When $X$ is even, we have
\[
\left|NI^+(X;H,H)-\exp(-\beta^{-1} xh)\mathbf I_{0,0}(x)\right| < C_3\mathbf F_{0,0}(x)\left(1\wedge (N^{-3/5}x^{-3} + N^{-1/40} )\right).
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Assuming the axiom of choice, the closed unit ball B in R^3 can be partitioned into finitely many pieces which can be reassembled by rigid motions (rotations and translations) into two disjoint copies of B; five pieces suffice (Robinson), and four do not. More generally (the strong form) any two bounded subsets of R^n, n >= 3, with nonempty interior are equidecomposable: one can be cut into finitely many pieces and moved by isometries onto the other. The pieces are necessarily non-measurable, so no contradiction with Lebesgue measure arises - the theorem shows that no finitely additive, isometry-invariant measure defined on ALL subsets of R^3 and normalising the ball can exist. In dimensions 1 and 2 the paradox fails: Banach showed that Lebesgue measure on R and R^2 extends to a finitely additive isometry-invariant measure on all subsets, because the isometry groups of R and R^2 are amenable (solvable), while SO(3) contains a free group on two generators, which is the source of the paradox (Hausdorff, 1914). Tarski's theorem (1929) makes this exact: a group action admits a paradoxical decomposition if and only if it carries no finitely additive invariant probability measure, i.e. it is non-amenable. With choice the result is a theorem; in ZF plus the axiom of determinacy, or in Solovay's model, every set of reals is measurable and the decomposition does not exist.

[Definition def:SC-infinity of arXiv:2608.11931, '\texorpdfstring{Nonlinear parabolic characterizations of stochastic completeness at infini'] A graph $G=(X,w,\kappa,\mu)$ satisfies \emph{stochastic completeness at infinity} \hyperref[def:SC-infinity]{\textup{{(SC\textsubscript{$\infty$})}}}{} if for some (and hence all) $t>0,$
$$e^{-tL}1+\int_0^t e^{-sL}\left(\frac{\kappa}{\mu}\right)\,\mathrm d s=1.$$
When $\kappa=0$ and the above holds, then $G$ is said to  satisfy \emph{stochastic completeness} \hyperref[def:SC]{\textup{(SC)}}{}.
Otherwise, a graph is said to be \emph{stochastically incomplete (at infinity)}.
title: Stochastic completeness at infinity

[Corollary cor:atomic of arXiv:2607.08551, 'Weighted-threshold Coupon Collection'] Fix $s>1$ and $t>0$. Then
\[
M_N^{(s)}(t)\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{L^1} M_\infty^{(s)}(t),
\]
and the limiting random variable is non-degenerate,
\[
\mathrm{Var}\bigl(M_\infty^{(s)}(t)\bigr)\ge
\bigl(q_1^{(s)}\bigr)^2 e^{-\lambda q_1^{(s)} t}\bigl(1-e^{-\lambda q_1^{(s)} t}\bigr)>0.
\]
In particular, the atomic regime does not collapse to a deterministic discovered-mass curve.

body:
[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2608.15914, 'Absorption cutoff and stationary singularities for rounded Gaussian random dynamical syste'] Assume $0<A<A_c(N)$, and let $x_0\in\R^N$ be deterministic. Run the
  chain $X^{(N)}$ from $X_0^{(N)}=x_0$ and $Y^{(N)}$ from
  $Y_0^{(N)}=Q_\varrho(x_0)$ with the same Gaussian matrices.
  There is $C_N<\infty$, depending only on $N$, such that the following holds.
  For $0<C_0<\infty$, define
  \begin{equation*}
    T_\varrho:=\left\lfloor C_0\log(1/\varrho)\right\rfloor .
  \end{equation*}
  There exists $p=p(A,N,C_0)$ satisfying
  \begin{equation}
    0
    \leq
    p
    \leq
    C_N(1+C_0)
    \left(
      1+\frac1{\gamma_{A,N}}
    \right),
  \end{equation}
  and
  \begin{equation}
    \Pp\left(
      \max_{0\leq t\leq T_\varrho}
      \norm{Y_t^{(N)}-X_t^{(N)}}_2
      >
      \varrho\,\left(\log(1/\varrho)\right)^p
    \right)
    \to0
  \end{equation}
  as $\varrho\downarrow0$.
title: Lemma 17 of arXiv:2608.15914

body:
[Theorem 2 (Cubic global thin obstacle solutions) of arXiv:2609.00703, 'Ellipsoidal Positivity Sets for Fractional Obstacle Problems with Quadratic Forcing'] Let \(n\ge2\), and let \(W\) be a global solution of the thin obstacle problem in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\)
with cubic growth and nonempty bounded positivity set on the thin space.
Then, after a translation in the thin variables, there exist \(K>0\) and a positive definite symmetric
matrix \(B\) such that
\[
\{W(\cdot,0)>0\}
=
\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\langle Bx,x\rangle<1\}
\]
and
\[
W(x,0)
=
K\bigl(1-\langle Bx,x\rangle\bigr)_+^{3/2}.
\]
In particular, the positivity set on the thin space is an ellipsoid.
Hence the conjecture of Fern\'andez-Real and Yu \cite[Conjecture~4.2]{FRY}
holds in the nonempty bounded-positivity case. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Cubic global thin obstacle solutions

On a finite connected graph with iid Uniform[1,2] edge weights and fixed terminals, define clipped off-edge thresholds a_e in [0,1] so that centered coordinate costs are min(U,a_e)-a_e+a_e^2/2 for U uniform on [0,1]. For a<=b, K(a,b)=a^2[b(2-b)/4-a/6], and K is symmetric. Under independent rate-one coordinate refresh, Var(T)=integral_0^infinity exp(-t)H(t)dt, where H(t)=sum_e E K(a_e(eta),a_e(eta^t)) and only off-edge coordinates are coupled inside H. Its limit is the first-order Hoeffding energy L, not generally zero. H(t)-L is the sum over |S|>=2 of |S|exp(-(|S|-1)t)||T_S||_2^2. A full-kernel integrable decay envelope for all t is impossible when L>0. No lattice exponent estimate is asserted.

Simple paths and positive weights
Independent Uniform[1,2] coordinates and independent refresh flags

[Definition landing of arXiv:2604.17170, 'CaTherine wheels from trees and Liouville quantum gravity'] A {\em ray} is a half-open interval in $Z$ (i.e.\/ a subspace homeomorphic to $[0,1)$).
It is a {\em proper ray} if the inclusion $[0,1) \subset Z$ is a proper embedding. 
A ray {\em lands} if it extends continuously to an embedding of $[0,1]$; the
image of $1$ is called the {\em landing point}.

A half-zipper has the {\em strong landing property} if every ray in $Z$ lands, and
if every point in $S^2$ is the landing point of some ray in $Z$.

body: [Definition def:cle_metric of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] Suppose that $\mathcal {L}$ is a random non-self-crossing loop in $\mathbf{C}$, and let $D$ be the regions surrounded by $\mathcal {L}$. Given $\mathcal {L}$, let $\Gamma_D$ be a conditionally independent ${\rm CLE}_{\kappa'}${} in each connected component of $D$, and let $\Gamma = \{\mathcal {L}\} \cup \Gamma_D$. We call a family of random metrics $(\metapproxres{\epsilon}{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma})_{V \in \metregions}$ coupled with $\Gamma$ that satisfies the assumptions above an \emph{approximate ${\rm CLE}_{\kappa'}${} metric}. In the case $\epsilon = 0$ we call $(\metres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma})_{V \in \metregions}$ a \emph{${\rm CLE}_{\kappa'}${} metric}. We call $\metapproxres{\epsilon}{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma}$ the \emph{internal metric in $V$}.

[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2609.02850, 'Canonical-row Chern flow on Bott--Samelson towers:\\ realizable-volume models for Schubert'] Let $f_k\in\RR[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ be homogeneous of degree $d+k$ for
$0\le k\le r$, and put
\[
 \widehat f(x,z)=\sum_{k=0}^r f_k(x)z^{r-k},
 \qquad
 S=\bigcup_{k=0}^r\Supp(f_k).
\]
Assume that $\Supp(\widehat f)$ is $M$-convex.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $S$ is $M^\natural$-convex and
\[
 S=\operatorname{conv}(S)\cap\ZZ^n.
\]
\item If $a_k\ne0$ for every nonzero layer, then
\[
 \Supp\!\left(\sum_{k=0}^r a_k f_k\right)=S.
\]
\item The parameter polynomial $\sum_{k=0}^r f_k(x)\beta^k$ has saturated
Newton polytope in $\ZZ^{n+1}$.
\end{enumerate}

[Definition defn:Whitney_McShane_operator of arXiv:2609.03129, 'A Closed-Form Formula for Consistent Lipschitz Regression on Metric Spaces with Sparse Neu'] Let $(X,\rho)$ be a bounded metric space and fix $N\in \mathbb{N}_+$.  The \textit{$N$-point Whitney-McShane operator} is the map
\[
\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{E}:
    (\operatorname{Lip}((X,\rho);1),\|\cdot\|_\infty)
    \times
    ([X\times \mathbb{R}]^N,\rho_1)
&\longrightarrow
    (\operatorname{Lip}((X,\rho);1),\|\cdot\|_\infty),
\\
    (f,\mathcal{D}_N)
&\longmapsto
    \mathcal{E}(f,\mathcal{D}_N),
\end{aligned}
\]
where, for every $\mathcal{D}_N\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} (x_n,y_n)_{n=1}^N\in [X\times \mathbb{R}]^N$, for each $z\in X$ by
\[
        \mathcal{E}(f,\mathcal{D}_N)(z)
    \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
        \max_{n\in[N]_+}
        \,
            \big\{
                [f(x_n)+y_n]-\rho(z,x_n)
            \big\}
.
\]
title: $N$-Point Whitney-McShane Operator

Let 1<=r<min(p,q), n>p+1, x_i iid N(0,I_p), and y_i=(W0+Delta)x_i+e_i, where e_i iid N(0,sigma^2 I_q) are independent of all inputs, W0 is fixed, and rank(Delta)<=r. Set X=[x_i], Y=[y_i], C=XX^T/n, and M=(Y-W0X)X^T(XX^T)^(-1)C^(1/2). Let W_hat=W0+trunc_r(M)C^(-1/2), where trunc_r is a best rank-r singular-value truncation. This is a global rank-constrained empirical least-squares estimator. There is a universal constant K such that E||W_hat-(W0+Delta)||_F^2 <= K*sigma^2*r*max(p,q)/n * E||C^(-1)||_op. The stronger n>p+1 assumption ensures that the inverse-covariance expectation is finite. This is the exact-rank isotropic specialization of Zindari-Mulayoff-Stich, arXiv:2605.19018, Theorem 2 (p.5) using Proposition 2 (p.3), with proof in Appendix V.1. It is a guarantee for the global estimator; it is not an initialization-specific convergence theorem for the factor GD iterates.

Normalize r>=1,delta<=1 and assume r/delta<=n^a for fixed a, so h=log_2(d*n*C*r/delta)=Theta(log n). Write the displayed precision certificate as A*s*h/sqrt(log_2 s), with fixed A>0, and require this certificate to be <=beta=c*log_2 n. body: In combinatorics, two Latin squares of the same size (order) are said to be orthogonal if when superimposed the ordered paired entries in the positions are all distinct. A set of Latin squares, all of the same order, all pairs of which are orthogonal is called a set of mutually orthogonal Latin squares. This concept of orthogonality in combinatorics is strongly related to the concept of blocking in statistics, which ensures that independent variables are truly independent with no hidden confounding correlations. "Orthogonal" is thus synonymous with "independent" in that knowing one variable's value gives no further information about another variable's likely value.
title: Mutually orthogonal Latin squares

body:
[Lem 252 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] If $\bX:\R^{N'}\to\R^N$ is $L$-Lipschitz, $\bg$ is a standard gaussian in $\R^{N'}$, and $\E[\|\bX(\bg)\|^2] = N$, then for any $\delta > 0$, there exists $c(\delta) > 0$ such that 
    \[
    \P\bigg(
    \bigg|\frac{\|\bX(\bg)\|^2}{N} - 1\bigg|
    \ge \delta\bigg)
    \le e^{-c(\delta)N}\,.\]

\begin{proof}
    Since $\bg \mapsto \|\bX(\bg)\|$ is $L$-Lipschitz, it follows from Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus} that $\|\bX(\bg)\|-\E\|\bX(\bg)\|$ is subgaussian with variance proxy $2L^2$, and satisfies the concentration bound \eqref{e:lip.subgaus}:
    \[
    \P\bigg( \Big|
    \|\bX(\bg)\| - \E\|\bX(\bg)\|\Big| \ge t
    \bigg) \le 2\exp\bigg\{-\frac{t^2}{2L^2}\bigg\}\,.
    \]
It follows that $\|\bX(\bg)\|$ has variance $O(L^2)$, which implies
    \[
     \frac{O(L^2)}{N}
     \ge
    \frac{\E[\|\bX(\bg)\|^2] - ( \E\|\bX(\bg)\|)^2}{N}
    =1- \frac{ ( \E\|\bX(\bg)\|)^2}{N}\,.
    \]
Combining the last two displays gives the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 252 of arXiv:2608.29416

  \]

[Lemma AveragedEstimate of arXiv:2411.06089, '{\Large \bf Averaging principle for semilinear slow-fast rough partial differential equati'] Suppose that conditions $(\mathbf{H1})$ and $(\mathbf{H2})$ hold.
For any $T>0$, $x\in \mathcal H$ and $\mathbf B=(B,B^2)\in \mathscr{C}^\gamma([0,T]; \mathbb R^d)$ with $\gamma \in (1/3, \gamma_0)$,
Eq.~(equation Averagedeq of the paper) has a unique global solution $(\bar{X},\bar{X}^\prime) \in \mathcal D_{\mathbf B}^{2\gamma, \eta}([0,T]; \mathcal H)$ with $\eta \in [0,\gamma)$ such that
$\bar{X}^\prime=G_1(\bar{X})$ and
$$\bar{X}_t=S_t x +\int_0^t S_{t-s} \bar{F}_1(\bar{X}_s)ds +\int_0^t S_{t-s} G_1 (\bar{X}_s) d \mathbf B_s, ~~~~ t\in [0,T].$$
Moreover, there exists a constant $C>0$ such that
\begin{equation}
	 \|\bar{X}\|_{\eta, 0} \leq C(1+\|x\|_{\mathcal H}).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma AveragedEstimate of arXiv:2411.06089

[Lemma 13 of arXiv:2608.04644, 'Khinchin's and Chung's Laws of the Iterated Logarithm at Time Zero for the Linear Stochast'] There  is a universal constant $K_0$ such that the following statement holds. Let $S$ be a bounded set and $\{X(s),s\in S\}$ be a separable Gaussian process.
Let $D_X(S) := \sup\left\{d_X(s, t):s, t \in S\right\}$ be the diameter of $S$ in the metric $d_X$. Then for any $u>0$,
\[
\mathbb P\left(\sup_{s,t\in S}   |X(s)-X(t)|\ge K_0\left(u+\int_0^{D_X(S)} \sqrt{\log N(S,d_X;\varepsilon)}  d\varepsilon    \right)  \right)\le \exp\left(-\frac{u^2}{D_X(S)^2}\right).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 13 of arXiv:2608.04644

[Proposition prop:entangled-recovery of arXiv:2607.18070, 'The Brownian loop-catcher'] Let $(P_1,\ldots,P_r)$ be the output records of independent normalized random walks
$\omega_i:a_i\to b_i$ ($1\le i\le r$) in Definition~(def:entangled of the paper), and let $\gamma_i$ be the corresponding
 entangled multipath LERW.  Independently sample an unrooted random-walk loop soup in $R$ with intensity $1$, and assign each loop that intersects $C_r$ to the smallest $i$ for which
it intersects $\gamma_i$, and then to the earliest path time $s$ on $\gamma_i$
at which such an intersection occurs.  If the loop visits $\gamma_i(s)$ more than once, choose uniformly one of those visits as its starting time. For each time on the entangled multipath LERW, order its assigned random-walk loops by an independent
uniform permutation and insert them in that order. Then conditioned on
$(P_1,\ldots,P_r)$, the resulting tuple of paths has the same law as the conditional law of $(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_r)$ given $(P_1,\ldots,P_r)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 6 (Critical rigidity) of arXiv:2609.03339, 'Exterior Serrin Rigidity for the Homogeneous \texorpdfstring{$k$}{k}-Hessian Equation\\'] Let $k=\frac{n}{2}$, and let $\Omega\Subset\R^n$ be smooth,
		bounded, strictly star-shaped, and strictly $(k-1)$-convex.  For some
		$\mathcal{A}>0$, suppose that $u\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\overline E)$  is a k-admissible solution of
			\begin{equation}
			\begin{cases}
				\sigma_k(D^2u)=0&\text{in }~\R^n\setminus\overline\Omega,\\
				u=0& \text{on}~\partial\Omega,\\
				u(x)-\mathcal{A}\log|x|=O(1)&\text{as }|x|\to\infty.
			\end{cases}
		\end{equation}	
	
	
	
	
	
		If $u_\nu=|Du|=c>0$ on $\partial\Omega$, then for some
		$x_0\in\R^n$,
		\[
		\Omega=B_R(x_0),\qquad
		R=\frac{\mathcal{A}}{c},\qquad
		u(x)=\mathcal{A}\log\frac{|x-x_0|}{R}.
		\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Critical rigidity

[Lemma 5 (Inverse-stable size-biased factor) of arXiv:2606.18458, 'Stable size-biasing and the positive scale-mixture order of generalized Gaussian laws'] Let $a>b>0$, set $\alpha=b/a\in(0,1)$, and let $S_\alpha$ be as in Lemma~2. Put
\[
W_0=S_\alpha^{-b},
\]
and let $W$ be the $W_0$-size-biased version of $W_0$. Then, for $\Repart s>-1$,
\begin{equation}
\E W^s=\frac{\Gamma(a(s+1))\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(b(s+1))\Gamma(a)}.

\end{equation}
Consequently, if
\[
V=2^{a-b}W,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
\E V^s=2^{(a-b)s}\frac{\Gamma(a(s+1))\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(b(s+1))\Gamma(a)},\qquad \Repart s>-1.

\end{equation}

body:
The model used by Wang-Huang-Li-Wu in arXiv:2609.02728 is Gaussian-feature, online least-squares regression. In the covariance eigenbasis, a feature vector phi has centered Gaussian law N(0,H) with H=diag(lambda_1,lambda_2,...) positive trace class, lambda_1>=lambda_2>=...>0. A label is y=<phi,theta_star>+epsilon with epsilon~N(0,sigma^2) independent of phi. The target has finite prediction energy sum_j lambda_j*|theta_star_j|^2<infinity; the pairing can equivalently be read as its mean-square-convergent Gaussian series. The population risk is R(theta)=E(<phi,theta>-y)^2/2, and the excess risk is Ecal(theta)=sum_j lambda_j*|theta_j-theta_star_j|^2/2=R(theta)-sigma^2/2. Their source/capacity assumptions are beta>1,s>0, lambda_j asymp j^(-beta) and lambda_j*|theta_star_j|^2 asymp j^(-(1+s*beta)), where asymp means upper and lower bounds by fixed positive constants, uniform in j. The label-noise standard deviation sigma is bounded above and away from zero by fixed constants (the constant-order noisy setting). At iteration k a fresh IID batch of B examples, independent of all past batches, gives the AVERAGED gradient g(theta;batch)=B^(-1)*sum_i phi_(k,i)*(<phi_(k,i),theta>-y_(k,i)). For a constant eta>0 and constant rho in[0,1), SGD uses theta_(k+1)=theta_k-eta*g(theta_k;batch); Polyak uses theta_(k+1)=theta_k-eta*g(theta_k;batch)+rho*(theta_k-theta_(k-1)); Nesterov first sets theta_k_la=theta_k+rho*(theta_k-theta_(k-1)) and uses theta_(k+1)=theta_k_la-eta*g(theta_k_la;batch). The source scaling-law analysis takes theta_0=theta_-1=0. For a one-pass data budget D, take T=D/B updates (or integer rounding at the exponent level), and B=D^(b+o(1)) with fixed b in[0,1). Hyperparameters can depend on D but are constant within each run. This protocol concerns final expected excess risk; it is not a finite-data repeated-epoch protocol, nor a theorem giving explicit constants in the critical-batch trade-off.
Definition of the specific source model; beta>1,s>0,uniform power-law comparison constants.
Fresh independent Gaussian features and independent Gaussian constant-order label noise; averaged minibatch gradients.
Zero initial iterate and zero initial momentum for the scaling-law protocol.

Let F_1,F_2 be identically distributed square-integrable variables with standard deviation s, and G_1,G_2 iid square-integrable variables on the same probability space. Suppose Delta_i=G_i-F_i>=0 have equal means and ||Delta_i||_2<=delta. Then 2(s-2delta)_+^2<=Var(F_1-F_2)<=2(s+2delta)^2. Independence is required only for G_1,G_2, and is not assumed for localization events, errors, or F_1,F_2.
square integrability
unconditional independence of G_1,G_2
identical F marginals and identical G marginals
nonnegative errors with equal means and the stated L2 bound

[Lemma lem:dtv-U-bound of arXiv:2507.16188, 'The noisy voter model with general initial conditions'] The following holds for every {\upshape\texttt{good}\xspace} collection $\{V_i\}_{i=1}^m$. Let $U_i$ and $\tau_i$ be as in (lem:Xt-from-V-to-U of the paper). Then, for some $C=C(q,\theta,\mathfrak{c}_0,\upalpha)>0$, the $d_{\textsc{tv}}^{\mathsf{x}_0}(U_i,t)$ from (eq:dtv-U-t-def of the paper) satisfy 
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^m d_{\textsc{tv}}^{\mathsf{x}_0}(U_i,t_1-\tau_i)^2 \mathbbm{1}_{\{\tau_i<t_1\}} \right] \leq C(1+t_1^3)e^{4(\log n)^{1-\frac{\upalpha}{2}}}n (\mathcal{A}^{(2)}_{t_1}(\mathsf{x}_0) \vee e^{-4\theta t_1}) + O(n^{-9})\,.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:dtv-U-bound of arXiv:2507.16188

body:
[Theorem 28 of arXiv:2609.01098, 'Gaussian upper bounds for averaged heat semigroups on graphs'] Let $o\in X$, $n>0$, $r\geq 0$, $C\geq 1$, $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, $q\colon [r,\infty)\to (0,\infty)$ monotone increasing with $q(t)\to\infty$ as $t\to\infty$, and
\[
A\geq  
\left((2C)^{3(2C)^{21n}}\cdot 1\vee  m(B(r)^{\frac{(2C)^{21n}}{q(r)}}\right)^\frac{q(r^2)}{q(r^2)-1}.
\] 
Assume \[
\mathcal{P}_{r}(t,o,o)
 \leq 
\frac{C}{\sqrt[\frac{q(t)}{q(t)-1}]{m(B(\sqrt t))}}
\]
for all $r^2\leq t\leq 2A^4r^2$ and
\[
\frac{m(B_x(s_2))}{m(B_x(s_1))}\leq C\left(\frac{s_2}{s_1}\right)^n
\]
for all $x\in B(2Ar)$ and $r\leq s_1\leq s_2\leq 2A^2r$.
Then, for all $U\subset B(r)$ satisfying $m(U)\geq \varepsilon m(B(r))$, we have 
\[
\lambda(U)
\geq 
\frac{C_n}{A^4r^2}
\left(
\frac{m(B(r))}{m(U)}\right)^{\frac{2}{N}},
\]
where $C_n=\frac{1}{C^{\frac{4}{n}}2^{5+\frac{4}{n}}}$ and 
\[
N\geq n\frac{q(r^2)}{q(r^2)-1}+ \frac{\ln\frac{1}{\epsilon}}{\ln A}+\frac{1}{q(r^2)-1}\ln(1\vee m(B(r))).
\]
title: Theorem 28 of arXiv:2609.01098

[Lemma 12 of arXiv:2506.11918, 'Central limit theorems for the Euler characteristic in the Random Connection Model for hig'] Let $F=\chi_a\big(\Delta_W\big)$.
There are constants $C_i>0$, $i\in\{1,\dots,7\}$, not depending on $W\in\Bf$, such that
\begin{align}
\int_{W^3} \E{ \left( \Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_2,U_2)}^1F \right)^2 \left( \Lambda_{(x_2,U_2),(x_1,U_1)}^1F \right)^2}^\frac{1}{2} \hspace{4cm} & \nonumber \\
\times \, \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_3,U_3),(x_2,U_2)}^2 F\right)^2 \left(\Lambda_{(x_2,U_2),(x_3,U_3),(x_1,U_1)}^2 F\right)^2}^\frac{1}{2}  \; \lambda^3 \, (\d {x}) &\;\leq\; C_1|W|,  \\[8pt]
\int_{W^3} \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_3,U_3),(x_2,U_2)}^2 F\right)^2 \left(\Lambda_{(x_2,U_2),(x_3,U_3),(x_1,U_1)}^2 F\right)^2} \; \lambda^3 \, (\d {x}) &\;\leq\; C_2|W|,  \\[8pt]
\int_W \E{ |\Lambda_{(x,U)}F|^3 } \; \lambda \, (\d x) &\;\leq\; C_3|W|,  \\[8pt]
\int_W \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x,U)}F\right)^4 }^\frac{3}{4} \; \lambda \, (\d x) &\;\leq\; C_4|W|,  \\[8pt]
\int_W \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x,U)}F\right)^4 } \; \lambda \, (\d x) &\;\leq\; C_5|W|,  \\[8pt]
\int_{W^2} 6\; \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1)}F\right)^4 }^\frac{1}{2} \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_2,U_2)}^2 F\right)^4 }^\frac{1}{2} \hspace{3.66cm} & \nonumber \\
+ 3\; \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_2,U_2)}^2 F\right)^4 } \; \lambda^2 \, (\d {x}) &\;\leq\; C_6|W|,  \\[8pt]
\int_W \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x,U)}F\right)^4 }^\frac{1}{2} \; \lambda \, (\d x) &\;\leq\; C_7|W|, 
\end{align}
where the integration is to be understood with respect to the points $x_i$.
title: Lemma 12 of arXiv:2506.11918

[Definition 8 of arXiv:2609.01574, 'A linear bound for Fujita's freeness conjecture'] Assume that $(X,\Delta)$ is log canonical near a closed point $x$ and that $X$ is smooth near $x$. Let $\mathfrak m_x\subset\mathcal O_X$ be the ideal sheaf of $x$. We call
\[

[Theorem thm:matrixBernstein of arXiv:2510.01021, '\Large Random Matrices, Intrinsic Freeness, and Sharp Non-Asymptotic Inequalities\relatedv'] Let $\{H_k\}_{k=1}^n$ be a sequence of independent random symmetric $d\times d$ matrices. Assume that each $H_k$ satisfies:
 \[
  \mathbb{E} H_k = 0 \text{ and } \lambda_{\max}\left( H_k \right) \leq R \text{ almost surely.}
 \]
Then, for all $t\geq 0$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb{P}\left[ \lambda_{\max}\left( \sum_{k=1}^n H_k \right) \geq t \right] \leq d \cdot \exp\left( \frac{-t^2}{2\sigma^2 + \frac23Rt} \right) \text{ where } \sigma^2 = \left\| \sum_{k=1}^n\mathbb{E}\left(H_k^2\right) \right\|.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
