[Dfn 2. dfn eq: restriction of a measure to a closed ball of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{The vague metric $d_{V}^{S, \rho_{S}}$}]
  We denote the set of Radon measures on $S$ by $\mathcal{M}(S)$.
  For $\mu \in \mathcal{M}(S)$,
  we write $\mu^{(r)}$ for the restriction of $\mu$ to $S^{(r)} \coloneqq \closure (B_{S}(\rho, r))$, 
  that is,
  $\mu^{(r)}$ is a finite Borel measure given by
  \begin{equation}  
    \mu^{(r)}(\cdot) 
    \coloneqq
    \mu|_{S^{(r)}}(\cdot)
    =
    \mu \left( \cdot \cap S^{(r)} \right).
  \end{equation} 
  We then define, for each $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal{M}(S)$,
  \begin{equation}
    d_{V}^{S, \rho_{S}}(\mu, \nu)
    \coloneqq
    \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-r} \left( 1 \wedge d_{P}^{S}(\mu^{(r)}, \nu^{(r)}) \right) dr.
  \end{equation}
title: Dfn 2. dfn eq: restriction of a measure to a closed ball of arXiv:2412.08236

body: [Definition def:standardWignerMatrix of arXiv:2510.01021, '\Large Random Matrices, Intrinsic Freeness, and Sharp Non-Asymptotic Inequalities\relatedv'] We will call a $d\times d$ symmetric random matrix a standard Wigner matrix when the upper triangular entries are i.i.d. standard Gaussian, i.e. for all $1\leq i\leq j\leq d$ we have $W_{ij}\sim \mathcal{N}\big(0,\frac1d\big)$, all independent.\footnote{When the diagonal entries are distributed accordingly to $\mathcal{N}\big(0,\frac2d\big)$ and the off-diagonal ones as $\mathcal{N}\big(0,\frac1d\big)$ the matrix is invariant to orthogonal conjugation and this case is refereed to as the \emph{Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE)}. We note that for a standard Wigner matrix, $\mathbb{E} W^2 = I$.}
title: Standard Wigner Matrix

Let d,ell>=1 be integers, rho>=0, and fix w in R^d with ||w||_2^2=d. Independently sample x_1,...,x_(ell+1) iid N(0,I_d/d) and epsilon_1,...,epsilon_(ell+1) iid N(0,rho), with the two families independent. Set y_i=x_i^T w+epsilon_i, s=[(d/ell)sum_(i=1)^ell y_i x_i; (1/ell)sum_(i=1)^ell y_i^2] in R^(d+1), and H=x_(ell+1)s^T in R^(d x (d+1)). The last pair is a fresh query, independent of the ell context pairs conditional on w. Now let w have an arbitrary Borel law Pi supported on the sphere ||w||^2=d; the covariate and noise sampling is independent of w. Let Gamma be a fixed d by (d+1) matrix, and define b=E_Pi[w], R=E_Pi[ww^T], and A=[R,(1+rho)b]. Define C_Pi as the symmetric block matrix with top-left (d/ell)I_d+[(1+1/ell)/(1+rho)]R, top-right (1+2/ell)b, bottom-left its transpose, and bottom-right (1+2/ell)(1+rho). For the predictor yhat=<Gamma,H>_F=tr(Gamma^T H), e(Gamma)=E[(y_(ell+1)-yhat)^2]=1+rho-(2/d)tr(Gamma A^T)+[(1+rho)/d]tr(Gamma C_Pi Gamma^T). This is the finite-dimensional formula of Appendix B Proposition 1 (B10), p.20. For uniform sphere tasks, b=0 and R=I_d. For a uniform law on a fixed pool of k sphere-normalized tasks, b=k^(-1)sum_i w_i and R=k^(-1)sum_i w_i w_i^T; the pool mean need not vanish. For a predictor trained on other data, the same identity holds conditionally on a frozen Gamma and test law/pool when the subsequent context and query are freshly sampled under this model. Every finite 1/ell term is retained; this is not the asymptotic approximation (B16), nor a theorem about Gaussian-task universality.

[Defn 2 of arXiv:2605.18751, '\mytitle'] Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be probability measures on \(E\), with likelihood ratio \(\ell\) as in~\eqref{def.ell}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]

\item \emph{Usual stochastic order} ($\st$): \(P\st Q\) if
\(\bar F_P(x)\le\bar F_Q(x)\) for every \(x\in E\).

\item \emph{Hazard-rate order} ($\hr$): \(P\hr Q\) if \(\bar F_P(x)/\bar F_Q(x)\) is nonincreasing wherever \(\bar F_Q(x)>0\) (equivalently, \(h_P(x)\ge h_Q(x)\) wherever both hazard rates are defined).

\item \emph{Likelihood-ratio order} ($\lr$): \(P\lr Q\) if \(\ell\) is nonincreasing on \(\supp(P)\cup\supp(Q)\).

\item \emph{Relative log-concavity} ($\lc$): when \(\supp(P)\) is an interval contained in \(\supp(Q)\), \(P\lc Q\) if \(\log\ell\) is concave on \(\supp(P)\).
\end{enumerate}
title: Definition 2 of arXiv:2605.18751

body: In mathematical analysis, the Minkowski inequality establishes that the L^p spaces satisfy the triangle inequality in the definition of normed vector spaces: for 1 <= p <= infinity and any f, g in L^p(mu) on a measure space, the sum f + g lies in L^p(mu) and ||f + g||_p <= ||f||_p + ||g||_p; the same inequality holds with sums in place of integrals for the sequence spaces l^p. The inequality is named after the German mathematician Hermann Minkowski.

\lim_{h\downarrow 0} \sup_{n} \sup_{\substack{t_{1},t_{2}\leq T\\
|t_{1}-t_{2}|\leq h}} P^{n}(|\xi^{(n)}_{t_{1}}-\xi^{(n)}_{t_{2}}|>

Then  one can find a sequence of integers $n'\to\infty$,

random processes $\tilde \xi_{t},\tilde \xi_{t}^{(n')}$

distributions of $\tilde \xi_{t}^{(n')}$ coincide with 
the corresponding finite-dimensional
distributions of $\xi_{t}^{(n')}$ and 
$$
P (|\tilde \xi_{t}-\tilde \xi_{t}^{(n')}|>\varepsilon) \to 0   
$$
as $n'\to\infty$ for any $\varepsilon>0$ and $t\geq0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Fix k>=1 integer, c>0, N/d^k -> c, a deterministic unit teacher direction u_d, iid uniform unit random feature directions v_i, Gaussian input G~N(0,I_d), and unrestricted real output coefficients. The population least-squares error for ReLU(u_d dot G) using the span of ReLU(v_i dot G) converges in L1 over feature directions to r=(t+a*(1-psi)+sqrt((t+a*(1-psi))^2+4*a*psi*t))/2, where psi=c*k!, a=E[ReLU(Z)*He_k(Z)]^2, t=sum_{j>k}E[ReLU(Z)*He_j(Z)]^2, Z is standard Gaussian and the Hermites are orthonormal. Normalize by Var(ReLU(Z))=(pi-1)/(2*pi) for relative risk. Odd k>=3 have a=0 and the curve is the constant t. Even k and k=1 use the Hu–Lu–Misiakiewicz population approximation theorem. This covers zero population ridge/approximation; finite-n Gaussian training and arbitrary positive population ridge are outside the claim. No novelty assertion is made.

  \item [$\mathrm{(ii)}$]$(\calM(X)_{\mathrm{fin}},d_{\BL^{\kappa}}^X)$ is separable.
  \item [$\mathrm{(iii)}$]Convergence with respect to $d_{\BL^{\kappa}}^X$ is equivalent to weak convergence.
  \item [$\mathrm{(iv)}$]Let $(Y,d^Y)$ be a metric space and fix an isometric embedding $f:X\to Y$.
  Then $\calM(X)_{\mathrm{fin}}\ni \mu\mapsto \mu\circ f^{-1}\in \calM(Y)_{\mathrm{fin}}$ is isometric 
  with respect to $d^X_{\BL^{\kappa}}$ and $d^Y_{\BL^{\kappa}}$. 
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition of arXiv:2411.15881, 'Stable Approximation for Call Function Via Stein's method'] For $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ in $\mathcal{C}_{b}^2$, define the operator as follows:
\[
(\mathcal{A}^{\alpha,\delta}f)(y)=d_\alpha \,
\int_{\infty}^{\infty} \frac{f(y+u)-f(y)-uf'(y)}{2|u|^{1+\alpha}}
\left[
(1+\delta){\bf 1}_{(0,\infty)}(u)+(1-\delta){\bf 1}_{(-\infty,0)}(u)
\right]
 du,
\]
where $d_\alpha = \left(
\int_0^\infty \frac{1-\cos u}{u^{1+\alpha}}du
\right)^{-1}$.

[Theorem thm:deconv of arXiv:2605.15545, 'Crossover from subcritical to critical decay: \\ random walk, self-avoiding walk, percolat'] Let $d \ge 1$ and
let $M,K_{\mathrm{IR}},\zeta>0$ be given.
Suppose $(Q,g)\in \mathcal{Q}_{M,K_{\mathrm{IR}},\zeta}$.
Let $\eta$ and $\Lambda$ be given by (equation eq:def_Lambda of the paper),
and let $x\in{\mathbb Z^d}$ be a nonzero vector in the same direction as $\eta$,
i.e., $\eta = \abs \eta \hat x$ ($\eta=0$ is permitted here).
If $d \le 2$, we further assume $\abs x \abs \eta \ge s_0$ for some $s_0 > 0$.
Then, as $\abs x \to \infty$,
\begin{equation} 
 G_{Q,g}  (x) :=
\int_0^\infty \mathrm{d} t    \int_{\mathbb T^d} \frac{\mathrm{d} k }{(2\pi)^d}
	e^{ik\cdot x} \hat g(k)  e^{-t [ \hat Q(0) - \hat Q (k) ] }
=  \mathbb{C}(x; \eta, \Lambda) \Bigl[\hat{g}(0) + O\Bigl(\frac 1 {\abs x^\delta}\Bigr) \Bigr]
\end{equation}
with some $\delta > 0$
and with the constant depending only on $d, \zeta, M, K_{\mathrm{IR}}, s_0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:stable-factor-barrier of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $k\geq5$, put $t=k-4$, and let $\mathcal L^{\mathrm{st}}_{h,k}$ be the
following explicitly defined set of labels.  Choose
$(u,v,b,c)\in U\times V\times B\times C$, define $p,q,r,s$ by
(equation eq:fullsparams of the paper), require $(p,q)=1$, and choose integer degrees
$a_i h\leq\ell_i\leq b_i h$ with $\gcd(p,\ell_i)=1$ for
$1\leq i\leq t$, where the fixed windows satisfy
(equation eq:prime-window-constants of the paper).  Starting from
$A_0=A_{p,q,r,s}$, define
\begin{equation}
 A_i=\Sigma_{\ell_i,p}A_{i-1}
 =\ell_i\mathbin{\cdot}A_{i-1}\cup\{p\}
 \qquad(1\leq i\leq t),
\end{equation}
and let $\mathcal L^{\mathrm{st}}_{h,k}$ be the set of all resulting labels
$|hA_t|$.  Put
\[
 \delta=1-\frac{1+\log\log2}{\log2}=0.086071\ldots.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 |\mathcal L^{\mathrm{st}}_{h,k}|
 \ll_k
 \frac{h^{k-1}}
 {(\log h)^\delta(\log\log h)^{3/2}}
 =o_k(h^{k-1}).
\end{equation}
Thus no refinement of collision estimates alone can give positive ambient
density from this stable full-residue chart.  This is a limitation of the
chart, not an upper bound for the full spectrum $\mathcal R(h,k)$.

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2608.21701, 'Superdiffusivity of random walks on the three-dimensional randomly oriented Manhattan latt'] There exists a constant $C<\infty$ such that, for every $m\ge0$, $z>1$, $\lambda\in(0,1)$, $n\ge0$, $j\in[3]^n$, $p\in\mathbb T_j^3$, and $k\in[3]$,
\begin{align}

\int_{\mathbb T_k^3} \frac{\rmd q} {\lambda+\theta(p,q)+\mathfrak l_m(\lambda,(p,q),z)} &\le 4\pi \left[ 1+ C\left( z^{-1/2} + \frac{(m+1)(1+\log z)}{z} \right) \right] \nonumber\\ 
&\quad\times {\rm UB}_m(\lambda+\theta_k(p),z)+C, \\
 \int_{\mathbb T_k^3} \frac{\rmd q} {\lambda+\theta(p,q)+\mathfrak u_m(\lambda,(p,q),z)} &\ge 4\pi \left[
1- C\left( z^{-1/2} + \frac{(m+1)(1+\log z)}{z} \right) \right] \nonumber\\
&\quad\times{\rm LB}_{m+1}(\lambda+\theta_k(p),z)- C{\rm LB}_{m+1}(1,z)-C.
\end{align}
Here, when $n=0$, we use the degree-zero convention from
Section~\ref{subsec:fourier.multipliers}.

Let (X, Sigma, mu) be any measure space and 1 <= p, q <= infinity with 1/p + 1/q = 1 (1/infinity = 0). For all measurable f, g: X -> C, ||fg||_1 <= ||f||_p ||g||_q (with the convention 0 * infinity = 0; so if f in L^p and g in L^q then fg in L^1 and |int fg dmu| <= ||f||_p ||g||_q). Equality case, 1 < p < infinity and ||f||_p, ||g||_q finite: ||fg||_1 = ||f||_p ||g||_q if and only if there are constants alpha, beta >= 0, not both zero, with alpha |f|^p = beta |g|^q mu-a.e. Generalized form: if 0 < p_1, ..., p_k <= infinity and 0 < r with 1/r = 1/p_1 + ... + 1/p_k, then ||f_1 ... f_k||_r <= ||f_1||_{p_1} ... ||f_k||_{p_k} (valid also for r < 1, by applying the two-factor case to |f_i|^r). Duality formula, with the semifiniteness caveat: for 1 <= p < infinity and f in L^p(mu), ||f||_p = sup{ |int fg dmu| : ||g||_{p'} <= 1 } over an ARBITRARY measure space; for measurable f with ||f||_p = infinity (1 < p < infinity), and for p = infinity, the identity requires mu to be SEMIFINITE. Counterexample without semifiniteness: X = {pt} with mu({pt}) = infinity; every g with ||g||_{p'} <= 1 and p' < infinity vanishes, so the supremum is 0, while for f = 1 one has ||f||_p = infinity for 1 < p < infinity and ||f||_infinity = 1.

[Theostar Longterm behaviors of $\mathrm{CBs}$ of arXiv:2605.06488, 'Continuous-state branching processes with L\'evy-Khintchine drift-interaction: Laplace dua'] Let $X$ be a $\mathrm{CB}(\Psi)$ process. Then,

\begin{enumerate}
\item One has $\lim_{t\rightarrow \infty}X_t=0$ a.s. if and only if $\Psi$ is critical or subcritical, i.e. $\Psi=\Sigma$, in the notation of Section (sec:LKfunction of the paper). In this case, $\mathrm{y}_t\to 0$ as $t$ tends to $\infty$.
\item One has $\lim_{t\rightarrow \infty}X_t=\infty$ a.s. if and only if $\Psi$ is immortal, i.e. $\Psi=-\Phi$, in the notation of Section (sec:LKfunction of the paper). In this case, $\mathrm{y}_t\to \infty$ as $t$ tends to $\infty$.
\item The process has positive probability  to converge to $0$ and to diverge to $\infty$ if and only if $\Psi$ is supercritical not immortal, i.e. $\Psi$ changes sign. In the latter case, the probability that $X$ goes to $0$ under $\mathbb{P}_x$ is given by $e^{-x\rho}$ where $\rho$ is the largest zero of $\Psi$ (equivalently the fixed point of the o.d.e (equation eq:ode of the paper) and limit of $\mathrm{y}$).
\item The process is absorbed at $0$ in finite time with positive probability if and only if $\int_{x_1}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{\Psi(u)}<\infty$ for some $x_1\in (0,\infty)$ (Grey's condition). The latter can only occur for non-immortal mechanism, and when the integral is finite, one has, 
\[\mathbb{P}_x(X_t=0)=e^{-x\mathrm{y}_t(\infty)}\in (0,1),\ \forall t\in [0,\infty), x\in [0,\infty).\]
\item The process is absorbed at $\infty$ in finite time with positive probability if and only if $\int_0^{x_1}\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{-\Psi(u)}<\infty$ for some $x_1\in (0,\infty)$ (Dynkin's condition\footnote{Harris [zbMATH02001586] cites Dynkin for the study of explosion}). The latter can only occur for supercritical mechanism and when the integral is finite, one has
\[\mathbb{P}_x(X_t=\infty)=1-e^{-x\mathrm{y}_t(0)}\in (0,1),\ \forall t\in [0,\infty), x\in (0,\infty].\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Longterm behaviors of $\mathrm{CBs}$

body:
DEFINITIONS. Let F be a class of measurable functions f: X -> [a, b], let S = (X_1, ..., X_n) be an i.i.d. sample from a distribution P on X, and let sigma_1, ..., sigma_n be independent Rademacher signs, independent of S. The empirical Rademacher complexity of F on S is R_hat_S(F) = E_sigma [ sup_{f in F} (1/n) sum_{i=1}^{n} sigma_i f(X_i) ], and the Rademacher complexity is R_n(F) = E_S [ R_hat_S(F) ]. Write P f = E f(X) and P_n f = (1/n) sum_i f(X_i). THEOREM. For every delta in (0, 1), with probability at least 1 - delta over the sample, simultaneously for all f in F: P f - P_n f <= 2 R_n(F) + (b - a) sqrt( log(1/delta) / (2n) ), and also P f - P_n f <= 2 R_hat_S(F) + 3 (b - a) sqrt( log(2/delta) / (2n) ) (a bound computable from the data). If F is closed under negation (f in F implies -f in F), the two-sided version sup_{f in F} |P f - P_n f| <= 2 R_n(F) + (b - a) sqrt(log(2/delta) / (2n)) holds with probability at least 1 - delta (for a general F apply the one-sided bound to F and to -F, each with delta/2, which replaces R_n(F) by R_n(F union -F)). Since E sup_f (P f - P_n f) <= 2 R_n(F), a class is uniformly Glivenko-Cantelli whenever R_n(F) -> 0. Standard values of R_n: a finite class bounded by B has R_n <= B sqrt(2 log |F| / n) (Massart); a class of indicators of VC dimension d has R_n <= sqrt(2 d log(e n / d) / n) and in fact O(sqrt(d / n)) (Dudley); linear predictors x -> <w, x> with ||w||_2 <= Lambda on inputs with ||x||_2 <= r have R_n <= Lambda r / sqrt(n); and for L-Lipschitz phi, R_n(phi o F) <= L R_n(F) (Ledoux-Talagrand contraction), which is how the bound passes from a class of predictors to a class of losses. In learning, with f the loss of a hypothesis, the theorem says the true risk of EVERY hypothesis in the class exceeds its empirical risk by at most 2 R_n plus a term of order sqrt(log(1/delta)/n), the modern replacement for VC bounds when the class is not a class of sets.
F a class of measurable functions with values in a bounded interval [a, b] (for the two-sided form with the stated constant the class should be closed under negation or one accepts an extra factor; see the references)
the sample is i.i.d. from P; delta in (0, 1)
measurability of the suprema (a countable class, or the usual separability assumptions) is assumed throughout

Hence E Phi(S) <= 2 R_n(F), and with Step 1 the first bound follows. Step 3 (the empirical version). R_hat_S(F) also has bounded differences (b - a)/n in each sample point, so by McDiarmid, with probability at least 1 - delta/2, R_n(F) <= R_hat_S(F) + (b - a) sqrt(log(2/delta)/(2n)); applying Step 1 with delta/2 as well and a union bound gives, with probability at least 1 - delta, Phi(S) <= 2 R_hat_S(F) + (b - a) sqrt(log(2/delta)/(2n)) + 2 (b - a) sqrt(log(2/delta)/(2n)) = 2 R_hat_S(F) + 3 (b - a) sqrt(log(2/delta)/(2n)). [Corollary cor:energy-finiteness-infinite-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Assume that the dyadic vector-weight law is energy-admissible.  Then, almost
surely on \(\{M>0\}\), the following assertions hold:
\[
    I_t(\mu)<\infty
    \qquad\text{for every }0<t<D_{\mathrm E}(X),
\]
and
\[
    I_t(\mu)=\infty
    \qquad\text{for every }D_{\mathrm E}(X)<t<1.
\]
If \(D_{\mathrm E}(X)=0\), the first assertion is vacuous.  If
\(D_{\mathrm E}(X)=1\), the second assertion is vacuous.

\[
\psi_{W_n(G)}(w)

[Definition def:cyclic of arXiv:2510.13572, 'Coalescence in Markov chains'] Consider an irreducible Markov chain on the state space $S$ with transition matrix $P$
and period $d$. There exists a unique partition
of $S$ into $d$ classes $S_0,S_1,\dots,S_{d-1}$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{j\in S_{r+1}} p_{i,j} = 1, \qquad i\in S_r,\ r=0,1,\dots,d-1,
\end{equation*}
where by convention $S_0 = S_d$. The sets $S_r$ are called the \emph{cyclic classes} of the chain.\hfill $\blacktriangleleft$

body: Theorem (campaign status: audited-pass): (S10 eq (2).) For every n >= 4, d_geo(A_n) = ceil(n/3). Lower bound: a feasible geometric quotient has at most r = n+1 signed classes, so Corollary 3.1 forces n+1 >= 2n+1-3d, i.e. d >= ceil(n/3). Upper bound: choose an independent U in V(C_n) with |U| = ceil(n/3) and take R = span{L_u = A+B_u : u in U}; modulo R, adding or deleting a vertex of U from a clique does not change its signed class, so classes are indexed by cliques of C_n - U, which has n-|U| vertices, n-2|U| edges and no clique bigger than an edge: at most 1+(n-|U|)+(n-2|U|) = 2n+1-3|U| <= n+1 classes. Notes: Uniform in n with NO computational input (earlier support had been exact finite searches only). Independently re-verified here by exhaustive search over all residual spaces of dim <= ceil(n/3)-1 spanned by zero-class forms and signed differences, n=4..8: zero feasible quotients (see local_rerun_exhaustive_dgeo_minimality).

[Proposition 2 (Finite-horizon memory-channel response) of arXiv:2608.19762, '2608.19762'] For $k\in\{m,v\}$,
\begin{align*}
    r_m(1)&=0,
    &
    r_m(2)&=b_m,
    &
    r_m(3)&=b_m(a+\beta_1),\\
    r_v(1)&=0,
    &
    r_v(2)&=b_v,
    &
    r_v(3)&=b_v(a+\beta_2),
\end{align*}
and
\begin{equation}
    r_k(4)
    =
    b_k
    \Bigl(
        a^2+a\beta_k+\beta_k^2
        +b_md_m+b_vd_v
    \Bigr).
    
\end{equation}

If $b_k\neq0$ and
\begin{equation}
    |a+\beta_k|>1,
    
\end{equation}
then
\[
    |r_k(3)|>|r_k(2)|.
\]
If, in addition,
\begin{equation}
    \left|
        a^2+a\beta_k+\beta_k^2
        +b_md_m+b_vd_v
    \right|
    >
    |a+\beta_k|,
    
\end{equation}
then
\[
    |r_k(4)|>|r_k(3)|.
\]
These finite-horizon amplification conditions can hold even when
$\rho(\overline A)<1$, so asymptotic stability does not preclude transient
growth in the response. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

A metric space (X, d) is a geodesic metric space if every pair of points x, y in X can be joined by a geodesic curve gamma: [0, 1] -> X such that the length of gamma equals d(x, y), meaning d(gamma(s), gamma(t)) = |s - t| * d(x, y) for all s, t in [0, 1].
(X, d) is a metric space

[Proposition eq:weighted-sharp-sparse of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:weighted-sharp-sparse}
Assume \(({\rm PT})_p\) and the critical-count ceiling
(equation eq:critical-count-ceiling of the paper).
If \(V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is Borel measurable and bounded below and \(k_N=o(N)\),
then
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{\rho\downarrow0}\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N
 \log\mathscr C_N^J\bigl(V;\mathcal A_N(k_N,\rho)\bigr)
 \le\Xi_p^{\rm sp}(V),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
 \Xi_p^{\rm sp}(V)
 :=
 \log(p-1)+
 \sup_{u\in\mathbb R}\left\{-V(u)-\frac{u^2}{2}\right\}.
\end{equation}
title: Weighted sparse-profile bound

[Lemma lem:exiF-hf of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] There exists a function $F:\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\to \mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}$ that is $\sigma(\{\mathcal{H}_i\}_{i=1}^k, \mathcal{Q}_{0,s}, \mathcal{M}_{t,1}, \{\mathcal{D}_i\}_{i=1}^k)$-measurable, and  satisfies the following conditions:
			\begin{itemize}
				\item On $\mathcal{E}[W]\cap\mathcal{E}_*$, for each $i\in \llbracket 1,k\rrbracket$, $F-\mathcal{H}_i\diamond \mathcal{Q}_{0,s}$ is constant on each interval $A_{i, j}$, $j\in\llbracket1, \ell(i) \rrbracket$.
				\item $F=-\infty$ outside of $\bigcup_{i=1}^k A_i$,
				\item For any $a>0$, with probability at least $1 - 2\exp(-ca)$ the following is true:  
                $$
                |F(x)-F(y)| \le a \log(|x-y|^{-1} + 2)\sqrt{|x-y|}
                $$
                for all $x, y \in \bigcup_{i=1}^k A_i$, $|x-y|\le |\log(r)|^{10}r^{2/3}$. 
			\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Method: Fluctuations of preferential-attachment distances and diameter structural reduction Result: If integer-valued X_n is centered by real c_n, every centered value lies in Z-c_n. Along a subsequence with fractional parts c_n tending to r, any weak limit is supported on Z-r. Two subsequences whose fractional parts have different limits can therefore have incompatible translated-lattice limits. Check: For a closed set staying a positive distance from Z-r, its probability is eventually0; the portmanteau theorem puts any weak limit on Z-r. The deterministic example X_n=floor(c_n) gives centered value minus the fractional part. Obstruction: A claimed continuous full-sequence limit without additional scaling would require checking this lattice obstruction. No centered distance law for the actual attachment model is obtained.

[Definition 17 of arXiv:2608.29075, 'The 2-Monoidal Structure of Symmetric Sequences'] Let $(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$ be a 2-monoidal category. A \textit{double monoid} in $\catname{C}$ is an object $A$ equipped with morphisms
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=scriptsize]
	{A \square A} & A && I & A && {A \circ A} & A && {J } & A,
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
	\arrow[from=1-7, to=1-8]
	\arrow[from=1-10, to=1-11]
\end{tikzcd}\]
    which turn $A$ into a monoid in both $(\catname{C},\square,I)$ and $(\catname{C},\circ,J)$, and make the following diagrams commute.
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{(A \circ A) \square (A \circ A)} && {(A \square A) \circ (A \square A)} \\
	{A \square A} & A & {A \circ A}
	\arrow["{\zeta_{A,A,A,A}}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{J \square J} & {A \square A} && {I \circ I} & {A \circ A} \\
	J & A && I & A
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{\mu_J}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
	\arrow[from=1-5, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\Delta_I}", from=2-4, to=1-4]
	\arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	& A \\
	I && J
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{{\iota_J = \epsilon_I}}"', from=2-1, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=1-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
    Dually, one can define \textit{double comonoids}. 

    A morphism between two double (co)monoids is a morphism of the two underlying (co)monoids. 
    
    The categories of double (co)monoids in the 2-monoidal category $(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$ are denoted by $\text{dMon}(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$ and by $\text{dComon}(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$, respectively.
title: Definition 17 of arXiv:2608.29075

Owner draft: independently checked proof (C013 v1). For a centered nondegenerate p-simplex S, p>=1, and nonnegative weights alpha_i of positive total T, the laws alpha_i*Unif(S) are jointly mixable with zero sum iff (p+1)*max_i alpha_i<=T. Necessity comes from extreme barycentric coordinates. Sufficiency uses the finite projection-diagonal lemma with c_i=(p+1)alpha_i/T to make a measurable frame with squared column norms alpha_i and frame operator T/(p+1) times identity. Haar-unitary squared moduli are Dirichlet(1,...,1), making each scaled simplex marginal correct and the weighted barycentric totals constant. Zero weights are point masses. The projection/Gram-Schmidt algorithm is Borel in the weights, so the coupling is valid conditionally on another tuple. Novelty UNKNOWN.

\[
        \mu_n:=\Pbb_{\nu_n}(K_0<n,K_1=n)

\[

Equivalently,
\[
        \mu_n=\nu_n(n-1)\frac{q^n}{n}.
\]

body: The Mandelbrot set (/ˈmændəlbroʊt, -brɒt/) is a two-dimensional set. It is defined in the complex plane as the complex numbers $c$ for which the function $f_{c}(z)=z^{2}+c$ does not diverge to infinity when iterated starting at $z=0$. In other words, it is the set of $c$ for which the sequence $f_{c}(0)$, $f_{c}(f_{c}(0))$, and so on, remains bounded in absolute value.

interval then $\mu_{*}$ is the unique minimiser of the strictly convex energy
$\mathcal F_{V}[\mu]=\int V\,\mathrm{d}\mu-\chi[\mu]$, the diffusion is its $W_{2}$-gradient
flow, and all statements of Sections~(sec:inequalities of the paper)--(sec:reverse of the paper) hold
verbatim with $\tfrac12x^{2}$ replaced by $V$: displacement convexity, the free LSI,
Talagrand and HWI inequalities, exponential relaxation to $\mu_{*}$, the JKO scheme, and

Let W have iid N(0,1) entries and v be an independent standard Gaussian vector. For any measurable g:R->[-1,1], set H=Wa/sqrt(n), b_j=v_j g(H_j), R=||b||^2/n, r=tr(D)/n and T=b^T W D W^T b/n^2. Then ||T-rR||_2<=9/sqrt(n), uniformly in q>0,a,D,g. The same conditional estimate holds for past-measurable a,D independent of the fresh W,v.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:dc969cd0f1d95e6342cc24b187d7c7c143166d09b25c2f460015416c0973f35c","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/dc/dc969cd0f1d95e6342cc24b187d7c7c143166d09b25c2f460015416c0973f35c.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:f3aeefd89b9bd0bd89a56e7f3aa2fc2ce4fb878722b532ee4aa00190646ee9e0","bundle_entry_key":"t250_w712_c021","bundle_id":"population.w712-t250-c021-c022-transpose-tanh-ntk","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Quantitative Tensor Programs and Gaussian shared-weight conditioning","draft":"w712/bundle_016.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:shared-gaussian-transpose-quadratic-rate","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C021 v1: a quantitative shared-Gaussian-transpose estimate

Kind: moved. Target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty unverified.
The Gaussian conditioning identity is standard; the point of recording
the estimate is to pay the transpose-reuse error in the specific NTK
program of C022. No claim of a new general conditioning theorem is made.

## Statement

Let n>=1, let a be a deterministic nonzero vector in R^n and set
q=||a||^2/n>0. Let D be a deterministic symmetric matrix with 0<=D<=I.
Let W have independent N(0,1) entries and let v be an independent
standard Gaussian vector in R^n. For a measurable g:R->[-1,1], define

    H=Wa/sqrt(n), b_j=v_j g(H_j), R=||b||^2/n,
    r=tr(D)/n, T=b^T W D W^T b/n^2.

Then

    ||T-rR||_2 <=9/sqrt(n).                         (1)

The bound is uniform over q>0, a, D, and g. In particular, if a and D
are random but measurable before the independent W,v are sampled, (1)
holds for the conditional L2 norm given that past, almost surely on
{a!=0}. This is not an assertion that W^T b is independent of H.

## 1. Exact conditional law, including its rank-one correction

Put P=I-aa^T/||a||^2. Decompose each Gaussian row of W into its
projection onto a and the orthogonal component. Conditional on H,

    W=H a^T/(sqrt(n)q)+G P,

where the rows of G are independent standard Gaussian vectors independent
of H. Conditional also on v, b is fixed, so G^T b has the law ||b||z
for an independent standard Gaussian z. Consequently the joint law of
H,v,W^T b/sqrt(n) is represented exactly by

    t=kappa a+sqrt(R)Pz, kappa=H^T b/(nq).          (2)

Here z is independent of H,v. When b=0 the representation still holds
with both terms zero; no division by ||b|| occurs. Since T=t^TDt/n,
its conditional mean and variance given H,v are

    m=R tr(DP)/n+kappa^2 a^TDa/n,
    Var_z(T)=2R^2 tr((PDP)^2)/n^2
                       +4R kappa^2 a^TDPDa/n^2.   (3)

For completeness the Gaussian formulas in (3) follow by diagonalizing
the symmetric PDP and using E z_i^2=1, E z_i^4=3 and independent
coordinates. Centered quadratic and linear terms have covariance zero
because every third Gaussian moment is zero. Expanding the linear term
in (2) gives exactly the second term in the variance. Thus (3) includes
the effect of the same W in the forward and transpose lines.

## 2. Uniform moment bounds; the apparent inverse q cancels

The H_j are iid N(0,q). Conditional on H, write

    U=sum g(H_j)^2, V=sum H_j^2 g(H_j)^2,
    V4=sum H_j^2 g(H_j)^4.

Gaussian moments of v give

    E_v[(H^Tb)^4]=3V^2,
    E_v[||b||^2(H^Tb)^2]=UV+2V4.

Since |g|<=1, U<=n, V,V4<=sum H_j^2. Also
E(sum H_j^2)^2=q^2(n^2+2n). Therefore

    E R^2<=1+2/n<=3,
    E(q^2 kappa^4)<=3(n^2+2n)/n^4<=9/n^2,
    E(q R kappa^2)<=(n+2)/n^2<=3/n.               (4)

These computations use the conditional Gaussian law of v. Bounded g
may depend on H but not on v or the residual G. The estimates have no
constant diverging as q tends to zero; q cancels against the H moments.

## 3. Centered fluctuation and conditional-mean correction

The matrix P is an orthogonal projection. Since D is a positive
contraction, tr((PDP)^2)<=n and a^TDPDa<=||a||^2=nq.
Equations (3)--(4) imply

    E(T-m)^2<=6/n+12/n^2.                          (5)

Use tr(DP)=tr(D)-a^TDa/||a||^2 to compare m to the proposed limit:

    m-rR=(a^TDa/n)kappa^2-R a^TDa/(n||a||^2).

Both coefficients are nonnegative, with a^TDa/n<=q and
a^TDa/||a||^2<=1. Thus (4) and the L2 triangle inequality give

    ||m-rR||_2<=(3+sqrt(3))/n.                     (6)

Another L2 triangle inequality, (5) and n>=1 yield

    ||T-rR||_2
       <=sqrt(6/n+12/n^2)+(3+sqrt(3))/n
       <=[sqrt(18)+3+sqrt(3)]/sqrt(n)
       <9/sqrt(n).

For the last strict bound, sqrt(18)<17/4 and sqrt(3)<7/4;
the corresponding squared comparisons are 288<289 and 48<49.
Replacing the strict inequality by <= proves (1).

## Boundaries, hypotheses and checks

The assertion includes n=1: P=0, but the rank-one term remains and (6)
still applies. It excludes a=0 only because q and its normalization are
undefined; the tanh application has a!=0 almost surely. A separately
defined zero-vector program is not inferred by dividing by q=0.
Symmetry and positivity of D supply the contraction trace bounds. Fresh
independent Gaussian v supplies the fourth moments in (4); measurability
of g with respect to H supplies its conditional status in those moments.
No independence is assumed between H and the backward vector t.

The restriction on what g may depend on is real. If instead g is allowed
to depend on both H_j and v_j, take q=1, a=(1,...,1), D=I, and
g(H_j,v_j)=sign(H_j v_j). Then b_j=|v_j|sign(H_j), R=mean v_j^2,
and (3) gives

    E(T-R)=(1-1/n)4/pi^2.

Indeed E|H_j v_j|=2/pi and E(H_j v_j)^2=1, so
E(kappa^2)=1/n+(1-1/n)4/pi^2; the projection correction subtracts 1/n.
At n=4096 the displayed bias is greater than 4095/16384>9/64,
using pi<4. Hence even the L1 lower bound exceeds 9/sqrt(n).
All other hypotheses remain intact. This refutes the weakened
future-dependent-g inference, not the stated theorem.

Positivity of D is convenient for the NTK application rather than a
necessary boundary of this estimate: the proof also works for symmetric
operator-norm contractions by bounding |a^TDa| instead. No necessity
claim for the stronger D hypothesis is intended.

The load-bearing checks are the normalization sqrt(n) in (2), the factor
n^2 in T, the two conditional Gaussian fourth-moment identities, the
power of q canceled in (4), and the term 4 in the noncentral variance.
The proof gives all of these algebraically. Exact finite checks are
supporting author checks, not sampled proofs of (1). Formalization remains

[Theorem 120 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Suppose that a discrete ensemble $X$ satisfies Assumptions~\ref{Assumptions_Theta}--\ref{Assumptions_analyticity}, that the equations \eqref{eq_equations_eqs} deterministically fix the filling fractions and that each segment $[\hat a_h^X, \hat b_h^X]$ contains exactly one band $(\alpha_h,\beta_h)$ of the equilibrium measure.

 There exists $\eps_0>0$ depending only on the constants in the assumptions and such that for any $\eps \in (0,\eps_0)$, any choice of pairwise disjoint segments $[\hat a_h^Y, \hat b_h^Y]$ indexed by $h \in [H]$ and satisfying
\[
\forall h \in [H]\qquad [\alpha_h-\eps ,\beta_h+\eps]\subset [\hat a_h^Y, \hat b_h^Y]\subset [\alpha_h-2\eps ,\beta_h+2\eps]\subset [\hat a_h^X, \hat b_h^X],
\]
and an \emph{integrality condition} spelled out below, there exists another discrete ensemble $Y$ with same number of segments $H$, same intensities of interactions $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$, and defined on segments $[\hat a_h^Y, \hat b_h^Y]$ indexed by $h \in [H]$, and there exists a constant $C > 0$ depending only on $\eps$ and on the constants in the assumptions for the ensemble $X$, having the following properties for $\N$ large enough depending only on the constants in the assumptions.
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item The ensemble $Y$ satisfies Assumptions~\ref{Assumptions_Theta}--\ref{Assumptions_analyticity} as well as Assumption~\ref{Assumptions_extra}, with constants that only depend on the constants in the assumptions for the ensemble $X$ and on $\eps$.
 \item There is an event $\mathcal{A}$ of probability at least $1-C\exp\big(-\frac{\N}{C}\big)$ in the ensemble $X$, such that the ensemble $Y$ is obtained by localizing to $\bigcup_{h = 1}^{H} [\hat{a}_h^Y,\hat{b}_h^Y]$ the ensemble $X$ conditioned on $\mathcal{A}$. In particular, the equilibrium measure for $Y$ coincides with the restriction to $\amsmathbb{A}^{Y}$ of the equilibrium measure for $X$.
 \item On $\mathcal{A}$, for any $h \in [H]$, each of the segments $[a_h^X,a_h^Y]$ either has no particles (if $[\hat{a}_h^{\prime\,X},\hat{a}_h^{\prime\,Y}]$ is void for $X$) or has no holes as in Definition~\ref{Definition_no_hole} (if $[\hat{a}_h^{\prime\,X},\hat{a}_h^{\prime\,Y}]$ is saturated for $X$). A similar property holds for the segments $[b_h^Y,b_h^X]$.
 \item For any $h \in [H]$, the filling fractions of the discrete ensemble $Y$ --- which are deterministic conditionally on $\mathcal{A}$ due to property 3. --- are obtained by subtracting from $\hat{n}_h^X$ the count of all particles in $[a_h^X,a_h^Y) \cup (b_h^Y,b_h^X]$ divided by $\N$ (there is something to subtract only if the corresponding rescaled and shifted segments are saturated for the ensemble $X$).
 \end{enumerate}
The aforementioned \emph{integrality condition} reads, for any $h \in [H]$
\begin{enumerate}
  \item If $a_h^X \neq -\infty$ and $[\hat a_h^{\prime\,X},\hat a_h^{\prime\,Y}]$ is void for $X$, we require $\N(\hat a_h^Y-\hat a_h^X)\in\amsmathbb Z_{\geq 0}$. If $a_1^X=-\infty$, we require that $\N \hat{a}_1^Y$ belongs to the lattice $\amsmathbb{L}$ in which $\ell_1$ varies.
  \item If $[\hat a_h^{\prime\,X},\hat a_h^{\prime\,Y}]$ is saturated for $X$, we require $\N(\hat a_h^Y-\hat a_h^X)\in \theta_{h,h} \amsmathbb Z_{\geq 0}$.
  \item Similar conditions are imposed on $\hat{b}_{h}^X,\hat{b}_h^Y$.
\end{enumerate}
We say that $Y$ is the localization of $X$ to $\amsmathbb{A}^{Y}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma conjugate-to-On of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $G$ be a compact Lie group, let $n\ge0$, and let $f_1,f_2\colon G\rightrightarrows {\textup{O}}(n)$ be homomorphisms. Then $f_1$ and $f_2$ are conjugate (i.e.\ homotopic in $\textup{Glo}$) if and only if for every $g\in G$ the two matrices $f_1(g)$ and $f_2(g)$ are conjugate in ${\textup{GL}}(n,{\mathbb{C}})$.
    \begin{proof}
        The condition is clearly necessary. To see that it is also sufficient, we first observe that $f_1$ and $f_2$ are conjugate if and only if they are conjugate as homomorphisms to ${\textup{GL}}(n,{\mathbb{R}})$ [broecker-tom-dieck]*{Exercise II.6.10.5}, i.e.\ if and only if the two representations $f_1^*{\mathbb{R}}^n$ and $f_2^*{\mathbb{R}}^n$ are isomorphic \emph{without} regarding the inner product. We will show that these representations become isomorphic after scalar extension to ${\mathbb{C}}$; forgetting the complex structure will then in particular give an isomorphism $f_1^*{\mathbb{R}}^n\oplus f_1^*{\mathbb{R}}^n\cong f_2^*{\mathbb{R}}^n\oplus f_2^*{\mathbb{R}}^n$ and counting the multiplicities of irreducible representations on each side yields the claim.

        To prove that $f_1^*{\mathbb{C}}^n$ and $f_2^*{\mathbb{C}}^n$ are isomorphic, it will suffice to show that their characters $\chi_i\colon g\mapsto\text{Tr}(f_i(g))$ agree [broecker-tom-dieck]*{Theorem II.4.12}. This follows at once from cyclic invariance of the trace and the assumption that $f_1(g)$ be conjugate to $f_2(g)$ for each fixed $g\in G$.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma conjugate-to-On of arXiv:2608.28504

[Lemma 22 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] Let $X=(X_{1},\dots,X_{n})$ and $Y=(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n})$ be vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. Then
\[
\prod_{i=1}^{n} X_{i}-\prod_{i=1}^{n} Y_{i}
=
\sum_{k=1}^{n}
(X_{k}-Y_{k})
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k-1} X_{i}\right)
\left(\prod_{i=k+1}^{n} Y_{i}\right).
\]

[Corollary cor:lumped-PF-bounds of arXiv:2605.16244, 'Analysis of a twisted Bose--Einstein Markov chain with applications to sampling Catalan st'] For $n\ge2$,
\[
 \lambda_2(\overline K_{\mathrm{PF}})
 =\frac{n}{2(n+1)}
 =\lambda_{2,\mathrm{PF}}.
\]
Moreover, for every $t\ge1$,
\[
 \max\left\{
  \frac{n}{n+2}\lambda_{2,\mathrm{PF}}^t,\,
  1-\frac{t+\log3}{\log n}
 \right\}
 \le d_{\mathrm{IPF}}(t)
 \le n\sqrt{\frac{n+1}{2}}\lambda_{2,\mathrm{PF}}^{t/2}.
\]
Consequently, for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$,
\[
 t_{\mathrm{mix},\mathrm{IPF}}(\varepsilon)=\Theta_\varepsilon(\log n).
\]

Let {x_t}_{t=1}^n be a sequence of dependent random vectors in R^p with zero mean E[x_t] = 0, where p = p_n can diverge much faster than sample size n (p >> n). The coordinate-wise sample mean vector is x_bar_n = (1/n) * sum_{t=1}^n x_t in R^p, with individual components x_bar_{i,n} = (1/n) * sum_{t=1}^n x_{i,t} for 1 <= i <= p.
E[x_t] = 0 for all t
p = p_n -> infinity as n -> infinity
title: High-Dimensional Sample Mean Vector

body:
[Lemma lem:beta.mgf of arXiv:2607.02013, 'Resolution of the Detection Threshold Conjecture for Random Geometric Graphs in the $d>n$ '] Let $x$ is sampled uniformly at random from the unit sphere $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Then $x$ is zero-mean and subgaussian with variance proxy $1/d$.

\begin{proof}
Fix a vector $v\in\mathbb{R}^d$.
Let $t=\|v\|$. Then $Z=\langle v,x\rangle/t$ is a symmetric random variable, and
    \[
    B=Z^2\sim\operatorname{Beta}\bigg(\frac{1}{2},
        \frac{d-1}{2}\bigg)\,.
    \]
It follows from the moment-generating function of the beta distribution that
    \[
    \mathbb E_x[\mathop{\rm exp}(\langle v,x\rangle)]
    = \mathbb E [\mathop{\rm exp}(tZ)]
    = 1 + \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{t^{2k}}{(2k)!}
        \prod_{r=0}^{k-1} \frac{1+2r}{d+2r} 
    \le 1 + \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{t^{2k}}{k! (2d)^k}
    = \mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(\frac{\|v\|^2}{2d}\bigg)\,,
    \]
which proves the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:beta.mgf of arXiv:2607.02013

[Thm Rakhmanov of arXiv:2412.00593, 'A new approach to strong convergence II.\\The classical ensembles'] Let $M, q\in \mathbb{N}$ with $q \leq M$, and let $h\in \mathcal{P}_q$.
Then
$$
	\sobnorm{h}{0}{[-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}]} 
	\leq C \max_{k=1,\ldots,2M} 
	\left| h\left( -1 + \tfrac{2k-1}{2 M} \right) \right|,
$$
where $C$ is a universal constant.
title: Rakhmanov

[Definition 3 of arXiv:2607.17662, 'On the Strong Law of Large Numbers under Sublinear Expectations'] A sublinear expectation $\mathbb{E} : \mathcal{H} \to \mathbb{R}$ is said to be \textit{continuous} if it satisfies:
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item[(1)] \textit{Lower-continuity:} If $X_n \uparrow X$, then
			$\mathbb{E}[X_n] \uparrow \mathbb{E}[X]$, where $0 \le X_n$, $X \in \mathcal{H}$.
			
			\item[(2)] \textit{Upper-continuity:} If $X_n \downarrow X$, then
			$\mathbb{E}[X_n] \downarrow \mathbb{E}[X]$, where $0 \le X_n$, $X \in \mathcal{H}$.
		\end{enumerate}
		
		A capacity $V : \mathcal{F} \to [0,1]$ is called a \textit{continuous capacity} if it satisfies:
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item[(1)] \textit{Lower-continuity:} If $A_n \uparrow A$, then
			$V(A_n) \uparrow V(A)$, where $A_n, A \in \mathcal{F}$.
			
			\item[(2)] \textit{Upper-continuity:} If $A_n \downarrow A$, then
			$V(A_n) \downarrow V(A)$, where $A_n, A \in \mathcal{F}$.
		\end{enumerate}
title: Definition 3 of arXiv:2607.17662

body: In probability theory, statistics and related fields, a Poisson point process is a type of mathematical object that consists of points randomly located on a mathematical space with the essential feature that the points occur independently of one another. The process's name derives from the fact that the number of points in any given finite region follows a Poisson distribution. The process and the distribution are named after French mathematician Siméon Denis Poisson. The process itself was discovered independently and repeatedly in several settings, including experiments on radioactive decay, telephone call arrivals and actuarial science.
title: Poisson point process

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Let finitely many symmetric tensors T_v of degrees k_v>=3 have distinct formal labels z_v. Form the formal Gaussian Hermite density ratio generated by exp(sum_v z_v T_v:t^(k_v)/k_v!), using probabilists Hermite tensors. For a complete Wick pairing with loopless contraction multigraph G and no isolated vertices, the grouping weight in the coefficient multilinear in the labels of the formal entropy integral (1+q)log(1+q)-q, after common tensor contractions and endpoint factorials are extracted, is chi_G derivative at one. Consequently disconnected graphs and graphs with an articulation vertex have zero weight; parallel edges are allowed. The identity is finite formal algebra: it does not assert convergence of an unbounded-input entropy series. The proof counts partitions of vertices into independent sets and differentiates chi_G(x)=sum_r S_G(r)(x)_r at x=1.
Finite formal coefficient extraction with distinct tensor labels
Probabilists multivariate Hermite normalization
Complete Wick pairing, no self-loop and no isolated vertex
No analytic convergence assumption is implicit

Target 1 finite algebraic lemma, proof draft, unaudited. The identity
may be known; novelty is unestablished. This lemma alone is not a
large-size matrix universality theorem.

Use probabilists' multivariate Hermite tensors, generated by
exp(t.x-|t|^2/2). Let a finite list of symmetric tensors T_v have
degrees k_v>=3. Give every tensor its own formal scalar label z_v.
Form the formal Gaussian density ratio whose Hermite generating
series is exp(sum_v z_v T_v:t^(k_v)/k_v!). Let q be this density ratio
minus one. Consider the coefficient multilinear in all z_v in the
formal entropy integral of (1+q)log(1+q)-q.

Fix a complete Wick pairing of the tensor endpoints. It cannot have
an edge between two endpoints in the same Hermite factor. Its
contraction multigraph G has tensor labels as vertices. Assume it
has no self-loops and no isolated vertices. Parallel edges are allowed.
After extracting the common tensor contractions and endpoint
factorials, the remaining grouping weight is exactly

                             chi'_G(1),             (1)

where chi_G is the usual chromatic polynomial of the underlying
simple graph. In particular the weight vanishes if G is disconnected
or has an articulation vertex. Two vertices joined by parallel edges
are allowed as one block and have weight one.

Proof. In a single density factor, extracting the product of a set of
distinct z-labels from the exponential gives that set's tensors in
one normal-ordered Hermite tensor. The factorial from the exponential
is canceled by its permutations of distinct labels. Thus a product
of r factors q assigns the vertices to r ordered nonempty groups.
For the fixed Wick pairing to be allowed, each group must be an
independent set of G. If S_G(r) counts partitions into r unordered
nonempty independent sets, there are r! such ordered assignments.

The scalar formal identity

 (1+q)log(1+q)-q=sum_(r>=2) (-1)^r q^r/[r(r-1)]

therefore gives grouping weight

                sum_(r>=2) (-1)^r (r-2)! S_G(r).     (2)

These are finite sums: r never exceeds the number of tensor labels.
Proper colorings with x available colors are counted by

                        chi_G(x)=sum_r S_G(r)(x)_r,

where (x)_r=x(x-1)...(x-r+1). This polynomial identity follows first
at each nonnegative integer x by grouping colorings according to
their nonempty color classes, then identically for all x. Since G
has an edge, S_G(1)=0. For r>=2,

                  (x)_r' at x=1=(-1)^(r-2)(r-2)!.

Differentiating the finite polynomial proves (1).

If G has at least two connected components, each has an edge because
there are no isolated vertices. Each component's chromatic polynomial
vanishes at x=1, so the product has a double zero there.

If G is connected and has an articulation vertex a, split it into
two nonempty edge-containing subgraphs G1,G2 meeting only at a.
Color a first. For every positive integer x, independently color
G1,G2 with that same color at a. This proves

                       chi_G(x)=chi_G1(x)chi_G2(x)/x

as a polynomial identity after multiplying by x. Both factors on the
right vanish at x=1. The denominator is nonzero there, so again
chi'_G(1)=0. This also covers further decompositions into blocks.

The argument is for distinct formal tensor labels, so equal-valued
tensors can be substituted afterwards. Dividing out the appropriate
label multiplicities does not change any of the vanishing statements.
Likewise replacing parallel edges by a single edge affects Wick
pairing multiplicities but not which groupings are legal. QED.

As a concrete check, the order-eight entropy star containing C8 and
two C4 tensors has an articulation vertex. In direct Hermite algebra,
the degree-eight chaos tensor is C8+35 sym(C4 tensor C4). The cross
term in its squared norm contributes +35/8!=+1/1152 times the fully
contracted star. The cubic entropy term contributes
-1/[2(4!)^2]=-1/1152 times the same contraction. They cancel exactly.
Dropping the composite term from the Hermite tensor would miss this.

[Dfn 4. dfn: resistance forms of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Resistance form and resistance metric, [Kigami_12_Resistance]}] 
  
  Let $F$ be a non-empty set.
  A pair $(\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{F})$ is called a \textit{resistance form} on $F$ if it satisfies the following conditions.
  \begin{enumerate} [label=(RF\arabic*), leftmargin = *]
    \item 
          The symbol $\mathcal{F}$ is a linear subspace of the collection of functions $\{ f : F \to \mathbb{R} \}$ 
          containing constants,
          and $\mathcal{E}$ is a non-negative symmetric bilinear form on $\mathcal{F}$
          such that $\mathcal{E}(f,f)=0$ if and only if $f$ is constant on $F$.
    \item 
          Let $\sim$ be the equivalence relation on $\mathcal{F}$ defined by saying $f \sim g$ if and only if $f-g$ is constant on $F$.
          Then $(\mathcal{F}/\sim, \mathcal{E})$ is a Hilbert space.
    \item
          If $x \neq y$, then there exists a function $f \in \mathcal{F}$ such that $f(x) \neq f(y)$.
    \item 
          For any $x, y \in F$,
          \begin{equation} 
            R_{(\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{F})}(x,y)
            \coloneqq
            \sup
            \left\{
            \frac{|f(x) - f(y)|^{2}}{\mathcal{E}(f,f)}
            :
            f \in \mathcal{F},\
            \mathcal{E}(f,f) > 0
            \right\}
            < \infty.
          \end{equation}     
    \item
          If $\bar{f}\coloneqq  (f \wedge 1) \vee 0$,
          then $\bar{f} \in \mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{E}(\bar{f}, \bar{f}) \leq \mathcal{E}(f,f)$ for any $f \in \mathcal{F}$.
  \end{enumerate}

[Lem 89 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] If $F$ is a grounded set and $F' = F \cup g$ is an enlargement in direction $s \in S\cup S^{-1}$, then
\[F'\cap sF' = (F\cap sF) \cup \{g\},\]
\[F'\cap s^{-1}F' = (F\cap s^{-1}F)\cup\{s^{-1}g\},\]
and
\[F'\cap tF' = F\cap tF \quad \hbox{for all}\ t \in (S\cup S^{-1})\setminus \{s,s^{-1}\}.\]
title: Lem 89 of arXiv:2507.08909

[Corollary cor:zero-gap-special-environment of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Let a full-centered letter $\mathsf C_i$ occur as an external typed
singleton immediately adjacent to a complete paired-marked or
literal-$W$ aggregate-Ricci block.  Keep the latter block and every joint
context intact.  On the plane-star decomposition
$\operatorname{ran}\mathsf J\oplus\operatorname{ran}\mathsf Q$, the
singleton multiplication map has the exact form
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}0&\mathsf S^-\\
                 \mathsf S^+&\mathsf V\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \|\mathsf S^-\|=\|\mathsf S^+\|\le N^{-1/2},
 \qquad
 \|\mathsf V\|\le1 .
\tag{3.3.1w$_{6a}$}
\]
Consequently the unsplit zero-gap environment has unit
operator/projective cost, while any exposed seed has its displayed
$N^{-1/2}$ debit.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Exact integral manipulation, Palm calculus, mass transport, limiting obstruction or conditional construction Result: Consider two equal radial densities proportional at large r to exp(b*r)*(1+r)^(-a), a>1. On a large L1 sphere, the split at radius s has weight proportional to (1+s)^(-a)*(1+R-s)^(-a). The contribution from epsilon*R<=s<=(1-epsilon)*R is O(R^(1-2a)), whereas either fixed endpoint region contributes order R^(-a). Their ratio tends to zero because a>1. Thus equal exponential growth alone need not force both factor radii to diverge; endpoint concentration can replace the tensor product of two boundary laws. Check: In the middle interval both denominators are bounded below by constants times R^a and its length is at most R. Near an endpoint, one denominator remains bounded while the other has order R^a. These independent upper and lower estimates establish the comparison. Obstruction: The model is not asserted to be a homogeneous geometric counterexample. A general theorem needs precise radial regularity, the endpoint mixture weights, and nondegeneracy of the resulting ideal diagram.

body:
[Lemma lem:tech_extent_lowerbound of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Let $\bm{Y}$ be a nonzero pure-jump L\'evy process on $\mathbb{R}^d$, let $\psi_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{u})$ denote its L\'evy-Khintchine exponent and $\nu_{\bm{Y}}$ its L\'evy measure.\\
{\normalfont(a)} If $\bm{Y}$ has finite variation and nonzero drift with direction $\bm{u}_*\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Then $|\psi_{\bm{Y}}(x\bm{u}_*)|\geqslant cx$ for some $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $x>0$.\\
{\normalfont(b)} Suppose there exist a locally finite measure $\rho$ on $(0,\infty)$ and a probability measure $\sigma$ on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ with
\[
\nu_{\bm{Y}}(A)
\geqslant \int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}\int_{(0,\infty)}\1_A(x\bm{v})\rho(\mathrm{d} x)\sigma(\mathrm{d}\bm{v}),
\qquad A\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}).
\]
Define $\Upsilon(x):=\int_{(0,x)}r^2\rho(\mathrm{d} r)$ for $x>0$, and, given any $c\in (0,1)$, suppose that $C_{c,\bm{u}_*}\coloneqq\{\bm{v}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}:|\langle \bm{u}_*,\bm{v}\rangle|\geqslant c\}$ has positive $\sigma$-measure $m:=\sigma(C_{c,\bm{u}_*})>0$ for some $\bm{u}_*\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Then we have
\[
|\psi_{\bm{Y}}(x\bm{u}_*)|\geqslant \frac{c^2m}{3}r^2\Upsilon(x^{-1})
\qquad\text{for all }x>0.
\]
In particular, if $c_\delta:=\inf_{x\in(0,1)}x^{\delta-2}\Upsilon(x)>0$ for some $\delta\in(0,2)$, then $|\psi_{\bm{Y}}(x\bm{u}_*)|\geqslant (c_\delta c^2m/3)x^{\delta}$, $x>1$.
title: Lemma lem:tech_extent_lowerbound of arXiv:2411.03609

[Definition 3 of arXiv:2604.13819, 'Convolution, cumulants and infinitesimal generators in the formal power series ring'] For $t\in \mathbb{R}\setminus \mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$, we define the \emph{$t$-deformed cumulants} $\{\kappa_{i}^{t}(A)\}_{i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}}$ of $A \in U$ by
$$
C^t[A](z) \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^\infty \kappa_i^t(A)z^i \coloneqq -\frac{z}{t} \frac{d}{dz}\log \left(1+ \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{t^{k}}{(t)_{\underline{k}}} a_{k} z^{k} \right).
$$
If $A\in U_d$ for some $d\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}$, we define the \emph{$d$-deformed cumulants} $\{\kappa_{i}^{d}(A)\}_{i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}}$ by
$$
C^d[A](z) \coloneqq \lim_{t\to d} C^t[A](z)\coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^\infty \kappa_i^d(A)z^i  = -\frac{z}{d} \frac{d}{dz}\log\left(1+ \sum_{k=1}^d \frac{d^{k}}{(d)_{\underline{k}}} a_{k} z^{k}\right).
$$
We call $C^t[A](z)$ the \emph{$t$-deformed cumulant transform} of $A$.
title: Definition 3 of arXiv:2604.13819

body:
[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2605.02002, 'Glauber dynamics for random field Ising models on bounded degree graphs and MLSI'] Let $\alpha\in(0,1)$, $G=(V,E)$ be a graph that has $\alpha$-stretched exponential growth, and the RFIM measure $\mu_G$ satisfies $\operatorname{WSM}(C)$ for some $C>0$. Further assume that $h=(h_u)_{u\in V}$ are i.i.d. random variables with a symmetric distribution around 0. Then for any $\epsilon>0$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$, we can find a randomized algorithm which runs in time $|V|^c$ for $c=c(\epsilon,\delta,\beta,C,\alpha,C_\alpha)>0$ and then generates a random configuration $\sigma^{\operatorname{alg}}\in\{-1,+1\}^V$ with law $\mu_G^{\operatorname{alg}}$ such that with $\mathbb{P}_h$-probability $1-\delta$,
$$
d_{TV}(\mu_G,\mu_G^{\operatorname{alg}})\leq\epsilon.
$$This randomized algorithm is the same as the algorithm defined in \cite{el2026fast}, Theorem 1.4, but defined on general graphs instead of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and with a different input of parameters. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 5 of arXiv:2605.02002

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Assume that a random variable $f:X\to\mathbb R$ has density $\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, in the sense that its law is given by $d\mu(x)=\varphi(x)dx$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The density must be positive, $\varphi\geq0$, and of mass one, $\int_\mathbb R\varphi(x)dx=1$.

\item $\mu(Z)=\int_Z\varphi(x)dx$, which can stand as an alternative definition for $\varphi$.

\item $E(\phi(f))=\int_\mathbb R\phi(x)\varphi(x)dx$, which can stand as well as a definition for $\varphi$.

\item The CDF is $F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x\varphi(t)dt$, and conversely, we have $\varphi(x)=F'(x)$.
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Theorem 42 (Physical fourth-moment theorem: exact zero stratum) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let $q\ge2$ and
\[
 X_{n,a}=I_q^{W_n}(f_{n,a}),
 \qquad
 \sup_n\sum_{a=1}^dq!\norm{f_{n,a}}^2<\infty.
\]
Write $\Sigma_n=\Cov(X_n)$, fix a free ultrafilter $\mathcal U$, and put
\[
 \xi_a=[f_{n,a}]_{\mathcal U}\in\cH_q,
 \qquad
 \Sigma=\Ulim\Sigma_n,
 \qquad
 \kappa_{n,a}=\E[X_{n,a}^4]-3\E[X_{n,a}^2]^2.
\]
The represented terminal has the intrinsic splitting
\begin{equation}
 T_a=\mathbb U_q^{-1}\xi_a
 =A_a^{\phys}+G_a^{\phys},
 \quad
 A_a^{\phys}=\mathbb U_q^{-1}P_{\cD_q}\xi_a,
 \quad
 G_a^{\phys}=\mathbb U_q^{-1}P_{\cK_q}\xi_a.
 
\end{equation}
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 \item $\displaystyle\sum_{a=1}^d\mathfrak Q_q(\xi_a)=0$,
 equivalently $\Ulim\sum_a\kappa_{n,a}=0$;
 \item for every $a$ and $1\le r<q$,
 $
  \Ulim\norm{f_{n,a}\otimes_rf_{n,a}}=0
 $;
 \item $\xi_a\in\cK_q$ for every $a$, equivalently
 $P_{\cD_q}\xi=0$;
 \item $A^{\phys}=0$ (equivalently, the limiting active part of
 the reduced Hilbert--Stein trajectory vanishes) and the represented
 laws converge along $\mathcal U$ to $N_d(0,\Sigma)$;
 \item for every $a$,
 $
  \Ulim\E[X_{n,a}^4]=3\Sigma_{aa}^2
 $.
\end{enumerate}
When these conditions hold, every mixed proper contraction also
vanishes:
\begin{equation}
 \Ulim\norm{f_{n,a}\otimes_rf_{n,b}}=0
 \qquad(1\le r<q,\ 1\le a,b\le d).
 
\end{equation}
Moreover, there is a finite constant $C_{q,d}$, depending only on
$(q,d)$, such that for every $n$ and $t\in\R^d$,
\begin{equation}
 \left|
  \E e^{it\cdot X_n}
  -e^{-\frac12t^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_nt}
 \right|
 \le C_{q,d}|t|^2
 \left(\sum_{a=1}^d\kappa_{n,a}\right)^{1/2}.
 
\end{equation}
Componentwise, the exact carré-du-champ comparison is
\begin{equation}
 \frac1{3q}\kappa_{n,a}
 \le
 \Var\bigl(\Gamma(X_{n,a},X_{n,a})\bigr)
 \le
 \frac{q-1}{3q}\kappa_{n,a}.
 
\end{equation}
Thus the fourth cumulants detect exactly, and not merely sufficiently,
the disappearance of the decomposable physical sector.

  \frac{1}{2}\bigl[\mathcal{L}_k^A + (\mathcal{L}_k^A)^\dagger\bigr],

[Corollary C:parabolic-profile of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take $\kappa \in (0, 1/2)$ and $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n/m \in [\kappa, \kappa^{-1}]$. Consider the process 
$$
\bar Y(j) = Y(1, j; n, m) - \mu(n, m+1- j), \qquad j\in\llbracket1,m \rrbracket,
$$
and fix a point $j_0 \in [1, (1-\kappa) m]$. Take any $\delta_0 > 0$. There exists some $c > 0$ depending only on $\kappa, \delta_0$, such that for all $\epsilon \in (0, n^{-1/3})$ we have
$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{j \in \llbracket1, m \rrbracket} \bar Y(j) - \frac{\delta_0|j-j_0|^2}{m} \ge \epsilon m\right) \le 2\exp(- c \epsilon^{3/2}m). 
$$
title: Corollary C:parabolic-profile of arXiv:2604.10020

body:
[Proposition prop:sharppinfini of arXiv:2603.00773, 'Long-time $L^p$ Wasserstein contraction for diffusion processes without global dissipativi'] Under Assumptions~(Assum:basic of the paper) and (assum:controllable of the paper), assume furthermore either one of these two conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\nabla b$ is bounded.
\item For any $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$, there exists $R>0$ such that for all  $t,\varepsilon>0$,
\[\mathbb P_x\left(|X_t-y|\leqslant \varepsilon\, \text{and}\, |X_s|\leqslant R\ \forall s\in[0,t]\right) >0\,.\]
\end{enumerate}
 Then, for any $t\geqslant 0$, $x\in\mathbb R^d$ and $v\in\mathbb S^{d-1}$,
\[\lim_{p\rightarrow \infty} \sup_{v\in\mathbb S^{d-1}} \left[ \mathbb E_x\left( |\Phi_t^X v|^p\right)\right]^{1/p} \geqslant \overline{\kappa}_\infty(t)\,.\]
In particular, $\lim_{p\rightarrow\infty} \kappa_p(t) \geqslant \overline{\kappa}_\infty(t)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:sharppinfini of arXiv:2603.00773

[Definition 37 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] \rm
 
 A \([0,\infty]\)-valued function
 $A_t(\omega),\ t \ge 0,\ \omega \in \Omega$
 is a PCAF if the following hold:
 \begin{itemize}
  \item[(A.1)] for each $t \ge 0$, $A_t(\cdot)$ is $\c{F}_t$-measurable,
  \item[(A.2)]
       there exist a set $\Lambda \in \c{F}_{\infty}$ called a defining set, and
       an exceptional set $N \subset E$ such that $\b{P}_x(\Lambda) = 1$
       for any $x \in E \setminus N$ and $\theta_t \Lambda \subset \Lambda$
       for any $t > 0$, and moreover,
       for each $\omega \in \Lambda$, ${A}_0(\omega) = 0$,
       $|A_t(\omega)| < \infty$ for any $t < \zeta(\omega)$,
       $A_t(\omega) = {A}_{\zeta(\omega)}(\omega)$ for any
       $t \ge \zeta(\omega)$ and
       \begin{align}
	{A}_{t + s}(\omega) = {A}_s(\omega) + {A}_t(\theta_s \omega),\
	\text{for any $t,s \ge 0$},
       \end{align}
  \item[(A.3)]
       for each $\omega \in \Lambda$, the map
       $t \mapsto {A}_t(\omega)$ is non-negative and continuous on
       $[0,\infty)$, where $\Lambda$ is the set defined in the above condition.
 \end{itemize}

body: In abstract algebra, an abelian group $(G,+)$ is called finitely generated if there exist finitely many elements $x_{1},\dots,x_{s}$ in $G$ such that every $x$ in $G$ can be written in the form $x=n_{1}x_{1}+n_{2}x_{2}+\cdots +n_{s}x_{s}$ for some integers $n_{1},\dots,n_{s}$. In this case, we say that the set $\{x_{1},\dots,x_{s}\}$ is a generating set of $G$ or that $x_{1},\dots,x_{s}$ generate $G$. So, finitely generated abelian groups can be thought of as a generalization of cyclic groups.

[Theorem 1 (General mixed-Sellke fluid limit) of arXiv:2608.22122, '2608.22122'] Under the stochastic construction and notation of Section~\ref{sec:model}, for every finite \(T>0\),
\[
\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}
\left\|
\bigl(s_N(t),\iota_N(t),r_N(t),A_N(t)\bigr)
-
\bigl(s(t),\iota(t),r(t),A(t)\bigr)
\right\|
\xlongrightarrow{\Pp}0
\]
as $N\to\infty.$

The deterministic limit is characterized by the  initial-value problem
\[
\dot A(t)
=
\tau\bigl[1-r_0-s_0G(A(t))\bigr]
-\gamma A(t),
\qquad
A(0)=0,
\]
together with
\[
s(t)=s_0G(A(t)),
\]
\[
r(t)=r_0+\frac{\gamma}{\tau}A(t),
\]
and
\[
\iota(t)=1-s(t)-r(t).
\]

Equivalently,
\[
A(t)=\tau\int_0^t\iota(u)\,du.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 13 of arXiv:2607.22416, 'A multi-player optimal stopping game based on a spider Brownian bridge'] Suppose that $p=0.5$, $\mathcal{G}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{1}$ are given by $\mathcal{G}_{1}(z)=z - \alpha$ and $\mathcal{L}_{1}(z)=  \theta z$, and that $\mathcal{G}_{2}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{2}$ are given by $\mathcal{G}_{2}(z)=-z - \alpha$ and $\mathcal{L}_{2}(z)=  -\theta z$.
 
The game admits at most three symmetric threshold-type Nash equilibria.

If $\theta \geq 1 + \max \{ 2 \alpha \left[ \alpha + (\alpha^2 + 1)\psi(\alpha) \right], \frac{1}{\alpha}(4+\alpha^2)\psi(\frac{\alpha}{2}) \}$ then there are no symmetric threshold-type Nash equilibria.

If $\theta \leq 1$ then there is a unique symmetric threshold-type Nash equilibria.

There are cases with more than one symmetric threshold-type Nash equilibria.

Let xi be a centred Gaussian element of a separable Hilbert space H with covariance eigenvalues lambda_1 >= lambda_2 >= ..., Lambda_k^2 = sum_{j>=k} lambda_j^2 (k = 1, 2), and let p_xi(x, a) be the density of ||xi - a||^2. (Thm 2.6) For every a in H: sup_{x>=0} p_xi(x, a) <= C kappa(Sigma_xi), C absolute, where kappa is defined in (2.1) and 0.9 (Lambda_1 Lambda_2)^{-1/2} <= kappa <= 1.8 (Lambda_1 Lambda_2)^{-1/2}; in particular the density is <= C' (lambda_1 lambda_2)^{-1/2}, uniformly in the dimension and the shift a. The proof bounds the density of the two-term sum (sqrt(lambda_1)Z_1 - a_1)^2 + (sqrt(lambda_2)Z_2 - a_2)^2 by 1/(2 sqrt(lambda_1 lambda_2)). (Thm 2.1) For Gaussian xi, eta: sup_x |P(||xi - a|| <= x) - P(||eta|| <= x)| <= C (kappa(Sigma_xi) + kappa(Sigma_eta)) (||lambda_xi - lambda_eta||_1 + ||a||^2).

 A_t=eta*[sum_i lambda_i*g_i,t^2/P_i,t^2]

 S_t=eta*max_i(lambda_i/P_i,t).

If A_t->38, each physical coordinate approaches EITHER its origin OR
its exact alternating scalar cycle. A cycling coordinate necessarily
has theta_i>38 and position amplitude a_i=eta/38-epsilon/lambda_i>0.
Consequently every corrected variance denominator CONVERGES, without
assuming this convergence. This includes parameters where the scalar cycle linearization has a
unit-modulus multiplier; it also permits stable and unstable cycles.
This conditional classification asserts neither their attraction nor
the generic occurrence of tracking. In particular theta=60 is not
being described as a neutral or attracting cycle.

Moreover the following are equivalent:

 (GAP) A_t->38 and liminf_t S_t>38;

 (GRADIENT) for some permutation(i,j), theta_j>38 and exactly one of

 CYCLE TYPE:
  theta_i>38, |g_i,t|->eta*lambda_i/38-epsilon>0,
  g_j,t/g_i,t->0;                                      (C)

 CRITICAL ORIGIN TYPE:
  theta_i=38, ||g_t||->0,
  g_j,t^2/(g_i,t^2+g_j,t^2)->0.                         (O)

In either type S_t->theta_j>38. Condition(C) forces coordinate i to
its cycle and j to its origin. Condition(O) has both coordinates at
their origins and an asymptotically critical-coordinate gradient.
In particular a persistent asymptotic top gap is IMPOSSIBLE if one
cap is strictly above38 and the other strictly below38. If both caps
are at most38, S_t<=38 at EVERY time, also excluding(GAP).

For epsilon=eta^p, substitute theta_i=eta^(1-p)*lambda_i. At p=1,

place of theta_i, with cycling GRADIENT amplitude eta*(lambda_i/38-1) and

give a finite-width band estimate, and does not equate liminf S>38
with the weaker property S_t>38 at every finite time while S_t->38.

Let I be the cycling set. Then

 P_i -> eta*lambda_i/38 for i in I,
 P_j -> epsilon for j outside I,
 S_t -> max({38 if I is nonempty} union {theta_j:j outside I}). (1)

The empty maximum is never needed: there are two coordinates.

[Theorem thm: Levy of arXiv:2411.17109, 'On the maximal correlation of some stochastic processes'] Let $(X_t,Y_t)$ be a two-dimensional L\'{e}vy process with the characteristic triple $(b,\Sigma,\nu)$. Define
\[\rho=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\Sigma_{12}/\sqrt{\Sigma_{11}\Sigma_{22}}, & \Sigma_{11}\Sigma_{22}>0,\\
0, & \Sigma_{11}\Sigma_{22}=0.
\end{array}\right.\]
Let $\mathrm{Op}(\nu)$ be the minimal constant $s$ such that the inequality
\[\int_{\mathbb{R}^2}\varphi(x)\psi(y)\,\nu(\mathrm{d}x,\mathrm{d}y)\leq s\sqrt{\int_{\mathbb{R}^2}(\varphi(x))^2\,\nu(\mathrm{d}x,\mathrm{d}y)\int_{\mathbb{R}^2}(\psi(y))^2\,\nu(\mathrm{d}x,\mathrm{d}y)}\]
holds for all measurable functions $\varphi(x)$ and $\psi(y)$ such that $\varphi(0)=\psi(0)=0$. Then we have that
\[R((X_t)_{t\geq 0},(Y_t)_{t\geq 0})=\max(|\rho|,\mathrm{Op}(\nu)).\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm: Levy of arXiv:2411.17109

body:
ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Examine whether the reflection-positivity chessboard argument can be pushed down from q >= q_c(d) large to q = 3 in d = 3 using improved contour entropy bounds. Result: The Kotecky-Shlosman argument proves a first-order transition when the entropy of contours (bounded by e^{c |contour|}) is beaten by the energy gain, which requires q large enough that log q exceeds a lattice-dependent constant; in d = 3 the best constants give q >= some number in the tens. Improving to q = 3 needs the exact contour entropy, which is not available; numerically the d = 3, q = 3 transition is weakly first order with a tiny latent heat, so any argument must be sharp to within a few percent, beyond what chessboard estimates give. Alternative route through the random-cluster representation: discontinuity is equivalent to non-uniqueness of the infinite-volume random-cluster measure at p_c, i.e. to the wired measure having an infinite cluster at p_c while the free one does not; for q > 4 in d = 2 this was done via the six-vertex transfer matrix, a planar tool. No d = 3 substitute. No result. Obstruction: Contour-entropy constants are far from sharp and the two-dimensional transfer-matrix route has no three-dimensional analogue.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0048-discontinuity-of-the-potts-phase-transition-on-z-d-for-q-3-d-3
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved

		\|Q_{s,t}^nf\|_{p'}\leq N(t-s)^{\frac{d}{2p'}-\frac{d}{2p}}\|f\|_{p}.
		\ee

[Proposition 26 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] If \(X\sim Q\), then \(X\) has a unique maximiser on \(I\) almost surely.
Put \(D_m=E_m\cap I\).  For all sufficiently large \(m\), this set is
nonempty; let \(S_m(f)\) denote the leftmost maximiser of \(f\) on \(D_m\).
If \(x_m,x\in\mathcal X\), \(x_m\to x\) locally uniformly, and \(x\) has a
unique maximiser \(S_I(x)\) on \(I\), then
\(S_m(x_m)\to S_I(x)\).

body:
[Lemma 2 of arXiv:2607.25645, 'Estimates of the total variation distance between laws of Sobolev mappings on Gaussian spa'] Let
$
f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)\colon \mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^k
$
be a mapping with $f_j\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ for $j=1,\ldots,k$.
Let
\[
J_f(x)=\bigl(\partial_i f_j(x)\bigr)_{\substack{1\le i\le n\\1\le j\le k}}
\]
be the Jacobian matrix of $f$, viewed as a $k\times n$ matrix, and let
$M_f=J_fJ_f^*$
be the corresponding Gram (Malliavin) matrix. 
Then, for $\Delta_f:=\det M_f$ and $A_f:=\operatorname{adj}(M_f)$, the following pointwise estimates hold:
\[
|\nabla \Delta_f|
\le
2k^{1-\frac{k}{2}}\,
\Delta_f^{1/2}
\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^k |\nabla f_j|^2\Bigr)^{\frac{k-1}{2}}
\Bigl(\sum_{m=1}^k \|D^2 f_m\|_{\rm HS}^2\Bigr)^{1/2},
\]
and
\[
\sup_{|\theta|=1}
\Bigl|
\sum_{i,j=1}^k \theta_i
\langle \nabla f_j,\nabla (A_f)_{i,j}\rangle
\Bigr|
\le
5k^{\frac32-k}
\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^k |\nabla f_j|^2\Bigr)^{k-1}
\Bigl(\sum_{m=1}^k \|D^2 f_m\|_{\rm HS}^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.
\]

Let $S_n = \frac{1}{n} X_n^T X_n$ with $X_n = Z_n \Sigma_n^{1/2}$, where $Z_n$ is $n \times p$ with i.i.d. entries of mean $0$, variance $1$ and finite fourth moment, $\Sigma_n$ is positive semidefinite with $\|\Sigma_n\|$ bounded, $p/n \to c \in (0, \infty)$, and the spectral distribution of $\Sigma_n$ converges weakly to $H$. Let $F^{c,H}$ be the limiting spectral distribution of $S_n$ (the Marchenko-Pastur-Silverstein law) and let $[a, b]$ be a closed interval, $a > 0$, lying outside the support of $F^{c,H}$ and outside the supports of $F^{c_n, H_n}$ for all large $n$ (the finite-$n$ laws built from $c_n = p/n$ and $H_n$). Then almost surely no eigenvalue of $S_n$ lies in $[a, b]$ for all $n$ large enough: $\mathbb{P}(\text{no eigenvalue of } S_n \text{ in } [a, b] \text{ for all large } n) = 1$. Corollary (Bai-Yin 1993, the case $\Sigma = I$): $\lambda_{\max}(S_n) \to (1 + \sqrt c)^2$ and, for $c < 1$, $\lambda_{\min}(S_n) \to (1 - \sqrt c)^2$ almost surely - the Marchenko-Pastur edges - and the finite fourth moment is necessary for the largest eigenvalue to converge. Consequence used throughout: an eigenvalue of a sample covariance strictly above $\sigma^2(1 + \sqrt c)^2$ (by a fixed margin) cannot come from an identity-covariance bulk, which is what licenses the bulk edge as a detection threshold in the spiked model, in Gavish-Donoho denoising, and in the median-based noise estimate.

body: In mathematics, the ideal class group (or class group) of an algebraic number field $K$ is the quotient group $J_{K}/P_{K}$ where $J_{K}$ is the group of fractional ideals of the ring of integers of $K$, and $P_{K}$ is its subgroup of principal ideals. The class group is a measure of the extent to which unique factorization fails in the ring of integers of $K$. The order of the group, which is finite, is called the class number of $K$.

[Lemma 16 (properties of precomposition operators) of arXiv:2609.01093, 'Ideal MHD below the classical well-posedness threshold'] Let $X=\mathrm{id}+w:\Rn_y\to\Rn_x$ be an orientation-preserving
bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism such that
\[
 \|dX\|_{L^\infty}+\|(dX)^{-1}\|_{L^\infty}\le\mathfrak m,
 \qquad 0<J_-\le\det dX\le J_+.
\]
Put $\Ufield:=dw$ and $\Kmat:=(dX)^{-1}$, and assume
$\Ufield,\Kmat-\mathrm{Id}\in Y^{s-1,1}$.  Recall $\mathcal{C}_{X}^\pm f=f\circ X^\pm$. Then, for every $0\le r\le s$,
\begin{equation}
 \|\mathcal C_Xf\|_{H^r_y}\le C_{\mathrm{comp}}(X,r)\|f\|_{H^r_x},
 \qquad
 \|\mathcal C_X^{-1}u\|_{H^r_x}\le C_{\mathrm{comp}}(X,r)\|u\|_{H^r_y},
\end{equation}
where, with $k(r):=\max\{\lceil r\rceil-1,0\}$,
\[
 C_{\mathrm{comp}}(X,r)\le C(n,s,r,v_{\rm A},\mathfrak m,J_\pm)
 \big(1+\|\Ufield\|_{Y^{s-1,1}}
        +\|\Kmat-\mathrm{Id}\|_{Y^{s-1,1}}\big)^{k(r)}.
\]
If these bounds hold uniformly for $X=X(t)$ on a compact interval $I$ and, in addition,
\[
 w\in C(I;H^s),\qquad
 \Ufield,\Kmat-\mathrm{Id}\in C(I;Y^{s-1,1}),
\]
then $u\in C(I;H^r_y)$ implies
$\mathcal C_{X(t)}^{-1}u(t)\in C(I;H^r_x)$. Independently of the Sobolev
time-regularity hypothesis above, suppose that $X(t)$ and $X(t)^{-1}$ vary
locally uniformly on $I$ and that the Jacobian and bi-Lipschitz bounds are
uniform. Then, for every $1\le q<\infty$, every $t_0\in I$, and every
$g\in L^q$,
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{t\in I}\|\mathcal C_{X(t)}^{\pm1}\|_{L^q\to L^q}<\infty,\qquad
 \lim_{t\to t_0}\|\mathcal C_{X(t)}^{\pm1}g
 -\mathcal C_{X(t_0)}^{\pm1}g\|_{L^q}=0.
\end{equation}
title: properties of precomposition operators

[Dfn 99 (SDE coefficients with ideal smoothing) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Abbreviating $\rho\equiv\rho_{\vY}$ for the occupation density of $\vY$, let us define
	\begin{align}
	
	B^i(t,y)
	&\equiv
	\frac{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi(t,y)}{\rho*\varphi(t,y)}\,,\\
	A^{ij}(t,y)
	&\equiv \frac{\rho_{Q^{ij}}*\varphi(t,y)}{\rho*\varphi(t,y)}\,.
	
	\end{align}
Let $\Sigma(t,y)$ be a matrix square root of $A(t,y)$, and let 
$\hvX$ be the solution to the SDE (in $d$ dimensions)
	\beq
	d\hvX(t) = B(t,\hvX(t))\,dt+
		\Sigma(t,\hvX(t))\,dW(t)\,,
	\eeq
where $W$ is a $d$-dimensional standard Brownian motion, with the initial condition that $\hvX(0)$ equidistributed as $\hvY(0)$. \textbf{In the abstract discussion of this section, we assume $B$ and $\Sigma$ are sufficiently regular that $\hvX$ is the unique solution of the SDE.}

body:
[Proposition 12 of arXiv:2609.01574, 'A linear bound for Fujita's freeness conjecture'] Let $(X,\Delta)$ be a pair, let $W\subset X$ be an lc center, and assume that $(X,\Delta)$ is log canonical over the generic point of $W$. Let $\nu\colon Z=W^\nu\to W$ be the normalization. Then there are a discriminant $b$-divisor $\mathbf B$ and a moduli $b$-divisor $\mathbf M$ over $Z$ with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] The trace $B_Z$ is effective, and
\[
 \nu^*\bigl((K_X+\Delta)|_W\bigr)\sim_{\mathbb Q}K_Z+B_Z+M_Z.
\]
\item[(ii)] There exist a smooth quasi-projective variety $Z'$ and a projective birational morphism $p\colon Z'\to Z$ such that $\mathbf K_Z+\mathbf B=\overline{K_{Z'}+B_{Z'}}$, $\mathbf M=\overline{M_{Z'}}$, and
$$
 K_{Z'}+B_{Z'}+M_{Z'}\sim_{\mathbb Q}p^*\nu^*\bigl((K_X+\Delta)|_W\bigr).
$$
Moreover, if $Z$ is projective, then $Z'$ is projective and $M_{Z'}$ is nef.
\item[(iii)] Let $\widetilde Z\to Z$ be a birational model and let $P$ be a prime divisor on $\widetilde Z$. For every lc place $T$ of $(X,\Delta)$ with center $W$, choose a log resolution $\pi\colon\widetilde X\to X$ on which $T$ appears and for which the induced rational map $T\dashrightarrow\widetilde Z$ is a morphism $f_T\colon T\to\widetilde Z$. If $K_T+\Delta_T=(K_{\widetilde X}+\Delta_{\widetilde X})|_T$, then
\[
 1-\mult_P\mathbf B
 =\inf_T\sup\Bigl\{\lambda\in\mathbb R\ \Bigm|\
 (T,\Delta_T+\lambda f_T^*P)
 \text{ is sub-lc over }\eta_P\Bigr\}.
\]
\end{enumerate}

body:
Let $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ with $X$ an $n \times p$ design of full column rank (treated as fixed), $E[\varepsilon] = 0$, and $\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = \Omega = \operatorname{diag}(\omega_1^2, \dots, \omega_n^2)$ - independent errors whose variances may differ across observations. Then the ordinary least-squares estimator $\hat\beta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y$ is unbiased and its exact covariance is the sandwich $$\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta) = (X^T X)^{-1}\, X^T \Omega X\, (X^T X)^{-1},$$ which reduces to the textbook $\sigma^2 (X^T X)^{-1}$ only when all $\omega_i^2 = \sigma^2$. THEOREM (White, 1980). With $r = y - X\hat\beta$ the residuals, the estimator $\hat V_{\mathrm{HC0}} = (X^T X)^{-1}\big(\sum_i r_i^2 x_i x_i^T\big)(X^T X)^{-1}$ is consistent for $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta)$ in the sense that $n\,\hat V_{\mathrm{HC0}} - n\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta) \to 0$ in probability as $n \to \infty$ with $p$ fixed, under finite fourth moments of the errors and of the regressors (the rows $x_i$ bounded or with $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \|x_i\|^4 = O(1)$) and $\frac{1}{n}X^T X \to$ a positive definite limit. No model for the $\omega_i^2$ is needed. In the ill-conditioned directions of $X^T X$ (nearly collinear regressors) the sandwich can exceed the homoscedastic formula by a large factor when the large residuals fall on the observations that determine those directions; the homoscedastic formula then badly understates the sampling noise of the coefficients.
fixed design X of full column rank
independent errors with mean zero and possibly different variances
finite fourth moments of errors and regressors; (1/n) X'X -> positive definite; p fixed as n -> infinity for the consistency statement

body: A Dirichlet character mod q is a completely multiplicative function chi from the integers to C, periodic with period q, vanishing exactly on integers sharing a factor with q, induced by a homomorphism from the unit group mod q to the circle. Its L-function is L(s, chi) = sum over n >= 1 of chi(n) n^{-s}, absolutely convergent for Re(s) > 1 with an Euler product over primes; for nonprincipal chi it extends holomorphically to C, and L(1, chi) is nonzero - the key analytic input to Dirichlet's theorem.
title: Dirichlet Character and L-Function

Let X be a set. A function mu* from the FULL power set of X to [0, +infinity] is an OUTER MEASURE if (1) mu*(empty set) = 0, (2) it is monotone: A contained in B implies mu*(A) <= mu*(B), and (3) it is countably subadditive: mu*(union over n >= 1 of A_n) <= sum over n >= 1 of mu*(A_n) for every countable family of subsets A_n of X, MEASURABLE OR NOT. Note that subadditivity is part of the definition in the abstract setting; the mathematical content lies in the fact that the standard constructions produce it. CONSTRUCTION FROM A COVERING FAMILY (a gauge): let E be a family of subsets of X containing the empty set and covering X by countably many of its members, and let rho : E -> [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0. Define mu*(A) = inf { sum over k >= 1 of rho(E_k) : E_k in E for all k and A contained in the union of the E_k }, with the convention that the infimum of the empty set is +infinity. Lebesgue outer measure on R^n is the case where E is the family of boxes (or open boxes, or cubes) and rho is the elementary volume. A set A is CARATHEODORY MEASURABLE for mu* if mu*(T) = mu*(T intersect A) + mu*(T minus A) for every test set T; these sets form a sigma-algebra on which mu* restricts to a complete countably additive measure (Caratheodory's theorem). CAUTIONS: an outer measure is defined on all subsets but is in general NOT additive on disjoint sets; it is not a measure on the power set; and the Caratheodory criterion, not the mere inequality in (3), is what recovers additivity.
X is a set and mu* is defined on the entire power set of X
for the construction: E contains the empty set and some countable subfamily of E covers X, so that every subset has at least one admissible cover
rho maps E into [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0; no additivity or monotonicity of rho is assumed
countable, not arbitrary, families are used in the subadditivity axiom
title: Outer measure and the outer measure generated by a covering family
