Sample $\phi \sim \mathrm{LF}_\mathbb{H}^{(\beta,0), (\beta, 1)}$, forest the boundary of $(\mathbb{H}, \phi, 0, 1)$, forest the boundary to get a forested quantum surface $\mathcal{D}^f$, restrict to the event that there is a point $p$ on the forested boundary arc from $0$ to $-\infty$ such that the generalized boundary length from $p$ to $0$ agrees with that from $0$ to $1$, let $q \in \partial \mathbb{H}$ be the boundary point on the same generalized quantum disk as $p$, and further restrict to the event that $q \in I$.

body:
[Lemma 18 of arXiv:2607.18862, 'Tamed Euler Schemes for Singular SDEs with Multiplicative L\'{e}vy Noise'] Let $\lambda,l,\epsilon>0$, $\alpha,\delta\in (0,1]$ be fixed numbers. Let $a_1$ be a symmetric $d\times d$ matrix, and let $a(x),\widetilde{a}(x)$ be a $d\times d$ matrix-valued functions. Assume that for any $x$, $a(x),\widetilde{a}(x)$ are both symmetric, satisfying
	\ce 
	\lambda^{-1}lI\leq a(x)+a_1,~\widetilde{a}(x)+a_1\leq \lambda lI,
	\de 
	where $I$ is the $d\times d$ unit matrix. Additionally, assume that
	\ce 
	\sup_y\|a(y)-\widetilde{a}(y)\|\leq \epsilon.
	\de 
	Let $h$ be a real function such that 
	\ce 
	|h(x)-h(y)|\leq \lambda|x-y|^\alpha 
	\de 
	for all $x,y\in\mR^d$. Let $\zeta,\xi,\eta$ be independent d-dimensional random vectors. Assume that $\zeta$ has normal distribution $\sN(0,I)$, $\eta$ has normal distribution $\sN(0,\sqrt{a_1})$ and $E[|\xi|^\alpha]< \infty$. Define an operater $T^*$ by the formula for Borel measure function $f$ on $\mR^d$
	\ce 
	T^*f(y)=\mE[f(y+\sqrt{a(y)}\zeta)]
	\de 
	and $T$ be the adjoint of $T^*$ in the $L_2$ sense. Let $1\leq i,j\leq d$ be fixed and define 
	\ce
	H(x)=\mE[h(x)(\partial_{x_i,x_j}^2Tf)(x+\eta+\xi)-(\partial_{x_i,x_j}^2T[hf])(x+\eta+\xi)],
	\de 
	\ce 
	F(x)=H(x)+\mE[\mathscr{L}_{\upsilon,R}^{g}Tf(x+\eta+\xi)].
	\de 
	Define $\widetilde{T}^*$, $\widetilde{T}$ and $\widetilde{F}(x)$ analogously, but with $\widetilde{a}$ replacing $a$. 
	
	(i)  We assume that there exists a constant $\beta\in(0,2]$ such that the function $g$ on $\mR^d$ satisfies 
	\ce 
	\|\varGamma_{0,\beta}^{0,R}g\|_{\infty}<\infty.
	\de 
	Then, for any $p\in (d/\beta\vee 1,\infty]$, $p'\in [p,\infty]$, and bounded Borel $f\in L_p(\mR^d)$,
	\be 
	\|F\|_{p'}\leq N\|f\|_{p}[(1+l^{-\frac{\alpha}{2}}\mE[|\xi|^\alpha])l^{\frac{\alpha}{2}-1 +\frac{d}{2p'}-\frac{d}{2p}}+l^{-\frac{\beta}{2}+\frac{d}{2p'}-\frac{d}{2p}}],
	\ee 
	where the constant $N$ depends only on $\lambda,\alpha,\beta, p, p'$.
	
	(ii)  We assume that there exists a constant $\beta\in(1,2]$ such that functions $g$ and $\widetilde{g}$ on $\mR^d$ satisfy
	\ce 
	\|\varGamma_{0,\beta}^{0,R}g\|_{\infty}<\infty,~	\|\varGamma_{0,\beta}^{0,R}\widetilde{g}\|_{\infty}<\infty.
	\de 
	Then, for any $p\in (2d/\beta,\infty]$, $p'\in [p,\infty]$, and bounded Borel function $f\in L_p(\mR^d)$,
	\be 
	\|F(x)-\widetilde{F}(x)\|_{p'}
	\leq N\epsilon\|f\|_{p}\bigg[(1+l^{-\frac{\alpha}{2}}\mE[|\xi|^\alpha])l^{\frac{\alpha}{2}-2 +\frac{d}{2p}-\frac{d}{2p'}}+ (1+\epsilon)l^{-\frac{1}{2}(\beta-\frac{d}{p'}+\frac{d}{p})}
	+l^{-\frac{1}{2}(1+\beta-\frac{d}{p'}+\frac{d}{p})}\bigg],
	\ee 
	where the constant $N$ depends only on $\lambda,\alpha,\beta, p, p'$.

body:
[Definition eq:deftildeupsilon of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] We define the family of elementary differentials $(\Upsilon^{\tau}: \tau\in\mathfrak{T})$, with $\Upsilon^{\tau} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]$, by using an induction in $\tau$. 
For the base case, we define  $\Upsilon^{\circ} = \big( \Upsilon^{\circ_{r}}\big)_{r \in \N} \in \prod_{r \in \N} \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\circ_{r}]$ by setting, in analogy with (equation eq:elem_diff1_base of the paper), 
\[
\Upsilon^{\circ_{r}}(x_{r}) = V(x_{r})\;.
\]
It is clear that one indeed has $\Upsilon^{\circ_{r}} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\circ]$. 
In other words, we could have just fixed a single $r \in \N$, applied the above formula, and then defined $\Upsilon^{\circ} = \pi_{\circ,\circ_{r}} \Upsilon^{\circ_{r}}$ and our construction would be well-defined in that it didn't depend on our initial choice of $r$. 

We now proceed to the inductive step. 
Suppose we have $\tau=[\tau_1,\dots,\tau_k]$, where $k > 0$, the $\tau_1,\dots,\tau_k$ are unlabelled, and $[\cdot]$ denotes joining the roots of unlabelled trees at a new unlabelled root. 
Our inductive assumption is that we have been given $\Upsilon^{\circ} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\raisebox{+0.05ex}{\includegraphics[scale=1.5]{figures/Xi.pdf}}]$, and $\Upsilon^{\tau_{j}} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}_j]$ for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant k$.

Next, fix any labelled $\underline{\tau} \in \tau$, and choose any labelled $\underline{\tau}_1,\dots,\underline{\tau}_k$ with $\underline{\tau}_j \in \tau_j$, such that $\underline{\tau} = [\underline{\tau}_1,\dots,\underline{\tau}_k]_{r}$ (here we use the notation of (equation eq:product_of_trees of the paper), and $r = r(\underline{\tau})$).
For every $\underline{\sigma}\in \{\circ_{r}, \underline{\tau}_1,\cdots,\underline{\tau}_k\}$, we first set
\begin{equs}
   \Upsilon^{\underline{\sigma}} \eqdef \iota_{\sigma,\underline{\sigma}} \Upsilon^{\sigma}\in\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\sigma}]\,.
\end{equs}
We then define $\Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ in analogy with (equation eq:elem_diff1 of the paper) by setting
\begin{equ}
\Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau})})
=
\big( \mathrm{d}^{k} \Upsilon^{\circ_r}(x_{r(\underline{\tau})}) \big) \big[ \Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}_{1}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau}_1)}),\cdots, \Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}_{k}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau}_k)}) \big]\,,
\end{equ}
and finally we can set
\begin{equ}
\Upsilon^{\tau} \eqdef
\pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}} \Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}}\;.
\end{equ}
In the next lemma we verify that $\Upsilon^{\tau}$ as defined above is well-defined, in that it does not depend on how we realised $\tau$ as the labelled tree $[\underline{\tau}_1,\dots,\underline{\tau}_k]_{r}$.

For integer K>=2 and N=K^3 vertices, independently draw C,C' to be the whole set with probability 1/K and otherwise one uniform vertex. They are independent, identically distributed and nonempty. For I=|C intersect C'|, P(I>0)=2/K-1/K^2+(1-1/K)^2/K^3 ->0, E I=K+2(1-1/K)/K+(1-1/K)^2/K^3 ->infinity, and E I^2=K^4+2(1-1/K)/K+(1-1/K)^2/K^3. Hence E I^2/(E I)^2 is asymptotic to K^2. This refutes a general first-moment inference, not the Ising conjecture.

body: A collection B of subsets of a set X is a basis (base) for a topology on X if (i) every point of X lies in at least one member of B, and (ii) whenever a point x lies in the intersection of two members B1, B2 of B, there is a member B3 of B with x in B3 and B3 contained in the intersection of B1 and B2. The topology generated by B consists of exactly those subsets U of X such that every point of U lies in some member of B contained in U; equivalently, the open sets are precisely the unions of subfamilies of B. Conversely, given a topological space (X, T), a subcollection B of T is a basis for T exactly when every open set is a union of members of B.
title: Basis for a topology

Fix an integer n >= 2 and let F_k = I_n(f_k) be a sequence living in the SAME n-th Wiener chaos, with E[F_k^2] = n! ||f_k||^2 converging to sigma^2 > 0. Then the following are EQUIVALENT: (i) F_k converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2); (ii) E[F_k^4] -> 3 sigma^4; (iii) the contractions satisfy || f_k contracted with f_k at r indices || -> 0 for every r = 1, ..., n-1. The theorem replaces the infinitely many moment conditions of the method of moments by a SINGLE fourth-moment condition. The hypothesis that the chaos order n is FIXED and the same for every k is essential and is the standard misquotation: for a general sequence of random variables, or for a sequence whose chaos order drifts, matching the fourth moment says nothing about normality - the fourth moment of a suitable two-point law is also 3 times the square of its variance. Also essential is sigma^2 > 0; degenerating variance is excluded. The quantitative form is due to Nourdin and Peccati via Malliavin-Stein: for F in the n-th chaos with E[F^2] = sigma^2, the total variation distance to N(0, sigma^2) is bounded by a constant depending only on n times the square root of ( E[F^4] - 3 sigma^4 ), so the fourth cumulant controls the rate as well as the limit. [Nualart and Peccati (2005), Ann. Probab. 33; Nourdin and Peccati (2009); see Nourdin and Peccati, Normal Approximations with Malliavin Calculus, Theorem 5.2.7]
all F_k lie in the SAME fixed chaos of order n >= 2
E[F_k^2] -> sigma^2 > 0
the equivalence is FALSE for sequences not confined to one chaos

Let B be a measurable random real symmetric n-by-n matrix with 0<=B<=I. On real symmetric matrices equipped with the spectral norm define Phi(X)=E[BXB]. For every integer k>=0, the induced operator norm satisfies ||Phi^k-Phi^(k+1)||_(op->op)<=3/(k+1). In particular, for iid orthogonal-projection updates e_(j+1)=P_j e_j, Q=E[I-P_j] and deterministic e_0, one has E[e_k^T Q e_k]<=3||e_0||^2/(k+1). This is independent of dimension, task count, rank and conditioning. For unit row normals and uniform row sampling it gives the full-task randomized Kaczmarz residual. This general inverse-time result was already available in June 2026; the April 2026 O(k^(-3/4-theta)) bound is superseded as a rate frontier.

[Lemma 18 of arXiv:2608.13687, 'Multiplicative chaos from random multiplicative functions'] For $\theta \in (0,1]$, the family of measures $(\mu^{\text{GMC}}_{N,0})_{N \geq 0}$ converges in probability in $\cM(\cI)$ as $N\to\infty$  to a non-trivial, non-atomic random measure denoted by $\mu_{\infty}^{\text{GMC}}$.
\begin{proof}
For  $\theta=1$,  this was shown in  \cite[Section 2.3.2]{goro-wong-3}, and their proof works for all $|f|^2\in \mathbf{P}_\theta$. 
For $\theta \in (0,1)$ and $|f|^2\in \mathbf{P}_\theta$, the  computations in \cite[Section 2.3.1]{goro-wong-3} still apply, and verify the hypotheses of \cite[Theorem~6.1]{SW20}, which in fact yields almost-sure convergence of $(\mu^{\text{GMC}}_{N,0})_{N\geq 0}$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Thm 3 of arXiv:2605.07369, '2605.07369'] {\bf(Moderate deviation principle for stochastic approximation $(X_n)_{n\ge 0}$)}
Let $(X_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be a stochastic process taking values in $\rr$ and satisfying the stochastic approximation algorithm  (\ref{sa-0}). Assume that the conditions (\ref{sa-2})-(\ref{g}) hold, and that $bg^{'}(x^*)<-1$.
Let $(b_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a sequence of positive numbers such that $b_n\rightarrow\infty$ and  $b_n=O(n^{\frac{1}{2(1+\gamma)}})$ for a constant $\gamma>0$.
Then, for any $r>0$, we have
$$
\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{b^2_n} \log \pp \left( h_n\left|X_{n+1}-x^*\right|>r b_n\right)=-\frac{r^2}{2 \sigma^2},
$$
where
$$
h_n:=\left(b^2\sum_{k=0}^n (k+1)^{-2} \left(\beta_{k+1}^n\left(b g^{'}\left(x^*\right)\right)\right)^2\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}
$$
and
$$
\beta_{k}^n\left(b g^{'}\left(x^*\right)\right):=\prod_{j=k}^n \left(1+\frac{b g^{'}\left(x^*\right)}{j+1}\right).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 26 (Matrix Bernstein Inequality, Thm. 6.2 in \cite{tropp2012user}) of arXiv:2604.23461, 'Scaling limit of Sinkhorn-rescaled Random Matrices \\ via Stability of Static Schrödinger '] Let $\{\bZ_k\}_{k=1}^{N}$ be a collection of independent, self-adjoint, random $d\times d$ mean zero matrices. Suppose the moment growth
	\[
	\E[\bZ_k^q]\preccurlyeq\frac{q!}{2}R^{q-2}\bA_k^2 \quad \text{ for } q=2,3,4,...
	\]
	Denote $\sigma^2=\|\sum_{k=1}^{N}\bA_k^2\|,$ then
	\[
	\P\left(\left\|\sum_{k=1}^{N}\bZ_k\right\|>t\right)\le \begin{cases}
		d\exp(-t^2/(4\sigma^2)) & \text{if } t\le \sigma^2/R,\\
		d\exp(-t/(4R))  & \text{if } t\ge\sigma^2/R.
	\end{cases}
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Matrix Bernstein Inequality, Thm. 6.2 in \cite{tropp2012user}

[Prop diff_S of arXiv:2603.29711, 'Strong Feller property, irreducibility,\\ and uniqueness of the invariant measure\\ for st'] Under the assumptions of Theorem~(th:wp of the paper),
let $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and $h\in H$.
Then, there exists a unique process $Y_\varepsilon^h$ such that, 
for every $T>0$,
\[
Y_\varepsilon^h \in L^\ell_\mathscr{P}
(\Omega; C([0,T];H) \cap L^2(0,T;V))\quad\forall\,\ell\geq1,
\]
and it holds, for all $t\in[0,T]$, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely, that 
\begin{multline*}
    (Y_\varepsilon^h(t),v)_H
    +\int_0^t(A^{\frac12}Y_\varepsilon^h(s), A^{\frac12}v)_H\,{\mathrm d} s
    +\int_0^t(\Psi''_{\beta,\varepsilon}(X_\varepsilon^x(s))Y_\varepsilon^h, v)_H\,{\mathrm d} s\\
    =(h,v)_H + \left(\int_0^t
    DG_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(X_\varepsilon^x(s))[Y_\varepsilon^h(s)]{\mathrm d} W(s), v\right)_H
    \quad\forall\,v\in V.
\end{multline*}
Moreover, $Y_\varepsilon^h$ satisfies (equation eq:Y of the paper) also in a mild sense, 
namely, for all $t\in[0,T]$, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely,
\[
    Y_\varepsilon^h(t)
    +\int_0^tS(t-s)
    \Psi''_{\beta,\varepsilon}(X_\varepsilon^x(s))Y_\varepsilon^h\,{\mathrm d} s
    =S(t)h + \int_0^tS(t-s)
    DG_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(X_\varepsilon^x(s))[Y_\varepsilon^h(s)]{\mathrm d} W(s).
\]
Furthermore, the approximated solution map 
$S_\varepsilon$
is Fr\'echet-differentiable and
\[
  DS_\varepsilon(x)[h]=Y_\varepsilon^h \quad\forall\,x,h\in H.
\]

	\(\bm\varphi^{n,t}\) satisfies

			\partial_t\bm\varphi^{n,t}(x,y)

			+
			n^2\mathbf P\bm\varphi^{n,t}(x,y)\mathbf 1_{\{y=x+1\}}  \\

			+
			\mathbf R_x\bm\varphi^{n,t}(x,y)

[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2609.02699, '\vspace{-0.5 cm}Gauge theory and symplectic structures'] Let $(M,g,J)$ be a K\"ahler manifold. For $B$ a unitary connection on $\mathcal L,$ take $A={A^\mathrm{Ch}}+2B,\beta=0$ and $\phi=\varphi\in\Omega^0(M,\mathcal L)\subset \Gamma(S_+)$. Then equations \eqref{Dirac}, \eqref{Curvature} reduce to vortex-like equations
\begin{align}
    \bar\partial_B \varphi=0\\
    i\Lambda F_B=\frac{c_m}{2}(r-|\varphi|^2)\\
    F_B^{0,2}=0
\end{align}
where $c_m$ is a positive constant depending only on the dimension $2m=n$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:irreg1 of arXiv:2412.03366, 'Regularity of Weighted Tensorized Fractional Brownian Fields and associated function space'] Almost surely, for every  $(\bar{j},\bar{k})$, one has
$$ c_{\bar{j},\bar{k}} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^2}\frac{e^{i(k_12^{-j_1}\xi_1 + k_22^{-j_2}\xi_2)}\widehat{\psi} (2^{-j_1}\xi_1)\widehat{\psi} (2^{-j_2}\xi_2)}{\phi_{\alpha,H}(\xi_1,\xi_2)}  d\hat{\bf{W}}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}).$$
In particular,
\begin{enumerate}
    \item if $\|\bar{j}-\bar{j}'\|_{\infty} >1$, the wavelet coefficients $c_{\bar{j},\bar{k}}$ and $c_{\bar{j}',\bar{k}'}$ are independent,
    \item there exist two constants $c,d>0$ such that 
    $$
   c \, 2^{-2 (\max (\bar{j}) H_\alpha^+ + \min (\bar{j}) H_\alpha^-  )} \leq \mathbb{E}[\, |c_{\bar{j},\bar{k}}|^2\, ] \leq d \, 2^{-2 (\max (\bar{j}) H_\alpha^+ + \min (\bar{j}) H_\alpha^-  )}
    $$
    for all $\bar{j},\bar{k}$. 
\end{enumerate}

A proposed route defines T_x as the union of all infinite geodesic rays from x and uses the valid stationary inequality P(bigeodesic through 0)<=one-half times sum_{x in S_n}P(-x in T_0). Its proposed closing estimate, that this raw shell sum vanishes along a subsequence or that the shell maximum is o(1/n), is unattainable whenever a ray exists from 0 almost surely: every ray crosses every surrounding shell and the sum is always at least 1. Keep the counting inequality; replace the closing quantity by genuinely two-sided extension witnesses or full boundary-geodesic occupation. The parent P0117 conjecture remains unresolved in this packet.

[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2606.27520, 'Critical curve of loop percolation on the $d$-regular tree'] For two vertices $x,y \in V(\mathbb{T}_d)$, denote by $x \wedge y$ their common ancestor. If there exists $M > 0$ such that for any $x,y \in V(\mathbb{T}_d)$ and any vertex set $A$ with the property that the removal of $x \wedge y$ would disconnect $x$ from $A$, 
\[
    \P_{\alpha, \kappa}( 0 \leftrightarrow x \mid 0 \leftrightarrow y, 0 \centernot\leftrightarrow A) \geq M  \P_{\alpha, \kappa}( 0 \leftrightarrow x \mid 0 \leftrightarrow x \wedge y),
\]
then 
\[
\theta(\alpha, \kappa) \leq \frac{4}{M} \frac{C_{\text{eff}}(0 \leftrightarrow \infty)}{1+C_{\text{eff}}(0 \leftrightarrow \infty)}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:char-eval of arXiv:2410.23944, 'Hitting time mixing for the random transposition walk'] Let $\lambda \vdash n$ and $\tau \in \mathfrak{S}_n$ be a transposition. Then 
\[\chi_{\lambda}(\tau) = - \chi_{\lambda'}(\tau) = d_{\lambda} \binom{n}{2}^{-1}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\binom{\lambda_i}{2} - \binom{\lambda_i'}{2}\bigg).\]
In particular, if $\lambda_1 \geq n - (\log n)^{2}$, then 
    \[\frac{\chi_{\lambda}(\tau)}{d_{\lambda}} = \frac{\binom{\lambda_1}{2}}{\binom{n}{2}} + O(n^{-2+o(1)}) = 1-\frac{2(n-\lambda_1)}{n}+ O(n^{-2+o(1)}).\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:char-eval of arXiv:2410.23944

body:
[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The language $H$ equals the well-defined concatenation $J.G$.
  \begin{proof}
    To every word $w \in H$ there is a \emph{coupon-counting
    function} $f_w\colon \{ 0, 1, \ldots, \lvert w \rvert \} \to \N$
    that tracks the current number of distinct coupons held.
    This means $f_w(0) = 0$ and $f_w(\lvert w \rvert) = m$.
    Choose the smallest $k$ for which $f(k) = m$ and let
    $j$ be the word formed from the first $k$ letters in $w$.
    Then $w$ has the decomposition $j.g$ for some word $g$
    of length $\lvert w\rvert - k$.
    But since $f(k) = f(\lvert w \rvert) = m$,
    each occurrence of $\D_i$ in $g$ must be eventually followed
    by $\C_i$. Hence $g \in G$. There can be no decomposition $j = u.v$
    with $u \in H$ and $v \neq \varepsilon$ because $k > 0$ was selected minimally.
    This establishes $j \in J$ and $w \in J.G$. Thus $H \subseteq J.G$.

    To show $J.G \subseteq H$, take some $j.g \in J.G$ and
    consider the coupon-counting function $f_{j.g}$.
    Then $f_{j.g}(\lvert j \rvert) = m$ but $g$
    recovers all coupons it drops,
    so $f_{j.g}(\lvert j\rvert + \lvert g \rvert) = 
    f_{j.g}(\lvert j \rvert) = m$. We conclude
    $j.g \in H$ and $H = J.G$.

    We could not have selected a longer word $j' \in J$ in the first
    paragraph because $j' = j.u$ would hold with $u \neq \varepsilon$.
    This gives the contradiction $j' \notin J$.
    So, the factorisation of words $w \mapsto (j, g)$ is unique;
    $J$ and $G$ are well-defined for concatenation.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 7 of arXiv:2605.14206

[Definition 13 of arXiv:2607.10486, 'Weak martingale solutions to stochastic Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system with transport '] Assume that $\rK$ is a separable infinite dimensional Hilbert space. A $\rK$-cylindrical Wiener process $W=(W(t): t \in [0,T])$ is a family of formal series
   \begin{equation}
      W(t)\coloneqq  \sum_{k=1}^\infty w_k(t) e_k, \;\; t \in [0,T], 
    \end{equation} 
    where  $\left(e_k: \; k \in \mathbb{N} \right)$ is an ONB of $\rK$ and $\left(w_k: \; k \in \mathbb{N} \right)$ is a sequence of iid standard Brownian motions on some fixed probability space. \\
    The space $\rK$ is often called the Reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or Cameron-Martin space, of the 
    cylindrical Wiener process $W$.

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Suppose that $\chi$ is injective. Let $V$ be a $k[G]$-module. Then the following properties hold. 

\medskip
{\bf (1)} If the $k[G]$-module $V$ has a lift $\mathcal V$ to $R$, then we have inequalities
$$\max\bigl(\jmath_V,\sum_{a\in\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z} [\ell_V(a)-\eta_V]\bigl)=\max\bigl(\jmath_V,\dim_k(V)-m\eta_V\bigr)\le r_{\mathcal V}\le\imath_V.$$
Moreover, if the character function $\ell_V$ is constant, then $m\mid r_{\mathcal V}$.

\smallskip
{\bf (2)} Suppose that $R$ contains $R_s$. The $k[G]$-module $V$ has a lift $\mathcal V$ to $R$ with $r_{\mathcal V}=0$ if and only if $\ell_V$ is a constant function and $\jmath_V=0$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} Suppose that $R$ contains $R_s$. Let $V_0:=\oplus_{(a,b)\in C_m\times\llbracket1,p^s-1\rrbracket} \mu_V(a,b)U_{a,b}$. Then the following three statements are equivalent.

\medskip\noindent
{\bf (3.a)} The $k[G]$-module $V$ has a lift to $R$.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (3.b)} The $k[G]$-module $V_0$ has a lift to $R$.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (3.c)} For each $a\in C_m$ we have an inequality 
\begin{equation}
\ell_{V_0}(a)\le \eta_{V_0}+\ell_{\soc_{k[H]}(V_0)}(a).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let f_n and f be probability density functions with respect to a common sigma-finite measure mu on a measurable space, and suppose f_n converges to f mu-almost everywhere. Then integral of |f_n - f| d mu converges to 0 as n tends to infinity, equivalently the probability measures with densities f_n converge to the probability measure with density f in total variation distance. [standard, e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples]

body:
[Lemma 58 of arXiv:2605.02430, '\textbf{Scaling limit of the range of tree-valued branching random walks in random environ'] We keep the above assumptions and notation. We fix $p\ino \bbN^*$. Let $\cC, \cC^{_{(n)}}_{^{\! }}\ino \ccC_{p}$ and $r_n \ino \bbN$, $n\ino \bbN$. Here, $\overline{X}_{n}\eqo (\bT, X_n)$, $n\ino \bbN$, stands for a $\ttm_\nu$-biased RW starting at $X_0\eqo \boo$. We assume the following. 
\begin{compactenum}

\smallskip

\item[$(a)$] $\cC^{_{(n)}}_{^{\! }}\!\!  \to \cC$ uniformly on every compact interval. 

\smallskip
 
\item[$(b)$] For all $n\ino \bbN$, there exist $a_n \ino (0, \infty)$ and $t_n\ino \bbT$ such that 
$C_s (t_n)\eqo a_n\, \cC^{_{(n)}}_{s/a_n}$, $s\ino \bbR_+$. 

\smallskip  
 
\item[$(c)$] There exists $r\ino \bbR_+$ such that $r_n/a_n \! \to \! r$. 

\smallskip
 
\end{compactenum}
Then for all $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_p \ino \bbR$, it holds $\bP$-a.s.~that
\begin{equation}

\widetilde{\ccL}_{\bT,X_{ r_n}} (a_n\,  \cC^{_{(n)}}_{\frac{\cdot}{^{a_n}}}\, ; \, \tfrac{1}{\sigma_\nu\sqrt{a_n}} \lambda_1, \ldots ,  \tfrac{1}{\sigma_\nu\sqrt{a_n}} \lambda_p) \underset{n\to \infty}{-\!\!\! -\!\!\! -\!\!\! -\!\!\! \longrightarrow } \ccL (\cC\, ; \, \lambda_1, \ldots , \lambda_p ),
\end{equation}
where we recall from (\ref{vutchi}) the definition of $\sigma_\nu$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 58 of arXiv:2605.02430

body:
[Proposition 9 of arXiv:2604.11682, 'Semilocalization for inhomogeneous random graphs'] Let $\nu > 0$. We define the threshold
  \begin{equation*}
    \xi = \xi_{\nu} = \frac{3(\nu + 1)(2 - 3\delta)}{(1 - \delta)(1 - 2\delta)}\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}\,.
  \end{equation*}
  The graph $G^{\pp}$ satisfies the following properties.
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item With $\nu$-high probability, for all $x \in \vertices$,
          $D_{x} - D^{\pp}_{x} \leq \xi/2$.
    \item There are no down-up paths in the graph $G^{\pp}$.
    \item The graph $G^{\pp}$ is a forest.
  \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 9 of arXiv:2604.11682

body: (1) U ≠ C is essential: there is no biholomorphism from C onto D, since any holomorphic map C → D is bounded, hence constant by Liouville's theorem. C and D are the two conformal types of simply connected Riemann surfaces with the sphere. (2) Simple connectivity is essential and is not repaired by 'the domain has no holes that matter'. The punctured disk D minus {0} is not conformally equivalent to D: a biholomorphism F : D minus {0} → D would be bounded, hence extend holomorphically to 0 with |F(0)| ≤ 1; the extension maps the disk into D by the open mapping theorem, so F(0) = F(z1) for some z1 ≠ 0, and openness near both points contradicts injectivity on D minus {0}. Likewise two annuli {1 < |z| < R} and {1 < |z| < R'} are conformally equivalent only when R = R': conformal type has a modulus, so 'both are doubly connected' is not enough. (3) The conclusion is interior. The Riemann map need not extend continuously to the boundary, and when it does it need not be injective there. For the slit disk U = D minus [0,1) (which is simply connected), the inverse of the Riemann map extends continuously to the closed disk, but each point of the open slit is the image of two boundary points, so no homeomorphism of the closures exists. The correct boundary statement is Carathéodory's theorem: if U is bounded by a Jordan curve, then the Riemann map extends to a homeomorphism of the closed domains. (4) Normalization: the map is unique only after fixing F(z0) = 0 and F'(z0) > 0; without it the family of Riemann maps is a three-real-parameter family (compose with any automorphism of D).
title: Pitfall: the Riemann mapping theorem needs simple connectivity, U ≠ C, and says nothing about the boundary

[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] Let $\{X_t\}$ be the $1$-column Kac walk on $\mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ started from any $X_0$.
For every $B<\infty$ there is a constant $C_B<\infty$ such that, for every $\eta\in(0,1/2)$ and every
\[
t\geq C_B n\log(n/\eta),
\]
one can couple $X_t$ to a Haar-distributed point $Y\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ so that
\[
\mathbb{P}[\|X_t-Y\|>n^{-B}]\leq \eta.
\]

[Defn slith of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] For a closed surface $S$ and a maximal lamination $\lambda$, let $\rho:\pi_1(S) \to \mathrm{PSL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ be an $n$-pleated representation (as in Definition (defn:pleat of the paper)), pleated along $\lambda$, with an associated $\rho$-equivariant limit map $\xi$ that assigns flags in $\mathbb{C}^n$ with the endpoints of leaves of $\tilde{\lambda}$. The \textit{slithering map} compatible with $\xi$  $$\Sigma:\tilde{\Lambda}^2 \to \mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$$ defined on the space of pairs of leaves of $\lambda$, such that $\Sigma(g_1,g_2)$ is a matrix in $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ that takes the transverse pair of flags associated with the endpoints of a leaf $g_2$ to that of a leaf $g_1$ (oriented in parallel), satisfying
\[
\Sigma(g,g)=\mathrm{id}, \qquad
\Sigma(g_1,g_3)=\Sigma(g_1,g_2)\Sigma(g_2,g_3),
\]
whenever $g_2$ separates $g_1$ from $g_3$. When $g_1$ and $g_2$ share an endpoint, $\Sigma(g_1,g_2)$ is the unique unipotent transformation that fixes the flag at the common endpoint and takes the flag at the other endpoint of $g_2$ to the flag at the other endpoint of $g_1$.
title: Slithering map

Let f be twice continuously differentiable on an open interval containing a root x* with f(x*) = 0 and f'(x*) != 0. Then there is a neighborhood U of x* such that for every initial guess x_0 in U, the Newton iterates x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n) are well-defined, remain in U, and converge to x*. Moreover there is a constant C > 0, depending on bounds for |f''| and 1/|f'| on U, such that |x_{n+1} - x*| <= C * |x_n - x*|^2 for all n, i.e. the convergence is locally quadratic.

f(x*) = 0 and f'(x*) != 0

Let d>=2, B_d={x in R^d:||x||_2<=1}, and 0<epsilon<1/2. A depth-2 sigma network here has the form b_0+sum_{i=1}^w v_i sigma(w_i^T x+b_i), with real finite parameters. Assume sigma:R->R has the following univariate approximation property (Assumption 1): there is a constant c_sigma>=1 such that every L-Lipschitz h:R->R constant outside [-R,R] can, for every delta>0, be uniformly approximated on R to error delta by a+sum_{j=1}^w alpha_j sigma(beta_j z-gamma_j), with w<=c_sigma R L/delta. Let f(x)=phi(||x||_2) be a 1-Lipschitz radial function on B_d. There exists such a network N with sup_{x in B_d}|N(x)-f(x)|<=epsilon and width w<=exp(C_sigma epsilon^(-9) log(d/epsilon)), where C_sigma depends only on sigma. This is the small-error regime of the printed theorem. It does not assert joint polynomial dependence on d and epsilon^(-1), bounded parameter magnitudes, or a training algorithm.

[Definition def-tp2 of arXiv:2507.01406, '{\Large On Iterated Lorenz Curves with Applications: The Multivariate Case }'] A density $h(u,v)$ on $[0,1]^{2}$ is \textit{totally
positive of order two} ($TP_{2}$) if for all $0\leq u_{1}<u_{2}\leq 1$ and $
0\leq v_{1}<v_{2}\leq 1$, 
\begin{equation}
h(u_{1},v_{1})\,h(u_{2},v_{2})\;\geq \;h(u_{1},v_{2})\,h(u_{2},v_{1}).

\end{equation}
Equivalently (under standard regularity so that conditional expectation and
density exist), for $H$ a bivariate distribution with density $h$, the
conditional mean $x\mapsto m_{2|1}^{H}(x)=E[\,X_{2}^{H}\mid X_{1}^{H}=x\,]$
is non-decreasing.
title: Definition def-tp2 of arXiv:2507.01406

[Thm 11 (Strong Law of Large Numbers) of arXiv:2608.30554, 'Strong law of large numbers for generalized operator means II'] Let $f$ be an operator monotone function on $(0, \infty)$ such that $f(1) = 0$ and $f'(1) = 1.$
    Let $Y_1, Y_2, \hdots$  be a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with probability law $\mu$ on $\mathbb{P}$ such that
     $$ \int_\mathbb{P} \|f(y)\|\log^{+}(\|f(y)\|) \: d\mu(y) < \infty.$$
     For any initial $\hat{S}_1\in\mathbb{P}$, the stochastic resolvent iteration $\hat{S}_{n+1}=J_{1 \over n+1}(Y_{n+1},\hat{S}_n)$ converges almost surely to $\Lambda_f(\mu)$ with respect to the Thompson metric.
     
     Similarly, for any initial $S_1\in\mathbb{P}$, the stochastic iteration $$S_{n+1}=M^f_{1 \over n+2}(Y_{n+1}, S_n)$$ converge almost surely to $\Lambda_f(\mu)$ with respect to the Thompson metric.

[Definition def:Borel of arXiv:2606.21391, 'Extreme points and faces in the moment problem'] The \emph{$\sigma$-algebra generated by} a family of subsets of $X$ is the smallest 
$\sigma$-algebra on $X$ that includes this family. A $\sigma$-algebra on $X$ is 
\emph{countably generated} if it is generated by a countable family of subsets of 
$X$. We assume topological spaces to be Hausdorff. The \emph{Borel $\sigma$-algebra} 
on a topological space $X$, denoted by $\mathcal{B}(X)$, is the $\sigma$-algebra generated 
by the open sets. Its elements are \emph{Borel sets} and the measures on $\mathcal{B}(X)$ 
are \emph{Borel measures}.

\[
 \sigma(\mathbf{X}^{0}_{N}:N\geq1)

\begin{equation}

\[

 L_{\mathbf{X}^{0}_{N}+\mathbf{Z}^{N}_{s,\tau_1}}

body:
Let (F_n) be an increasing filtration with F_infinity the sigma-algebra it generates, and let Y be in L^1. Then E[Y | F_n] converges almost surely and in L^1 to E[Y | F_infinity]. Taking Y = 1_A for A in F_infinity gives LEVY'S 0-1 LAW: P(A | F_n) -> 1_A almost surely, so the conditional probability of any event in the limit sigma-algebra converges to 0 or 1. Applied to a tail event of an independent sequence, where F_n is generated by the first n variables and P(A | F_n) = P(A) by independence, this yields Kolmogorov's 0-1 law as a corollary. The theorem is about an INCREASING family; the corresponding statement for a decreasing family is Levy's downward theorem and needs its own proof. The limit is conditional on F_infinity and not on F - the two differ, and writing E[Y | F] would be wrong unless F_infinity = F up to null sets. [standard; e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales, Theorem 14.2]
(F_n) increasing, F_infinity generated by their union
Y integrable

body:
[Prop switching ergodic monomolecular of arXiv:2507.09421, 'Stability of randomly switching stochastic reaction networks with asymptotically linear tr'] In Example (ex:switching ergodic monomolecular of the paper), $\mathcal R_1$ and $\mathcal R_2$ are evanescent whenever $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$. For any $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, the mixed process is evanescent as long as $\kappa$ is small enough, but is exponentially ergodic as long as $\kappa$ is large enough.
\begin{proof}
Notice that the respective matrices in different individual environments as well as the stationary environment are given by 
\[
    M_1=\begin{bmatrix}-4&2\varepsilon\\ 2(1-\varepsilon)&0\end{bmatrix},\quad
    M_2=\begin{bmatrix}0&2(1-\varepsilon)\\ 2\varepsilon&-4\end{bmatrix},\quad
    M=\begin{bmatrix}-2&1\\ 1&-2\end{bmatrix}
\]
Note that the eigenvalues of $M_1$ and $M_2$ are $-2\pm2\sqrt{1 + \varepsilon - \varepsilon^2}$. For $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ we have $\varepsilon>\varepsilon^2$, and hence the larger eigenvalue is positive. Since both off-diagonal entries of $M_1$ and $M_2$ are nonzero, it follows from Proposition (prop:dec/inc direction of the paper)(ii) that there exist vectors $v^1,v^2\in\mathbb R^2_{>0}$ such that $v^iM_i\in\mathbb R^2_{>0}$. By Corollary (cor:one-environment-transience of the paper) we conclude that both $\mathcal R_1$ and $\mathcal R_2$ are evanescent for any nonzero state; the existence of inflow reactions means this state is evanescent as well. Similarly, by Theorem (thm:slow-switching-transience of the paper) we conclude that all states are evanescent for the mixed process whenever $\kappa$ is sufficiently small.

However, one sees that if $v=(1,1)$ then $vM=-v$, so by Theorem (thm:fast-switching-ergodicity of the paper) the mixed process converges exponentially fast whenever $\kappa$ is sufficiently large. Since the state space is irreducible, it follows by definition that the mixed process is exponentially ergodic whenever $\kappa$ is sufficiently large.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop switching ergodic monomolecular of arXiv:2507.09421

Let H be a complex Hilbert space and (U(t))_{t∈R} a family of unitary operators on H with U(0) = I, U(t+s) = U(t)U(s) for all s,t ∈ R, and t ↦ U(t)x continuous for each x ∈ H (strong continuity). Then there is a unique self-adjoint, generally unbounded operator A with domain D(A) = { x ∈ H : lim_{t→0} (U(t)x − x)/t exists in H }, defined by iAx = lim_{t→0}(U(t)x − x)/t, such that U(t) = e^{itA} in the sense of the Borel functional calculus. D(A) is dense and invariant under each U(t), and for x ∈ D(A) the map t ↦ U(t)x is differentiable with d/dt U(t)x = iA U(t)x = i U(t) A x. Conversely, every self-adjoint A generates such a group via e^{itA}. Application: A = Δ with domain H²(R^n) is self-adjoint, and the propagator e^{itΔ} of the free Schrödinger equation is the corresponding unitary group; likewise the free wave evolution is a unitary group on Ḣ¹ × L².
H a complex Hilbert space
U(t) unitary for every t, U(0)=I, U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)
strong continuity: t ↦ U(t)x continuous for every x ∈ H

[Definition Def: q-adically refining of arXiv:2604.05941, 'Banach spaces of continuous paths with finite $p$-th variation'] Fix an integer $q\ge2$. A partition sequence $\mathbb P=(\mathbb P^n)_{n\ge0}$ on $[0,1]$ is called \emph{$q$-refining} if, for each $n\ge0$,
    \[
        \mathbb P^n=\{0=t_0^n<t_1^n<\cdots<t_{q^n}^n=1\}, \qquad \text{and} \qquad
        t_i^n=t_{qi}^{n+1} \quad \text{for all } i = 0, \cdots, q^n.
    \]
    We call $\mathbb P$ \emph{dense} if $\bigcup_{n\ge0}\mathbb P^n$ is dense in $[0,1]$.

[Thm exponent of arXiv:2505.24821, 'Asymptotics for the harmonic descent chain and applications to critical beta-splitting tre'] We have that 
    \begin{enumerate}[ref=(\roman*)]
        \item  $x_{n+1} < x_n$ for all $n \geq k$. In particular, for any fixed $k$, the limit $x \coloneqq \lim_{n \to\infty} x_n$ exists.
        \item  For all $n \geq k$, $x_n - x = O(\frac{kx_k}{n-k})$.
        \item 
        For fixed $c \geq 2$ and $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$, and for $k$ sufficiently large, $x_{k+m} \leq \frac{c^\ell x_k}{mh_k}$ for each $m \leq k^{d_\ell}$ where $d_\ell = 1-\frac{1}{c+1} - 2^{-\ell}$.

        \item  For fixed $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $x_n - x = n^{-\gamma_*+o(1)}$, where $\gamma_*$ is the solution to 
        \begin{equation}
        \sum_{i=1}^\infty \left(\frac{1}{i} - \frac{i}{(i+1)(i+1-\gamma)}\right) = 0 
        \end{equation}
        with $1.5 < \gamma_* < 2$.
        \item  For all $\epsilon > 0$ and $k = o(n/\log^3 n)$, there exist $0 < c(k, \epsilon) < C(k, \epsilon) = O_\epsilon(x_k k^{0.01})$ such that $c(k, \epsilon)(n / k)^{-\gamma_*-\epsilon} \leq x_n - x \leq C(k, \epsilon)(n / k)^{-\gamma_*+\epsilon}$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm exponent of arXiv:2505.24821

[Dfn 3 of arXiv:2604.01748, 'Largest-loop-first loop-erased random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^{4}$'] Let $m \ge 0$ be an integer. A sequence of points 
 $$\lambda = [\lambda(0), \lambda(1), \cdots, \lambda(m)] \subset \mathbb{Z}^{d}$$ is called a path of length $m$ if $|\lambda(k) - \lambda(k+1)| = 1$ for all $0 \le k \le m-1$. We write $\text{len}\, (\lambda) = m$ for the length of $\lambda$. For $0 \le a \le b \le m$, we set $\lambda[a,b] = [\lambda(a), \lambda(a+1), \cdots, \lambda(b)]$ to denote the portion of the path $\lambda$ between times $a$ and $b$. Furthermore, $\lambda$ is said to be a simple path if $\lambda(j) \neq \lambda(k)$ for all $0 \le j < k \le m$.

     Let $\lambda_{1} = [\lambda_{1}(0), \cdots, \lambda_{1}(m_{1})]$ and $\lambda_{2} = [\lambda_{2}(0), \cdots, \lambda_{2}(m_{2})]$ be two paths in $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ of lengths $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$, respectively, and suppose that $\lambda_{1}(m_{1}) = \lambda_{2}(0)$. We define the concatenation of $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$, denoted by $\lambda_{1} \oplus \lambda_{2}$, by
$$\lambda_{1} \oplus \lambda_{2} = [ \lambda_{1} (0), \cdots , \lambda_{1} (m_{1}) , \lambda_{2} (1), \cdots , \lambda_{2} (m_{2})]. $$
    Then $\lambda_{1} \oplus \lambda_{2}$ is a path of length $m_{1}+m_{2}$.
title: Definition 3 of arXiv:2604.01748

[Theorem 11 of arXiv:2608.19832, 'Sharp Convex Concentration for Symmetric Random Tensors with Subgaussian Coordinates'] Let \(A,B\subset\R^n\) be measurable sets with positive \(\Pp\)-probability.
Put
\[
 Q_A=\Pp(\,\cdot\mid A),
 \qquad
 Q_B=\Pp(\,\cdot\mid B),
\]
\[
 H_A=\log\frac1{\Pp(A)},
 \qquad
 H_B=\log\frac1{\Pp(B)}.
\]
There is a coupling \((X,Y)\) with \(X\sim Q_B\) and \(Y\sim Q_A\) such
that
\begin{align}
 \sum_i\E\left[\E(\abs{X_i-Y_i}\mid X)^2\right]
 &\le CK^2\big[\Psi_n(H_A)+\Psi_n(H_B)\big],
 \\
 \sum_i\E\left[\E(\abs{X_i-Y_i}\mid Y)^2\right]
 &\le CK^2\big[\Psi_n(H_A)+\Psi_n(H_B)\big],
 \\
 \E\norm{X-Y}^2
 &\le CK^2\big[
 \sqrt{nH_A}+H_A+\sqrt{nH_B}+H_B
 \big],
 
\end{align}

log-Hessian condition
\begin{equation}
  -\beta_0I\;\preceq\;\nabla^2\log p_0\;\preceq\;-\alpha_0I,
  \qquad 0<\alpha_0\le\beta_0<\infty .
\end{equation}
 Then
\textup{(S)} holds: with $m_s:=e^{-\int_0^s\beta}\in[m_{\min},m_{\max}]\subset(0,\infty)$,
\[
  \opnorm{\nabla^2\log p_s}\le\frac{\beta_0}{m_s^2}\le\frac{\beta_0}{m_{\min}^2},
  \qquad|\Delta\log p_s|\le\frac{d\beta_0}{m_{\min}^2},
\]
and $|\nabla\log p_s(x)|\le A_*(1+|x|)$ with
$A_*=\max\{\sup_{s\le T}|\nabla\log p_s(0)|,\ \beta_0m_{\min}^{-2}\}<\infty$.

[Definition Stepping operator of arXiv:2606.21556, 'Mean field limit of non-exchangeable interacting diffusions on co-evolutionary networks'] For any fibered probability measure \(\mu \in \mathcal{P}_{\nu}(\mathcal{X}\times [0,1])\) and any measurable partition \(\mathcal{P}=\{S_1,\ldots,S_k\}\) of \([0,1]\), we define the step function \(\mu_{\mathcal{P}}\) as 
	\[
	\mu_{\mathcal{P}}^{\xi}= \sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathds{1}_{S_i}(\xi) \mu_{S_i} , \quad \textrm{for } \textrm{a.e. } \xi \in [0,1],
	\]
	where \(\mu_{S_i}=\frac{1}{\nu(S_i)}\int_{S_i} \mu^{\xi} d\xi\in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})\) is the average probability
 	measure over the set \(S_i\). If \(\nu(S_i)=0\), we set \(\mu_{S_i}\) to be an arbitrary probability measure in \(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})\).
title: Stepping operator

  \end{enumerate}

body: In computational complexity theory, an interactive proof system is an abstract machine that models computation as the exchange of messages between two parties: a prover and a verifier. The parties interact by exchanging messages in order to ascertain whether a given string belongs to a language or not. The prover is assumed to possess unlimited computational resources but cannot be trusted, while the verifier has bounded computation power but is assumed to be always honest. Messages are sent between the verifier and prover until the verifier has an answer to the problem and has "convinced" itself that it is correct.
title: Interactive proof system

body: [Lemma 15 of arXiv:2609.02732, 'Conservation of mass for solutions of Leibenson's equation on Riemannian Manifolds'] Assume that any non-negative bounded solution $u$ to (\ref{evoeq}) in $M\times [0, T)$, $T\in (0, \infty]$ with non-negative initial function $u(\cdot, 0)=u_0\in L^{1}(M)\cap L^{\infty}(M)$ has the property of \textit{mass conservation}. Fix some $\lambda>0$. Then there is no non-trivial non-negative function $v\in L^{1}(M)\cap L^{\infty}(M)$ with $v^{q}\in W^{1, p}(M)$ such that \begin{equation}-\Delta_pv^{q}=\lambda v,\end{equation} weakly in $M$.
title: Lemma 15 of arXiv:2609.02732

body:
[Theorem 14 (Homotopy detection under inclusions) of arXiv:2609.01882, '\textbf{Coxeter Descents and Parabolic Homotopy Colimits}\\[2mm] \large A Hochster-type de'] Let $G$ be compact, connected, simply connected, and semisimple, and let $\mathcal K\subseteq\mathcal L\subseteq2^S$. The natural map
\[
  \XK(G)\longrightarrow X_{\mathcal L}(G)
\]
is a homotopy equivalence if and only if, for every $D\subseteq S$, the inclusion
\[
  \mathcal K_D\longrightarrow\mathcal L_D
\]
induces isomorphisms on all augmented reduced integral homology groups, including degree $-1$.

In the synchronous nearest-neighbor particle-hole process on Z^d with iid initial excess eta satisfying P(eta=1)=P(eta=-1)=p, P(eta=0)=1-2p, 0<p<1/2, stationary capacity-one holes and the source coupling conventions, let H_t(x) indicate an unfilled hole and A_t(x) count active particles after round t. For every k distinct sites x_1,...,x_k and every nonnegative measurable function F of the entire active-count field, E[F(A_t) product_i H_t(x_i)] <= [p/(1-p)]^k E[F(A_t)]. In particular E[H_t(x) A_t(z)] <= [p/(1-p)]h_t, where h_t=E H_t(0)=E A_t(0). The estimate holds at each finite t; it does not assert conditional stochastic domination. Novelty: UNCHECKED (mixed-observable extension); deletion method KNOWN. Status: independently checked proof.
0<p<1/2; P(η=±1)=p each and otherwise zero
Stationary capacity-one holes; synchronous finite-time nearest-neighbor dynamics
F nonnegative and depends only on active-count field

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:ffcd4dd91fa05e1493a1b49064a14f9195b7bc835ede03b225ca9ca7cec5ec2a","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/ff/ffcd4dd91fa05e1493a1b49064a14f9195b7bc835ede03b225ca9ca7cec5ec2a.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:a31d174696b39217c23e18b76d86886c8a46b0b980c4086414d1bd398b3b5ce2","bundle_entry_key":"i0005-c8","bundle_id":"population.i0005-palm-reductions-and-comparisons-004","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"interacting particle systems and comparison fields","draft":"w661/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.particle-hole:sparse-particle-hole-mixed-observable-deletion-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0005-C8 v1: mixed hole–active deletion inequalities

Novelty: UNCHECKED. Extension of the KNOWN unvisited-hole deletion argument in source Lemma 8.4 and own C5. No earlier explicit mixed-moment statement found in the limited source searches. This result is valid in all dimensions, but does not give the time-dependent thinning needed by C7.

Use the sparse iid critical law P(η=1)=P(η=−1)=p, P(η=0)=1−2p with 0<p<1/2, stationary capacity-one holes and synchronous nearest-neighbor dynamics on Z^d. Let q=p/(1−p). For a finite set K of k distinct sites and any nonnegative measurable function F of the entire active-particle count field at a fixed finite time t,

E[F(A_t) product_{x∈K}H_t(x)]≤q^k E[F(A_t)].

The assertion allows expectations equal to infinity, in which case the inequality is interpreted in the extended nonnegative sense. In particular, with h_t=EH_t(0)=EA_t(0),

E[H_t(x)A_t(z)]≤q h_t,
E[H_t(x)1_{A_t(z)>0}]≤q P(A_t(z)>0)≤q h_t.

No independence or negative association of surviving holes and active particles is claimed.

## Proof

On E_K={H_t(x)=1 for all x∈K}, every specified initial value equals −1 and no particle has arrived at any specified site by time t. For each subset J⊂K replace the initial −1 values at J by zero, leaving every other sign and every walk/stack/tie variable fixed. The modified dynamics agree with the original particle dynamics through t: before a first putative arrival at a modified site, nothing affecting any particle has changed, so such an arrival would also occur in the original dynamics, a contradiction. Hence the active-count field A_t is identical in every image, and F(A_t) is unchanged.

These 2^k images are disjoint, because their initial coordinate assignments on K distinguish exactly which values are zero versus −1. Let c=(1−2p)/p. For a bounded nonnegative F, the image weighted expectation is exactly c^{|J|}E[F(A_t)1_{E_K}], by conditioning on all variables except the k specified initial coordinates. The transformations are injective with the prescribed original values restored. Their union is a subset of the full probability space. Since F is unchanged on each image,

E[F(A_t)]≥sum_{J⊂K}c^{|J|}E[F(A_t)1_{E_K}]
=(1+c)^k E[F(A_t)1_{E_K}]
=q^{−k}E[F(A_t)1_{E_K}].

This proves the inequality for bounded F. Apply it to min(F,m) and use monotone convergence as m→∞ to cover every nonnegative measurable F. The change-of-coordinate argument is finite, even if F depends on infinitely many active counts; at fixed t all specified hole-survival events have finite propagation cones, and the deletion leaves the entire particle evolution unchanged through t.

For F(A)=A(z) or 1_{A(z)>0}, translation invariance and critical signed-density conservation give the displayed specializations. The same moment bound holds at x=z, where the left side is zero. Active counts have finite expectation because the initial particles that can reach a site by t lie in a finite ball and there is at most one initial particle per site.

## Application and limitation

C7's mixed sum has the upper bound q h_t|B_{2R}|. This is useful at R=O(p^−1/d). At R=O(h_t^−1/d), dividing by h_t gives an upper bound of order q/h_t, which grows without limit for fixed p as h_t→0. Thus this all-time mixed inequality does not establish the mean-spacing mixed bound required for a fixed-law counterexample.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:1c3dcea0c0d9581690e0b39d8bdb7899bedd14af1bcebf941ddc1ef05029982c","revision_digest":"sha256:994ccdb83ec12ad25a0cb1fa8dde79fa7b7190fc787c00fcabe9d49326cfe6fc","source_id":"own-work:w661:I0005-C8:v1","source_revision":"v1; 2026-10-14T06:00:17.3108952+03:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

$\lambda_{\sigma,m}=\sigma^{-m}\cH(c\sigma^{m-1})-a_0$ for every $\sigma>0$ and $m\ge0$. Hence, for every fixed $m>1$ and $N\ge1$,
\[
\lambda_{\sigma,m}=-a_0+\sum_{k=1}^{N}h_{2k}c^{2k}\sigma^{(2k-1)m-2k}+O\!\left(\sigma^{(2N+1)m-2N-2}\right),
\]
where $\cH(v)=\sum_{k\ge1}h_{2k}v^{2k}$ near $0$ and $h_2=(2D_2)^{-1}$, $h_4=-D_4/(24D_2^4)$, $h_6=(10D_4^2-D_2D_6)/(720D_2^7)$. In particular,
\[
\lambda_{\sigma,2}=\frac{c^2}{2D_2}-a_0-\frac{D_4c^4}{24D_2^4}\sigma^2+\frac{(10D_4^2-D_2D_6)c^6}{720D_2^7}\sigma^4+O(\sigma^6).
\]
If $0\le m<1$ and $J(R_+-t)=Kt^\nu(1+o(1))$ as $t\downarrow0$, with $p=\nu+1$ and $A=K\Gamma(p)$, then
\[
\lambda_{\sigma,m}=\frac{c}{R_+\sigma}\left[(1-m)|\log\sigma|+p\log|\log\sigma|+C_{m,c,J}+o(1)\right]-a_0,
\]
where $C_{m,c,J}=\log c+p\log(1-m)-p\log R_+-\log(R_+A)-1$.

body: Three hypotheses of the De Giorgi-Nash-Moser theorem are load-bearing, and each fails concretely. (1) Scalar. The theorem is false for systems: De Giorgi (1968) exhibited, for n >= 3, a linear elliptic system with bounded measurable coefficients satisfying the Legendre-Hadamard and even the strong ellipticity condition whose weak solution is u(x) = x |x|^{-gamma} for an explicit gamma with 1 < gamma < n/2 - a solution in H^1 that is unbounded, hence not even locally bounded, let alone Hoelder. So a referee must check that an application of De Giorgi-Nash-Moser or of Moser's Harnack inequality is to a single equation, not to a system, and that the maximum-principle-based truncations used in the proof are available. (2) The energy class u in H^1_loc. A distributional solution whose gradient is only in L^p for some p < 2 need not be bounded. In the plane take A(x) = I + (mu - 1) x x^T/|x|^2 with mu > 1 (uniformly elliptic, bounded, measurable, discontinuous only at the origin). In polar coordinates div(A grad u) = (1/r) d/dr ( r mu u_r ) + (1/r^2) u_{theta theta}, so u = r^s cos(theta) solves the equation away from 0 exactly when mu s^2 = 1. The choice s = -1/sqrt(mu) in (-1,0) gives u = r^{-1/sqrt(mu)} cos(theta), which is unbounded at 0, lies in W^{1,p}_loc precisely for p < 2/(1 + 1/sqrt(mu)) < 2, and is a distributional solution across the origin (the flux through small circles tends to 0 because s > -1). (3) The Hoelder exponent depends on the ellipticity ratio and cannot be improved to Lipschitz. The same coefficients with s = +alpha, i.e. mu = 1/alpha^2, give the H^1 solution u = r^alpha cos(theta) of a uniformly elliptic equation with ellipticity ratio alpha^{-2}: it is exactly C^{0,alpha} at the origin and no better. Hence the exponent alpha(n, Lambda/lambda) in the theorem must degenerate to 0 as Lambda/lambda tends to infinity, and 'bounded measurable coefficients give Lipschitz solutions' is false. Gradient bounds require continuity (or Dini/Hoelder continuity) of the coefficients.
title: Pitfall: De Giorgi-Nash-Moser Needs a Scalar Equation and an Energy-Class Solution

[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2609.02850, 'Canonical-row Chern flow on Bott--Samelson towers:\\ realizable-volume models for Schubert'] Let
\[
 \widehat f(x,z)=\sum_{\alpha\in S}c_\alpha
 x^\alpha z^{D-|\alpha|}
\]
be a nonzero homogeneous polynomial of degree $D$, and assume that
$\Supp(\widehat f)=\widehat S_D$ is $M$-convex.  Then $S$ is
$M^\natural$-convex and
\begin{equation}
 S=\operatorname{conv}(S)\cap\ZZ^n.
\end{equation}
Consequently, every polynomial whose support is $S$ has saturated Newton
polytope.

body: [Definition of arXiv:2605.02226, 'Finitely Dependent Processes on Subshifts'] A subshift of finite type $ X \subset A^{G}$ satisfies the $k$-extension property if there exists a finite collection $ \mathcal{F} $ of forbidden patterns for which $ X = X(\mathcal{F})$ and such that any locally allowed pattern $ w$ supported on a set $S \subset G$ which extends to a locally allowed pattern on $ S \cdot \mathbf{B}(k) $, is globally allowed.  $ X$ has finite extension property (FEP) if it satisfies $ k$-extension property for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For simple random walk on the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or more generally on critical random media with anomalous volume growth, Kesten's argument establishes subdiffusive behavior, that the walk's typical displacement after n steps is of order n^{1/d_w} with walk dimension d_w > 2 rather than the diffusive n^{1/2}, by combining a volume-growth estimate showing balls of radius r typically contain of order r^{d_f} points, with d_f the fractal (volume) dimension of the cluster, and an effective-resistance estimate R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) of order r^{zeta}, reflecting the long dangling ends and low-conductance bottlenecks characteristic of the critical cluster. The expected exit time from a ball of radius r is then of order r^{d_f+zeta} (volume times resistance: the Einstein relation d_w = d_f + zeta), so the displacement is of order n^{1/(d_f+zeta)}, subdiffusive when d_f + zeta > 2; the Nash/heat-kernel machinery or a direct expected-exit-time computation turns the two estimates into bounds. In balls of the intrinsic (graph) metric with unit conductances R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) <= r, so zeta <= 1 there: for the high-dimensional incipient infinite cluster the intrinsic volume grows as r^2 and the resistance as r, giving d_w = 3. The argument does not give the exact value of the subdiffusivity exponent in most dimensions, only bounds, with the precise exponent known rigorously only in specific settings such as sufficiently high dimension or tree-like/hierarchical models, and it is specific to critical (not subcritical or supercritical) percolation geometry, where the fractal, tree-like structure with many bottlenecks is essential to the argument. Typical failure: Assuming the subdiffusivity exponent established for one setting, such as high-dimensional or tree-based incipient infinite clusters where exact computation is possible, transfers to two-dimensional critical percolation, where the exact random-walk dimension remains a major open problem; volume-growth and resistance-growth exponents are model- and dimension-specific quantities that must be independently estimated rather than imported across models with superficially similar critical geometry. Canonical reference: Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Barlow, Jarai, Kumagai and Slade, 2008, Communications in Mathematical Physics.
the walk is on the incipient infinite cluster or a similarly statistically self-similar critical random graph
a known or boundable volume-growth exponent d_f for balls in the cluster
a known or boundable effective-resistance-growth exponent reflecting the bottleneck/dangling-end structure
typically also requires the cluster's law to have appropriate scale-invariance, or at least comparable behavior across scales

[Cor finite-order of arXiv:2608.30847, 'An Almgren-type formula for planar $p$-harmonic functions'] Let $u$ be a nonconstant planar $p$-harmonic function and $x_0\in\Omega$.  If $u(x_0)=0$, then $u$ has finite vanishing order at $x_0$ in the following sense: either $D u(x_0)\ne0$ and the order is $1$, or $x_0$ is critical and
$$
  |u(x_0+r\theta)|\le Cr^{\lambda_N(p)},

  \sup_{\theta\in\mathbb S^1}|u(x_0+r\theta)|\ge c r^{\lambda_N(p)}
$$
for all sufficiently small $r>0$, with constants $c,C>0$.

[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] For any subclasses \(\mathcal{T}, \mathcal{T}_n\) and \(n\in \mathbb{N}\), the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(\left(\bigcap_n \mathcal{T}_n \right)_{loc} = \bigcap_n (\mathcal{T}_n)_{loc}\) and \(\left(\bigcup_n \mathcal{T}_n \right)_{loc} \supset \bigcup_n (\mathcal{T}_n)_{loc}\).
\item \(\left(\bigcap_n \mathcal{T}_n \right)_{col} \subset \bigcap_n (\mathcal{T}_n)_{col}\) and \(\left(\bigcup_n \mathcal{T}_n \right)_{col} = \bigcup_n (\mathcal{T}_n)_{col}\).
\item If \(\mathcal{T}_1 \subset \mathcal{T}_2\), then \((\mathcal{T}_{1})_{loc} \subset (\mathcal{T}_{2})_{loc}\) and  \((\mathcal{T}_{1})_{col} \subset (\mathcal{T}_{2})_{col}\).
\item For any \(\{F_k\}_k \in \nest\), \(\mathcal{T}_{loc} \subset \mathcal{T}(\{F_k\}) \subset \mathcal{T}_{col}\).
\item \((\mathcal{T}_{loc})_{loc} = \mathcal{T}_{loc}\) and \((\mathcal{T}_{col})_{col} = \mathcal{T}_{col}\).
\item \(\mathcal{T}_{loc} \subset (\mathcal{T}_{loc})_{col} \subset \mathcal{T}_{col}\) and \(\mathcal{T}_{loc} \subset (\mathcal{T}_{col})_{loc} \subset \mathcal{T}_{col}\).
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition propmain2e of arXiv:2605.01878, '\Large Random trade timing and power-law tails in realized prices'] Let $(X_t, t\geq 0)$ be a Markov modulated L\'{e}vy process, described in Section (smain1a of the paper) and let the trade time $T$, described in Sections (smain1b of the paper)-(smain1c of the paper), satisfy (equation itm of the paper) and (equation itmadd of the paper). 
Suppose that Assumption (asshol of the paper) holds and there exists $\alpha>0$ such that $r_D(A(-\alpha)) = \lambda_{\min}$.
Then such $\alpha$ is unique, and the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*)]
\item There exist constants \(0<C_1\le C_2<\infty\) such that
\begin{align} 
\widetilde M C_1 \le (\log y)^{-\beta} y^\alpha \mathbb{P}(P_T>y) \le \widetilde M C_2 
\end{align}
for sufficiently large $y$, where $\beta$ is determined by the following case distinction:
 \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), ref=(\alph*)]
    \item  If $\lambda_{\min} = \lambda_1 < \mu_1$, then $\beta = 0$.
    \item  If $\lambda_{\min}  = \mu_1 < \lambda_1$, then $\beta = r_1-1$.
    \item  If $\lambda_{\min}  = \lambda_1 =  \mu_1$, then $\beta = r_1$.
\end{enumerate}
    \item    Suppose, in addition, the nonlattice condition in Proposition (propmain of the paper)\,(propmainb of the paper) holds, and $\lambda_{\min}=\lambda_1 < \mu_1$ or $\lambda_{\min}  = \mu_1 < \lambda_1$ with $r_1 = 1$. Then,  as $y\to\infty$,
\[
\lim_{y \to \infty}  y^\alpha \mathbb{P}(P_T>y) = \widetilde M/\alpha.
\]
\end{enumerate}
In (propmain2ea of the paper) and (propmain2eb of the paper), $\widetilde M \coloneqq \lim_{s \to -\alpha}(s+\alpha)^{\beta+1} M_T(s)$, which is positive.
title: Proposition propmain2e of arXiv:2605.01878

body:
[Definition Def_ExtendedIsometry of arXiv:2609.02848, 'The universal moduli space of non-degenerate $\Z/2\Z$~harmonic spinors'] The \defined{extended gauge group} of $S$ is the tame Fréchet Lie group $\widehat\mathscr{G}(S)$ constructed as follows:
  \begin{enumerate}  
  \item
    
    An \defined{extended isometry} of $S$ is a diffeomorphism $u \in \Diff(S)$ for which there exists a diffeomorphism $\check u \in \Diff(X)$ such that $u$ defines an isometry $S \cong \check u^*S$.
    These form a subgroup $\widehat\mathscr{G}(S) \leqslant \Diff(S)$.    
  \item
    A moment's thought shows that extended isometries lift to $\mathrm{O}(r)$--equivariant diffeomorphisms of $\Fr(S)$,
    the orthogonal frame bundle of $S$;
    in fact, $\widehat\mathscr{G}(S) = \Diff(\Fr(S))^{\mathrm{O}(r)}$, abusing notation.
    By [Molitor2010:UnimodularAutomorphisms],
    $\widehat\mathscr{G}(S) \leqslant \Diff(\Fr(S))$ is a tame Fréchet Lie subgroup.
  \item
    From the above perspective,
    $\widehat\mathscr{G}(S)$ acts smoothly and tamely on $S = \Fr(S) \times_{\mathrm{O}(r)} \mathbb{R}^r$ and $X = \Fr(S) \times_{\mathrm{O}(r)} \set{*}$ from the left
    by
    \begin{equation*}
      u \cdot [p,\phi] \coloneq [u(p),\phi]
      \quad\text{and}\quad
      u \cdot [p,*] \coloneq [u(p),*],
    \end{equation*}
    respectively.
    As a consequence,
    it acts smoothly and tamely on $\Gamma\paren{X,S}$, $\mathbf{Dir}$, and $\mathbf{Ram}$ from the right by pullback.
    \footnote{
      
      The reader should be warned that $\widehat\mathscr{G}(S)$ does not lift to an action on $\mathbf{Ram}^0$;
      however, the action lifts locally.
      This is sufficient for (Prop_TransformToNormalForm of the paper).
    }
    \qedhere
  \end{enumerate}
title: Definition Def_ExtendedIsometry of arXiv:2609.02848

body: Fix d >= 2 and let E(Z^d) be the set of nearest-neighbour edges of the integer lattice. Assign to each edge e an independent random weight tau_e >= 0 with common distribution F; the collection (tau_e) is the environment. The PASSAGE TIME of a finite lattice path gamma is T(gamma) = sum over the edges of gamma of tau_e, and the passage time between vertices x and y is T(x,y) = inf over finite paths from x to y of T(gamma). T is a random pseudometric on Z^d: it is symmetric, satisfies the triangle inequality, and vanishes on the diagonal, but T(x,y) = 0 is possible for x != y when F has an atom at 0. A GEODESIC from x to y is a path attaining the infimum. Geodesics need not exist for a general F, and when F(0) is at least the critical probability p_c(d) the infimum can be 0 and attained by infinitely many paths; when F(0) < p_c a geodesic exists almost surely for every pair, and it is almost surely unique for every pair when F is continuous, since ties then have probability 0. The standing notation in the literature is T(0, x) for the point-to-point time, mu or g for the time constant, chi for the fluctuation exponent and xi for the wandering exponent; the store already records that those exponents are DEFINED differently by different theorems and are not interchangeable. [standard; e.g. Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Chapters 1 and 4]

[Lemma lem:closure of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] For $2\le|S|\le3$ let
$K_S=\operatorname{conv}\{B_{ij}:i,j\in S,\ t_i\ne t_j\}$ (discard $S$ with no valid
pair). Then
\[
  \inf_{\substack{\operatorname{supp} q\subseteq S\\ |\mu(q)|<1}}C(q)
  \;=\;\operatorname{dist}^2\bigl(0,K_S\bigr),
  \qquad
  \inf_{\substack{|\operatorname{supp} q|\le3\\ |\mu(q)|<1}}C(q)
  \;=\;\min_{S}\operatorname{dist}^2(0,K_S) .
\]
For three pairwise distinct directions the interior of the edge-weight
triangle is attained by positive weights (via
$q_1{:}q_2{:}q_3=\frac{d_{23}}{\alpha_{23}}{:}\frac{d_{13}}{\alpha_{13}}
{:}\frac{d_{12}}{\alpha_{12}}$), the vertices by two-point supports, and
non-degenerate edge interiors only as limits with $|\mu|\to1$; if two of the
three directions coincide, the corresponding segment of $K_S$ is attained
exactly. Moreover, for three distinct directions the three points
$B_{ij},B_{ik},B_{jk}$, when distinct, are never collinear over $\mathbb{R}$.

\[
\Phi_p(\mathrm{Maj}_n) > \Phi_p(f)\qquad\text{for all unbiased }f\neq \mathrm{Maj}_n.
\]

Suppose that $ \theta_{\varepsilon, m(\varepsilon)} $ is the solution of (equation Galerkin approximation equations-delta=0 of the paper) with $ \theta_{\varepsilon, m(\varepsilon)}(0)\sim \mathcal{G}(0,\varepsilon P_{m(\varepsilon)}/2)$, then there exists $\eta_0>0$ such that for every  $ \eta \in\left[0, \eta_0\right]$, under the scaling regime (equation scaling-m of the paper), we have

	$$

body:
[Thm main:shocks of arXiv:2604.12963, 'Shocks, instability, and the twenty networks\\ of infinite geodesics in the Directed Lands'] The following hold for all $\omega$ in a full $\mathbb{P}$-probability event and all $\theta\in\Theta^\omega$. 
\begin{enumerate}[label={\rm(\alph*)}, ref={\rm\alph*}] \itemsep=1pt
\item If $(x,s)\notin\IG\theta$, then it is either not a shock or is a proper double shock. Proper double shocks can only occur at stability points.
\item A point $(x,s)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ is the tip of a stability island if and only if there exists a misordered pair of $\theta-$ and $\theta+$ shock interfaces $\tau^-$ and $\tau^+$ emanating from $(x,s)$ such that, for every $r<s$,
$\tau^-([r,s])\setminus{\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta+}\neq\varnothing$
and $\tau^+([r,s])\setminus{\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta-}\neq\varnothing$.
Moreover, every such tip is a \emph{pns} point. 
\item A point $(x,s)$ is a \emph{snowbird shock} if and only if it is the bottom of a stability island. In that case, the tip of the island is the point at which the geodesics $\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{-}$ and $\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{+}$ first separate. Furthermore, $(x,s)$ is the point where the misordered pair of $\theta\pm$ interfaces from the tip reintersect.
\item A point $(x,s)$ is a $\theta-$ {\rm(}respectively $\theta+${\rm)} hugging shock if and only if it lies on the left {\rm(}respectively right{\rm)} boundary of a stability island and is neither the tip nor the bottom of that island.
\item If $(x,s)$ is a dust point {\rm(}i.e.\ $(x,s)\in\mathcal D^\theta${\rm)}, then it is either a \emph{pns} point or a single shock. Conversely, single shocks occur only at dust points. If $(x,s)$ is a pns point, then it is either the tip of a stability island or a dust point. 
\item Fix a stability island. Then each of the first, third, and fourth configurations on the third {\rm(}respectively fourth{\rm)} row in Figure (fig:geodesics of the paper) occurs on a set of starting points that is dense in the right {\rm(}respectively left{\rm)} boundary of the island.  The second configuration in that row occurs on a set of isolated points along the same boundary, which accumulates at the tip of the island.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition randomcoveringset of arXiv:2506.10448, 'Hitting probabilities and the Ekstr\"om--Persson conjecture'] Let $\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and consider the probability space
$(\Omega,\mathbb{P})$, where $\Omega:=(\spt\mu)^{\mathbb{N}}$ and $\mathbb{P}:=\mu^{\mathbb{N}}$.
Let $\underline{r}$ be {a} sequence of positive numbers. Given
$\omega \in \Omega$, the \emph{random covering set} generated by the sequence
$\underline{r}$ is the limsup set
\[
E_{\underline{r}}(\omega)\coloneqq\limsup_{k\to\infty}B(\omega_{k},r_k)
  =\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigcup_{k=n}^{\infty}B(\omega_{ k},r_k).
\]

body:
[Lemma 4 (Euclidean score reduction) of arXiv:2609.02362, '\textbf{Farthest-cell triplet entropy: high-dimensional shell limits and hyperbolic curvat'] For the independent query $(R_{0,d},U_{0,d})$ and prototypes
$(R_{i,d},U_{i,d})$, $i=1,2,3$, the farthest-distance ordering is the
ordering of
\begin{equation}
  S_{i,d}
  =
  \lambda_d\xi_{i,d}-Z_{i,d}+r_{i,d},
  \qquad
  Z_{i,d}
  =
  \sqrt d\,\langle U_{0,d},U_{i,d}\rangle.
  
\end{equation}
Conditionally on the prototypes,
\[
  (Z_{1,d},Z_{2,d},Z_{3,d})
  \Rightarrow N(0,I_3)
\]
in probability \cite{diaconisfreedman1987}.  Moreover,
\[
  \max_{1\leq i\leq3}|r_{i,d}|
  \xrightarrow{p}0
\]
when $\lambda_d=O(1)$, whereas
\[
  \frac{1}{\lambda_d}
  \max_{1\leq i\leq3}|r_{i,d}|
  \xrightarrow{p}0
\]
when $\lambda_d\to\infty$.

Let (M,g) be a Riemannian (or pseudo-Riemannian) manifold. There exists a unique affine connection nabla on M, called the Levi-Civita connection of g, that is (1) torsion-free: nabla_X Y - nabla_Y X = [X,Y] for all smooth vector fields X, Y, and (2) compatible with the metric: X(g(Y,Z)) = g(nabla_X Y, Z) + g(Y, nabla_X Z) for all smooth vector fields X, Y, Z.

[Proposition 1 (Blindness of two-moment discrepancies) of arXiv:2608.24881, 'What FID Hides: Detecting, Ranking, and\\ Diagnosing Deviations in Generative Evaluation'] Let $M(P,Q)$ be a discrepancy determined only by the means and covariances
of $P$ and $Q$, with $M(P,Q)=0$ whenever these moments agree. For every distribution $P$ on
$\mathbb R^d$ with finite second moments and nonzero covariance, there exists $Q\neq P$ with the same
mean and covariance. Hence $M(P,Q)=0$; in particular, $\operatorname{FID}(P,Q)=0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Blindness of two-moment discrepancies

body:
Load-bearing hypothesis: uniqueness in Kruzhkov's theorem is for ENTROPY solutions; the integral (weak) formulation alone, even with Rankine-Hugoniot satisfied at every jump, does not determine the solution. Counterexample 1 (Burgers, f(u) = u^2/2, datum u0 ≡ 0): besides u ≡ 0 the function u(x,t) = 0 for x < -t/2, u = -1 for -t/2 < x < 0, u = 1 for 0 < x < t/2, u = 0 for x > t/2 is a weak solution — every jump satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot (speeds -1/2, 0, 1/2 respectively) — yet it is not an entropy solution (the jump from -1 up to 1 is an expansion shock violating Oleinik/Lax). Counterexample 2 (Burgers with u0 = 0 for x < 0, u0 = 1 for x > 0): the stationary-in-shape expansion shock u = 0 for x < t/2, u = 1 for x > t/2 satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot, but the entropy solution is the rarefaction u = 0 for x ≤ 0, u = x/t for 0 ≤ x ≤ t, u = 1 for x ≥ t. In both cases the wrong solutions create information (characteristics emanate from the shock) instead of destroying it, and they are not vanishing-viscosity limits. Auditor's check: a proof that constructs 'a' weak solution and then calls it 'the' solution — or that computes shock speeds from Rankine-Hugoniot without verifying admissibility — is incomplete; check Oleinik's chord condition at every jump (for convex flux: the state must jump DOWN as x increases).
Burgers' equation f(u) = u^2/2 in one dimension
Weak solutions are only required to satisfy the integral identity; jumps must satisfy Rankine-Hugoniot but may still be inadmissible
Uniqueness is restored by the Kruzhkov entropy inequalities (equivalently, for piecewise smooth solutions, by Oleinik's chord condition at each jump)
title: Pitfall: Weak Solutions of a Conservation Law Are Not Unique without an Entropy Condition

[Lemma lem:positive-part of arXiv:2604.13968, 'Divisible sandpiles via random walks in random scenery'] Let $(Z_i)_{i\in I}$ be a finite collection of independent mean-zero random variables
		with $|Z_i|\leq b_i$ a.s.\ for deterministic $b_i>0$.
		Let $B^2\coloneqq\sum_{i\in I}\var(Z_i)$.
		If $\max_{i}b_i^2\leq B^2$, then there exists a universal constant~$c_\star>0$ such that $\mathbb{E}\bigl[\bigl(\sum_{i\in I}Z_i\bigr)^{\!+}\bigr]\geq c_\star B$.

[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2608.22746, 'Generative Neural Networks for Sinkhorn Distributionally Robust Hypothesis Testing'] [Gradient Convergence of Smooth HyCNNs] 
    Let $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be a Lipschitz continuous convex function, and $\{\widehat{\mathsf{HyCNN}}_n^{\tau}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of smooth HyCNNs with hyperparameters $L_n \cdot h_n = \mathcal{O}({\varepsilon_n}^{-d})$ for any $\varepsilon_n>0$, where $\widehat{\mathsf{HyCNN}}_n^{\tau}: \mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$. 
    Assume that $ \widehat{\mathsf{HyCNN}}_n^{\tau} \to f $. Then 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For almost every $\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d$, $\nabla \widehat{\mathsf{HyCNN}}_n^{\tau} (\boldsymbol{x}) \to \nabla f(\boldsymbol{x})$.  
        \item If $f$ is Lipschitz smooth, the gradient sequence $\nabla \widehat{\mathsf{HyCNN}}_n$ converges to $\nabla f$ uniformly at a rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{\varepsilon_n} \right)$. 
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: PageRank (PR) is an algorithm used by Google Search to rank web pages in their search engine results. It is named after both the term "web page" and co-founder Larry Page. PageRank is a way of measuring the importance of website pages. According to Google:PageRank works by counting the number and quality of links to a page to determine a rough estimate of how important the website is. The underlying assumption is that more important websites are likely to receive more links from other websites.

body: In the theory of abelian groups, the torsion subgroup of an abelian group is the subgroup of consisting of all elements that have finite order. [Definition of arXiv:2608.30346, '\textbf{Classification complexity of homeomorphism group actions}'] Let \(X,Y\) be standard Borel spaces and \(E,F\) be two equivalence relations on \(X,Y\) respectively. We say that \(E\) is \textit{Borel reducible} to \(F\) denoted by \(E \leq_B F\), if there exists a Borel mapping \(f: X \to Y\) called a \textit{reduction} such that
    \[x E y \iff f(x) F f(y)\]
    for all \(x,y \in X\). We say that \(E\) is \textit{Borel bireducible} to \(F\) denoted by \(E \sim_B F\), if \(E \leq_B F\) and \(F \leq_B E\). We write \(E <_B F\) if \(E \leq_B F\) and \(F \not \leq_B E\).

body: [Definition def:closed-orth-spc of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] An orthogonal space $X$ (possibly equipped with an action of a compact Lie group) is called \emph{closed} if for every linear isometric embedding $V\to W$ of finite-dimensional inner product spaces $V,W$, $X(V)\to X(W)$ is a closed embedding.

If $v\in C^{4,\alpha}_\delta(Y)$ and \(L_{\omega_k}v=0\), then $v=0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 14 of arXiv:2608.27433

body:
[Lem 7 of arXiv:2608.21312, 'Interface between competing random walks on a cycle'] For $n\ge0$ and $d\ge1$, let $Y_{U,n}$ be the shifted ATD walk as in \eqref{eq:shifted ATD walk} with $U=\tau^{(2)}_{0}$. Then the probability density function $f_{n}(x)$ of $Y_{U,n}$ for all $x\in \bR$ satisfies
\[
f_{n}(x)\le\frac{C}{(n+d)^2},
\]
for some universal constant $C>0$.

[Proposition 1 (Functional Blaschke-Santal\'o) of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] Let $f:\R^n\to\R_+$ be a measurable function such that $0<\int f <+\infty$. Then, there exists $z\in \R^n$ with the following property: 
\\
for every measurable function $g:\R^n\to\R_+$ and measurable function $\Omega:\R_{+}\to\R_{+}$ satisfying
$$f(x+z)g(y)\le \Omega^{2}(\langle x,y\rangle ) \quad \text{for every } x,y\in \R^n \text{ such that } \langle x,y\rangle >0,$$
        one has
         \begin{equation}
         
         \int_{\R^n} f(x)dx\int_{\R^n} g(y)dy\le
        \left( \int_{\R^n} \Omega({|x|^{2}})dx\right)^2.\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Functional Blaschke-Santal\'o

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \(L>0\) and \(a>1\). Define
\(\mathsf A_{a,L}:L^2(B_{a,L},\mathrm dA)\to L^2(0,\infty)\) by
\[
        (\mathsf A_{a,L}f)(\xi)
        :=
        \int_{B_{a,L}}\overline{u_\xi(z)}f(z)\,\mathrm dA(z).
\]
Then \(\mathsf A_{a,L}\) is Hilbert--Schmidt,
\(K_{B_{a,L}}=\mathsf A_{a,L}^*\mathsf A_{a,L}\), and \(K_{B_{a,L}}\) is a
positive trace-class operator with \(\operatorname{tr}(K_{B_{a,L}})=L\lambda_a\).

[Lemma lem:scalar_DR_variance of arXiv:2609.02491, 'Generalised Random Parking for Trapeziums on a Strip'] Let $F:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be locally bounded and continuous for all sufficiently large arguments. Suppose that, for some $C_0\in\mathbb{R}$ and all sufficiently large $x$,
\begin{equation}
F(x+a) = \frac{1}{x} \mleft( \int_0^xF(t)\,\mathrm{d} t + \int_\delta^{x+\delta}F(t)\,\mathrm{d} t \mright) + \frac{C_0}{x} + p(x+a), 
\end{equation}
where $ |p(x)|\le C\mathcal R_2(x)$ for all sufficiently large $x$. Then, there exists a constant $\rho\ge0$ such that
\[
F(x) = \rho\cdot (x+\varsigma ) + \mathcal{O}(\mathcal R_2(x)).
\]
title: Lemma lem:scalar_DR_variance of arXiv:2609.02491

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2606.19115, 'Finite free perpetuities'] Let $p \in \tilde{\pols}_{\le n}(\C)$ be written in the form 
    \[
    p(z) = \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} \coef{k}{n}(p) z^{n-k}.
    \]
    Then, for any $0 \le d \le n$, the $d$-fold normalized derivatives satisfy:
            \[ \partial_n^d p(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-d} (-1)^k \binom{n-d}{k} \coef{k}{n}(p) z^{n-d-k}. \]
            and
        \[ D_n^d p(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-d} (-1)^k \binom{n-d}{k} \coef{k+d}{n}(p) z^{n-d-k}. \]
title: Lemma 9 of arXiv:2606.19115

body:
Let $S = n^{-1} X^T X = \sum_{i=1}^M \lambda_i u_i u_i^T$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\mathbb{R}^M$ with population covariance $\Sigma$, and let $M/n \to c \in (0,1)$. Among rotation-equivariant estimators $\sum_i d_i u_i u_i^T$ the Frobenius-optimal choice is the oracle $d_i^* = u_i^T \Sigma u_i$, whose large-dimensional limit is $\lambda_i / |1 - c - c\lambda_i \breve m_F(\lambda_i)|^2$ with $\breve m_F(\lambda) = \lim_{\eta \downarrow 0} m_F(\lambda + i\eta)$, $m_F(z) = \int dF(t)/(t - z)$ the Stieltjes transform of the limiting sample spectral distribution $F$ (Ledoit-Peche 2011). Writing $\operatorname{Im} \breve m_F(\lambda) = \pi f(\lambda)$ and $\operatorname{Re} \breve m_F(\lambda) = \pi H_f(\lambda)$, $H_f(x) = \pi^{-1} \mathrm{PV}\!\int f(t)/(t - x)\,dt$, the oracle reads $\tilde d_i = \lambda_i / \big[(\pi c \lambda_i f(\lambda_i))^2 + (1 - c - \pi c \lambda_i H_f(\lambda_i))^2\big]$. Ledoit and Wolf (2020) estimate $f$ and $H_f$ from the sample eigenvalues themselves with the Epanechnikov kernel $\kappa(x) = \tfrac{3}{4\sqrt5}(1 - x^2/5)^+$ and the eigenvalue-proportional bandwidth $h_j = \lambda_j n^{-1/3}$: $\tilde f(x) = M^{-1}\sum_j \kappa((x - \lambda_j)/h_j)/h_j$ and $\tilde H_f(x) = M^{-1}\sum_j H_\kappa((x - \lambda_j)/h_j)/h_j$, where $H_\kappa(x) = -\tfrac{3x}{10\pi} + \tfrac{3}{4\sqrt5\pi}(1 - x^2/5)\log\big|\tfrac{\sqrt5 - x}{\sqrt5 + x}\big|$. The resulting estimator $\hat\Sigma = \sum_i \tilde d_i u_i u_i^T$ has no tuning constant, is positive definite when $c < 1$, and its Frobenius loss (and its minimum-variance-portfolio loss) converges to the oracle's; for $c > 1$ a separate formula handles the $M - n$ null eigenvalues.
rows i.i.d. with finite twelfth moments (the Ledoit-Wolf condition)
M/n -> c in (0,1) for the stated form; the population spectral distribution has compact support (Ledoit-Peche take it bounded away from zero)
the sample eigenvalues are distinct (they are, almost surely)

body:
[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is a proved mean-conditioning case of Svante Janson's Problem 20.3 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Let w_j >= 0, w_0 > 0, Phi(z) = sum_{j>=0} w_j z^j, and rho be its radius of convergence. Choose a fixed tau in (0,rho], with Phi(tau) < infinity, and define pi_j = w_j tau^j/Phi(tau), mu = sum j pi_j > 0, and sigma^2 = sum (j-mu)^2 pi_j in (0,infinity). Allow either tau < rho, or tau = rho with finite sigma^2. Let integers m_n satisfy m_n - n mu = O(1), and restrict to feasible sizes. Draw (Y_1,...,Y_n) with probability proportional to product_i w_{Y_i}, conditional on sum_i Y_i = m_n, and put N_d = number of i with Y_i = d. For any fixed finite set D of nonnegative integers, ((N_d-n pi_d)/sqrt(n))_{d in D} converges in distribution to a centered multivariate Gaussian vector. Its diagonal covariance is V_dd = pi_d(1-pi_d) - (d-mu)^2 pi_d^2/sigma^2; for distinct d,e its covariance is V_de = -pi_d pi_e - (d-mu)(e-mu)pi_d pi_e/sigma^2. Degenerate Gaussian coordinates are allowed. In Janson's parameters, Psi(t) = t Phi'(t)/Phi(t), lambda = mu, and nu = lim_{t upward to rho} Psi(t), so the two cases are 0 < lambda < nu and lambda = nu with finite variance. The stronger O(1) centering hypothesis is explicit here; mere convergence m_n/n -> lambda is not being asserted to justify centering by the fixed law pi. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
The tilt is fixed, mu > 0, and 0 < sigma^2 < infinity.
m_n-n mu = O(1), with positive conditioning probability.
D is finite; tau is interior or is the finite-variance boundary tilt.
