For unit teacher theta_N and population losses Phi_N(x)=phi(x.theta_N) on S^(N-1), with one fixed phi independent of N, Assumption A is phi_prime(m)<0 on (0,1). The information exponent is an integer k>=1 such that phi is C^(k+1)([-1,1]), its derivatives of orders 1,...,k-1 vanish at zero, phi^(k)(0)<0, and its (k+1)-st derivative is bounded on [-1,1]. For H_N=L_N-E L_N, Assumption B requires uniform constants C_1,iota>0 with sup_(x in S^(N-1)) E[(grad_S H_N(x).theta_N)^2]<=C_1 and sup_(x in S^(N-1)) E||grad_S H_N(x)||^(4+iota)<=C_1*N^((4+iota)/2). The source algorithm uses fresh independent samples and positive spherical step delta_N/N followed by unit normalization. Define alpha_c(N,1)=1, alpha_c(N,2)=log N, alpha_c(N,k)=N^(k-2) for k>=3. These definitions concern a rank-one population loss and online updates. They do not by themselves establish a mean-field two-layer network theorem or a frequency ordering. The fixed-phi condition is essential here; this card does not substitute an arbitrary N-dependent profile.

body: In computer science and telecommunications, Hamming codes are a family of linear error-correcting codes. Hamming codes can detect one-bit and two-bit errors, or correct one-bit errors without detection of uncorrected errors. By contrast, the simple parity code cannot correct errors, and can detect only an odd number of bits in error. Hamming codes are perfect codes, that is, they achieve the highest possible rate for codes with their block length and minimum distance of three. Richard W. Hamming invented Hamming codes in 1950 as a way of automatically correcting errors introduced by punched card readers. In his original paper, Hamming elaborated his general idea, but specifically focused on the Hamming(7,4) code which adds three parity bits to four bits of data.
title: Hamming code

[Theorem 18 (\cite{NuPe,NP-book}) of arXiv:2606.14812, 'Joint convergence in Wiener chaos via transport hierarchy and Malliavin covariances'] Fix an integer $n\geq 1$ and consider a sequence 
	$(F_k=I_n(f_k), k\geq 1)$ of square integrable random variables 
	in the $n$th Wiener chaos. Assume that
	\begin{equation}
		\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathbf{E}[F_k^2] 
		= \lim_{k\to\infty}n!\|f_k\|^2_{H^{\odot n}} = 1.
	\end{equation}
	Then the following statements are equivalent:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $(F_k)$ converges in distribution to $N(0,1)$ as 
		$k\to\infty$.
		\item $\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathbf{E}[F_k^4]=3$.
		\item $\lim_{k\to\infty}\|f_k\otimes_l f_k\|_{H^{\otimes 2(n-l)}}
		=0$ for $l=1,2,\ldots,n-1$.
		\item $\|DF_k\|_H^2$ converges to $n$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ as 
		$k\to\infty$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 44 of arXiv:2605.02430, '\textbf{Scaling limit of the range of tree-valued branching random walks in random environ'] Let $\nu$ be a supercritical offspring distribution whose mean is denoted by $\ttm_\nu$. 
We assume that $ \sum_{k\in \bbN} k^{2} \nu(k) \leko \infty$. Let $(\bT, \boo)$ be 
either a GW($\nu$)-tree as in Definition \ref{GWfordef} $(\textbf a)$ (in this case: $\boo\eqo \varnothing$) or an infinite GW($\nu$)-tree as in Definition \ref{GWptdef} or an invariant GW($\nu$)-tree as in 
Definition~\ref{definvRW}. Let $\overline{X}_n \eqo (\bT, X_n)$, $n\ino \bbN$, be a $\mathtt m_\nu$-biased RW on $\bT$ such that $X_0 \eqo \boo$. Then, for all $n, p\ino \bbN^*$, the following holds true. 
\begin{compactenum}

\smallskip

\item[$(i)$] If $\bT$ is a GW($\nu$)-tree, $\bP \big(\max_{1\leq k\leq n} |X_k| \geq p \big) \leq 4 ne^{-p^2/2n}$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(ii)$] If $\bT$ is an invariant GW($\nu$)-tree, $\bP \big(\max_{1\leq k\leq n} \big|  \bbn X_k \bbn   \big| \geq p \big) \leq 8 n^3e^{-(p-1)^2/2n}$. 

\smallskip

Let $\mathcal{K}$ be an essentially small tensor-triangulated category. A thick subcategory $\mathcal{P} \subsetneq \mathcal{K}$ is a prime thick $\otimes$-ideal if $a \otimes b \in \mathcal{P} \implies a \in \mathcal{P}$ or $b \in \mathcal{P}$. body:
[Proposition 13 (Exact linearity of the separatrix; cf.\
Paper~III, Prop.~5.1) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] Under \textup{(S1)--(S4)}, a distribution lies in the separatrix
if and only if it annihilates every normal direction:
\[
\pi\in\Sigma\iff\langle\pi,\mathbf n_\nu\rangle=0\ \ \forall\nu
\iff\langle\pi|_O,\mathbf d_O\rangle=0\ \ \text{for every orbit }O,
\]
and explicitly, on the whole simplex,
\[
\Sigma
=\Bigl\{\pi\in\Delta_{m-1}:\
\sqrt{\kappa(z)}\,\pi_z=\sqrt{\kappa(\sigma(z))}\,\pi_{\sigma(z)}\
\text{for every orbit}\Bigr\},
\]
with the weights of neutral sites unconstrained. Note that the
linear form of the condition already covers the boundary strata: if
one of $\pi_z,\pi_{\sigma(z)}$ vanishes so does the other, so no
orbit can carry mass at a single site --- which is how Paper~III's
ratio condition, stated only on orbits of positive mass, is
subsumed here. Equivalently:
$\Sigma$ is the intersection of the simplex with a linear subspace
of $\mathbb R^m$ of codimension $r=n_{\mathrm{pair}}$; the
interior part $\Sigma^\circ$, which the spherical
picture below uses, is the corresponding relatively open subset. We
write
\[
\Sigma^\circ:=\Sigma\cap\Delta^\circ_{m-1}
\]
throughout, and keep the distinction firmly: the \emph{algebraic}
statements of this section hold on $\Sigma\subseteq\Delta_{m-1}$,
closed simplex included, while every \emph{Riemannian} statement ---
distances, geodesics, isometries, Hessians --- is made on
$\Sigma^\circ\subseteq\Delta^\circ_{m-1}$, where the Fisher--Rao
metric is defined.
This recovers, through the orbit collapse, the affine characterisation
of the separatrix obtained in Paper~III, and prepares it for the
spherical representation.

body:
[Theorem 1 (Stable convergence of the local linearization error) of arXiv:2608.16256, 'Error Distribution of the Local Linearization Method for Stochastic Differential Equations'] Under the standing assumptions, assume additionally that
\[
    f\in C^3(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d).
\]
Let \(W=(W^{\alpha\beta})_{1\le\alpha,\beta\le q}\) be a
\(q^2\)-dimensional standard Brownian motion independent of \(\mathcal F\),
defined on an extension of the original probability space.  Let \(U\) be the
unique continuous solution of
\begin{equation}
    dU_t^i
    =
    f^i_j(X_t)U_t^j\,dt
    +
    \frac{1}{4\sqrt3}
    f^i_{jk}(X_t)
    \sigma^j_\alpha
    \sigma^k_\beta
    \bigl(
        dW_t^{\alpha\beta}
        +
        dW_t^{\beta\alpha}
    \bigr),
    \qquad
    U_0=0 .
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
    \hat U^n
    \Rightarrow^{\mathrm{st}}
    U
    \qquad
    \text{in } C([0,1],\mathbb R^d).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Stable convergence of the local linearization error

body:
[Lem 3 of arXiv:2608.02103, '$p$-Adic Diffusion and Random Walks on $[0,1]$'] The map $\rho$ satisfies 
\begin{align*}
\rho\left( p^mn+p^k\mathbb{Z}_p\right)&= p^{-m}\rho(n)+[0,p^{-k}]
\\
\rho\left(\mathbb{Q}_p\setminus \{p^mn+p^k\mathbb{Z}_p\}\right)
&=  \mathbb{R}_+ \setminus\left(p^{-m}\rho(n)+[0,p^{-k}]\right)
\end{align*}
for $n\in \mathbb{Q}_p / \mathbb{Z}_p$ and $m,k \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $k\geq m$, and it is a bijection
\[
\mathbb{Q}_p\setminus N_p\cong\mathbb{R}_+\,,
\]
where 
\[
N_p=\mathset{\frac{a}{p^n}\mid a\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\mathset{0},\;n\ge1}\,,
\]
viewed as a subset of $\mathbb{Q}_p$.

body:
[Definition def:ribbon-record of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] A rooted orthogonal-Weingarten ribbon record $\Gamma$ of degree $m$
consists of the dart set
$\{1,\ldots,m\}\times\{L_0,L_1,R_0,R_1\}$; its coefficient boxes and
color labels; perfect matchings $p,q,r$ giving the row,
coefficient-column, and rooted trace wiring; all local wedge and
direct/cross signs; the distinguished root boundary; and the following
orthogonal-Weingarten path data.

Partition the darts into the independent Haar-color classes
$\mathscr H_\Gamma$ (there is one class when all entries come from one
Haar matrix).  If $a\in\mathscr H_\Gamma$ contains $m_a$ coefficient
occurrences, put $k_a=2m_a$, so it has $2k_a=4m_a$ darts, and denote by
$p_a,q_a$ the restrictions of $p,q$.  The rooted dart order chooses a
deterministic relabelling $\sigma_a$ with
$\sigma_a\cdot e_{k_a}=p_a$, where
\[
 e_k=\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\ldots,\{2k-1,2k\}\},
\]
and put
$\mathfrak m_a=\sigma_a^{-1}\cdot q_a\in\mathcal P_2(2k_a)$.
The orthogonal Weingarten graph has vertex set
$\bigsqcup_{j\ge0}\mathcal P_2(2j)$.  At level $j$ it has a solid arrow
\[
 \mathfrak n\longrightarrow(i,2j-1)\cdot\mathfrak n,
 \qquad 1\le i<2j-1,
\]
and it has a dashed arrow
$\mathfrak n\dashrightarrow\mathfrak n^\downarrow$ when
$\{2j-1,2j\}\in\mathfrak n$, where $\mathfrak n^\downarrow$ is
obtained by deleting that pair.  The record chooses, for every $a$, one
\emph{individual} path $\gamma_a$ from $\mathfrak m_a$ to the empty
pairing.  It uses exactly $k_a$ dashed arrows; write $s_a$ for its number
of solid arrows.  If $\mu_a$ is the coset type of $\mathfrak m_a$, define
\[
 d_a:=|\mathfrak m_a|=k_a-\ell(\mu_a)
      =k_a-\#(p_a\vee q_a),
 \qquad
 g_a:=s_a-d_a\ge0,
 \qquad
 g_{\rm Wg}:=\sum_{a\in\mathscr H_\Gamma}g_a.
\]
Thus $g_{\rm Wg}$ is the total number of solid arrows beyond shortest
orthogonal-Weingarten paths; unlike the unitary excess, it need not be
even.

Let $w_\Gamma$ be the scalar coefficient of this chosen product path,
including the bounded local wedge and direct/cross coefficients.  Write
$\operatorname{Contr}^{\rm raw}_{\Gamma,\tau}$ for the typed raw
contraction determined by the record and its circuit state, and put
\[
 F_\Gamma=\#(p\vee r),\qquad
 \ell_\Gamma=\#(p\vee q)
      =\sum_{a\in\mathscr H_\Gamma}\#(p_a\vee q_a),\qquad
 \omega_\Gamma=n^{F_\Gamma}w_\Gamma,\qquad
 \mathcal A_\Gamma=w_\Gamma
       \operatorname{Contr}^{\rm raw}_{\Gamma,\tau}.
\]
Thus $w_\Gamma$ is a scalar coefficient, not the value or norm of an
open contraction; $\omega_\Gamma$ merely expresses the same coefficient
in once-normalized original-circuit units.
title: Rooted ribbon record and raw coefficient

body:
[Definition 1 (Symmetric matrix normal (SN) distribution) of arXiv:2606.28678, '2606.28678'] Let $M\in \mathcal{S}^d$ and $\Psi,\Sigma\in \mathcal{S}_{++}^d$ be such that $\Psi\Sigma = \Sigma\Psi$. A random matrix $\mathfrak{Z}\in \mathcal{S}^d$ is said to have an SN distribution with mean $M$ and scales $\Psi,\Sigma$, written
\[
\mathfrak{Z}\sim \mathcal{SN}_{d\times d}(M,\Psi,\Sigma),
\]
if $\vecs(\mathfrak{Z})\sim \mathcal{N}_{q_d}(\vecs(M),\Omega_{\Psi,\Sigma})$. In particular, $\EE[\mathfrak{Z}] = M$ and $\Var(\vecs(\mathfrak{Z})) = \Omega_{\Psi,\Sigma}$. The density, with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $\mathcal{S}^d$ induced by the isometry $\vecs$, is
\[
S\mapsto \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{q_d/2}|\Omega_{\Psi,\Sigma}|^{1/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}(\vecs(S-M))^{\top}\Omega_{\Psi,\Sigma}^{-1}\vecs(S-M)\right\}, \qquad S\in \mathcal{S}^d.
\]
title: Symmetric matrix normal (SN) distribution

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:109871f01d4f6b4ab823e5b0b019fea88818232bfdcfd78da7d6755f76a2e669","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/10/109871f01d4f6b4ab823e5b0b019fea88818232bfdcfd78da7d6755f76a2e669.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:49331acff4a65667e72885df2d3d58dd5e4993043ec230db85ff3dd996378bce","bundle_entry_key":"stationary-rigidity","bundle_id":"population.adam-piecewise-potential-boundary-and-stationary-rigidity-007","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"adaptive optimization and discrete dynamics","draft":"w706/bundle_007.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.adam:adam-stationary-active-curvature-threshold-origin-product-two-cycles","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"T421-W706-019 v1; target1; kind special; proof (unaudited).

STATEMENT AND LIMIT
Consider UNCORRECTED Adam, b=9/10,d=999/1000, epsilon outside the square
root, on a positive diagonal quadratic with two eigenvalues. Suppose
eta*lambda_i/epsilon>38 for i=1,2. Let K be a compact fully invariant
set of physical states (nonnegative raw variances), and let pi be an
invariant Borel probability measure on K. Suppose pi-almost surely

 sum_i lambda_i*y_i^2*w_i,next*(w_i,next-2)=0.              (1)

Here y_i=x_i/(c*eta), c=1/19, and w_i=c*eta*lambda_i/
(sqrt(v_i)+epsilon). Equation (1) says that scaled active curvature is
38 wherever the gradient is nonzero, with its numerator identity
extended by zero at zero gradients.

Then pi is supported on the nine product states obtained by choosing
in each coordinate either the origin or one of the two cycle phases

 (y,mu,V)=(0,0,0), or (+/-a,-/+c*a,a^2),
 a=1/2-e, e=epsilon/(c*eta*lambda), mu=m/(c*eta*lambda),
 V=v/(c*eta*lambda)^2.

Equivalently pi is a convex combination of the origin atom and the four
uniform measures on the product/axis two-cycles (two axis cycles and two
relative-phase product cycles). If zero gradient has pi-probability zero,
the origin atom is absent.

This is a stationary equality classification. It does NOT show that an
ordinary corrected trajectory with active curvature tending to38 converges
to one of these cycles. Sparse excursions or heteroclinic pieces of an
omega-limit set are not excluded by this proof. In particular it does not
settle the two-supercritical target or upgrade claim016 to that range.

1. THE SOURCE POTENTIAL APPLIES TO BOUNDED FULL ORBITS
Use Fong--Yang arXiv2608.20638v2, Appendix H.1.2, equations105,117--123,
Lemma H.5 and its six-case proof, pp.54--58. Source notation in a scalar
coordinate is p=w_t,w=w_(t+1),u=w/p,y=y_t,z=y_(t-1),Delta=y-z.

Every state in K has a bounded full orbit: repeatedly select predecessors
in K using F(K)=K. The variance recursion gives V_t>=nu*y_(t-1)^2 and
the second-moment/speed identities F1/F2. The eventual condition F3
(p>1 implies w>c) in the source in fact holds at every point of such a
full bounded orbit. Unroll its momentum and variance from time t-N.
The source Step1 argument bounds sqrt(V_next)+e by

 (1+b)*sqrt(d/(d-b^2))+e + O(b^N*p*|mu_(t-N)|).

Here p<=1/e and boundedness makes the last term tend to zero. Moreover
d/(d-b^2)<9 and e<1/2, so the remaining bound is less than
3*(1+b)+1/2<1/c. Thus F3 holds strictly. All the source's remaining
identities and inequalities are pointwise, with no initialization
condition. Its potential inequality therefore holds at every point of K.

The previous position is a single-valued continuous function of the
current state: z=y+p*mu/c, since y=z-p*mu/c. Hence the printed piecewise
potential Phi is a BOREL function of the scalar state. It is bounded on
K: e>0 bounds p, positions and moments are bounded, and Gamma is bounded.
No continuity of Phi is asserted; claim018 records its boundary jump.

2. EQUALITY CASES OF THE SCALAR MARGIN
Set Psi=Phi(Fz)-Phi(z)-y^2*w*(w-2). The source proves Psi>=0.
The following stricter conclusions are extracted from its proof.

(a) p,w<=1. The exact quadratic expression from Step3 has a positive
definite (Delta,y) matrix. Its determinant is

 (c/2)*w*[(1-b^2*u^2)*(2-w)-(c/2)*(1+b)^2*w],

and its first diagonal entry is c*(1-b^2*u^2)/2>0. Since
u^2<=1/d and 0<w<=1, strict positivity follows from

 1-b^2/d-(c/2)*(1+b)^2 =697/7400>0.

Thus Psi=0 requires y=Delta=0, hence mu=0. The scalar state is a point
on the pure-variance axis y=mu=0 with p,w<=1.

(b) p<=1<w. Step4 has a positive definite quadratic part. For its
coefficients A,B,C the determinant identity printed there is

 AC-B^2/4=c*C/2+b^2*u^2/(1+b)*[c/2-(1-b/2)*(w-1)^2].

The bracket is strictly positive because 1<w<=d^(-1/2)<=1+c.
If y=Delta=0, the quadratic vanishes but V_next=d*V<V and the upward
crossing makes Gamma(V)-Gamma(V_next)>0. Thus Psi>0 always.

(c) p>1>=w. Step5 gives Psi>=y^2*H(w)>0; y is nonzero in this case
by the variance recursion. F3 proved above supplies w>c as required.

(d) p,w>1 and y=0. Step6 gives Psi>=A*Delta^2+
Gamma(V)-Gamma(dV). A>0 and the unclipped Gamma is strictly increasing
for V>0. Thus equality forces Delta=0 and V=0, giving the origin.

(e) p,w>1 and y!=0, u<=b. The source's strict lower bound is
Psi/y^2>=171/50000-6/2375>0.

(f) p,w>1 and y!=0, b<=u<d^(-1/2). Source Step6 bounds Psi/y^2
below by a quadratic form in X=p-2, Z=Delta/y-2, tau=u-1. The (X,Z)
block is positive definite with determinant >=(6/25)*w^2. Its Schur
complement in tau is strictly positive: writing U=1/p in (0,1), the
available coefficient exceeds (243/10)*U while the cost is at most
(625/27)*U^2. Their difference is at least (311/270)*U>0.
Consequently equality forces tau=X=Z=0. Thus p=w=2 and Delta=2*y.
The variance recursion then gives V=V_next=a^2 and |y|=a; the previous
step relation gives mu=-c*y. These are exactly the cycle phases.

The source partition writes u<d^(-1/2). At the endpoint equality in
the speed bound would require y=0 and e=0 or V=0. With e>0 and y!=0,
u=(sqrt(V)+e)/(sqrt(dV+nu*y^2)+e)<d^(-1/2), as required.

Thus the only possible zero-margin scalar states are the origin, the
cycle phases, and a segment of the pure-variance axis below curvature1.
Any positive-variance point on that axis exits this last zero-margin
region after finitely many iterates: V decays geometrically to zero and
eventually crosses w=1, where case(b) has strictly positive margin.

3. INTEGRATE THE BOUNDED BOREL POTENTIAL
Let L=sum_i lambda_i*Phi_i, also bounded Borel. Since pi is invariant,
integral(L composed F-L) d pi=0. Equation (1) and the source inequality
give, pi-almost surely,

 L(Fz)-L(z)=sum_i lambda_i*Psi_i(z)>=0.

Its integral is zero, so each nonnegative Psi_i vanishes almost surely.
Invariance implies that, on a single pi-full set, Psi_i(F^n z)=0 for
every integer n>=0 and both coordinates (a countable intersection).
Section2 excludes every positive pure-variance state from this set.
Thus each scalar marginal lies on the origin or exact two-cycle.
The nine product states and the invariant weights stated above follow.

No independence of coordinates, ergodicity of pi, continuity of Phi, or
passage of integrals of discontinuous functions under weak convergence
was used. In particular one must not apply this proof to empirical weak
limits before establishing equation(1) for that invariant limit measure.

[Conj 6 (Algebraic Integrability Conjecture) of arXiv:2609.00974, 'On Algebraic Integrability\\ of Vector Fields \\ with Rational Function Coefficients\\ tha'] Let $K/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ be an algebraic extension of fields. Let $\F$ be a foliation on $K$, which admits a model over the ring of integers $\cO_L$, where $L$ is a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$.

    The following are equivalent:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The foliation $\F$ is algebraically integrable, i.e., it is of the form $\F=\op{Der}_{W}(K)$ for a subfield $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\subset W\subset K$.
        \item For almost all primes $p$ and all maximal ideals $q$ over $p$ in $\cO_L$ the reduction modulo $q$ of $\F$ is $p$-closed, i.e., it defines a $1$-foliation.
    \end{enumerate} (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Algebraic Integrability Conjecture

[Lemma of arXiv:2608.25065, 'Detection of first homology via random geometric graphs in the thermodynamic regime'] \label[lemma]{very likely to get at least one loop}
    There exist $c, c_1 > 0$
    depending on $\lambda_-,\lambda_+,d,Q$
    such that for any $\epsilon >0$
    the following holds. 
    There exists $R_0=R_0(\epsilon,\lambda_-,\lambda_+,d,Q)$
    such that for all $R \ge R_0$ we have
    \[
        \mathbb{P}( E'_x \mbox{ holds for some } x \in [-\epsilon R+Q\log R, \epsilon R - Q \log R]^d)
        \ge 
        1-e^{-c_1 \epsilon^d R}
    \]
    and if $\lambda_- > \lambda_c(d)$,
    \[
        \mathbb{P}( E_x \mbox{ holds for some } x \in [-\epsilon R+Q\log R, \epsilon R - Q \log R]^d)
        \ge 
        1-e^{-c_1 \epsilon^d R}.
    \]

[Proposition 4 (Characterizing equation for the mgf of the stationary distribution) of arXiv:2606.00781, '2606.00781'] The moment generating function (mgf) $g:[0,1]\to[0,\infty)$ of the stationary distribution $\mu$ of $X$, defined via $g(x):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mu_nx^n/n!$ for all $x\in[0,1]$, satisfies for every $x\in[0,1]$ the
   equation
   \begin{equation} 
      2dxg'(x)+2\int_{(0,1]}\frac{g(x)-g(x(1-t))}{t}\,\Lambda({\rm d}t)\ =\
      dxg(x)+\int_{(0,1]}\frac{e^{xt}-1}{t}g\big(x(1-t)\big)\,\Lambda({\rm d}t)
   \end{equation}
   with $d:=\Lambda(\{0\})$. Conversely, if $g$ is the mgf of some distribution on $[0,1]$ and if $g$ satisfies
   the equation (\ref{inteqn}) for all $x\in[0,1]$, then $g$ is the mgf of the stationary distribution $\mu$ of $X$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Characterizing equation for the mgf of the stationary distribution

Let f:[0,1]->R be 1-Lipschitz and 0<epsilon<1/2. Set n=2 ceil(4 epsilon^(-3)). There exists an even real polynomial p(z)=p_0+sum_{j=1}^{n/2} p_(2j) z^(2j), of degree at most n, such that sup_{z in [0,1]}|p(z)-f(z)|<=epsilon and |p_(2j)|<=2^n for j>=1. The constant coefficient p_0 is not bounded uniformly over all such f; additive constants of f are unrestricted. The coefficient bound is exponential 2^n, not the product 2n.

[Definition 37 of arXiv:2609.04033, 'From configuration spaces to graph complexes via $\mathbf{FA}$-modules'] Given $n$ and $r$ we define the chain complex $(\mathsf{TT}(n,r), d_{\mathsf{TT}})$ as follows.  The underlying graded vector space is

$$ \mathsf{TT}(n,r) = \left(\ds\bigoplus_{i=0}^{\lfloor (n-r+1)/2\rfloor} \Sigma^{2i-r+2}\mathsf{T}(n,2i+1,r-2)\right)\oplus \Sigma^{1-r}\mathsf{T}(n,0,r-1).$$	
The differential $d_{\mathsf{TT}}$ is of the form $d_{\mathsf{TT}}= d_{\mathsf{T}} + (-1)^{E} d_R$ 
where $d_\mathsf{T}$ is the differential on each summand, and where $d_R\colon \mathsf{T}(n,1,r-2) \to \mathsf{T}(n,0,r-1)$ is defined to take the unique blue marking and turn it red. 

The fact that $d_{\mathsf{TT}}^2 = 0$ follows immediately from the fact that edge contraction and changing the color of a marking commute; the sign ensures they anti-commute.
title: Definition 37 of arXiv:2609.04033

[Proposition 4 (Control of the good event) of arXiv:2604.25470, 'A mathematical analysis of hierarchical Hopfield models'] Fix $\delta\in(0,1)$ and $\rho\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $m:=\lfloor \delta L\rfloor+1$.
		Define
		\[
		q_-^{\mathrm{true}}
		:=
		\mathbb P\bigl(|\xi^\mu|_1<\theta\bigr),
		\qquad \mu\in S_\alpha,
		\]
		and suppose that there exists a deterministic quantity $\overline q_+\ge 0$ such that
		\[
		q_+:=\max_{\mu\notin S_\alpha}\mathbb P\bigl(x_\mu=1\mid \eta^{(\alpha)}\bigr)
		\le \overline q_+
		\qquad\text{almost surely.}
		\]
		Then
		\[
		\mathbb P\bigl(\mathcal G_\alpha(\delta,\rho)^c\bigr)
		\le
		\binom{L}{m}\bigl(q_-^{\mathrm{true}}\bigr)^m
		+
		\frac{\bigl((M-L)\overline q_+\bigr)^{\rho+1}}{(\rho+1)!}.
		\]
		In particular, if
		\[
		\binom{L}{m}\bigl(q_-^{\mathrm{true}}\bigr)^m \xrightarrow[N_f\to\infty]{}0
		\qquad\text{and}\qquad
		(M-L)\overline q_+ \xrightarrow[N_f\to\infty]{}0,
		\]
		then
		\[
		\mathbb P\bigl(\mathcal G_\alpha(\delta,\rho)^c\bigr)\xrightarrow[N_f\to\infty]{}0.
		\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let N be a positive integer and X a random variable with values in D(N); put F(n) = P(X | n) for n | N (the event that X divides n). Then P(X = n) = sum_{d | n} mu(n/d) F(d), with mu the arithmetic Moebius function. Conversely, a real function F on D(N) equals n -> P(X | n) for some law on D(N) if and only if F(N) = 1 and every value p(n) = sum_{d | n} mu(n/d) F(d) is nonnegative. Monotonicity cannot replace nonnegativity: on D(6), F(1) = 0, F(2) = F(3) = 3/5, F(6) = 1 is order-preserving with F(6) = 1, yet p(6) = F(6) - F(2) - F(3) + F(1) = -1/5.
N is a positive integer
X takes values in the positive divisors of N

body:
[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; the criterion reproduces the source's worked example, and every algebraic step was confirmed symbolically] This is the proved kernel inequality used for the campaign answer to Problem 3.3 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240). Let mu be a probability measure on R whose support has diameter at most one, and for R>0 define xi_R(u)=the integral over x in the real line of [(x-u)^2+R^2]^(-1) mu(dx). If xi_R'(u_0)=0 and xi_R''(u_0)>=0, then xi_R(u_0)>=1. Equality forces R^2=3/4 and mu=(delta_{u_0-1/2}+delta_{u_0+1/2})/2, where delta_a denotes a unit point mass at a. The proof decomposes the mean-zero-derivative constraint into one- and two-atom extreme measures and checks the two polynomial inequalities written out in the record. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
mu is a probability measure with support diameter at most one.
R>0; u_0 is stationary with nonnegative second derivative.
metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:ad622d5bf73c04228172964ae7fb91c69d3036e499260717b4c5e352163cc6cc","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/ad/ad622d5bf73c04228172964ae7fb91c69d3036e499260717b4c5e352163cc6cc.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:9d13417b75738e2fc15d10e3322f651494c6abbbfcb1c6c7d810fcc69a74ead5","bundle_entry_key":"hasebe-ueda-problem-3-3-stationary-cauchy-kernel-lower-bound","bundle_id":"population.probability-campaign-results-20260914-001","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"codex-prob1000-nodes-1010/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.free:hasebe-ueda-problem-3-3-stationary-cauchy-kernel-lower-bound","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"Translate so that $u_0 = 0$ and write $s = R^2$ and $\varphi(d) = 1/(d^2+s)$. The three quantities in
play are
$$F = \int \varphi \, d\mu = \xi_R(0), \qquad G = \int \frac{d}{(d^2+s)^2}\,d\mu = -\tfrac12 \xi_R'(0),
\qquad H = \int \frac{3d^2-s}{(d^2+s)^3}\,d\mu = \tfrac12\xi_R''(0),$$
and the hypotheses are $G = 0$ and $H \ge 0$. All three are linear in $\mu$.

Consider the set $K$ of probability measures $\nu$ on $\operatorname{supp}\mu$ with $G(\nu)=0$. It is
convex and weak-* compact, and its extreme points carry at most two atoms, since a measure subject to
normalisation and one further linear constraint can be perturbed inside $K$ as soon as its support has
three points. By Choquet's theorem $\mu$ is a barycentre of extreme points, and $F$, $G$ and $H$
integrate accordingly. An extreme point with a single atom must be $\delta_0$, because $G(\delta_x)=0$
forces $x=0$. So it is enough to understand a *pair*: atoms at $-a$ and $b$ with $a,b>0$ and
$a+b \le 1$.

For such a pair the condition $G=0$ determines the two weights, and writing $A = a^2+s$, $B = b^2+s$ and
$\Delta = bA^2+aB^2 > 0$,
$$F - 1 = \frac{\Phi}{\Delta}, \qquad H = \frac{\Psi}{\Delta AB}, \qquad
\Phi = bA(1-A) + aB(1-B), \qquad \Psi = bB(3a^2-s) + aA(3b^2-s).$$
In terms of $D = a+b$ and $m = ab$ both collapse:
$$\frac{\Psi}{D} = 3m^2 + s(6m - D^2) - s^2, \qquad
\frac{\Phi}{D} = 3m^2 + m(1-D^2) + s(1-2m) - s^2 .$$

**Lemma A.** *If $\Psi \ge 0$ then $s \le \tfrac34 D^2$.* The quantity $\Psi/D$ is increasing in $m$, so
it is largest at $m = D^2/4$, where it equals $(3D^2-4s)(D^2+4s)/16$. For that to be nonnegative,
$s \le \tfrac34 D^2$.

**Lemma B.** *If $0 \le s \le \tfrac34$ and $D \le 1$ then $\Phi \ge 0$.* The quantity $\Phi/D$ is
concave in $s$, so on $[0,\tfrac34]$ it is least at an endpoint. At $s=0$ it is $m(1+3m-D^2) \ge 0$. At
$s = \tfrac34$ it is a convex function of $m$ whose derivative at $m = D^2/4$ is $(D^2-1)/2 \le 0$, so it
decreases on $(0, D^2/4]$ and is least at $m = D^2/4$, where it equals $(1-D^2)(D^2+3)/16 \ge 0$.

## Putting it together

Let $\mu$, $R$ and $u_0$ be as in the proposition, and decompose $\mu$ into extreme points as above.

Since $H(\mu) \ge 0$, some extreme point $\kappa$ has $H(\kappa) \ge 0$. It cannot be $\delta_0$, for
which $H = -1/s^2 < 0$. So $\kappa$ is a pair, and Lemma A gives $s \le \tfrac34 D_\kappa^2 \le \tfrac34$.

Now every extreme point has $F \ge 1$. For $\delta_0$ this is $F = 1/s \ge 4/3$. For a pair it is Lemma
B, which needs only $s \le \tfrac34$ and diameter at most one, and in particular does not care about the
sign of that pair's own $H$. Averaging, $F(\mu) \ge 1$, which is the proposition.

Equality is rigid. Lemma B is an equality only at $D=1$, $m=D^2/4$ and $s = \tfrac34$, that is, two atoms
of equal weight at $\pm\tfrac12$ with $R^2 = \tfrac34$: the symmetric Bernoulli law at its critical
radius, rescaled. So the symmetric Bernoulli is the unique extremal measure, which is why the constant it
produces is the answer.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:41d53089fc9154dfc68427cb689fc659cab94c6fae196dceb869ccf188d76c60","revision_digest":"sha256:9b4c7b6d3b0ec8dff2722e778fc17fe40b74161b32c5838f250300a75f180ac4","source_id":"doi:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15","source_revision":"problem source: ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374; own campaign record: 2026-09-14","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma 34 of arXiv:2608.27372, 'Universality and sharp thresholds for ellipsoid fitting'] Assume $(x_i)_{i\le n}$ satisfy the hypotheses of
	Proposition~\ref{prop:light-tail-quotient}. Fix $L\ge2$ and
	$\eps\in(0,1)$. There exists
	$C=C(L,\eps,K_x)>0$ such that the following holds.

	Fix $K>0$. Consider $\ell\in\{2,\ldots,L\}$, $\mathcal I\subset[n]$, and
	$t\in\R^n$ supported on $\mathcal I^c$ with $\|t\|_2=1$ and $\|t\|_{\infty}\leq (Kd)^{-1/2}$. Then, for every
		$\gamma\ge C K^{-1/2}$, and $\mathcal F_{\ell-1}^{\mathcal I}$-measurable $B_\ell\in\R^{p_\ell\times q_\ell}$,
	$$
	\mathbf 1_{\mathcal G_\ell^{\mathcal I}(t)}
	\P\left(
		\|\mathcal L_{X,\ell}^*t+B_\ell\|_*\le\gamma d
	\,\middle|\,
	\mathcal F_{\ell-1}^{\mathcal I}
	\right)
	\le
	\mathbf 1_{\mathcal G_\ell^{\mathcal I}(t)}
	(C \gamma)^{m_{t,\ell}q_\ell}.
	$$

body: The characteristic-function route to the quadratic-form bounded-density conjecture is VIABLE, not a dead end (correction of an earlier note). ||p||_inf <= (1/2pi) integral|phi_Q|. Three large eigenvalues each contribute a stationary-phase factor |t|^{-1/2}, so |phi_Q(t)| ~ |t|^{-3/2}, just inside integrability; two give |t|^{-1}, divergent - that is why three. The 'dead end' rested on the 3-D uniform ball (|phi|~1/t), which is not a projection of a product of 1-D densities and so not a valid instance. Measured integral|phi|/(2pi): 6.3 separable-uniform, 6.5 delocalized, 3.3 bimodal, 4.5-6.0 for the adversarial edge law 1{cos(s x^2)>1/2} - its bump at frequency s is killed by the other two directions and shrinks as s grows. So the whole conjecture reduces to ONE uniform oscillatory-integral estimate integral|phi_Q| <= 2 pi C over all A with three large eigenvalues and all laws <=1 (C~7; sharp density constant 3sqrt2). The per-direction van der Corput is still non-uniform; the estimate must be joint over the three directions.

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Let r_n<=q_n tend to infinity with r_n/q_n->gamma in (0,1], and let B_n be biorthogonally invariant real r_n by q_n signals with finite second moments. Let mu_n be their empirical singular-value laws after dividing the matrices by sqrt(r_n). If E W2(mu_n,mu)^2->0 for a deterministic finite-second-moment probability law mu on [0,infinity), then i_n(s)=I(B_n;sqrt(s)B_n+G_n)/(r_n*q_n) converges locally uniformly on s>=0 to a finite concave function i_mu. The law mu may have atoms, including a zero atom, and need not have finite logarithmic energy. Apply Theorem 4 only to regular spectral approximations with bounded smooth densities on compact intervals away from zero; shared-Haar Gaussian information continuity then pays the limit exchange. For X_N=U_N V_N^T/sqrt(N), with independent arrays of fixed centered iid real unit-variance factor laws of sizes N by M and P by M, finite fourth moments, and positive finite limits P/N,M/N, the Gaussian-factor reference B_N has the needed expected spectral W2 convergence by unaudited claim 008. At every differentiability point s>0 of its limiting normalized MI, m_B_N(s)->2*i_mu_prime(s) and limsup_N[m_X_N(s)-m_B_N(s)]<=0, where m_Q=E||Q-E[Q|sqrt(s)Q+G]||_F^2/(NP). This follows from the Haar comparison in unaudited claim 006. The possible exceptional SNR set is at most countable; pointwise MMSE extremality there remains open. Raw-product loss gaps are divided by N. Novelty of this continuity consequence and application is unestablished; all new proof dependencies remain unaudited.
Real matrices and standard independent Gaussian channel noise; Frobenius error divided by the number of entries.
Generic extension: biorthogonal invariance, finite second moments, positive finite rectangular aspect limit and expected spectral W2 convergence after dividing the signal by sqrt(number of rows).
Product consequence: positive finite limits P/N,M/N; independent fixed centered iid unit-variance real factor laws with finite fourth moments.
Published Theorem 4 is used only for compact bounded spectral densities away from zero and bounded deterministic singular profiles; its Assumptions 2,3 and aspect bound are checked.
The existing entropy/coupling arguments in claims 006 and 008 remain unaudited dependencies.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:6a6ca6a63166d44d3d9cf9391583d684e5e68cfd473148bf446c647856003226","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/6a/6a6ca6a63166d44d3d9cf9391583d684e5e68cfd473148bf446c647856003226.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:4ff0a7bdc107601cb716445557a06517fa517d47ab08abe6e8d67724f83df970","bundle_entry_key":"rotational-mi-limit-spectral-atoms-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-mi-limit-spectral-atoms-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:rotational-mi-limit-spectral-atoms-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Extending a rotationally invariant MI limit through spectral atoms

Target 2, proof draft, unaudited. Novelty is unestablished. The extension
uses a published theorem for regular spectral densities and our existing
entropy-continuity lemma; it is not a new derivation of the published
spherical-integral formula.

## 1. Statement and the external input

Let r_n<=q_n be positive integers, r_n->infinity, and r_n/q_n->gamma in
(0,1]. Let B_n be biorthogonally invariant real r_n by q_n matrices with
finite second moments. Let mu_n be the empirical distribution of the r_n
singular values of B_n/sqrt(r_n). Assume that a deterministic probability
measure mu on [0,infinity), of finite second moment, satisfies

    E W2(mu_n,mu)^2 -> 0.                              (1)

The claim is that

    i_n(s)=I(B_n;sqrt(s)B_n+G_n)/(r_n*q_n)

converges to a finite concave function i_mu(s) for every s>=0, locally
uniformly in s. Here G_n has independent standard real Gaussian entries.
No density, finite logarithmic moment or finite logarithmic energy of mu
is required. In particular mu may have a zero atom.

The external input is Pourkamali-Macris, arXiv:2403.04615, Theorem 4,
equation (14), PDF p6. In its real Gaussian model this establishes the
normalized MI limit for biorthogonally invariant signals S_n whose
empirical singular-value laws converge almost surely to a compactly
supported density satisfying Assumption 2 (including finite logarithmic
moment and logarithmic energy of its symmetrization), and whose empirical
second moments are almost surely bounded (Assumption 3), when q_n/r_n
is bounded. The source uses noise of entry variance 1/r_n: its posterior
Gaussian quadratic has exponent -r_n||Y-sqrt(s)S||_F^2/2 (equation (65)).
Set S_n=B_n/sqrt(r_n) and multiply the observation by sqrt(r_n); the MI
and normalization are exactly i_n(s) above. Theorem 4 is invoked as stated,
not reproved here. Its proof explicitly includes fixed singular values
with independent Haar frames, in Section 5.6.1, equation (68), PDF p19.

## 2. Approximating laws that meet every spectral hypothesis

There exist measures mu_k with bounded smooth densities supported in
[a_k,b_k] subset (0,infinity), such that W2(mu_k,mu)->0. One construction
is to couple A~mu with

    A_k=min(A,R_k)+2*epsilon_k+epsilon_k*Z,

where R_k->infinity, epsilon_k->0, and Z is independent with a smooth
bounded density compactly supported in [-1,1]. The resulting density is
smooth, bounded and supported inside [epsilon_k,R_k+3*epsilon_k].
The L2 coupling error tends to zero by the finite second moment of A
and the triangle inequality. This proves the W2 approximation assertion.

For each k, let mu_(n,k) put mass 1/r_n on the mid-quantiles
F_k^(-1)((j-1/2)/r_n), j=1,...,r_n. They converge in W2 to mu_k;
bounded support and convergence of the quantile step functions almost
everywhere give this by dominated convergence. Define B_(n,k) to have
these singular values multiplied by sqrt(r_n), with independent Haar
left and right frames.

In the source convention S_(n,k)=B_(n,k)/sqrt(r_n), its limiting spectral
density is mu_k. Its symmetrization is a bounded density supported in
two compact intervals separated from zero. Thus its log absolute moment
is finite. Its logarithmic energy is finite as well: the singularity
|log|x-y|| is locally Lebesgue integrable and the density is bounded,
while the support is compact. The empirical second moments are bounded
deterministically by b_k^2. The aspect bound follows from gamma>0.
These verify Assumptions 2,3 and the aspect condition separately for
each fixed k. Theorem 4 gives a finite limit

    i_k(s)=lim_n I(B_(n,k);sqrt(s)B_(n,k)+G_n)/(r_n*q_n).

## 3. Continuity pays for the two limits

Couple B_n and B_(n,k) by the same Haar frames and pair their decreasing
singular values. The normalized squared cost is

    delta_(n,k)^2
      = (r_n/q_n) E W2(mu_n,mu_(n,k))^2.

By (1), the deterministic quantile convergence and the L2 triangle
inequality for the random W2 distance,

    limsup_n delta_(n,k) <= sqrt(gamma)*W2(mu,mu_k).    (2)

The Gaussian-smoothed entropy continuity bound from claim 006 gives

    |i_n(s)-i_(n,k)(s)| <= sqrt(s)*delta_(n,k).        (3)

Applied also to two deterministic-quantile approximating models, it gives

    |i_j(s)-i_k(s)| <= sqrt(s*gamma)*W2(mu_j,mu_k).    (4)

Here the finite empirical quantile W2 distances converge to the distance
between their limiting laws. Equation (4) shows that i_k are Cauchy
uniformly on every [0,S]. Denote their limit by i_mu. Passing n->infinity
in (3), then k->infinity using (2), proves i_n(s)->i_mu(s). More precisely
the same argument with sup_(0<=s<=S) in (3) proves locally uniform
convergence, because the regular-model i_(n,k) converge locally uniformly.
For that last assertion, pointwise convergence from Theorem 4 plus the
common Lipschitz bound on i_(n,k) suffices: their derivatives are at most
E||B_(n,k)||_F^2/(2*r_n*q_n)<=b_k^2/2. A finite grid proves uniform
convergence on [0,S], including zero, without any derivative interchange.

The limits are finite: the zero estimator and I-MMSE give
0<=i_n(s)<=s E||B_n||_F^2/(2*r_n*q_n), whose upper bounds stay finite
by (1). Finite-dimensional Gaussian-channel information is concave in s;
therefore its finite limit is concave too. This proves the statement.

## 4. Gaussian-factor reference at all positive finite aspect ratios

Let B_N=U_G V_G^T/sqrt(N), with factors N by M and P by M and independent
standard Gaussian entries. Transpose when needed, set r=min(N,P),
q=max(N,P), and use the singular-value law of B_N/sqrt(r). Claim 008,
Section 3, supplies expected W2 convergence to a deterministic finite-
second-moment law; its scaling from sqrt(N) to sqrt(r) is deterministic
and has a positive finite limit. This dependency remains unaudited.
Positive finite limits P/N and M/N ensure r/q->gamma>0 and bounded
normalized second moments. The preceding result therefore supplies a
finite Gaussian-reference MI limit for every s>=0, including when the
limiting product spectrum has an atom at zero.

Now take fixed centered iid unit-variance real non-Gaussian factor laws
with finite fourth moments and the same dimensions. Claim 008 also
supplies their expected singular-profile coupling to the reference.
Apply the already proved abstract comparison in claim 006. At every
differentiability point s>0 of the finite concave reference limit i_mu,

    m_B_N(s) -> 2*i_mu'(s),
    limsup_N [m_X_N(s)-m_B_N(s)] <= 0.               (5)

The exceptional set is at most countable, fixed by the reference limit.
At an arbitrary s>0, the weaker left-derivative bound from claim 006
still holds. This does not assert a reference MMSE limit at a corner,
nor pointwise domination there. Raw product losses require division of
their gap by N, as in claim 014. The main all-SNR Target 2 remains open
at possible nondifferentiability points; differentiability has not been
proved by the smooth spectral approximations.

An explicit warning example is useful: concave C1 functions can converge
uniformly to min(s,1), which has a corner. For epsilon>0 take f_e(s)=s
on s<=1-epsilon, f_e(s)=1 on s>=1+epsilon, and
f_e(s)=1-(s-1-epsilon)^2/(4*epsilon) between. The pieces and first
derivatives match at both endpoints; the derivative decreases from one
to zero. The uniform error from min(s,1) is epsilon/4. Thus no
differentiability conclusion follows merely from smoothing and a
uniform MI estimate.

## 5. What is new here, and what remains unchecked

The compact-support wording in the header of source Proposition 2 does
not remove the density obligation by itself. Its Appendix D.1 proof,
specifically Lemma D.1, invokes Assumptions 2 and 3 and finite
non-commutative entropy when applying Theorem 1.1 of Guionnet-Huang.
An atomic input cannot be inserted on the strength of that header alone.
The present argument deliberately applies Theorem 4 only to the regular
mu_k, verifies those hypotheses there, and then uses a separate
dimension-uniform information-continuity estimate. This is why it pays
the obstruction recorded in mmse_source_obstruction.md rather than
ignoring that earlier source check.

This draft discharges the input-density and zero-atom obstruction to
using the published MI-limit theorem, under explicit expected-W2 input
control. It does not claim a new spherical-integral theorem or a new
formula for the reference MI. Novelty of this continuity extension and
its T287 application is not established. The least-trusted dependencies
are the existing unaudited spectral W2 proof (claim 008), and application
of the source theorem to the stated fixed-profile Haar approximants.
The latter is supported by the source's own equation (68), not by an
assumption that the finite-dimensional prior has a Lebesgue density.

[Corollary 11 of arXiv:2605.30616, 'Brownian motion: the hyperbolic number setting'] Let $\left(X,\sigma\left(X\right),\mu\right)$ be a $\mathbb{H}$-valued
probability space, and let $L_{X}^{2}=L^{2}\left(X,\sigma\left(X\right),\mu\right)$
be the $\mathbb{R}$-Banach space equipped with the $\mathbb{H}$-indefinite
inner product $\left[,\right]$. If 
\[
f=f_{+}e_{+}+f_{-}e_{-},\;\;g=g_{+}e_{+}+g_{-}e_{-}\in L_{X}^{2},
\]
then 
\[
\left[f,g\right]=\left\langle f_{+},g_{+}\right\rangle _{2}e_{+}+\left\langle f_{-},g_{-}\right\rangle _{2}e_{-}\in\mathbb{H},
\]
where $\left\langle ,\right\rangle _{2}$ is the $\mathbb{R}$-definite
inner product on the usual $L^{2}$-spaces $L^{2}\left(X,\sigma\left(X\right),\mu_{e}\right)$
for all $e\in\left\{ \pm\right\} $. So, this $\mathbb{R}$-Banach
space $L_{X}^{2}$ is $\mathbb{H}$-indefinite-inner-product $\mathbb{H}$-bi-module
in the sense of \cite{MR5000850}.

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.26834, 'Small-time annealed large deviations principle for one-dimensional diffusions in a random '] Under assumption $H_1$, for each $\theta \in (0,1)$, there exist deterministic constants
		\[
		C=C(\theta)>0,\qquad N=N(\theta)>0,
		\]
		such that for $\Pbb$-a.e. $W$, one has for any $0<t<1, \ r>0$ and $ x \in \R$
		\begin{equation}
			P_x^W(\tau_{D_W(x,r)}\le t)
			\le C t^{-N}\exp\left(C M(D_W(x,r)) \right)
			\exp\left\{-a_\theta\frac{r^2}{t}\right\},
		\end{equation}
		where the constant $M(D_W(x,r))$ was defined in (\ref{01}) and 
		\begin{equation*}
			a_\theta=\frac{(1-\theta)^2}{2(1+\theta)}.
		\end{equation*}
		In particular, $a_\theta\uparrow 1/2$ as $\theta\downarrow0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.26834

[Lemma l.expdecay of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let $Q_1, Q_2$ be two marking functions on finite marked point processes. Let $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ be a marked point process such that the ground process $\mathcal{P}$ satisfies the Palm correlation bound~(equation e:bd_palmcorr of the paper) for $m =1$.
 Suppose for $p\in\mathbb{N}$, $i=1,2$ that there are   fast decreasing functions $\varphi_{i,p}$ as in (equation varphibd of the paper) such that 
\begin{equation}
\sup_{1 \leq n < \infty} \sup_{x_1,\ldots,x_p \in W_n} \mathbb{P}_{\bk x1p}
\bigl(Q_i(\tilde{x}_1, \tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n)>r\bigr) \le \varphi_{i,p}(r),\quad r > 0.
\end{equation}
 Then 
for all $p \in \mathbb{N}$ there are fast decreasing functions ~$\tilde\varphi_p$ such that
$$
\sup_{1 \leq n < \infty} \sup_{x_1,\ldots,x_p\in W_n}\mathbb{P}_{\bk x1p}\left( \max_{x \in \mathcal{P}_n :  |x - x_1| \leq Q_1(\tilde{x}_1, \tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n)} Q_2(\tilde{x}, \tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n) > r \right) \leq   \tilde{\varphi}_p(r), \quad r > 0.
$$
If the assumption (equation e:Q12tails of the paper) holds with the supremum taken up to $n = \infty$, i.e., $\sup_{1 \le n \le \infty}$, then the conclusion  remains valid with  $\sup_{1 \le n \le \infty}$.
title: Tail bounds for the maximum of fast decreasing marks

[Lemma L:Int-16 of arXiv:2606.23865, 'Uniform-in-time Gaussian fluctuations for multiscale nonlinear stochastic systems via Mall'] For $0 \le u \le s \le w \le r \le t$, let the term $\mathcal{J}_{16}(t;\varepsilon,\eta)$ be defined as follows:
\begin{multline*}
\mathcal{J}_{16}(t;\varepsilon,\eta)  \triangleq K \int_{u=0}^t \int_{s=u}^t \int_{w=s}^t \int_{r=w}^t  e^{-2 \alpha (t-r)} e^{- \alpha(t-s)} e^{- \alpha(t-w)}   e^{-\frac{\lambda}{\eta} (r-u)} e^{-\frac{\lambda}{\eta} (s-u)} e^{-\frac{\lambda}{\eta} (r-w)} \\
\times e^{-\frac{\lambda}{\eta} (w-s)}     dr \thinspace dw \thinspace ds \thinspace du.
\end{multline*}
Then, there exists a time-independent positive constant $K$ such that
$$ \mathcal{J}_{16}(t;\varepsilon,\eta) \le K \eta^3.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma L:Int-16 of arXiv:2606.23865

body: In mathematics, an action of a group $G$ on a set $S$ is, loosely speaking, an operation that takes an element of $G$ and an element of $S$ and produces another element of $S.$ More formally, it is a group homomorphism from $G$ to the automorphism group of $S$ (the set of all bijections on $S$ along with group operation being function composition). One says that $G$ acts on $S.$

\[
A_1^{(v)}
:=\Big\{
N_v^{\mathrm{rec}}([0,k^{-1/3}])=0,\ 
N_v^{\mathrm{rec}}\big((k^{-1/3},\,\tfrac{1}{12}\log k]\big)\ge 1,\ 
N_v^{\mathrm{sus}}\big((\tfrac{1}{12}\log k,\,\tfrac{1}{6}\log k]\big)\ge 1
\Big\},
\]
with $N_v^{\text{rec}}, N_v^{\text{sus}}$ the Poisson processes defined in the modified Harris construction. Then $A_1^{(v)}$ is \\ $\mathcal{G}(v, \{u_1,\dots, u_k\})$ measurable, with $\mathcal{G}(v, \{u_1,\dots, u_k\})$ defined in Definition~\ref{def:local_graphical_data} for all sufficiently large $k$,
\[
\mathbb{P}\!\left(A_1^{(v)}\right)\ \ge\ 1-k^{-\min\{1,\rho\}/18}.
\]

body:
Let A be an n x n matrix over a field. A has a factorisation A = L U with L unit lower triangular (ones on the diagonal) and U upper triangular if and only if every leading principal submatrix A_k = A[1..k, 1..k], k = 1, ..., n - 1, is invertible (for invertible A this is equivalent to all n leading principal minors being nonzero); when it exists the factorisation is unique for invertible A, and u_kk = det A_k / det A_{k-1}. In general, for every A there is a permutation matrix P with P A = L U (Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting: at each step the row with the largest remaining entry in the pivot column is swapped into the pivot position); for invertible A the factors are then unique given P. The elimination costs 2 n^3 / 3 flops; solving A x = b afterwards costs 2 n^2 by one forward and one back substitution; the determinant is the product of the u_kk times the sign of P. Partial pivoting is backward stable in practice (the growth factor is bounded by 2^{n-1} in the worst case, attained by Wilkinson's example, but is small on almost all matrices), whereas elimination without pivoting can be unstable on matrices with small pivots even when A is well conditioned. Symmetric positive definite matrices need no pivoting (Cholesky); diagonally dominant matrices need none either.

Seek L = [[L', 0], [m^T, 1]], U = [[U', u], [0, s]]; multiplying out, L U = [[L' U', L' u], [m^T U', m^T u + s]], so u = L'^{-1} b, m^T = c^T U'^{-1} and s = d - m^T u are forced and exist (L', U' invertible), which gives existence and, by the same forcing, uniqueness when all factors are invertible. The minor formula u_kk = det A_k / det A_{k-1} follows from det A_k = u_11 ... u_kk. Partial pivoting: at step k the k-th column of the current matrix, restricted to rows k..n, is not identically zero if A is invertible (otherwise the first k columns would be dependent), so a nonzero (indeed the largest) pivot can be swapped into place; recording the swaps as a permutation P, the elimination runs to completion on P A, and each elimination step is multiplication by a unit lower triangular Gauss transform, whose inverses multiply to L. Uniqueness given P follows from the first part. The growth-factor bound: with partial pivoting every multiplier has modulus at most 1, so each step at most doubles the largest entry, giving 2^{n-1}; Wilkinson's matrix (1 on the diagonal and last column, -1 below the diagonal) attains it. [Prop EGF of arXiv:2605.07920, 'Primitive Sequences for Probability Measures on Compact Intervals'] Let
    \[
    G_X(z) := \sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb{E}[X^n] z^n
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad
    \tilde{G}_X(z) := \sum_{n=0}^\infty \varepsilon_n z^n.
    \]
    Then the following hold:
    \begin{propitems}
        \item $G_X$ has radius of convergence $1/\|X\|_\infty$, and in particular it is finite if and only if $\|X\|_\infty > 0$.
        \item $\tilde{G}_X$ is an entire function.
    \end{propitems}

\[ 
\Upsilon(f+g;\Pi_N) = \Upsilon(f;\Pi_N) + \O(e^{-\alpha \sqrt{N}})  
\]
where the implied constant depends on $e^{\|f\|}$, $C$, $\alpha$ and $\delta$.

body:
[Lem transprop of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] Let $\mathcal N$ be a transparent (weighted planar) network of order $n$, with weight
matrix $A$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If a path in another network reaches sink-$r$ and if the network is concatenated with $\mathcal N$, then it can be continued
through the path $h_r$ without changing its weight. More generally, a vertex-disjoint family reaching pairwise distinct
levels $I\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}$ can be continued through the paths
$\{h_r:r\in I\}$, without changing either its weight or its
vertex-disjointness.

\item If $\mathcal N'$ is another transparent network, then the
concatenation $\mathcal N\mathcal N'$ is transparent.

\item Let $D=\emph{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)$ be an invertible diagonal matrix.  There is a transparent network with
weight matrix $DAD^{-1}$.  

\item There is a transparent network with weight matrix $SAS^{-1}$ where  $S$ is the side-reversal matrix (see (equation eq:S of the paper)). 
\end{enumerate}

Let $\tilde q_* = q_0$, so that condition~\ref{it:8.2} is satisfied, and $(\tilde p,\tilde \zeta,\tilde \zeta^\Ising) = (p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$. We will couple $\tilde{X}(q_0)=X(q_*)$ and

[Lemma lem:BBG-lem5 of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Let Assumption~(ass:Wass of the paper) hold. Then, for every $N\ge2$ and every initial
configuration $(x^N_1(0),\ldots,x^N_N(0))\in(\mathbb R^d)^N$, the
$N$-particle SVGD system~(equation eq:svgd-continuous of the paper) associated with the kernel (equation eq:bilinear-matern-kernel of the paper)
has a unique global classical solution. Moreover, there exists
$C\in(0,\infty)$ such that, for all $T>0$,
\[
        \int_0^T \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \|x^N_i(t)\|^2\,dt
        \le
        CT+\frac{C}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N V(x^N_i(0)).
\]
Further, under the initialization in Assumption~(ass:Wass of the paper),
\begin{equation}
        \sup_{N\ge2}
        \mathbb E\left[\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N V(x^N_i(0))\right]
        <\infty .
\end{equation}
The corresponding mean-field equation (equation eq:mf-svgd of the paper)
is globally defined in the weak continuity-equation sense and satisfies, for all
$T>0$,
\[
        \int_0^T \int_{\mathbb R^d}\|x\|^2\,\mu_t(dx)\,dt
        \le
        CT+ C\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(x)\,\mu_0(dx) < \infty.
\]

[Lemma lem:delta1-delta2-reduction of arXiv:2604.07711, 'Central Limit Theorem for Random Partial\\ Sphere Coverings in High Dimensions'] Let $U_1,U_2$ be independent random points on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ with distribution $\sigma$, and define
\[
    p_N := \mathbb{P}\big(C_N(U_1)\cap C_N(U_2)\neq\varnothing\big).
\]
Then
\[
    \delta_1\le \frac{4}{N^4}\,p_N
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad
    \delta_2\le \frac{16}{N^4}\,p_N^2.
\]

[Lemma lma:realformsign of arXiv:2608.26564, 'Real ideal points, Conway spheres, and left-orderable Dehn fillings'] Let $R_\theta = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}\cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
\begin{enumerate}
	\item If $A = G(\varepsilon \left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&s\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right))G^{-1}$ with $\varepsilon = \pm 1$, $s \neq 0$, and $G = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} g_{11} & g_{12} \\ g_{21} & g_{22} \end{smallmatrix}\right) \in GL_2(\mathbb{R})$, then $\mathfrak{d}(A) = \varepsilon s(g_{11}^2 + g_{21}^2)/\det G$. In particular, $\mathfrak{d} \neq 0$ on noncentral parabolic matrices, and two noncentral parabolic matrices of the same trace are $SL_2(\mathbb{R})$-conjugate if and only if their $\mathfrak{d}$-signs agree.
	\item If $A = GR_\theta G^{-1}$ with $0 < \theta < \pi$, then $\mathfrak{d}(A) = -\sin\theta\,(g_{11}^2 + g_{12}^2 + g_{21}^2 + g_{22}^2)/\det G$. In particular $\mathfrak{d} \neq 0$ on elliptic matrices, and two elliptic matrices of the same trace are $SL_2(\mathbb{R})$-conjugate if and only if their $\mathfrak{d}$-signs agree.
	\item The sign of $\mathfrak{d}$ on an elliptic matrix depends only on its rotation direction: if $\operatorname{tr} A = 2\cos\theta_A$ with $0 < \theta_A < \pi$, then $\mathfrak{d}(A) < 0$ if and only if the projective action of $A$ has rotation number $\theta_A/\pi$, and $\mathfrak{d}(A) > 0$ if and only if it has rotation number $-\theta_A/\pi$.
	\item For $\Omega = \mathrm{Ad}_{\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)}$, we have $\mathfrak{d}(\Omega(A)) = -\mathfrak{d}(A)$.
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition prop:tailrl-closed-form-weights of arXiv:2609.02987, 'Tail Likelihood Reinforcement Learning'] For every $i=1,\ldots,N$,
\begin{equation}
\omega\bigl(r_{(i)}\bigr)
=
\sum_{k=1}^{i}
\frac{r_{(k)}-r_{(k-1)}}{N-k+1}.

\end{equation}
Equivalently, all weights follow the recurrence
\begin{equation}
\omega\bigl(r_{(i)}\bigr)
=
\omega\bigl(r_{(i-1)}\bigr)
+
\frac{r_{(i)}-r_{(i-1)}}{N-i+1},
\qquad
\omega\bigl(r_{(0)}\bigr)=0.

\end{equation}
title: Closed-form empirical weights

[Proposition prop:supercritical of arXiv:2604.13968, 'Divisible sandpiles via random walks in random scenery'] Let~$G = (V,E)$ be an infinite, locally finite, connected graph, let~$(X_n)_{n\geq 0}$ be simple random walk on~$G$, and let $(\xi(v))_{v\in V}$ be i.i.d.\ and independent of the walk with
		$\mathbb{E}[\xi] \in (0, \infty]$. If $A_n(x)\to\infty$ for some $x\in V$, then $\sup_n\mathbb{E}_x[S_n\mid\xi]=\infty$ almost surely.
		In particular, if the degree is bounded by~$d$, then $A_n(x)\geq n/d\to\infty$, so the conclusion holds on every infinite bounded-degree graph.

body:
Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable map $T: X \to X$ is measure-preserving if $\mu(T^{-1} A) = \mu(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{B}$ (preimages, not images: $T$ need not be injective, and for non-invertible $T$ the condition $\mu(TA) = \mu(A)$ is neither implied nor required). The system is a probability-preserving system when $\mu(X) = 1$. A set $A$ is (strictly) invariant if $T^{-1}A = A$, and invariant mod $\mu$ if $\mu(T^{-1}A \,\triangle\, A) = 0$; every set invariant mod $\mu$ differs from a strictly invariant set by a null set. $T$ is ergodic if every invariant set has measure $0$ or full measure; equivalently (for a probability measure) every measurable $f$ with $f \circ T = f$ a.e. is a.e. constant; equivalently every set $A$ with $T^{-1}A \subset A$ mod $\mu$ (or $T^{-1}A \supset A$ mod $\mu$) has measure 0 or 1. The invariant $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{I} = \{A : T^{-1}A = A\}$ is what the ergodic averages converge to conditional expectations onto. Ergodicity is not the same as mixing (mixing implies ergodic, not conversely: an irrational rotation of the circle is ergodic but not mixing), and it is not preserved by passing to powers ($T^2$ may fail to be ergodic when $T$ is, e.g. the rotation by $1/2$ on two points).
T is measurable
invariance is expressed through preimages T^{-1}A
title: Measure-preserving transformation; ergodicity

[Corollary cor:1d_case of arXiv:2411.07878, 'Bernstein-type and Bennett-type inequalities for unbounded matrix martingales'] Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be scalar random variables satisfying assumptions of Theorem~(thm:martingale of the paper) with
    \[
    \sigma^2_i \coloneqq \E [X^2_i | \mathscr{F}_{i-1}],
    \quad
    U_i \coloneqq \norm*{(X_i)_{+} | \mathscr{F}_{i-1}}_{\psi_{\alpha}}.
    \]
    Fix $\sigma > 0$, $U \ge K > 0$ and define the event
    \begin{equation}
    
        E \coloneqq \lrc{\sum^n_{i = 1} \sigma_i^2 \le \sigma^2, \quad
        \sum^n_{i = 1} U^{2}_i \le U^2, \quad
        \max_{i \in [n]} U_i \le K}.
    \end{equation}
    Then, with probability at least $1 - \mathbb{P}(E) - e^{-\mathrm{x}}$,
    \begin{equation}
        \max_{k \in [n]} \sum^k_{i=1} X_i \le \sigma \sqrt{2 \mathrm{x}} + \frac{4 Kz \mathrm{x}}{\min\left\{2 \alpha z^{\alpha},\, \hspace{0.2em}\underline{\log}\hspace{0.2em} \left(\left( \frac{Kz}{\sigma}\right)^2 \mathrm{x} \right)  \right\}}.
    \end{equation}
   The same holds for (equation res:ber of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.15874, '2608.15874'] Let $(M_n,\cF_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a martingale in $\cH$ with $M_0=0$ and increments
\[
  X_n=M_n-M_{n-1},
  \qquad
  \E[X_n\mid\cF_{n-1}]=0,
  \qquad
  \norm{X_n}\le1\quad\text{a.s.}
\]
Write
\[
  V_n=\sum_{i=1}^n\E[X_i\otimes X_i\mid\cF_{i-1}],
  \qquad n\ge0.
\]
Then, for every $\rho>0$,
\[
  \roundb{U_\rho^h(M_n,V_n)}_{n\ge0}
\]
is a nonnegative supermartingale with initial value one. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Method: Uniform Lipschitz height models and their interfaces structural reduction or obstruction Result: Conditioning an interior height on all other heights gives a uniform law on its feasible interval, intersected with the odd integers in the discrete model. The interval endpoints are the maximum of neighbor heights minus the slope bound and the minimum plus the bound. Check: For real slope bound1 and six neighboring heights0,0,0,0,0,1, the feasible interval is[0,1], so the conditional mean is1/2 while the neighbor average is1/6. These neighbor values satisfy their mutual triangular-edge constraints. One must first control the effective large-scale field and then the discontinuous operation of extracting its zero interface.

[Proposition prop:birth-cycle-change of arXiv:2608.29719, 'Persistence Pairing Graphs: Tracking Changes of Selected Homology Bases'] Let $k<i$ be positive cell indices of the same dimension such that $R_k=R_i=0$. For any $a\in\Bbbk$, let $V'$ be a matrix given by
\[
V'_i=V_i+aV_k
\]
and, for $\ell\neq i$, $V'_\ell=V_\ell$. Then $V'$ is upper unitriangular and dimension preserving, and
\[
DV'=R.
\]
Thus, $(R,V')$ has exactly the same reduced matrix and the same persistence pairs as $(R,V)$.

Suppose further that the interval $u$ has birth index $i$, dies at $t$, and that the interval $v$ with birth index $k$ survives beyond $t$. If $w_{ur}$ and $w'_{ur}$ denote the transition coefficients before and after the change, then
\[
w'_{uv}=w_{uv}+a
\]
and, for $r\neq v$, $w'_{ur}=w_{ur}$.

On paths 0,...,n, put conductance c_n=1 for odd n and 2 for even n, normalized counting measure, and spatial scale 1/n. Graph metric-measure spaces converge and resistance is between half and all of graph distance. The stationary variable-speed walks accelerated by n^2 have no common limit of finite-dimensional laws: their cosine two-time covariance tends for t>0 to (1/2)exp(-pi^2*t) along odd n and (1/2)exp(-2*pi^2*t) along even n. This weighted-path example diagnoses the need for actual scaled resistance convergence; it is not a counterexample to an IIC scaling limit.

Status: proof written; w346 KEEP pending. This weighted-path example diagnoses a reduction, not the unweighted IIC itself.

For each n>=2 take the path with vertices 0,...,n, normalized counting measure and distance |i-j|/n. Put conductance c_n on every edge, with c_n=1 for odd n and c_n=2 for even n. These metric-measure spaces converge to the interval with uniform measure. Effective resistance is |i-j|/c_n, so it is uniformly between half and all of graph distance, yet the resistance distance divided by n has no single limit.

Let the continuous-time variable-speed walk have generator L_n h(i)=c_n*sum_{j adjacent i}(h(j)-h(i)), start in its uniform stationary law, and accelerate time by n^2. Its process laws do not have a single scaling limit along all n.

Proof: the nonconstant eigenfunction u_n(i)=cos(pi*(i+1/2)/(n+1)) has eigenvalue -lambda_n, where lambda_n=2*c_n*(1-cos(pi/(n+1))). Its uniform mean is zero and its uniform second moment is 1/2. Thus

    E[u_n(X_0)*u_n(X_(n^2*t))]=(1/2)*exp(-n^2*lambda_n*t).

u_n is uniformly close to the fixed spatial observable cos(pi*i/n). For any fixed t>0, the displayed bounded two-time expectation tends to (1/2)*exp(-pi^2*t) along odd n and (1/2)*exp(-2*pi^2*t) along even n. A common limit of finite-dimensional laws would force the same bounded continuous expectation, a contradiction. Also the endpoint hitting mean from 0 is n(n+1)/(2*c_n), independently confirming the two time constants.

Every graph here is a tree; both volume and resistance orders are controlled. To use a resistance-form convergence theorem for the IIC one must establish actual scaled resistance and measure convergence, matching embedding and time normalization, rather than replace convergence by constant-factor estimates. The example does not assert that the IIC has this alternation, or that its scaling limit fails.

Checks: finite generator eigenvectors and stationary correlations, plus exact endpoint hitting systems. body:
[Thm robust of arXiv:2601.19145, 'Stochastic Persistence in Infinite Dimensions'] Suppose $\mathcal{M}$ (resp. $\mathcal{M}_0$) decomposes as $\Theta \times \tilde{\mathcal{M}}$ (resp. $\Theta \times \tilde{\mathcal{M}_0}$), where $\Theta$ is a compact metric space such that $\{\theta\} \times \tilde{\mathcal{M}}$ is an invariant set ((inv-set of the paper)) for every $\theta \in \Theta$.
    
    Fix some $\theta_0 \in \Theta$. Suppose (as1 of the paper)--(as-compact of the paper) hold, except (as-V of the paper)(as-alpha of the paper) is replaced with: ``$\mathcal{L} V$ extends to a continuous function $H: \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}$ and there is a constant $\Lambda < 0$ such that $\sup_{\mu \in P_{inv}(\{\theta_0\} \times \mathcal{M}_0)} \mu H \leq \Lambda < 0$." Then for all $\theta$ sufficiently close to $\theta_0$, the results of (main of the paper) hold on $\{\theta\} \times \mathcal{M}$. To be more specific, let $\{Y_t^x\}_{t \geq 0, x \in \tilde{\mathcal{M}}}$ be the Markov process on $\tilde{\mathcal{M}}$ such that $(\theta, Y_t^x) = X_t^{(\theta,x)}$ (this is well-defined because $\{\theta\} \times \tilde{\mathcal{M}}$ is an invariant set). Then we have:

    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item For all $x \in \tilde{\mathcal{M}}_+ \coloneqq \tilde{\mathcal{M}}_0^c$ we have that, almost surely, all limit points $\mu$ of $\tilde{\mu}_t^x \coloneqq (1/t)\int_0^t \delta_{Y_s^x(\omega)}ds$ as $t \to \infty$ satisfy $\mu(\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_+) = 1$.
        \item $Y_t$ is stochastically persistent, meaning for all $\epsilon > 0$ there exists a compact set $\mathcal{K}_\epsilon \subset \tilde{\mathcal{M}}_+$ such that for all $x \in \tilde{\mathcal{M}}_+$ $$\mathbb{P}(\liminf_{t \to \infty} \tilde{\mu}_t^x(\mathcal{K}_\epsilon) \geq 1 - \epsilon) = 1 \,.$$
        \item $P_{inv}(\{\theta\} \times \tilde{\mathcal{M}}_+)$ is nonempty.
    \end{enumerate}

[Conj 8 (\cite{HallEak2025}) of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] Let $b_0$ be an invertible operator in a $W^\ast$-probability space $(\A,\tau)$.  Define
\[ \tilde{p}_0(z) = \tau[|b_0-z|^{-2}] \qquad \& \qquad \tilde{p}_2(z) = \tau[b_0^\ast b_0|b_0-z|^{-2}] \]
where, as usual, for any operator $a\in\A$, $|a|^2:=a^\ast a$.  Define $T(b_0,\cdot)\colon\C\to\R_+$ by
\begin{equation}  T(b_0,z) = \frac{\log(\tilde{p}_2(z))-\log(|z|^2\tilde{p}_0(z))}{\tilde{p}_2(z)-|z|^2\tilde{p}_0(z)}.
\end{equation}
For each $t>0$, define the open precompact set $\Sigma(b_0,t)$ by
\begin{equation}  \Sigma(b_0,t) = \{z\in\C\colon T(b_0,z)<t\}. \end{equation}
Let $b(t,\zeta)$ be a free multiplicative Brownian motion (see Notation \ref{notat.ovweparam}) freely independent from $b_0$.  Then the support of the Brown measure of $b_0b(t,\zeta)$ is equal to the image $\overline{\Sigma(b_0,t,\zeta)}$ of $\overline{\Sigma(b_0,t)}$ under the map $\Psi^{b_0}_{t,\zeta}$ of \eqref{eq.Psi}. (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: \cite{HallEak2025}

For each $\ell=1, 2, \dots, n-1$, we denote by $\{\m{u_0}{u_{\ell}}\}$ the event that $\{\s{u_0}{u_{\ell}}\} \cap \{\ns{u_0}{u_{\ell+1}}\}$.
We define $\{\cam{u_0}{u_{n}}\}$ inductively as follows
\[\{\cam{u_0}{u_{n}}\}:=\{\s{u_0}{u_{n}}\}\cup\bigcup_{\ell=1}^{n-1}\{\m{u_0}{u_{\ell}}, \cam{u_{\ell}}{u_{n}}\}, \text{for } n \geq 2,\]
with the initial condition $\{\cam{u_0}{u_1}\}:=\{\s{u_0}{u_1}\}$.
In addition, we denote the complement of $\{\cam{u_0}{u_n}\}$ by $\{\ncam{u_0}{u_n}\}$.

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2607.23887, '2607.23887'] Let $X,Y$ be independent standard real Gaussian random variables and let
$P\in\C[X,Y]$ satisfy $\E(P^m)=0$ for every $m\ge1$. Write $P$ in the
coordinates \eqref{eq:coords}. Then either every monomial occurring in $P$ has
weight at least $1$, or every monomial occurring in $P$ has weight at most
$-1$. Consequently, for every $Q\in\C[X,Y]$,
\[
  \E\bigl(QP^m\bigr)=0 \qquad\text{whenever } m>\deg Q .
\]
In particular $\GMC(2)$ holds, with the explicit threshold $m\ge\deg Q+1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Outer vertex-isoperimetry of regular plane tessellations (18 September 2026) proves that for an infinite (d,f)-regular plane tessellation G with finite d, f >= 3, 1/d + 1/f <= 1/2 and face degree f >= 5, the outer vertex-isoperimetric constant equals the edge-isoperimetric constant: h_V(G) = h_E(G) = (d-2) sqrt(1 - 4/((d-2)(f-2))); in particular h_V(H_{5,5}) = sqrt(5). Together with the triangular and quadrangular cases of Haslegrave and Panagiotis, this answers the finite-faced regular/co-regular part of Question 6.20 of R. Lyons and Y. Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks; arbitrary transitive plane graphs, the further class in the question, are not covered. The proof rests on a general principle: an infinite simple graph of maximum degree Delta has equal edge and outer vertex-isoperimetric constants whenever its edge constant is at least Delta - 3, and the constant 3 is optimal uniformly in the degree. Paper (PDF): https://github.com/yspennstate/outer-vertex-isoperimetry (commit 9dff9a1b89b3); ResearchGate record 414470838. Not refereed.
title: Lyons-Peres Question 6.20 answered for finite-faced regular tessellations: the outer vertex-isoperimetric constant of a (d,f)-regular plane tessellation with f >= 5 is (d-2) sqrt(1 - 4/((d-2)(f-2))) (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/outer-vertex-isoperimetry)

body: [Theo 59 of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] For the ferromagnetic (nearest-neighbor) Ising model in dimension $d \ge 2$, Gaussian concentration holds in the uniqueness regime. In the phase coexistence regime $\beta \ge \beta_c(d)$, it fails for every shift-invariant ergodic Gibbs measure. More precisely, for $\beta < \beta_c(d)$, the unique Gibbs measure $\nu_\beta$ satisfies Gaussian concentration, whereas for $\beta \ge \beta_c(d)$ no shift-invariant ergodic Gibbs measure satisfies Gaussian concentration.

body:
Let V have n elements and X a random subset. The law of X is invariant under all permutations of V if and only if q(A) = P(A subset of X) depends only on |A|, say q(A) = a_|A|. Then P(|X| = r) = p_r = binom(n, r) sum_{j=0}^{n-r} (-1)^j binom(n - r, j) a_{r+j}, and given |X| = r, X is uniform over the r-subsets. A real sequence a_0, ..., a_n is the profile of some exchangeable random subset if and only if a_0 = 1 and every p_r >= 0, and the law is then unique. Monotonicity is not enough: for n = 2, a = (1, 3/5, 1/10) is nonincreasing in [0, 1] but gives p_0 = -1/10.

[Corollary eq:subquadratic-local-cost of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[corollary]{cor:general-tail-obstruction}
Assume that the distinguished coordinate has law \(\mu\).  Suppose that
for some \(M<\infty\), \(\eta>0\), \(\delta>0\), and a sequence
\(a_k\to\infty\), (equation eq:conditional-remainder-cost of the paper) holds with
\(a=a_k\) for every sufficiently large \(k\), and
\begin{equation}
 \overline I_\mu(a_k,\eta)\le\left(\frac12-\delta\right)a_k^2
\end{equation}
for all sufficiently large \(k\), then, for every sufficiently large
\(k\), setting \(B_k=[a_k-M,a_k+\eta+M]\),
\begin{align}
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Crt}_{N,\max}^J(B_k)
 &>\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_{N,\max}^G(B_k),\\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Crt}_N^J(B_k)
 &>\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_N^G(B_k).
 
\end{align}
If the joint coefficient array is invariant in law under global sign
reversal \(J\mapsto-J\), the analogous strict inequality holds for local
minima in \(-B_k\).

[Lem 1 (Lemma 4.7 \& 4.8 of \cite{JX20-a}) of arXiv:2608.30173, '2608.30173'] (i) For every $1\le p<\infty$, we can find a constant $C$ depending only on $n,\Omega,p$ and $u_\infty$ such that
\[
\|f\|_{L^p(\om)} \le C \Big \|\Delta f+\frac{n+2}{n-2} r_\infty u_\infty^{\frac{4}{n-2}} f \Big\|_{L^p(\om)}+C \sup_{1\le l\le L} \Big|\int_\om u_\infty^{\frac{4}{n-2}} \phi_l f \,\ud x\Big|
\]
for all $f\in W^{2,p}(\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$.

(ii) There exists a constant $C$ depending only on $n,\Omega$ and $u_\infty$ such that
\begin{itemize}
\item
\[
\|f\|_{L^{\frac{n+2}{n-2}}(\om)}\le C \Big \| \Pi(\Delta f+\frac{n+2}{n-2}r_\infty u_\infty^{\frac{4}{n-2}} f )\Big\|_{L^{\frac{n(n+2)}{n^2+4}}(\om)}+C \sup_{1\le l\le L} \Big|\int_\om u_\infty^{\frac{4}{n-2}} \phi_l f \,\ud x \Big|
\]
for all $f\in W^{2,\frac{n(n+2)}{n^2+4}}(\Omega)\cap W^{1,\frac{n(n+2)}{n^2+4}}_0(\Omega)$.
\item
\[
\|f\|_{L^{1}(\om)}\le C \Big \| \Pi(\Delta f+\frac{n+2}{n-2}r_\infty u_\infty^{\frac{4}{n-2}} f )\Big\|_{L^{1}(\om)}+C \sup_{1\le l\le L} \Big|\int_\om u_\infty^{\frac{4}{n-2}} \phi_l f \,\ud x \Big|
\]
for all $f\in W^{2,1}(\Omega)\cap W^{1,1}_0(\Omega)$.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:eta-kappa of arXiv:2411.10419, 'Lower bounds on the top Lyapunov exponent for linear PDEs driven by the 2D stochastic Navi'] For any $ \mathbf{q} > 2$ and $ \kappa \in (0, 1] $, we set $\hat M_i = (M_0 - i) \vee \kappa^{-\mathbf{q}}$ and define the  time $ \eta$ as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item Set $ \tau_{0} =0 $ and then for every $ i \geqslant 0 $:
\begin{equs}[e:def-tau-sigma-i]
\sigma_{i} &= \inf \{ t \geqslant
\tau_{i}  \; \colon \; M^{(2)}_{t} \geqslant \hat M_i \}\wedge \{ 
\tau_{i} + t_{\star}^{\kappa, \delta} (\hat M_i)\} \;,\\
\tau_{i+1} &= \inf \{ t \geqslant  \tau_{i}  \;\colon \; M_{t} \leqslant \hat M_{i+1}\}  \;,
\end{equs}
where $ t_{\star}^{\kappa, \delta} (M)$ is defined in (equation e:tsd of the paper). 
\item Define $ L = \min \{i \geqslant 0\,:\, \hat M_{i} \leqslant \kappa^{- \mathbf{q}} \}$ and the ``final step'' $i_{\mathrm{fin}}= \min \{ i \geqslant 0  \; \colon \; \sigma_{i} < \tau_{i+1} \} \wedge L$.
\item Finally, we set
$\eta = \sigma_{i_{\mathrm{fin}}}$.
\end{itemize}

		\[
		\mathbb A^\alpha

		\text{ and }\mathcal G\in\mathrm{OP}\mathcal S^0\text{ such that }
		\mathcal A=\mathcal L+\mathcal G

		of $\mathcal A$. A family $\mathscr N\subset\mathbb A^\alpha$ is called

		$\mathcal A=\mathcal L_{\mathcal A}+\mathcal G_{\mathcal A}$ for every

		\[
		\{\mathcal L_{\mathcal A}:\mathcal A\in\mathscr N\}

		\{\mathcal L_{\mathcal A}+\mathcal L_{\mathcal A}^*:
		\mathcal A\in\mathscr N\},
		\quad
		\{\mathcal G_{\mathcal A}:\mathcal A\in\mathscr N\}
		\]
		are bounded in $\mathrm{OP}\mathcal S^0$.

$$
In particular, if
  $f\in E_{q,p,\beta'}$, then for any $C\in \bC$

linear part and satisfying assumptions (1) and (2) of Theorem \ref{thm.correlated-refined}.

$
\theta:R\rightarrow F
$
such that

and  the induced 
group homomorphism 
$\Theta:\Aff(R)^2\to \Aff(F)^2$ is such that the measure $\Theta_\ast \eta$ on $\Aff(F)^2$ is still supported on pairs with a common linear parts and satisfies the assumptions (1) and (2) of $\eta. $

Let P be a probability measure on a discrete space X with Markov generator L. P is said to satisfy a modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality with constant alpha > 0 if for every positive function f on X, Ent_P(f) <= (1 / (2 * alpha)) * E_P[ - f * L(log f) ]. For product spaces under the discrete gradient, this relates Ent(exp(lambda * f)) to coordinate perturbations.

\begin{equation*}
M_n=L_{m-S_{n\wedge\sigma_m}}(J_{n\wedge\sigma_m})+
\sum_{\ell=0}^{n\wedge\sigma_m-1}G_{m-S_\ell}(J_\ell),
\qquad n\geq0,
\end{equation*}

is an $(\mathcal F_n)$-martingale.

body: [Defn def:isotopy of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a $C^0$-foliation. A \textbf{$C^0$-isotopy} of $\mathcal{F}$ is a topological isotopy $h_t : M \rightarrow M$ such that $\mathcal{F}_t = h_t(\mathcal{F})$ is a continuous path of $C^0$-foliations. In particular, the plane fields $T \mathcal{F}_t$ exist and vary continuously with $t$. This $C^0$-isotopy is \textbf{$\varepsilon$-small}, if $d\big(h_t(x),x\big)<\varepsilon$ for all $x\in M$ and furthermore $T\mathcal{F}_t$ is $\varepsilon$-close to $T\mathcal{F}$.

body:
[Lemma janson1 of arXiv:2606.09488, 'The temporal stochastic block model'] Let $r \in \mathbb{N}$, $(\lambda_i)_{i\in [r]} \in (\mathbb{R}^+)^r$ and $X_i \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_i)$ be independent random variables. Define
$$ \mu = \mathbb{E}\left[ \sum_{i=1}^r X_i \right] = \sum_{i=1}^r \frac{1}{\lambda_i}, \quad \quad \lambda_* = \min_{i \in [r]} \lambda_i. $$
Then, for $\epsilon >0$, we have 
$$ \mathbb{P}\left[ \sum_{i=1}^r X_i \geq (1+\epsilon)\mu \right] \leq (1+\epsilon)^{-1} e^{-\lambda_* \mu (\epsilon-\log(1+\epsilon))}.$$

[Lem lem-testfunction of arXiv:2608.30807, 'Isodiametric-type upper bounds for Steklov eigenvalues'] Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Fix $k\in \mathbb{N}$ and suppose that $u_1,\ldots,u_{k+1}\in H^1(\Omega)$ satisfy $\int_{\partial\Omega}u_i^2d\sigma>0$ for all $i=1,\ldots,k+1$. Assume moreover that, whenever $i\neq j$,
\[
\int_{\Omega}\nabla u_i\cdot \nabla u_jdx=\int_{\partial\Omega}u_iu_jd\sigma=0.
\]
Then we have
\[
\sigma_k(\Omega)\leq \max_{1\leq i\leq k+1}\mathcal{R}_{\Omega}(u_i).
\]

body: [Definition 242 (The characteristics for the compressible Euler system) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] A surface $S \subset \R\times\Sigma$ (or curve $\ell \subset \R\times\Sigma$) is a \emph{characteristic} if at every point $p \in S$ (or $p \in \ell$), the co-normal space to $S$ (or $\ell$) at $p$, defined to be $\{\bm{\upxi} \in T_p^*(\R\times\Sigma) \, | \, \bm{\upxi}(V) = 0 \text{ for all } V \in  T_pS \}$ (or  $\{\bm{\upxi} \in T_p^*(\R\times\Sigma) \, | \, \bm{\upxi}(V) = 0 \text{ for all } V \in  T_p\ell \}$), is a subset of $C_p^*$ (or $P_p^*$).
title: The characteristics for the compressible Euler system

[Definition Distance to monotonicity of arXiv:2505.02685, 'On the Spectral Expansion of Monotone Subsets of the Hypercube'] For a function $f:\{0,1\}^{n}\rightarrow\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$, we define
\[
\mathsf{dist}_{2}^{\mathsf{mono}}(f)\vcentcolon= \inf_{g\in \mathsf{mono}}\sqrt{\Exu{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}{\big(f(x)-g(x)\big)^{2}}},
\]
where $g$ ranges over all monotone increasing functions from $\{0,1\}^{n}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$.
title: Distance to monotonicity

body: [Definition def:history of arXiv:2412.00279, 'Optimal local storage policy based on stochastic intensities and its large scale behavior'] A filtration $\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$ in $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$ (i.e. an increasing family of $\sigma$-algebras contained in $\mathcal{F}$)  is \emph{a history} of the simple locally finite point process $\Phi$ if $\Phi((a,b])$ is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable for all $a<b\leqslant t$. The \emph{natural history} of $\Phi$ is $\mathcal{F}_t=\sigma\left(\Phi((a,b]):a<b\leqslant t\right)$ the smallest filtration satisfying this property.
