[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] We have the following estimate for the binomial coefficients,
$$\binom{N}{K}\approx\left(\frac{1}{t^t(1-t)^{1-t}}\right)^N$$
in the $K\simeq tN\to\infty$ limit, with $t\in(0,1]$. In particular we have
$$\binom{2N}{N}\approx4^N$$
in the $N\to\infty$ limit, for the central binomial coefficients.

body: [Proposition 2 ($\gamma$-folding) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] For a norm with gain $\gamma$ feeding a linear map $W$, $\;\big(x_{\mathrm{norm}}\odot\gamma\big)W^\top=x_{\mathrm{norm}}\big(W\diag(\gamma)\big)^\top$. Hence setting $W\leftarrow W\diag(\gamma)$, $\gamma\leftarrow \mathbf 1$ preserves the function exactly and moves a per-channel scale entirely onto the weights. Where a norm feeds several projections, as both norms of \Cref{sec:anatomy} do, the substitution is applied to each of them before $\gamma$ is reset. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

    Furthermore, for any sequence $\beta^N\to v$ with $|v|<\beta_0$ the conditions in Assumption \ref{ass:SRI} are satisfied by the sequence $\boldsymbol q_{\beta^N}^{(2)}.$

DRAFT; proof (unaudited), no claim of novelty or a solved spectral gap. Let d>=2, beta>0, let A,B be positive even C2 functions on S^(d-1), and let B0 be constant. Write L(ru)=A(u)r^4-2B(u)r^2+B0, r_*=sqrt(B/A), F=B0-B^2/A and Z(u)=integral_0^infinity r^(d-1)exp[-beta(A(u)r^4-2B(u)r^2)]dr. E_u denotes its normalized radial conditional. Then grad log Z=-beta(A/B)E_u[r^2]grad F-(d/4)grad log A. If K=4r_*^3 grad A-4r_* grad B, then Hess F=r_*^4 Hess A-2r_*^2 Hess B-K tensor K/(8B); nonzero critical points of L correspond to critical points of F and have Hessian inertia equal to the positive radial block 8B plus Hess F. For empirical real phase retrieval with fixed unit teacher v, A(u)=mean_i(a_i.u)^4, B(u)=mean_i(a_i.v)^2(a_i.u)^2, B0=mean_i(a_i.v)^4, iid standard Gaussian measurements a_i and m>=d, almost surely the angular marginal is not stationary at v, simultaneously for all beta>0: grad log Z(v)=-d grad A(v)/(4A(v)) is nonzero. Conditioning on z_i=a_i.v, grad A(v) is centered Gaussian on v-perp with covariance (16/m^2)sum_i z_i^6 times the identity, which is positive almost surely. For any deterministic empirical sample with A>0 and M4=mean_i|a_i|^4, |grad log A|<=4(M4/A)^(1/4). Thus the entropy force is at most d(M4/a0)^(1/4) if A>=a0>0. Neither a polynomial Poincare constant nor a quantitative displacement of angular critical points is supplied.
d>=2, beta>0
A,B positive, even and C2 on the sphere; B0 constant
M4=mean|a_i|^4 for the empirical quartic derivative bound

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:6f1d4919c789f453820e66d3e087321134100f003343dfa9ff8a4af03d3d5f07","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/6f/6f1d4919c789f453820e66d3e087321134100f003343dfa9ff8a4af03d3d5f07.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:9d0b1896cd0a966d531f1fb9da25f164c57179e2592f3e177154676bde7804d7","bundle_entry_key":"profile-entropy","bundle_id":"population.t321-angular-profile-entropy-score-unaudited","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability and statistical learning","draft":"w724/bundle_003.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.functional.inequalities:empirical-phase-retrieval-angular-profile-entropy-score-w724-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Radial optimization versus the actual angular Gibbs marginal

T321 Target 2. Kind: reduction. Status: proof (unaudited).
No polynomial spectral gap, empirical landscape theorem, or novelty is claimed.

Assume d>=2, beta>0 and even C2 functions A,B on the unit sphere with A>0
and B>0. Compactness gives uniform positive lower bounds. Let B0 be constant,
L(ru)=A(u)r^4-2B(u)r^2+B0, r>0. Set

 r_*(u)=sqrt(B/A), F(u)=B0-B(u)^2/A(u), q(u)=B(u)/sqrt(A(u)).

1. The unique positive radial minimum is r_*. Its radial second derivative
is 8B>0. The profile gradient is grad F=r_*^4 grad A-2r_*^2 grad B.
Writing K=4r_*^3 grad A-4r_* grad B, differentiation of the radial stationary
equation gives grad r_*=-K/(8B). A second differentiation of F=L(r_*,u)
therefore gives the spherical Hessian identity

 Hess F=r_*^4 Hess A-2r_*^2 Hess B-K tensor K/(8B).       (1)

This is the Schur complement of the positive radial Hessian block. At a
critical point of F, the point r_*u is a critical point of L, and conversely
every nonzero critical point of L has this form. The Hessian quadratic form
of L in polar coordinates is congruent to diag(8B,Hess F), by completing
the square in the radial displacement. At a critical point this coordinate
Hessian also represents the ambient Hessian under an invertible change of
coordinates; hence their inertia is the same. In particular a negative
profile Hessian direction corresponds to a negative ambient Hessian
direction, and conversely. Local minima correspond as well because

 L(ru)=F(u)+A(u)(r^2-B(u)/A(u))^2.                      (2)

The origin is excluded from these statements. Passing to the antipodal
quotient preserves them locally because A,B,F,r_* are even.

2. The true angular marginal is proportional to

 Z(u)=integral_0^infinity r^(d-1)exp[-beta(A r^4-2B r^2)]dr.

The constant B0 cancels. Substitute s=A(u)^(1/4)r to get the exact identity

 Z(u)=A(u)^(-d/4) J_beta(q(u)),
 J_beta(q)=integral_0^infinity s^(d-1) exp[-beta(s^4-2q s^2)]ds. (3)

In particular this is an integral, not merely exp(-beta F). Let E_u denote
expectation under the radial conditional at u. Differentiating the
normalized integral gives

 grad log Z=-beta E_u r^4 grad A+2beta E_u r^2 grad B.

Integration of the derivative of r^d exp[-beta(A r^4-2B r^2)] gives
4beta A E_u r^4=d+4beta B E_u r^2. Its two boundary values are zero:
d>0 controls zero and beta A>0 controls infinity. Substitution yields

 grad log Z=-beta (A/B) E_u r^2 grad F-(d/4) grad log A. (4)

Every normalization and derivative is justified by a uniform quartic tail
dominator on the compact sphere; its polynomial factors are integrable.
Formula (4) is also obtained by differentiating (3), using F=B0-q^2.
It retains both radial-angular dependence and the dimension d.

At a critical point of F, grad log Z=-(d/4)grad log A. Thus a profile critical
point is a marginal critical point if and only if grad A vanishes there.
Consequently (1) alone does not transfer the strict-saddle decomposition
of the empirical loss to the angular marginal. A quantitative displacement
and Hessian control, or a decomposition that directly handles the entropy
term in (4), is still required. No assertion that empirical critical points
actually move by any particular amount is made.

For clarity, critical-point coincidence can fail in this general coefficient
class: on S^1 take theta modulo 2pi, A(theta)=exp(eta sin(2theta)),
q(theta)=q0+delta cos^2(theta), B(theta)=sqrt(A(theta))q(theta), with eta>0,
q0>0 and delta>0. All coefficients are even under the antipodal map theta
->theta+pi. F has its minima at theta=0 modulo pi, where F'=0 but
(log Z)'=-d eta/2 !=0, by (4) with d=2. This is a deterministic coefficient
example, NOT an empirical phase-retrieval sample and NOT a counterexample
to Target 2.

More directly, the mismatch occurs at the empirical teacher itself. For
the empirical coefficients, at u=v one has A(v)=B(v)=B0 and
grad B(v)=grad A(v)/2. Provided A(v)>0, F(v)=0 and grad F(v)=0, while (4)
gives, for every beta>0,

 grad log Z(v)=-(d/(4A(v)))grad A(v).                    (4a)

For iid standard Gaussian measurements and fixed unit v in dimension
d>=2, grad A(v) is nonzero almost surely. To see this, write a_i=z_i v+w_i
where z_i are iid N(0,1) and w_i are independent standard Gaussian vectors
on v-perp, independent of all z_i. Then grad A(v)=(4/m)sum_i z_i^3 w_i.
Conditional on the z_i, this is a centered Gaussian on v-perp with covariance
(16/m^2)sum_i z_i^6 times the identity. That scalar is positive almost surely,
so this Gaussian has no atom at zero. Thus whenever the full sample spans
R^d and A,B are positive everywhere, the actual angular marginal almost
surely is not stationary at the exact teacher direction, simultaneously
for every beta>0. For m>=d these positivity assumptions hold almost surely:
all z_i are nonzero and the measurements span, making both quartic A and
weighted quadratic B positive on the sphere. This is an exact finite-sample
fact, not an approximation or a claim of a large shift. The marginal's
critical point can still approach the teacher as beta grows.

3. The entropy gradient has a useful deterministic sample bound. If
A(u)=mean_i(a_i.u)^4 and M4=mean_i|a_i|^4, then Holder with exponents
4/3 and 4 and projection onto the tangent space give

 |grad_S A|<=4 A^(3/4) M4^(1/4),
 |grad_S log A|<=4 (M4/A)^(1/4).                       (5)

Indeed, the ambient derivative is 4 mean_i(a_i.u)^3 a_i; take its norm,
then apply Holder to mean_i |a_i.u|^3 |a_i|. Orthogonal projection cannot
increase a vector norm. If A>=a0>0, the entropy term in (4) is thus at most
d(M4/a0)^(1/4). On the already-used sample event A>=1/4 and
M4<=2d(d+2), this is at most d[8d(d+2)]^(1/4).

This polynomial bound does not make the entropy term small relative to
the profile force: the latter vanishes at profile critical points. No
implicit-function displacement estimate follows without quantitative
Hessian, derivative and neighborhood controls. Equations (1)-(5) specify
the next missing premise of the angular decomposition route rather than
proving a gap. All statements remain unaudited; no numerical or formal
proof certificate is asserted.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:512b7913667af871a93751f90143f82261cfd7ee32c3c3abd540f095b5a556c6","revision_digest":"sha256:ad6d864f7aeba53a0c7ed206fa2ce4be0f1ac99467e3c9649c18c7989b2be73d","source_id":"own-work:w724:T321:C009:v1","source_revision":"C009-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

If there exists a positive weight $p$ and $M<\infty$ such that
\[
\sup_{\lambda}\frac1{p(\lambda)}\int |k(\lambda,\mu)|p(\mu)\dd\mu\le M,
\qquad
\sup_{\mu}\frac1{p(\mu)}\int |k(\lambda,\mu)|p(\lambda)\dd\lambda\le M,
\]
then $\norm{K}_{\op}\le M$.

body: [Corollary of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Assume that \(S\) is an embedded surface which is transverse to the almost pseudo-Anosov flow \(\varphi\). If \(S\) is not a fiber of \(M\), then \(\partial \Theta(\widetilde{S})\neq \emptyset\) and any infinite leaf ray \(L\) in \(\mathcal{F}_{S}^{\pm}\) must limit to a closed leaf and spiral toward it.

[Corollary cor:false-twin-stability of arXiv:2609.02845, 'Degeneracy bounds, stability, and a sharp gap for $B$-colorings'] Let $d$, $\Delta$, and $s$ be integers satisfying $1\le d\le\Delta$ and $0\le s<d$.  Let $G$ be a finite simple
$d$-degenerate graph with $\Delta(G)\le\Delta$ and $q_B(G)\ge d\Delta-s$.  Then some vertex $v$ has distinct neighbors
$u_1,\ldots,u_d$ such that $d_G(u_1)=\Delta$ and
\[
  \sum_{j=2}^{d}|N_G(u_1)\setminus N_G(u_j)|\le s,
  \qquad
  \sum_{j=2}^{d}|N_G(u_1)\oplus N_G(u_j)|\le2s.
\]
Consequently, at least $d-s$ of $u_1,\ldots,u_d$ have degree $\Delta$ and the same open neighborhood.  In particular, $G$
contains copies of $K_{d-s,\Delta}$ and $K_{d,\Delta-s}$.

PROOF (UNAUDITED). For normalized tanh features u_q, extended by u_0(z)=z, define delta(q,r,c)=1-E[u_q(X)u_r(Y)] for standard Gaussians of correlation c. Uniformly for q,r,s in [0,1] and c in [-1,1], |delta(q,r,c)-delta(s,s,c)| <= (121/2)(q-r)^2+20(1-c)(|q-s|+|r-s|). For c<1 its relative version has coefficients 242 and 80, dividing the contrast term by 1-c. For n independent fresh paired rows, E[(Qnew-Rnew)^2 | past] <= [(1-(q+r)/12)^2+3/n](q-r)^2+8qr(1-c)/n. These remove the absolute-Lipschitz loss in the deterministic gap comparison and expose the weighted radial-contrast term still needed for a multi-layer recursion.
q,r,s in [0,1]; c in [-1,1]; relative comparison only for c<1
Fresh paired Gaussian rows, independent across rows and conditional on completed past; integer n>=1

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:7076d4393689293319a7309eaf3c96e6c5b82dcaf126753efdf511edf8798e81","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/70/7076d4393689293319a7309eaf3c96e6c5b82dcaf126753efdf511edf8798e81.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:945ca18bb0a98db18e19c44e0797808647334210146f2f927f040de71041804d","bundle_entry_key":"tanh_gap_radial_comparison","bundle_id":"population.w712-t250-c011-gap-radial-comparison","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Quantitative Gaussian-process limits and empirical Gram matrices","draft":"w712/bundle_007.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:tanh-population-gap-angular-factor-and-radial-contrast-recursion","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C011 v1: angular-factor comparison and radial-contrast recursion

Kind: moved. Target: 1, the reviewer's two-input relative-gap rung.
Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty unverified. This is a component lemma,
not the claimed multi-layer relative rate.

## Statement

Let F(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2 for a standard Gaussian Z. On [0,1] define
h_q(z)=tanh(sqrt(q)z)/sqrt(q), h_0(z)=z, a(q)=||h_q||_2,
u_q=h_q/a(q). For a standard Gaussian pair (X,Y) with correlation c set
H(q,r,c)=E[u_q(X)u_r(Y)] and delta(q,r,c)=1-H(q,r,c).
For all q,r,s in [0,1] and c in [-1,1],

    |delta(q,r,c)-delta(s,s,c)|
      <= (121/2)(q-r)^2 + 20(1-c)(|q-s|+|r-s|).       (1)

For c<1 this gives the scale-free comparison

    |delta(q,r,c)/delta(s,s,c)-1|
      <= 242 (q-r)^2/(1-c) + 80(|q-s|+|r-s|).         (2)

For c=1 the reference gap is zero and (2) is NOT asserted; (1) still holds.

For a fresh independent collection of n standard Gaussian pairs of
correlation c, let

    Q'=mean tanh(sqrt(q)X_i)^2,
    R'=mean tanh(sqrt(r)Y_i)^2, e=q-r.

For every integer n>=1,

    E[(Q'-R')^2]
      <= [(1-(q+r)/12)^2+3/n] e^2
           + 8qr(1-c)/n.                             (3)

If q,r,c are measurable with respect to the completed network past and
the paired rows are fresh conditional on that past, (3) holds conditionally.
No future state, gradient, or sensitivity is conditioned on. In particular
at a state with equal q=r, the new contrast has zero conditional mean and
second moment at most 8q^2(1-c)/n. Equal marginal variances are not preserved
pathwise.

## 1. Uniform feature estimates

Audited C002 v2, steps 1-2, gives q/4<=F(q)<=q for 0<=q<=1,
and increasing concave F with F(0)=0 and F(q)<=q-q^2/6.
Hence 1/2<=a(q)<=1, including q=0, and |h_q(z)|<=|z|.
For t>=0,

    tanh(t)-t sech(t)^2
      = integral_0^t 2v sech(v)^2 tanh(v) dv <= 2t^3/3.

Differentiation yields |partial_q h_q(z)|<=|z|^3/3 for q>0;
at zero its continuous extension is -z^3/3. This polynomial envelope
justifies differentiation and continuity in Gaussian L2 by dominated
convergence. Thus |a'(q)|<=sqrt(15)/3<2 and

    |partial_q u_q(z)| <= (2/3)|z|^3+8|z|,
    ||partial_q u_q||_2 <= (2/3)sqrt(15)+8 <= 11.      (4)

Here E Z^6=15 and E Z^2=1. The last inequality follows from
sqrt(15)<=9/2. These are uniform bounds; endpoint derivatives are
one-sided and all parameter integrals are over [0,1]. In particular

    ||u_q-u_r||_2 <= 11|q-r|.                        (5)

The derivative in the input variable is

    w_q(z):=partial_z u_q(z)=sech(sqrt(q)z)^2/a(q),
    w_0(z)=1, 0<w_q(z)<=2.

For q>0, the derivative of the numerator in q has absolute value
|z tanh(sqrt(q)z) sech(sqrt(q)z)^2/sqrt(q)|<=z^2.
Its limit at zero is -z^2. Using a>=1/2 and |a'|<2 gives

    |partial_q w_q(z)| <= 2z^2+8,
    ||w_q-w_s||_1 <= 10|q-s|.                       (6)

The L1 norms refer to a standard Gaussian marginal, independent of the
joint correlation used below.

## 2. The gap separates into shape and angular parts

Price's identity, as in Voigtlaender, arXiv:1710.03576, Theorem 1 and
Corollary 2, gives for -1<c<1

    partial_c H(q,r,c)=J(q,r,c):=E[w_q(X)w_r(Y)].

The features have at most linear growth; their input derivatives are
bounded. Thus the identity applies at interior correlations. Coupling
Y=cX+sqrt(1-c^2)Z with independent X,Z, polynomial domination gives
continuity of H and J at both endpoints. Since |J|<=4, integration and
passage to either endpoint are justified. In particular

    delta(q,r,c)
      = (1/2)||u_q-u_r||_2^2 + integral_c^1 J(q,r,t)dt. (7)

No centered sample covariance is involved in this population identity.
At q=r=s the shape term is zero. For the same correlation t, subtract
the products w_q(X)w_r(Y) and w_s(X)w_s(Y). The triangle inequality,
the bound |w|<=2, and (6), without any independence of X,Y, give

    |J(q,r,t)-J(s,s,t)|
      <=20(|q-s|+|r-s|).                             (8)

Subtract (7) for the two states, integrate (8) over an interval of length
1-c, and use (5). This proves (1), including c=-1 and c=1.

## 3. A nonzero reference gap and relative comparison

Let b=E[Zu_s(Z)] and v(z)=u_s(z)-bz. Then E[Zv(Z)]=0 and
||v||_2^2=1-b^2. Gaussian conditional expectation E[X|Y]=cY gives
E[Xv(Y)]=E[Yv(X)]=0, including both degenerate endpoint pairs.
Cauchy-Schwarz therefore implies

    H(s,s,c)=b^2 c+E[v(X)v(Y)] <= b^2 c+1-b^2,
    delta(s,s,c)>=b^2(1-c).                          (9)

For s>0, the elementary inequality tanh(t)>=t/sqrt(1+t^2) for t>=0,
oddness, and F(s)<=s yield

    b >= E[Z^2/sqrt(1+sZ^2)]
      >= 1/sqrt(1+3s) >= 1/2.

The middle step is Jensen for the convex function x->(1+sx)^(-1/2)
under the probability measure with density Z^2, whose Z^2 mean is 3.
For s=0, b=1 directly. Consequently delta(s,s,c)>0 for c<1 and
delta(s,s,c)>=(1-c)/4. Dividing (1) by this lower bound proves (2):
(121/2)*4=242 and 20*4=80. No division by a zero endpoint gap is made.

## 4. Conditional contrast recursion

The scalar function f(t)=tanh(sqrt(t))^2 is 1-Lipschitz on [0,infinity):
for t>0 its derivative is [tanh(sqrt(t))/sqrt(t)]sech(sqrt(t))^2 in [0,1],
and its continuous derivative at zero is 1. Hence for A=sqrt(q)X,
B=sqrt(r)Y,

    |tanh(A)^2-tanh(B)^2| <= |A^2-B^2|.

Gaussian fourth moments give

    E[(A^2-B^2)^2]
      =3q^2+3r^2-2qr(1+2c^2)
      =3(q-r)^2+4qr(1-c^2)
      <=3(q-r)^2+8qr(1-c).                          (10)

The last step uses 1+c<=2 and 1-c>=0; it holds also for c=-1.
For independent paired rows, the variance of their mean difference is
the single-row variance divided by n. Bounding that variance by its
second moment and using (10) gives

    Var(Q'-R') <= [3e^2+8qr(1-c)]/n.               (11)

The mean is F(q)-F(r). For t>0, concavity and F(0)=0 imply
0<=F'(t)<=F(t)/t<=1-t/6. Differentiation is justified, for example,
by the derivative bound Z^2 for tanh(sqrt(t)Z)^2. At zero the derivative
is 1 by dominated convergence. Integrating this derivative bound between
q and r, in either order, gives

    |F(q)-F(r)| <= |q-r|[1-(q+r)/12].             (12)

The bracket is at least 5/6 because q+r<=2, so squaring preserves (12).
Add the square of this mean to (11) to obtain (3). The conditional
version uses precisely the same calculation after fixing the past;
only the fresh paired rows are independent.

## What remains open

C010 controls empirical gap noise relative to delta(Q_l,R_l,c_l).
Equation (1) removes the inappropriate absolute-Lipschitz comparison
with the GP state: its common-variance error carries the angular gap.
Equation (3) exhibits how fresh sampling creates radial contrast.
Neither is a closed relative multi-layer recursion. To iterate (2), one
must control the weighted term (Q_l-R_l)^2/(1-c_l) jointly with the
angle and the marginal errors, and compare the angle to the deterministic
angle. Replacing random denominators by their expectations or multiplying
unconditional moment bounds is not justified. No such step is asserted.

## Source and verification scope

Prior inputs: reviewer-PASS C002 v2 scalar facts; Voigtlaender's primary
Price identity at the locator above. C010 motivated this lemma but its
inverse-Lipschitz constant and unaudited moment theorem are not needed
in this proof. The new comparison and recursion await independent audit;
literature novelty has not been established. Any finite arithmetic checks
verify only their stated polynomial or rational identities, not the
analytic proof or the full target.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:518f766b67426759f30e8af49671a3b9d8d16c68f200bc9351ef0e8fa9d8db47","revision_digest":"sha256:ad83a72ff6e090c157d65d37c37ef544d8a8f16bcecdcf5091c33640dfc49344","source_id":"own-work:T250-w712-C011-v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20T19:28:50.001126+00:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Thm of arXiv:2608.25065, 'Detection of first homology via random geometric graphs in the thermodynamic regime'] \label[thm]{need at least rlogr}
    Let $0< \underline{\lambda} \le \overline{\lambda} < \infty$.
    Then there
    exists $q(\underline{\lambda},\overline{\lambda}, d) > 0$
    such that,
    if $\underline{\lambda} \le nr^d \le \overline{\lambda}$, then
    \[
        \mathbb{P}(
        \exists z \in \ker(Z_1(G_M(n;r)) \to H_1(M)) \setminus Z_1^{q r|\log r|}(G_M(n;r)))
        \to 1
    \]
    as $r \to 0$.
    Moreover,
    if $\underline{\lambda} >\lambda_c$,
    $z$ above can be chosen
    to lie in the largest component $\mathring{G}_M(n;r)$ of $G_M(n;r)$.
    In particular, in this case we have
    \[
        \mathbb{P}\left(\begin{array}{c} Z_1(G_M(n;r))/Z_1^{qr|\log r|}(G_M(n;r))
        \not \cong H_1(M) \mbox{ and } \\ Z_1(\mathring{G}_M(n;r))/Z_1^{qr|\log r|}(\mathring{G}_M(n;r))
        \not \cong H_1(M)
        \end{array}\right)
        \to 1
    \]
    as $r \to 0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 199 (Harmless wave equation error terms) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] Let $1 \leq N \leq \Ntop$.
We define $\HarmlessWave{N}$ to be any term
that satisfies the following pointwise estimate 
on $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarboot)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$:
	\begin{align} 
		\left| \HarmlessWave{[1,N]} \right|
		&
		\lesssim \left|\comdersmall^{[1,N+1]; \le 1}\velocityarray\right| + \left|\tander^{\le N} (\vortrenormalized,\GradEnt)\right| + 
				\left| \comdersmall^{[1,N];\le 1} \controlvars \right| + \left| \tandersmall^{[1,N]}\badcontrolvars\right|.
	\end{align}
title: Harmless wave equation error terms

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a sequence of general complex Wishart matrices
$$W_N=Y_NY_N^*\in M_N(L^\infty(X))$$
with $Y_N$ being $N\times M$ complex Gaussian of parameter $1$, we have
$$\frac{W_N}{N}\sim\max(1-t,0)\delta_0+\frac{\sqrt{4t-(x-1-t)^2}}{2\pi x}\,dx$$
with $M=tN\to\infty$, with the limiting measure being the Marchenko-Pastur law $\pi_t$.
title: Unnumbered theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'

[Ppn 197 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any subsequential limit $\Q$ as obtained by Proposition~\ref{p:tightness}, let $\mu\sim\Q$ and $(\Gamma,\Upsilon,\mathcal{E})\sim\mu$ (so $\mathcal{E}\equiv0$). Denote the limiting processes as 
	\begin{align}\nonumber
	\Gamma
	&\equiv \Big(
	D^{\RomI}=D=Y^{\RomI},
	Q^{\RomII},Q^{\RomII,\RomIII},Q^{\RomIII},Q^{\Ising}
	\Big)\,,\\
	\Upsilon
	&\equiv\Big( 
	Z^{\RomII}=Y^{\RomII},
	Z^{\RomIII}=Y^{\RomIII},
	Z^{\Ising}=Y^{\Ising}
	\Big)\,.
	
	\end{align}
Then $\Gamma$ is a finite-variation process, while $\Upsilon$ is a martingale. For each $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$, the covariation of $Z^\sigma$ with $Z^\tau$ is given by $Q^{\sigma,\tau}$, where
$Q^{\sigma,\Ising}\equiv0$ for $\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII\}$. 
 The ``$\frozen$'' variant of the statement also holds. 

\begin{proof}
Suppose $\Q_N\to\Q$ along some subsequence of integers $N\to\infty$.
By Corollary~\ref{c:tightness}, this means there exists a Skorohod coupling of the disorder matrices $\bG^N$ for which, with probability one over $(\bG^N)_{N\ge1}$, we have
$\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}\Rightarrow \mu$ with $\mu\sim\bar{\Q}$. Let $\cG(s)$ be the filtration generated by the limiting process $(\Gamma,\Upsilon)$. It follows from \eqref{e:def.drift} that if 
$0\le s\le t\le 1$, then for all $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$ and $A\in\cG(s)$, we have 
	\beq
	\bE_{\bG^N}\bigg[ \Big( Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(t)
		-Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(s)\Big)
		\ind\{A\}\bigg]
	=\bE_{\bG^N}\bigg[ \Big( D^{\bullet,\sigma}(t)
		-D^{\bullet,\sigma}(s)\Big)
		\ind\{A\}\bigg]\,,
	\eeq
where $\bE_{\bG^N}$ denotes expectation with respect to $\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}$.
Now fix an event $A\in\cG(s)$. Let $L_R,U_R$ be bounded continuous $\cG(s)$-measurable functions such that $L_R \le \ind\{A\} \le U_R$, and both $L_R,U_R$ converge to $\ind\{A\}$ in the limit $R\to\infty$. Moreover, we can arrange for the convergence to happen fast enough so that
	\beq
	\E_N\Big(U_R-L_R\Big) \le \frac{o_R(1)}{R}\,,
	\eeq
where we recall that $\E_N$ denotes the overall expectation.
Define also the function
	\[
	I_R(x) = \max\Big\{\min\{x,R\},-R\Big\} \in[-R,R]\,.
	\]
Let $\bE$ denote expectation with respect to $\mu$.
Since $\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}\Rightarrow\mu$, for fixed $R$ we have
	\begin{align*}
	\lim_{N\to\infty}
	\bE_{\bG^N}\bigg[ I_R\Big( Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(t)
		-Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(s)\Big)
	L_R \bigg]
	&=\bE\bigg[ I_R\Big(Y^\sigma(t)-Y^\sigma(s)\Big) L_R\bigg]\,,\\
	\lim_{N\to\infty}
	\bE_{\bG^N}\bigg[ I_R\Big( 
		D^{\bullet,\sigma}(t)-D^{\bullet,\sigma}(s)\Big)
	L_R\bigg]
	&=\bE\bigg[ I_R\Big(D^\sigma(t)-D^\sigma(s)\Big) L_R\bigg]
	\end{align*}
(and likewise with $U_R$ in place of $L_R$).
We then bound
	\begin{align*}
	&\bigg| \bE_{\bG^N}\Big[ I_R
		\Big( Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(t)-Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(s)\Big)
	L_R \Big] - \bE_{\bG^N}\Big[ 
		\Big( Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(t)-Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(s)\Big)
		;A\Big]\bigg| \\
	&\qquad\le R\bE_{\bG^N} \Big(U_R-L_R\Big)
	+ \bE_{\bG^N} \bigg[
	\Big| Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(t)-Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(s)\Big|
	; \Big| Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(t)-Y^{\bullet,\sigma}(s)\Big| \ge R\bigg]
	\end{align*}

	\[

	\]

\eqref{e:ind.A.approx}.

[Thm Theorem: Reduction to Host--Kra factors of arXiv:2605.16921, '${\ASL_n}(\mathbb Z)$ invariant random subsets of $\mathbb Z^n$'] Let $(X, \mu)$ be an $\ASL_d(\mathbb{Z})$-system. Let $k \geq 1$, let $v_1, \ldots, v_k \in \mathbb{Z}^d \setminus \{0\}$ be pairwise distinct, and let $f_1, \ldots, f_k \in L^\infty(X)$ be $\SL_d(\mathbb{Z})$-invariant. Set $K := 2^{d-1}k$. Then
    $$ \mathbb{E}\left[(v_1 \cdot f_1) \cdots (v_k \cdot f_k)\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[\bigl(v_1 \cdot \mathbb{E}[f_1 \mid Z^{K}(X)]\bigr) \cdots \bigl(v_k \cdot \mathbb{E}[f_k \mid Z^{K}(X)]\bigr)\right],$$
    where $Z^{K}(X)$ denotes the $K$-th Host--Kra factor of $X$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm Theorem: Reduction to Host--Kra factors of arXiv:2605.16921

			\]
			admits a finite right limit at every $t\in[0,T)$ and a finite
			left limit at every $t\in(0,T]$.
			
			\item Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a process with regulated trajectories.
			For $s\in(0,T]$, we define its left limit and left jump by
			\[
			\mathcal{X}_{s-}
			:=
			\lim_{u\uparrow s}\mathcal{X}_u,
			\qquad
			\Delta_-\mathcal{X}_s
			:=
			\mathcal{X}_s-\mathcal{X}_{s-},
			\]
			with the convention $\Delta_-\mathcal{X}_0=0$.
			
			For $s\in[0,T)$, we define its right limit and right jump by
			\[
			\mathcal{X}_{s+}
			:=
			\lim_{u\downarrow s}\mathcal{X}_u,
			\qquad
			\Delta_+\mathcal{X}_s
			:=
			\mathcal{X}_{s+}-\mathcal{X}_s,
			\]
			with the convention $\Delta_+\mathcal{X}_T=0$.
			
			The trajectories of a regulated process have at most countably
			many discontinuities; see
			[DudleyNorvaisa2011].
			
			\item Let
			\[
			\mathsf{K}:\Omega\times[0,T]\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}
			\]
			be a regulated process of finite variation. Then $\mathsf{K}$
			admits the decomposition
			\[
			\mathsf{K}
			=
			\mathsf{K}^c+\mathsf{K}^d+\mathsf{K}^g,
			\]
			where $\mathsf{K}^c$ is continuous, the càdlàg pure-jump process
			$\mathsf{K}^d$ is defined by
			\[
			\mathsf{K}^d_t
			:=
			\sum_{0<s\leq t}\Delta_-\mathsf{K}_s,
			\qquad t\in[0,T],
			\]
			and the càglàd pure-jump process $\mathsf{K}^g$ is defined by
			\[
			\mathsf{K}^g_t
			:=
			\sum_{0\leq s<t}\Delta_+\mathsf{K}_s,
			\qquad t\in[0,T].
			\]
			The above sums converge absolutely along each trajectory since
			$\mathsf{K}$ has finite variation.
			
			In particular,
			\[
			\mathsf{K}_t
			=
			\mathsf{K}^{\ast}_t
			+
			\sum_{0\leq s<t}\Delta_+\mathsf{K}_s,
			\qquad t\in[0,T],
			\]
			where
			\[
			\mathsf{K}^{\ast}
			:=
			\mathsf{K}-\mathsf{K}^g
			=
			\mathsf{K}^c+\mathsf{K}^d
			\]
			is the càdlàg, or right-continuous, part of $\mathsf{K}$.
			The process $\mathsf{K}^g$ is the left-continuous pure-jump part
			of $\mathsf{K}$.
		\end{itemize}
title: Regulated processes

body: For the l^p norm on R^2 and the axis direction e_2, the dogleg excess of a midpoint-displaced point v = (d, r/2) is exactly asymptotic to (2^p/p) d^p / r^{p-1} as d/r -> 0 (second-order Taylor of (1 + x^p)^{1/p}). Consequently the enclosing-ball (quadratic lower) curvature condition excess >= c d^2/r holds at the axis if and only if p <= 2: for p < 2 the excess is of larger order than quadratic (the condition holds with room), at p = 2 it is exactly quadratic with constant 2, and for every p > 2 the contact is quartic or flatter and the enclosing-ball constant is ZERO. The curvature hypothesis consumed by localization arguments is therefore genuinely restrictive - entire familiar norm families fail it at their axis directions - and cannot be discharged by convexity or symmetry alone. Numerically verified: measured excess/predicted ratios 0.9995-1.0000 across p in {1.5, 2, 3, 4} at two offsets, and the quadratic test excess/(d^2/r) converges to a constant for p <= 2 and to zero for p > 2.

[Definition 3 of arXiv:2605.02002, 'Glauber dynamics for random field Ising models on bounded degree graphs and MLSI'] Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph and $\mu_G$ be the RFIM measure on $G$. We say that $\mu_G$ satisfies $\operatorname{WSM}(C)$ for some $C>0$ if for all vertices $v\in V$ and $r\geq 1$, we have 
    $$
\mathbb{E}_h[d_{TV}(\mu_G(\sigma_v\in\cdot\mid \sigma_{\partial B_r(v)}=+),\mu_G(\sigma_v\in\cdot\mid \sigma_{\partial B_r(v)}=-))]\leq Ce^{-r/C}.
    $$Here $\partial B_r(v)$ is the boundary of $B_r(v)$ in $V$ and $B_r(v)$ is the ball of radius $r$ around $v$ with respect to the graph distance on $G$. We use $\sigma_{\partial B_r(v)}=+$ (resp. $\sigma_{\partial B_r(v)}=-$) to denote the all plus (resp. all minus) boundary condition.
title: Definition 3 of arXiv:2605.02002

body: Ergodic theory is a branch of mathematics that studies statistical properties of deterministic dynamical systems; it is the study of ergodicity. In this context, "statistical properties" refers to properties which are expressed through the behavior of time averages of various functions along trajectories of dynamical systems. The notion of deterministic dynamical systems assumes that the equations determining the dynamics do not contain any random perturbations, noise, etc. Thus, the statistics with which we are concerned are properties of the dynamics.

[Lemma lem:second_moment_recurrences of arXiv:2609.02491, 'Generalised Random Parking for Trapeziums on a Strip'] Let $B_\mathcal{P}$ and $B_\mathcal{T}$ be defined as in~(equation eq:defn_B_s of the paper). For all $x>(3a-b)/2$, it follows that
\begin{align}
B_{\mathcal{P}}(x)
&=
\frac{1}{x-a} \mleft( \int_0^{x-a}B_{\mathcal{P}}(t)\,\mathrm{d} t + \int_\delta^{x-\varsigma }B_{\mathcal{T}}(t)\,\mathrm{d} t \mright) + q_{\mathcal{P}}(x), \quad \text{ and } \\
B_{\mathcal{T}}(x)
&=
\frac{1}{x-a} \mleft( \int_\delta^{x-a}B_{\mathcal{T}}(t)\,\mathrm{d} t + \int_0^{x-\varsigma }B_{\mathcal{P}}(t)\,\mathrm{d} t \mright) + q_{\mathcal{T}}(x), 
\end{align}
where
\begin{align}
q_{\mathcal{P}}(x) 
&=
\frac{1}{x-a} \mleft( \int_0^{x-a} e_{\mathcal{P}}(t)e_{\mathcal{T}}(x-\varsigma -t)\,\mathrm{d} t + \int_\delta^{x-\varsigma } e_{\mathcal{T}}(t)e_{\mathcal{P}}(x-\varsigma -t)\,\mathrm{d} t \mright),\quad \text{ and } \\
q_{\mathcal{T}}(x)
&=
\frac{1}{x-a} \mleft( \int_0^{x-a-\delta} e_{\mathcal{T}}(t+\delta)e_{\mathcal{T}}(x-a-t)\,\mathrm{d} t + \int_0^{x-\varsigma }  e_{\mathcal{P}}(t)e_{\mathcal{P}}(x-\varsigma -t)\,\mathrm{d} t \mright). 
\end{align}

[Theorem 17 of arXiv:2606.29512, '2606.29512'] Let Assumptions \ref{assumption1}, 
\ref{assumption2}, \ref{assumption3}  and \ref{assumption2c} hold.  
Then every admissible solution admits an $\cH$-valued c\`adl\`ag modification. 
Moreover,  there exists a constant 
$N=N(d,r)>0$
such that if $u$ is an admissible solution 
to \eqref{SNS5}--\eqref{div5}--\eqref{bin5} satisfying 
$\hat u\leq \delta/N$, then 
$$
\E e^{-\psi_{t}}|u_t-v_t|^2_{\cH}
\leq \E |u_0-v_0|_{\cH}^2\quad\text{for $t\in[0,T]$} 
$$
for any admissible solution $v$ of \eqref{SNS5}--\eqref{div5}--\eqref{bin5} 
on $[0,T]$ with $\cH$-valued initial condition 
$v_t|_{t=0}=v_0$, where 
$$
\psi_t=N\int_0^t\beta_s\,ds,
\quad 
\beta_s
=\hat u^2+\bar u_s^2+\lambda^2_s+\tilde\lambda^2_s+\vartheta^2+\chi^2_s+\kappa_s

with a constant  $N=N(d,r,\delta)$. In particular, if $u_0=v_0$

[Definition 14 of arXiv:2605.03236, 'Stochastic It\^o Equations and Parabolic Second-Order Equations with singular Drift'] Given a domain $\cO\subset\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$, the
(right)  {\em parabolic boundary }of $\cO$ is the set of all points
$(t_{0},x_{0})$ belonging to the boundary $\partial \cO$ of $\cO$ (as
a set in $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$) for each of which one can find a continuous
function $x_{t}\in\bR^{d}$ and a
\index{$S$@Miscelenea!parabolic boundary}
\index{$S$@Miscelenea!$\partial'$}
 number $\delta>0$ such that $x_{t_{0}}=x_{0}$
and $(t,  x_{t})\in \cO$ for $t\in[t_{0}-\delta, t_{0})$.
The parabolic boundary of $\cO$ is denoted by $\partial^{\prime}\cO$.

[Prop geods-dust of arXiv:2604.12963, 'Shocks, instability, and the twenty networks\\ of infinite geodesics in the Directed Lands'] Let $\omega\in\Omega_0$, $\theta\in\Theta^\omega$, and  $(x,s)\in\IG\theta$. Suppose that $(x,s)$ is not on the boundary of any stability island. Then the following are the only three possible $\theta$-directed geodesic configurations out of $(x,s)$, and each of the three occurs on a set of starting points that is dense in $\IG\theta$. See the first three configurations on the second row of Figure (fig:geodesics of the paper).
    \begin{enumerate}[label={\rm(\alph*)}, ref={\rm\alph*}] \itemsep=1pt
        \item $(x,s)\not\in{\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta-}\cup{\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta+}$. Then $(x,s)\in\IGpns\theta$.
        
        \item $(x,s)\in {\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta-}$. Then $(x,s)\not\in{\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta+}$, there are no distinct middle geodesics out of $(x,s)$, and
        \[
        \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s,\infty)}\preceq \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s,\infty)}\prec\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s,\infty)} = \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s,\infty)}.
        \]

        \item $(x,s)\in {\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta+}$. Then $(x,s)\not\in{\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta-}$, there are no distinct middle geodesics out of $(x,s)$, and
        \[
        \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s,\infty)}= \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s,\infty)}\prec\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s,\infty)} \preceq\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s,\infty)}.
        \]
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop geods-dust of arXiv:2604.12963

body: [Corollary co-uncited-4 of arXiv:2411.12623, 'Random signed measures'] For any random signed measure $\xi$ on $S$ and any sub $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{G}$ of $\mathcal{F}$, there exist $\mathcal{G}$-measurable kernels $\eta_+ = \mathbb{E}[\xi_+|\mathcal{G}]$ and $\eta_- = \mathbb{E}[\xi_-|\mathcal{G}]$ and pre-kernel $\eta = \mathbb{E}[\xi|\mathcal{G}]$ from $\Omega$ to $S$, such that $\eta_+(B) = \mathbb{E}[\xi_+(B)|\mathcal{G}]$ a.s. for all $B\in\hat{\mathcal{S}}$ and similarly for $\eta_-$ and $\eta$. If $\mathbb{E}[|\xi|]$ is locally finite, then $\eta_+$ and $\eta_-$ are random measures on $S$ and $\eta=\eta_+-\eta_-= \mathbb{E}[\xi|\mathcal{G}]$ is a random signed measure on $S$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\[
 s(\theta)\succ s(\eta)
\]
and $s(\theta)$ is not a permutation of $s(\eta)$, then
\begin{equation}
 M_{p,n,t}(\theta)>M_{p,n,t}(\eta).
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\[
 \widetilde A_{p,n,t}(\theta)>
 \widetilde A_{p,n,t}(\eta).
\]

    \]

[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2608.26618, 'A Unified Descriptive-Complexity Framework for Model Selection under Correlated Designs'] Let $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_n)^\top$ be independent, mean-zero
sub-Weibull $(\alpha,\zeta)$ random variables for all $i$ and some $\alpha\in(0,2]$.
Then, for every deterministic vector $a \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $t>0$, we have
\begin{equation*}
\Pr\!\Big(
\big|a^\top\varepsilon\big|
\ge t
\Big)
\ \le\
2\exp\!\left\{
-c_{\alpha,\zeta}
\min\!\left(
\left(\frac{t}{\sigma\|a\|_2}\right)^2,\,
\left(\frac{t}{\sigma\|a\|_2}\right)^\alpha
\right)
\right\}.
\end{equation*}

\end{equation}

[Definition of arXiv:2411.19255, 'Moderate, large and super large deviations principles for Poisson process with uniform cat'] A family of random variables $\xi_T(1)$ satisfies large deviation principle (LDP)  on  $\mathbb{R}$ with a rate function
	$I = I(x): \mathbb{R} \rightarrow [0,\infty]$ and normalizing function
	$\psi(T)$ such that $\lim_{T\rightarrow\infty}\psi(T) = \infty$,
	if for any $c \geq 0 $ \ the set $\{ x \in \mathbb{R}: I(x) \leq c \}$  is a compact set
	and, for any set $B \in \mathfrak{B}(\mathbb{R})$ the following inequalities hold:
	$$
	\limsup_{T \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{\psi(T)} \ln \mathbf{P}(\xi_T(1) \in B ) \leq - I([B]),
	$$
	$$
	\liminf_{T \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{\psi(T)} \ln \mathbf{P}(\xi_T(1) \in B )\geq -I((B)),
	$$
	where $\mathfrak{B}(\mathbb{R})$ is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\mathbb{R}$, $I(B) = \inf\limits_{x \in B} I(x)$,
	$I(\emptyset) = \infty$.

Let (X, Sigma, mu) be a measure space and 1 <= p < infinity with conjugate exponent p'. For g in L^{p'}(mu) define Lambda_g(f) = int_X f g dmu. (a) If 1 < p < infinity, then g -> Lambda_g is an isometric isomorphism of L^{p'}(mu) onto the dual space (L^p(mu))*, for an arbitrary measure space. (b) If p = 1 and mu is sigma-finite (more generally, localizable), then g -> Lambda_g is an isometric isomorphism of L^infinity(mu) onto (L^1(mu))*. In particular L^p is reflexive for 1 < p < infinity. For 1 < p < infinity the map is isometric over every measure space; for p = 1 it is isometric as soon as mu is semifinite, and without sigma-finiteness (or localizability) it need not be surjective. The case p = infinity is genuinely different and is NOT covered: the analogous map L^1(mu) -> (L^infinity(mu))* is isometric when mu is semifinite but in general not surjective, so (L^infinity)* is in general strictly larger than L^1 (see the pitfall).

body: A Riemannian metric g on a smooth manifold M is a smooth assignment to each point p in M of a positive-definite symmetric bilinear form g_p on the tangent space T_pM: g_p: T_pM x T_pM -> R is bilinear and symmetric, satisfies g_p(v,v) > 0 for every nonzero v in T_pM, and p |-> g_p(X(p),Y(p)) is a smooth function of p for any pair of smooth vector fields X, Y. The pair (M,g) is called a Riemannian manifold. The metric g determines lengths of tangent vectors, angles between them, and, by integration along curves, the length of any piecewise smooth curve and the induced distance function between points of M.
title: Riemannian Metric

[Lemma 34 of arXiv:2608.26619, 'Uniqueness of Positively Curved Ancient Ricci Flows on Surfaces with Boundary'] Let $g(\psi,\theta,t) = u(\psi,t)g_{0}$, $0\leq t< T$ be a radially symmetric {Ricci flow with boundary} on $\old$ solving \eqref{2DRF}. The quantity $$E(\psi,t) := R(\psi,t) - \frac{|\nabla h|^2}{h(1-h)}$$
defined in \eqref{eq_E} satisfies
$$\partial_tE - \Delta_{g(t)} E \geq E^2.$$
Above, $R$ denotes the scalar curvature, $h(\psi,t) = 1 - \sqrt{\frac{u(\psi,t)}{u_\fl(\psi)}}$ as in \eqref{eq_h}, and $u_{\fl}$ is the conformal factor associated with the flat disk as in \eqref{eq_flat}.

[Definition 3 of arXiv:2608.25725, 'Gr\"obner Bases for Alexander Fitting Ideals of Links'] For \(k\ge0\), define
\[
\AG_k(G,\phi)
 :=\mathcal G_P\!\left(\PP(E_k(G,\phi))\right).
\]
We call this the \emph{\(k\)th Alexander--Gr\"obner invariant} of
\((G,\phi)\). The target \(\Z^\ell\) is understood with its fixed ordered
standard basis. The reduced Gr\"obner basis of the unit ideal is \(\{1\}\),
and that of the zero ideal is the empty set. By
Theorem~\ref{thm:CF-invariance} and uniqueness of reduced Gr\"obner bases,
\(\AG_k(G,\phi)\) depends only on \((G,\phi)\).

[Thm nclt of arXiv:2604.10602, 'Fractional Navier-Stokes Equations with Caputo Derivative Driven by Hermite Noise'] Let $(\xi_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a stationary centered Gaussian sequence with covariance $\rho(n)=\mathbb{E}[\xi_0\xi_n]\sim n^{2H-2}$ as $n\to\infty$. For $k\ge1$, let $H_k$ be the Hermite polynomial of degree $k$ normalized so that $\mathbb{E}[H_k(\xi)^2]=k!$. Define
\[
S_N(t) = \frac{1}{N^H} \sum_{n=1}^{[Nt]} H_k(\xi_n), \qquad t\ge 0.
\]
Then, as $N\to\infty$, the finite-dimensional distributions of $S_N(t)$ converge to those of the Hermite process $Z_H^k(t)$. Moreover, let $u^N$ be the mild solution of (equation eq:main of the paper) with $\dot{S}_N$ in place of $\dot{Z}_H^k$. Under the assumptions of Theorem~(thm:exist of the paper), we have
\[
u^N \xrightarrow{\text{law}} u \quad \text{in } C([0,T];\dot{H}^\nu),
\]
where $u$ is the mild solution of the original problem. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let (Omega, T) be a MINIMAL topological dynamical system, Omega a compact metric space and T a homeomorphism, and let V: Omega -> R be continuous. For each omega in Omega let H_omega be the discrete Schrodinger operator on l^2(Z) given by (H_omega u)(n) = u(n+1) + u(n-1) + V(T^n omega) u(n). By minimality the spectrum sigma(H_omega) is one and the same compact set Sigma contained in R for every omega. For an energy E in R define the Schrodinger cocycle (T, A^E) over (Omega,T), where A^E(omega) is the SL(2,R) matrix with rows (E - V(omega), -1) and (1, 0); its iterates are A^E_n(omega) = A^E(T^{n-1}omega) ... A^E(omega), and they transfer solutions of the difference equation u(n+1) + u(n-1) + V(T^n omega)u(n) = E u(n). The cocycle is UNIFORMLY HYPERBOLIC if there is a continuous T-invariant splitting R^2 = E^s(omega) + E^u(omega) and constants C > 0, lambda > 1 with ||A^E_n(omega)v|| <= C lambda^{-n}||v|| for v in E^s(omega) and ||A^E_{-n}(omega)v|| <= C lambda^{-n}||v|| for v in E^u(omega), for all n >= 0 and all omega; equivalently (for SL(2,R) cocycles over a compact base) ||A^E_n(omega)|| >= C lambda^n for all omega and all n >= 0. THEOREM (R. Johnson): E belongs to R \ Sigma if and only if the cocycle (T, A^E) is uniformly hyperbolic. Equivalently, Sigma is exactly the set of real energies at which the Schrodinger cocycle fails to be uniformly hyperbolic. The same statement holds in the continuum setting for Schrodinger operators -u'' + V(T_t omega)u on the line with a minimal flow, which is Johnson's original formulation, and it is the standard dictionary between spectral theory and the dynamics of the transfer-matrix cocycle. SHARP EDGES. (a) UNIFORM hyperbolicity is far stronger than a positive Lyapunov exponent, and this is the single most often misused point. In the supercritical almost Mathieu operator, and more generally in the localisation regime, the Lyapunov exponent L(E) is positive at EVERY energy of the spectrum; those energies are in Sigma, so the cocycle there is non-uniformly hyperbolic. 'Positive exponent' therefore does NOT imply 'in the resolvent set'; only uniformity does. (b) Minimality of the base is used twice: to make sigma(H_omega) independent of omega, and to propagate the exponential dichotomy from one orbit to all of Omega. For a non-minimal base the spectrum can genuinely depend on omega and the statement must be reformulated (typically with the union of the spectra over the support of an ergodic measure, or over the whole base), so do not apply the equivalence verbatim outside minimality. (c) The theorem characterises the RESOLVENT set, which is open; correspondingly uniform hyperbolicity is an open condition in E and in the cocycle, whereas positivity of the Lyapunov exponent is not open. (d) The statement is for real E; for non-real E the operator is invertible anyway and the associated cocycle is not an SL(2,R) cocycle.
Omega is a compact metric space and T: Omega -> Omega is a homeomorphism
(Omega, T) is minimal
V: Omega -> R is continuous
H_omega is the discrete Schrodinger operator with potential n -> V(T^n omega) on l^2(Z) (equivalently, the continuum Schrodinger operator over a minimal flow)
E is a real energy
uniform hyperbolicity is understood with constants uniform over all of Omega

From the two solutions one builds the Green kernel G_omega(m,n) of (H_omega - E)^{-1} in the standard way, and the exponential dichotomy bounds give |G_omega(m,n)| <= C' lambda^{-|m-n|} with constants independent of omega. A kernel with uniform exponential off-diagonal decay defines a bounded operator on l^2(Z), so H_omega - E is boundedly invertible for every omega, i.e. E is not in Sigma. Bounded invertibility of the operator for all omega is equivalent, through Sacker-Sell exponential dichotomy theory applied to the first-order system defined by the transfer matrices, to the existence of an exponential dichotomy for the cocycle over the closure of the orbit; the dichotomy projections are then continuous in omega, and minimality makes them globally defined on Omega. body:
Let X be a topological space and f: X -> (-infinity, +infinity] an extended-real function. f is lower semicontinuous (lsc) at a point x0 if for every real a < f(x0) there is a neighbourhood U of x0 with f(x) > a for all x in U. f is lsc on X iff any one of the following equivalent conditions holds: (i) the superlevel set {x : f(x) > a} is open for every real a; (ii) the sublevel set {x : f(x) <= a} is closed for every real a; (iii) the epigraph {(x,t) in X x R : t >= f(x)} is closed in X x R. If X is first countable (in particular metric), lower semicontinuity at x0 is equivalent to liminf_{x -> x0} f(x) >= f(x0). f is upper semicontinuous iff -f is lsc, and f is continuous iff it is both. Standard facts, each of which is the reason lsc is worth naming: (1) the pointwise SUPREMUM of an arbitrary family of lsc functions is lsc; (2) a sum of finitely many lsc functions is lsc provided no (+infinity) + (-infinity) occurs, and a nonnegative multiple of an lsc function is lsc; (3) a nondecreasing pointwise limit of continuous functions is lsc, and conversely on a METRIC space every lsc function bounded below is the pointwise nondecreasing limit of a sequence of Lipschitz functions (Baire); (4) the indicator 1_A is lsc iff A is open; (5) WEIERSTRASS FORM: if X is compact and f is lsc then f attains its infimum on X, because the sublevel sets {f <= a} are closed and have the finite intersection property. This is the form in which lsc is used in the direct method of the calculus of variations: coercivity plus lsc on a compact (or weakly compact) set yields a minimiser. SHARP EDGES, i.e. what is NOT true. (a) lsc buys you MINIMA only, never maxima: on the compact space [0,1] the function f(x) = x for x < 1, f(1) = 0 is lsc (every superlevel set {f > a} is (a,1) or [0,1] or empty), its supremum is 1 and it is not attained. (b) The supremum of lsc functions is lsc but the INFIMUM of infinitely many lsc functions need not be: on R the continuous functions f_n(x) = max(0, 1 - n|x|) have pointwise infimum the indicator of {0}, whose superlevel set {f > 1/2} = {0} is not open. (c) 'lsc at every point' is genuinely weaker than continuity; an lsc function may be discontinuous on a dense set. (d) Statement (3) uses metrizability of X; on a general topological space an lsc function need not be a pointwise limit of continuous functions (it is a supremum of continuous functions on compact Hausdorff or, more generally, normal spaces, by Urysohn/Katetov-Tong, but for arbitrary X no such representation is available). (e) In integration theory the useful instance is Fatou's lemma, which says exactly that f -> integral f is lsc along pointwise convergence of nonnegative measurable functions; no upper semicontinuity holds there without a domination hypothesis.
X is a topological space
f takes values in the extended reals (-infinity, +infinity]
for the liminf characterisation, X is first countable (e.g. metric)
for the attainment-of-the-infimum statement, X is compact
for the approximation by Lipschitz functions, X is metric and f is bounded below

[Corollary cor:diamond-gauge-equiv-NAHM of arXiv:2608.02772, 'Non-Abelian Hirota-Miwa Equations for the KPZ Universality Class'] Under the substitution
    \begin{equation}
        C_i(u) = G(Tu)G(S_i u)^{-1}, \qquad
        \Lambda_i(u) = -G(u)U_{0i}(u)G(S_i u)^{-1},
    \end{equation}
    the $C$-diamond (equation eq:diamond-C-ij of the paper) reduces to the
    compatibility condition for (equation eq:gauge-system of the paper), while the
    $\Lambda$-diamond (equation eq:diamond-L-ij of the paper) and mixed
    diamond (equation eq:diamond-mixed-ij of the paper) become, respectively,
    \begin{align}
        U_{0i}(u)U_{0j}(S_i u)
        &= U_{0j}(u)U_{0i}(S_j u),
         \\
        U_{0j}(S_i u) + U_{0i}(Tu)
        &= U_{0i}(S_j u) + U_{0j}(Tu).
        
    \end{align}
    These are the specializations of
    (equation eq:NAHM-quadratic of the paper)
    and (equation eq:NAHM-shifted-cycle of the paper) to the triple
    $(0, i, j)$.  Moreover, the definition
    $U_{ij} = U_{0j} - U_{0i}$ extends these to the full
    quadratic relation (equation eq:NAHM-quadratic of the paper) for all
    distinct triples in $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$.
title: Corollary cor:diamond-gauge-equiv-NAHM of arXiv:2608.02772

    \underline{\textsf{\textbf{E}}} X

    \overline{\textsf{\textbf{E}}} X~.

Let $K$ be a real separable Hilbert space. The $d_2$ probability distance between two $K$-valued random variables $F$ and $X$ is defined by $d_2(F, X) := \sup_{h \in \mathcal{F}_2(K)} |\mathbb{E}[h(F)] - \mathbb{E}[h(X)]|$, where the test function class is $\mathcal{F}_2(K) := \{ h \in C_b^2(K; \mathbb{R}) : \sup_{x \in K} \|D^2 h(x)\|_{\mathcal{L}(K)} \le 1 \}$.

F, X \in L^2(\Omega; K)

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2607.08242, 'Convergence of random sums in non-commutative probability'] Suppose $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi)$ is an NCP. 

Let $\{a_i\}$ be self-adjoint variables such that, $\varphi(a_i)=0, \varphi(a_i^2)=1$, and  $\sup_i|\varphi(a_i^m)| < \infty$ for every positive integer $m$. 
Then the following hold for $S_n:=a_1+\cdots +a_n$.\vskip5pt

\noindent (i) If $\{a_i\}$ are free, then $S_n/\sqrt{n}\stackrel{*}{\to} s$.

\vskip5pt

\noindent (ii) If $\{a_i\}$ are independent, then $S_n/\sqrt{n}\stackrel{*}{\to} z$.

\vskip5pt

\noindent (iii) If $\{a_i\}$ are half-independent, then $S_n/\sqrt{n}
\stackrel{*}{\to} r_S$.

\vskip3pt

[Prop p.axioms of arXiv:2507.16056, 'Conditional GMC within the stochastic heat flow'] Take $q\in(0,\infty),\theta'\in\mathbb{R}$, and any probability space that houses random $M'_{[s,t]}\in\mathcal{M}_+(\Gamma_{[s,t]})$ for $s<t\in q\mathbb{D}$. Write $Z'_{s,t}:=M'_{[s,t]}\circ\margin{\{s,t\}}^{-1}$ for the time-$\{s,t\}$ marginal.
If for all $t_0<\cdots<t_{\ell}\inq\mathbb{D}$ we have that
\begin{enumerate}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\item 
$M'_{[t_0,t_1]},\ldots,M'_{[t_{\ell-1},t_{\ell}]}$ are independent, 
\item 
$M'_{[t_0,t_\ell]}\circ\margin{\{t_0,\ldots,t_\ell\}}^{-1} = Z'_{t_0,t_1}\circ\cdots\opdotZ'_{t_{\ell-1},t_{\ell}}$\ , and
\item 
$
	\mathbf{E} Z'_{s,t} {}^{\otimes n}
	=
	\mathrm{d} x\, \mathrm{d} x' \, \mathcal{Q}^{[\![n]\!],\theta'}(t-s,x,x')
$
for all $s<t \in q\mathbb{D}$ and $n=1,2,3,4$,
\end{enumerate}
then $M'_{[0,q ]}$ is equal in law to $M^{\theta'}_{[0,q ]}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

    \item If $X, Y\in\mathcal{G}$, then $\max\{X, Y\}\in \mathcal{G}$ \citep[][Proposition 2]{CS25}.

    \item if $X, Y\in\mathcal{H}$, then $\max\{X, Y\}\in \mathcal{H}$ \citep[][Proposition 3]{CHSZ25}.

    \item If $X, Y\in\mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}^\ast$], then $\max\{X, Y\}\in \mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}^\ast$].
    \end{itemize}

  \item[{\rm (vii)}] If $X\in \mathcal{H}$, then $(X-c)_+\in\mathcal{H}$ for any $c\in\R_{++}$ \citep[][Proposition 5]{CHSZ25}. \\
       If $X\in \mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$], then $(X-c)_+\in\mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$] for any $c\in\R_{++}$.

  \item[{\rm (viii)}] Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent such that $X\in\mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}$, $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$]. If $Y$ is non-negative, then $(X-Y)_+\in \mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}$, $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$].

  \item[{\rm (ix)}]  If $X\in \mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$], then $[X|X>c] \in \mathcal{V}$ [resp. $\mathcal{H}$, $\mathcal{H}^\ast$] for any $c\in\R_{++}$. However, $[X|X>c]\notin \mathcal{G}$ for any $c\in\R_{++}$.

body: In graph theory, the Robertson–Seymour theorem (also called the graph minors theorem) states that the undirected graphs, partially ordered by the graph minor relationship, form a well-quasi-ordering. Equivalently, every family of graphs that is closed under taking minors can be defined by a finite set of forbidden minors, in the same way that Wagner's theorem characterizes the planar graphs as being the graphs that do not have the complete graph $K_{5}$ or the complete bipartite graph $K_{3,3}$ as minors.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Bound the coefficients' growth from the lace expansion's structure and compare with the Borel condition. Result: Borel summability (Watson/Nevanlinna) needs the remainder after N terms to be bounded by C K^N N! (2d)^{-N} uniformly in a sector, and the coefficients to grow at most like K^N N!. The known coefficients a_1 = 1, a_2 = 1, a_3 = 7/2 and the computed higher ones (Mertens-Moore numerics) grow rapidly, consistent with factorial growth. The lace expansion gives the coefficient a_i as a sum over lace diagrams with i-th order random-walk contributions; the number of lace diagrams at order N grows like N! (the laces are essentially permutations of intervals), and each contributes O(1) after the 1/(2d) powers are extracted, so the factorial growth of a_N is plausible, and the remainder estimate of the same form would follow from a bound on the contribution of all diagrams of order >= N by K^N N! (2d)^{-N}. The lace expansion's remainder term is controlled in the existing proofs of the expansion only as O((2d)^{-N}) with an N-dependent constant not tracked; tracking it gives, at best, the factorial bound if the number of order-N diagrams is bounded by K^N N!, which I believe is correct for the diagrams counted with their symmetry factors. The uniform-in-sector (complex d) statement needed for Borel summability is meaningless for the lattice; one would need an analytic continuation in a parameter playing the role of 1/(2d), e.g. the spread-out range or a long-range exponent, and then the Nevanlinna condition in that parameter. So the honest reduction: Borel summability requires (i) K^N N! bounds on the lace-expansion remainder, plausible and unproved, and (ii) an analytic interpolation in the expansion parameter, for which no natural candidate is known. This mirrors the situation for the self-avoiding walk connective constant expansion (Graham's Borel-type bounds) mentioned in the source. Obstruction: No analytic interpolation in 1/(2d); remainder constants not tracked.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0080-borel-summability-of-the-1-d-expansion-of-the-percolation-threshold
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved
title: Attempt on Borel summability of the 1/d expansion of the percolation threshold

[Definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a set $X$, which can be finite, countable, or even uncountable, a discrete probability measure on it is a linear combination as follows,
$$\mu=\sum_{x\in X}\lambda_x\delta_x$$
with the coefficients $\lambda_i\in\mathbb R$ satisfying $\lambda_i\geq0$ and $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$. For $f:X\to\mathbb R$ we set
$$\int_Xf(x)d\mu(x)=\sum_{x\in X}\lambda_xf(x)$$
with the convention that each Dirac mass integrates up to $1$.

[Corollary 2-l12 of arXiv:2412.04015, 'Linear fluctuation of interfaces in Glauber-Kawasaki dynamics'] Fix a function
$F\colon {\mathbb R}_+ \times (\sqrt{K} {\mathbb T} \times {\mathbb T}^{d-1}) \to {\mathbb R}$
and a cylinder function $f$. Then, there exists a finite constant
${\mathfrak c}({\boldsymbol u}^N)$, depending only on ${\boldsymbol u}^N$, $f$ and $d$, uniformly
bounded in $N$, such that
\begin{align*}
& {\mathbb E}_{\nu^N} \Big[\, \Big|\,
\int_0^t \, 
\sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_N} \widehat {F_{s}}(Ax) \,
(\Xi^{\rm c} _{{\boldsymbol u}^N (\cdot), x} f) (\eta (s))
\, ds \, \Big| \,\Big]
\\
&\quad \;\le \;
{\mathfrak c}({\boldsymbol u}^N) \, \Big\{ \frac{1}{K_N} \;+\;
K_N\,  \int_0^t (\, 1 + \Vert F(s)\Vert^2_\infty\,)\, \big[ \,
H_N(f^N_s)  + (N/\ell_N)^d \,\big] \, ds\; \Big\}
\\
& \quad \; + \;
\int_0^t \frac{1}{\gamma_s}  \big\{\, H_N(f^N_s) +
\log 2 \, \big\} \; ds
\;+\; {\mathfrak c} ({\boldsymbol u}^N) \,  K\, N^{d-2}\, \int_0^t   \gamma_s \,  {\mathfrak m}_K (F(s))^2\,
\, e^{c ({\boldsymbol u}^N) \, \gamma_s\,  {\mathfrak m}_K (F(s)) \, \epsilon_N }\; ds
\end{align*}
for all $t>0$, $\gamma\colon [0,t] \to (0,\infty)$.  In this equation,
$f^N_s$ is given by (equation 2-34c of the paper), $(\ell_N : N\ge 1)$ is the sequence
introduced in the statement of Theorem (mt1 of the paper), and
$\epsilon_N = K^{1/2}/N$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorema 2 ({\Cref{criterion-decomp-log}}) of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let \(X\) be a smooth \(k\)-variety of dimension \(d\), and let \(D\)
be a simple normal crossings divisor on \(X\).  Then the following
conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The pair \((X,D)\) is log HT-split.
\item There is an isomorphism
\begin{equation}
F_{*}\Omega_{X/k}^{\bullet}(\log D)
\simeq
\bigoplus_{i=0}^{d}
\Omega_{X/k}^i(\log D)[-i]
\end{equation}
in \(\mcalD_{\qcoh}(X)\).
\end{enumerate}
If \(X\) is projective, these equivalent conditions imply logarithmic
Akizuki--Nakano vanishing and the \(E_1\)-degeneration of the
logarithmic Hodge-to-de Rham spectral sequence (\Cref{vanishing}). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: {\Cref{criterion-decomp-log}}

Write f = u + iv with real u, v. If f is complex-differentiable at z = x + iy then the partial derivatives satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equations u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x there, and f'(z) = u_x + i v_x. Conversely, if u, v have continuous first partials satisfying the Cauchy-Riemann equations on an open set, then f is holomorphic there. Consequently u and v are harmonic (Laplace equation), and are harmonic conjugates.
f = u + iv on an open set; sufficiency needs continuous partials

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The chi law of parameter $n\in\mathbb N$, appearing as
$$\chi_n=law\left(\sqrt{f_1^2+\ldots+f_n^2}\right)$$
with $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ being independent, each following $g_1$, has density given by
$$\chi_n=\frac{x^{n-1}e^{-x^2/2}}{2^{n/2-1}\Gamma(n/2)}\,dx$$
and its moments are given by the following formula, valid for any $k\in\mathbb N$,
$$M_k=2^{k/2}\frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{n+k}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)}$$
with $\Gamma$ being as usual the gamma function.

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2606.17381, 'Large deviation principle for friendship-biases\\ in Galton--Watson trees'] {\bf [Properties of the rate function]}

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\rm (a)}] On $\cD$, $(x,s) \mapsto J(x,s)$ is marginally convex and achieves its unique zero at $(x^*,s^*)$ given by
\[
(x^*,s^*) = \big(\|G(\nu^*)\|_1,G(\nu^*)/\|G(\nu^*)\|_1\big)
\] 
with $\nu^* = (\zeta^{\otimes 2})^{\otimes 3}$, which equals
\[
x^* = \frac{1}{1-p}, \qquad s^* = \big((1-p)-(1-p)^4,\, p^3 + (1-p)^4,\, p-p^3\big).          
\]
\item[{\rm (b)}] 
For every $(x,s) \in \mathrm{int}(\cD)$, the infimum defining $J(x,s)$ is achieved and equals
\[
J(x,s) = -\lambda(x,s) - x \sum_{\chi \in S} s^\chi \lambda^\chi (x,s), 
\]
where $\lambda(x,s)$ and $\lambda^\chi(x,s)$, $\chi \in S$, are Lagrangian multipliers that uniquely solve four equations involving rational functions whose coefficients depend on $(x,s)$ and $p$ (see Section \ref{sec:ProofLDP2}).
\item[{\rm (c)}]
On $\mathrm{int}(\cD)$, $(x,s) \mapsto J(x,s)$ is analytic and marginally strictly convex.
\item[{\rm(d)}] 
$\mathrm{int}(\cD) = \big\{(x,s)\in(0,\infty)\times\mathcal S_2\colon\, 1 < x < \infty,\,s^- < 1/x < s^-+s^0 < 1 < 3s^-+s^0\big\}$.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 4 of arXiv:2606.17381

[Prop GTASEP of arXiv:2510.23430, 'On the Martin boundary for discrete TASEP'] Let $\lambda,\mu$ be partitions such that $l(\mu)\leq t$, and $n\in\mathbb Z_{\geq 0}$. Then
$$
\mathbb P(Y(t+n)=\lambda+\delta\mid Y(t)=\mu+\delta)=p^{|\lambda|-|\mu|}(1-p)^nG^{(0,-p)}_{\lambda/\mu}(1^n).
$$
In particular, $\mathbb P(Y(n)=\lambda+\delta)=p^{|\lambda|}(1-p)^nG^{(0,-p)}_{\lambda}(1^n)$.

[Lemma omega-fewer-quantifiers of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $X\in\cat{$\bm G$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Sp}$ be levelwise closed, i.e. for all inner product spaces $V\in \textbf{\textup{O}}$, $X(V)$ is a closed orthogonal $G$-space. Then $X$ is a $G$-global $\Omega$-spectrum if and only if $\tilde\sigma({\mathcal{U}}_H)^\varphi\colon X(V)({\mathcal{U}}_H)^\varphi\to(\Omega^WX(V\oplus W)(\mathcal U_H))^\varphi$ is a weak homotopy equivalence for every homomorphism of compact Lie groups $\varphi\colon H\to G$, some (hence any) complete $H$-universe ${\mathcal{U}}_H$, and all $H$-representations $V,W$.
    \begin{proof}
        The assumptions guarantee that both $X(V)$ and $\Omega^WX(V\oplus W)$ are closed orthogonal $(G\times K)$-spaces for all $K$-representations $V,W$. Thus, Lemma~(lemma:we-between-closed of the paper) shows that $X$ is a $G$-global $\Omega$-spectrum if and only if \[\tilde\sigma({\mathcal{U}}_H)\colon X(V)({\mathcal{U}}_H)\to\Omega^WX(V\oplus W)({\mathcal{U}}_H)\]
        is a $\mathcal G_{H,K\times G}$-equivariant weak equivalence for all compact Lie groups $H,K$ and all $K$-representations $V,W$. As ${\mathcal{U}}_H$ is also a complete universe for every closed subgroup of $H$ (Remark~(rk:universe-subgroup of the paper)), this is equivalent via replacing $H$ by its subgroups to $\tilde\sigma({\mathcal{U}}_H)$ inducing a weak homotopy equivalence on $(\psi,\varphi)$-fixed points for all compact Lie groups $H$ and $K$, $K$-representations $V$ and $W$, and homomorphisms $\psi\colon H\to K$ and $\varphi\colon H\to G$. Restricting $V$ and $W$ to $H$-representations along $\psi$, this simplifies to the condition from the statement of the lemma, finishing the proof.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma omega-fewer-quantifiers of arXiv:2608.28504

\[
  \tilde r(x)
  :=\frac{\chi^2(P(x,\cdot)\|\pi)}{\log(1/\pi(x))}
  =\frac{\sum_{i=2}^n\lambda_i^2\,\phi_i(x)^2}{\log(1/\pi(x))}.
\]
Then $r(x)\le\tilde r(x)$ pointwise, $\bar r_\pi\le\mathbb{E}_\pi[\tilde r]$,
and $M\le\max_x\tilde r(x)$.

[Definition 13 of arXiv:2608.29157, 'Dilator-based analysis of $\KP$'] A \emph{$\rmbeta$-language} is a many-sorted first-order language $\calL$ with a distinguished type $\ord$ together with a distinguished binary predicate $\le_\ord$, and the only terms in $\calL$ of type $\ord$ are variables. In particular, we do not allow constant symbols of type $\ord$ or function symbols of value $\ord$. A \emph{$\rmbeta$-theory} is a theory in some $\rmbeta$-language.
    
    A structure $M$ in a $\rmbeta$-language $\calL$ is a \emph{pre-$\rmbeta$-model} if the \emph{ordinal part} $(\ord^M,\le_\ord^M)$ of $M$ is a linear order. If the ordinal part of $M$ is a well-order, we call $M$ a \emph{$\rmbeta$-model}.
    We also define the following semantic implication notions: For a $\rmbeta$-language $\calL$ and a $\rmbeta$-theory $T$ in $\calL$, and a formula $\phi$ in $\calL$,
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $T\vDash_{\pre\rmbeta} \phi$ if every pre-$\rmbeta$-model of $T$ satisfies the universal closure of $\phi$. We call $\phi$ is \emph{pre-$\rmbeta$-valid in $T$}.
        \item $T\vDash_{\rmbeta} \phi$ if every $\rmbeta$-model of $T$ satisfies the universal closure of $\phi$. We call $\phi$ is \emph{$\rmbeta$-valid in $T$}.
    \end{enumerate}
    We omit $T$ in the previous notations when $T=\varnothing$.

A real $n \times n$ matrix $A = (a_{ij})$ is nonnegative ($A \ge 0$) if all entries are $\ge 0$, and positive ($A > 0$) if all entries are $> 0$. Associate to $A \ge 0$ the directed graph $G(A)$ on vertices $1, \dots, n$ with an edge $i \to j$ iff $a_{ij} > 0$; then $(A^m)_{ij} > 0$ iff there is a walk of length $m$ from $i$ to $j$. $A$ is irreducible if $G(A)$ is strongly connected (every vertex reaches every other), equivalently if there is no permutation matrix $P$ with $P A P^{\mathsf T} = \begin{pmatrix} B & C \\ 0 & D\end{pmatrix}$ with $B, D$ square nonempty blocks, equivalently (for $n \ge 2$) if $(I + A)^{n-1} > 0$; a $1 \times 1$ matrix is irreducible by convention (some authors exclude the zero $1\times1$ matrix). The period (index of imprimitivity) $h$ of an irreducible $A$ is the greatest common divisor of the lengths of all closed walks in $G(A)$; it does not depend on the vertex, and $h = 1$ iff $A$ is aperiodic. $A$ is primitive if $A \ge 0$ and $A^m > 0$ for some $m \ge 1$; for nonnegative matrices, primitive $\iff$ irreducible and aperiodic, and then $A^m > 0$ for all $m \ge (n-1)^2 + 1$ (Wielandt's bound). Every positive matrix is primitive. Warnings: irreducible does not imply primitive (the cyclic permutation matrix of an $n$-cycle is irreducible with period $n$); a matrix with a positive diagonal entry that is irreducible is automatically primitive; irreducibility is a property of the zero pattern only, not of the magnitudes; a matrix with some negative entries is outside this theory entirely.
A is a square real matrix with nonnegative entries

body: Theorem (campaign status: proved): No boundary-preserving admissible sign basis repairs the NAE-star absorption failure. Whatever the basis takes as its single private member (q, or one Y_j, up to sign), two of the three forms - call them Y_i, Y_k - remain, and for EVERY signed selector choice their residuals are linearly independent. Their span therefore has dimension at least 2 while its private projection has dimension at most 1, so the span contains a nonzero pure-boundary vector. With R_< = 0, connector absorption is impossible. Notes: Proof of the independence: the residual Y_i -/+ g retains at least one of the two boundary coordinates x_i, z_i private to that row; a residual from Y_k meets at most one of x_i, z_i, since a basis selector has at most one such boundary coordinate and the sole nonboundary basis form is supported on the j-th pair; if the two were proportional, the first would have to cancel one of its own pair coordinates by selecting it and would then have no support on x_k, z_k, while the second necessarily retains one - contradiction. Quantifier is over ALL boundary-preserving admissible sign bases AND all signed selector choices. R_< = 0 is essential: the leak is fatal only when ancestors have paid nothing.

[Lemma of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] Let $\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_l \in \mathbb{R}$, and $l$ is fixed. Then the Harish-Chandra integral satisfies, for every fixed $r \in \mathbb{N}$,
  \[ \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \log \text{} H \text{} C (x_1, \ldots, x_r,
     0^{N - r} ; N \theta_1, \ldots, N \theta_l, 0^{N - l}) = \sum_{i = 1}^r
     \sum_{j = 1}^l \log (1 - \theta_j x_i)^{- 1}, \]
  where the above convergence is uniform in a neighborhood of $0^r$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2608.26974, 'Why not to use the Gaussian kernel'] Consider a stationary strictly positive-definite kernel $k(x, y) = \Phi(x - y)$ for a continuous and integrable $\Phi \colon \R^d \to \R$.
  Suppose that there are $C \geq 0$ and $a > 0$ such that $(\mathcal{F}\Phi)(\omega) \leq C \exp(-a \lVert \omega \rVert_2)$ for all $\omega \in \R^d$.
  Let $\sigma \geq 0$.
  If $X_n = \{x_1, \ldots, x_n \}$ for a sequence $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^\infty \subset \R^d$ of pairwise distinct points whose closure has non-empty interior, then
  \begin{equation*}
     \sup_{x \in K} \V_\sigma(x \mid \mathcal{D}_n) \to 0 \quad \text{ as } \quad n \to \infty \quad \text{ for any compact } \quad K \subset \R^d.
  \end{equation*}
title: Theorem 9 of arXiv:2608.26974

body: [Definition Brownian Continuum Random Tree of arXiv:2512.17747, 'On exponentially height-penalized random trees'] The Brownian Continuum Random Tree (BCRT in short) [aldous1991continuum] is the random real tree $(T_{\mathbf{e}},\rho_{\mathbf{e}},d_{\mathbf{e}},\sigma_{\mathbf{e}})$, where $(\mathbf{e}(t):0\leq t\leq 1)$ is the standard Brownian excursion, and $\sigma_{\mathbf{e}}$ is the pushforward of the Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$ under the projection map of the quotient $\sim$.

  \]

[Corollary cor:product-compact-box of arXiv:2606.21006, 'Law of the Iterated Logarithm for Weighted Sums of Functionals of Long-Memory Gaussian Seq'] For \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in\mathbb R^m\), define
\[
\Psi_n(x):=\prod_{j=1}^m \psi_n(x_j),
\qquad
\Psi(x):=c_f^{m/2}\prod_{j=1}^m |x_j|^{(\alpha-1)/2}.
\]
Let
\(
D_R:=[-R,R]^m,
\quad
K_{\varepsilon,R}:=\{x\in D_R:\min_{1\le j\le m}|x_j|\ge\varepsilon\}.
\)
Then for every \(R>0\), every \(\varepsilon\in(0,R)\), and every \(\eta\in(0,\alpha)\),

\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)]
\(
\sup_{x\in K_{\varepsilon,R}}
|\Psi_n(x)-\Psi(x)|
\longrightarrow0;
\)

\item[(b)] for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\(
|\Psi_n(x)|^2
\le
C_{R,\eta}\prod_{j=1}^m |x_j|^{\alpha-1-\eta},
\qquad
x\in D_R;
\)

\item[(c)]
\(
\|\Psi_n-\Psi\|_{L^2(D_R)}
\longrightarrow0.
\)
\end{itemize}

[Proposition prop: rad_blow of arXiv:2412.07690, 'A law of large numbers concerning the distribution of critical points of random Fourier se'] Fix a box $B\subset \mathscr{V}$ and $r<\dist(B,\mathscr{V})$.  Denote by $S=S(r,B)$ the compact set set
\[
S=\big\{\, v\in \mathscr{V};\;\;\dist(v,B)\leq r\,\,\big\}.
\]
Suppose that $F\,\big\vert_B$ is $C^2$,  $2$-ample and $J_1$-ample, i.e., for any ${\boldsymbol{v}}\in B$ the Gaussian vector $\big(\, F(v),F'(v)\,\big)$   is nondegenerate.  Define 
\[
w_F:B^2_*\to {\mathbb R}, \,\, w_F({\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{y}})=|{\boldsymbol{x}}-{\boldsymbol{y}}|^{m-2}\rho_F^{(2)}({\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{y}}).
\]
There exists a constant $C(m, \vol[B], r)>0$,  that depends only on $m$, $\vol[B]$  and $r$ such that
\begin{equation}
\sup_{{\boldsymbol{p}}\in B^2_*}|{w}_F({\boldsymbol{p}})\,\big\vert \leq  C(m,\vol[B], r)\Vert \EuScript{K}_F\Vert^{3m-1/2}_{C^6(S\times S)}.
\end{equation}
In particular $\var\big[\, Z_B\,\big]<\infty$.

body:
[Definition 11 (Octahedron recurrence) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{def:oct}
We use the max-plus form of the octahedron recurrence, in the sense of
\cite{KTW,Speyer,NarSheffTao}.  One starts with real values assigned to a
stepped surface in the parity sublattice of \(\mathbb Z^3\).  A local move
replaces one face of an elementary octahedron by the opposite face.  If the
six vertices of this octahedron are
\[
(i,j,k\pm 1),\qquad (i\pm 1,j,k),\qquad (i,j\pm 1,k),
\]
and all values except \(F(i,j,k+1)\) are already known, then the missing value
is defined by
\[
F(i,j,k+1)
=
\max\{F(i+1,j,k)+F(i-1,j,k),\,
F(i,j+1,k)+F(i,j-1,k)\}
-F(i,j,k-1).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
F(i,j,k+1)+F(i,j,k-1)
=
\max\{F(i+1,j,k)+F(i-1,j,k),\,
F(i,j+1,k)+F(i,j-1,k)\}.
\]
Iterating these local moves transports the data from one stepped surface to
another.  In the hive setting this transport is the
Knutson--Tao--Woodward/Speyer piecewise-linear, volume-preserving bijection
between the two hive decompositions corresponding to associativity
\cite{KTW,Speyer,NarSheffTao}; we denote it by \(\oct\).

For the applications below, Proposition~\ref{gt-rem}(iv) first lets us regard
Gelfand--Tsetlin patterns as hives with one large-gap side.  With this
identification, \(\oct\) sends a pair of Gelfand--Tsetlin patterns, equivalently
a double hive, to an augmented hive, or to a pair of hives glued along their
common boundary.  Throughout the paper \(h_n\) denotes the hive component of
this image when the input is the deformed GUE double hive.
title: Octahedron recurrence

body:
[Definition 8 of arXiv:2603.24616, 'Pinning in non-critical half-space geometric last passage percolation'] Let $\Sigma \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ and $\Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval. A {\em $\Sigma$-indexed line ensemble $\mathcal{L}$} is a random variable defined on a probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ that takes values in $\left(C (\Sigma \times \Lambda), \mathcal{C}_{\Sigma}\right)$. Intuitively, $\mathcal{L}$ is a collection of random continuous curves (sometimes referred to as {\em lines}), indexed by $\Sigma$, each of which maps $\Lambda$ into $\mathbb{R}$. We will often slightly abuse notation and write $\mathcal{L}: \Sigma \times \Lambda \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, even though it is not $\mathcal{L}$ which is such a function, but $\mathcal{L}(\omega)$ for every $\omega \in \Omega$. For $i \in \Sigma$, we write $\mathcal{L}_i(\omega) = (\mathcal{L}(\omega))(i, \cdot)$ for the curve of index $i$ and note that the latter is a map $\mathcal{L}_i: \Omega \rightarrow C(\Lambda)$, which is $\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{C}$ measurable. 

We say that a line ensemble $\mathcal{L}$ is {\em non-intersecting} if $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely $\mathcal{L}_i(t) > \mathcal{L}_j(t)$ for all $i < j$ and $t \in \Lambda$. We say that a line ensemble $\mathcal{L}$ is {\em ordered} if $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely $\mathcal{L}_i(t) \geq \mathcal{L}_j(t)$ for all $i < j$ and $t \in \Lambda$. If $[a,b] \subseteq \Lambda$, we let $\mathcal{L}_i[a,b]$ denote the restriction of $\mathcal{L}_i$ to $[a,b]$, and note that the latter is a measurable map $\mathcal{L}_i[a,b]: \Omega \rightarrow C([a,b])$. If $\Sigma_1 \subseteq \Sigma$ and $[a,b] \subseteq \Lambda$, we let $\mathcal{L}\vert_{\Sigma_1 \times [a,b]}$ denote the restriction of $\mathcal{L}$ to $\Sigma_1 \times [a,b]$, which is a measurable map $\mathcal{L}\vert_{\Sigma_1 \times [a,b]}: \Omega \rightarrow C(\Sigma_1 \times [a,b])$.
title: Definition 8 of arXiv:2603.24616

body: [Theorem theo:roel of arXiv:2603.21634, 'Individual-based stochastic model with unbounded growth, birth and death rates: a tightnes'] Let $T \geq 0$, $\left(P^{K}\right)_{K \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of probability measures on $\mathbb{D}([0,T],(\mathcal{M}_{\omega}(\mathbb{R}^{*}_{+}),v))$, and $D$ be a dense countable subset of $\mathcal{C}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{*}_{+})$ for the topology of uniform convergence. Assume that for all $f \in D \cup \{ \omega\}$, $\left(\pi_{f}*P^{K}\right)_{K \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a tight sequence of probability measures on $\mathbb{D}([0,T],\mathbb{R})$, where $\pi_{f} * P^{K}$ is the usual pushforward of $P^{K}$ by $\pi_{f}$. Then $\left(P^{K}\right)_{K \in \mathbb{N}}$ is tight on $\mathbb{D}([0,T],(\mathcal{M}_{\omega}(\mathbb{R}^{*}_{+}),v))$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma lem:regularized_solutions of arXiv:2609.01984, 'Instantaneous shrinking of supports for stochastic PDEs\footnote{JY was supported by a KIA'] For each $n\ge1$, equation (equation eq:regularized-measure-equation of the paper) has a unique
nonnegative solution $u_n$. Moreover, for every bounded stopping time
$\tau\le T$, every $p\ge2$, and every $\kappa\in(0,1/2)$,
\[
    u_n\in\mathcal H_p^{1/2-\kappa}(\tau).
\]
In addition, if $(1-2\kappa)p>6$ and
\[
    \frac1p<\mathbb{a}<\mathbb{b}<
    \frac14-\frac{\kappa}{2}-\frac1{2p},
\]
then
\[
    u_n\in
    C^{\mathbb{a} -1/p}
    \bigl([0,\tau];C^{1/2-\kappa-2\mathbb{b}-1/p}(\mathbb{R})\bigr)
    \qquad\text{a.s.}
\]
Furthermore, for every $\rho>0$, there exists $N_n= N(\nu,\kappa,p, \mathbb{a}, \mathbb{b}, \mathbb{c}_1 ,T, n)$ such that 
\begin{equation}

    \mathbb{E}
    \left\|
        u_n\zeta_{\rho/p}
    \right\|_{C^{\mathbb{a} -1/p}
    ([0,\tau];C^{1/2-\kappa-2\mathbb{b} -1/p})}^p
    \le
    N_n+
    N_n\|\mu_0\zeta_{\rho/p}\|_{U_p^{1/2-\kappa}}^p.
\end{equation} Consequently,
\begin{equation}

    \mathbb{E}
    \left[
        \sup_{t\le\tau,\ x\in\mathbb{R}}
        u_n(t,x)^p e^{-\rho|x|}
    \right]
    \le N_n.
\end{equation}

body:
[Definition def:qualify of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] Let $z\in\mathcal Z_i$ and write $\pi_z(s)=z+\gamma_{s-\tau\beta}$ for the reference path issued
from $z$. Throughout this definition $X_v$ and $\mathcal R_v$ denote the trajectory and the
recovery marks of $v$ in the configuration $\omega$ of (sec:graphical of the paper), before the
substitution of (sec:auxpath of the paper). Only $\pi_z$ and $\mathcal A^{(i,\tau)}_{\to v}$ are auxiliary
objects of the cell. The set $\Upsilon_z$ defined below is thus a functional of $\omega$ and of
the auxiliary objects of $(i,\tau)$ alone, and the two are independent. A particle $v$
\emph{qualifies at $t_j$}, $j\in\mathcal J'$, if
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $|\pi_z(t_j)-X_v(t_j)|\le r/2$;
\item $v$ displaces by at most $r/4$ during $[t_j,t_j+\mathfrak d]$; and
\item $\mathcal A^{(i,\tau)}_{\to v}$ has a mark in $[t_j,t_j+\mathfrak d]$.
\end{enumerate}
It \emph{qualifies freshly at $t_j$} if in addition $|\pi_z(t_k)-X_v(t_k)|>r/2$ for every
$k\in\mathcal J'$ with $k>j$. We let $\Upsilon_z$ be the set of particles which qualify freshly at
some $j\in\mathcal J'$, carry no recovery mark during $[\tau\beta,\tau\beta+T_L]$, and remain in
the reduced super-cube $Q^{*}_-(i)$ throughout $[\tau\beta,\tau\beta+T_L]$.
title: Qualifying proximity to a reference path

body: [Thm 2 (Unique ergodicity) of arXiv:2606.27035, 'R\'emy's diffusion on Brownian trees'] Let $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}^{\, \bullet}$ be any rooted real tree equipped with a mass measure with total mass $1$ and a marked point different from the root. Let $B$ be an independent Brownian motion. Then $\frac{1}{ \sqrt{1+t}} \cdot \Psi(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}^{\, \bullet}, B)_t$ converges in distribution towards $ \boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}_{2\mathbb{e}}^{\, \bullet} = (\mathcal{T}_{2 \mathbb{e}}, X)$ as $t\to\infty$ in the marked Gromov--Hausdorff--Prokhorov topology. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
