[Theorem thm:nogradient of arXiv:2510.22778, 'Free denoising diffusion models'] Let $f\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R})$ with $f>0$. Suppose the spectral flow of (equation eq:opsde of the paper) is, for
every initial law, the $m$-mobility Wasserstein gradient flow of an energy
\[
  E[\mu]=\int W\,\mathrm{d}\mu+\tfrac12\iint K(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x)\mathrm{d}\mu(y),
  \qquad K\ \text{symmetric and }C^{2}\ \text{off the diagonal},
\]
with a continuous mobility $m>0$, that is
$\partial_{t}\mu+\partial_{x}\big(\mu\,m\,\partial_{x}\tfrac{\delta E}{\delta\mu}\big)^{-}=0$
reproduces (equation eq:opvelocity of the paper). Then $m$ and $f$ are both constant. In particular,
for non-constant $f$ the flow is not a Wasserstein gradient flow of
any such energy, and the convexity method of Section~(sec:inequalities of the paper) does not
apply.

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.02711, 'Differentiability of the Leading Lyapunov Exponent \\ of a linear differential equation...'] The study of evolution in temporally fluctuating environments often relies on the analysis of Lyapunov exponents, which quantify the exponential growth of populations. However, when model parameters depend on a stochastic process, calculating the selection gradient—a key tool for predicting the evolution of phenotypic traits—becomes a mathematical challenge. While the periodic case has been resolved, a general approach for random environments remains to be developed. This article proposes a rigorous method to: \begin{enumerate} \item Establish the differentiability of the leading Lyapunov exponent $\Lambda(z)$ with respect to a parameter $z$, providing an explicit integral formula for its derivative $\Lambda'(z)$. \item Develop a numerical algorithm to compute $\Lambda'(z)$ by solving an extended differential equation. \item Apply these results to the analysis of mutant invasion in a resident population at equilibrium, identifying the selection gradient as the derivative $\Lambda'(z)$. \end{enumerate} \footnote{\today}

[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2608.19179, 'A random walk on $p$-groups with a symmetric perfect pairing'] Suppose $M$ is symmetric and non-singular. Then $\Delta_S$ satisfies
   \[
   \Delta_S \Big[ \Ker(M) \Big]=
   \Ker 
   \begin{mat}{ccc|c}
   & & & *\\
   & M& &\vdots\\
   & & & *\\ \hline
   * & \hdots & * & *
   \end{mat} \hspace{1in} \text{ for all } \, M
   \]
   where the entries denoted by $*$ are uniformly random variables, that are independent, subject to the symmetry condition. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Attempt to derive g_alpha from the PWIT recursive distributional equation for the resolvent at z, then differentiate in z. Result: The density is g_alpha(r) = (1/2pi) Delta_z of the log-potential U(z) = -integral log|z-w| dmu_alpha(w), and U is expressed through the limit of the singular-value law of the shifted operator on the PWIT, whose Stieltjes transform satisfies a fixed-point equation in a 2x2 matrix-valued function with alpha-stable-type nonlinearity (as in Bordenave-Caputo-Chafai). The z-dependence enters only through the off-diagonal entries; at z = 0 the equation closes on a single positive stable random variable, which is why g_alpha(0) is explicit. For z not 0 the fixed point involves a two-parameter family of stable laws (radial and angular parts), and I could not reduce it to a scalar equation; the isotropy only removes the angular variable of z, not of the recursion. Tail check: the stated tail r^{2(alpha-1)} e^{-alpha r^alpha/2} is consistent with the expected behaviour that eigenvalues of modulus r come from rows with an exceptionally large entry of size r^alpha, whose density in the stable domain is r^{-alpha-1} ... the exponential factor indicates instead a large-deviation of a sum of alpha-stable variables of the Poisson-Dirichlet type. No closed form. Obstruction: The matrix-valued PWIT fixed point does not reduce to a scalar equation away from z = 0.

body: [Defn 7 of arXiv:2608.12804, 'Scaling Limits for Ising Models on Inhomogeneous Random Graphs and Applications'] Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a Polish space and $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal S)$ denote the set of all probability measures on the Borel $\sigma$-field on $\mathcal S$, equipped with the topology $\Gamma$ of weak convergence. Let $\{\mu_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ be a family of $\mathcal P(\mathcal S)$-valued random probability measures defined on a common probability space $(\Omega,\mathscr{F},\P)$ (i.e. each $\mu_n$: $(\Omega,\mathscr{F}) \to (\mathcal P(\mathcal S), \mathcal{B}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal S),\Gamma\bigr))$ is a measurable function, where $\mathcal{B}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal S),\Gamma\bigr)$ denotes the Borel $\sigma$-field on $\mathcal P(\mathcal{S})$ generated by $\Gamma$). We say that $\mu_n$ converges weakly in probability to a measure $\mu \in  \mathcal P(\mathcal S)$, if for all $U \in \Gamma$ containing $\mu$, we have $$\P(\mu_n \in U) \rightarrow 1.$$

body:
Let f be a C^1 diffeomorphism of a compact Riemannian manifold M and mu an f-invariant Borel probability measure. Since M is compact, log of the norm of Df and of Df^{-1} are bounded, hence integrable, so Oseledets' multiplicative ergodic theorem applies: for mu-a.e. x there are finitely many numbers lambda_1(x) > lambda_2(x) > ... > lambda_{k(x)}(x) (the LYAPUNOV EXPONENTS at x) and a Df-invariant splitting of the tangent space

  T_x M = E_1(x) + ... + E_{k(x)}(x),   Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(f x),

such that for every nonzero v in E_i(x) the limit of (1/n) log |Df^n_x v| as n -> +-infinity exists and equals lambda_i(x). The functions x -> lambda_i(x) and the multiplicities dim E_i(x) are measurable and f-invariant, and if mu is ergodic they are constant almost everywhere; the subspaces E_i(x) are measurable and Df-equivariant, Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(fx). The splitting is in general only MEASURABLE, not continuous, and the convergence is not uniform in x.

Two structural facts that every application uses. (1) TEMPEREDNESS: any measurable positive function that is subexponential along orbits -- such as the angle between the Oseledets subspaces, or the norm of the change to Lyapunov (adapted) coordinates -- can be chosen tempered, meaning (1/n) log of its value at f^n x tends to 0; this is what lets one build Lyapunov charts in which Df is uniformly contracting on the negative-exponent bundle at the cost of a chart size that shrinks subexponentially along the orbit. (2) PESIN BLOCKS: for each l one collects the points where the Oseledets estimates hold with uniform constants depending on l; the resulting sets Lambda_l are COMPACT (after discarding a null set and restricting the subbundles continuously), increase in l, exhaust a full-measure set, and carry uniform hyperbolic-like estimates. They are NOT f-invariant -- an orbit wanders between blocks -- which is exactly why non-uniformly hyperbolic statements are local-and-measurable rather than uniform.

A point x is called (non-uniformly) hyperbolic when no exponent at x is zero; the stable bundle E^s(x) is the sum of the E_i(x) with lambda_i(x) < 0 and the unstable bundle the sum of those with lambda_i(x) > 0. Zero exponents are the obstruction: nothing in this framework says anything about directions with zero exponent.
M is a compact Riemannian manifold and f a C^1 diffeomorphism of M
mu is an f-invariant Borel probability measure (compactness makes the Oseledets integrability condition automatic)
the exponents and multiplicities are measurable and f-invariant, constant a.e. when mu is ergodic; the subspaces are measurable and Df-equivariant
the Oseledets splitting is measurable, generally not continuous, and the Pesin blocks are not invariant

body:
The gcd of two positive integers a >= b is computed by repeated division: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), terminating when the remainder is 0, at which point the last nonzero remainder is gcd(a, b). Running the steps backward (the extended Euclidean algorithm) produces integers x, y with ax + by = gcd(a, b) (Bezout coefficients). It runs in O(log min(a,b)) division steps.
a, b positive integers

If the number of tests plus the mean-zero condition is less than2^m, a nonzero f exists in their common nullspace. Rescale it to supnorm1. Then the process passes every supplied test but E[X_(m+1)|F_m]=f(Y) is nonzero. Check: The witness T*=m+1 on{f(Y)>0} and m otherwise is a stopping time and has E X_T*=E f_+>0. Predetermined test rules are functions of the revealed-bit history; their final-time continuation indicators do not depend on the unknown terminal value. The construction does not claim f or T* is computationally efficient. Obstruction: A polynomial number of linear tests alone cannot reproduce the full martingale property. Selecting a useful computational subclass requires an explicit representation, complexity bound and error tolerance; the nullspace construction does not supply that theory.

Own-work draft, C007 version 2, proof (unaudited); priority not established. For every m>=1 and 0<eta<=1, consider the depth-three mean-field model h_i=sigma(w_i x), z_j=m^(-1)sum_i B_ji h_i, f=m^(-1)sum_j a_j sigma(z_j), with sigma(z)=z/[4(1+z^2)]. Data have x=1 and y Bernoulli(1/2). Every w_i,a_j,B_ji is initially 1/4; these point-mass random variables are independent iid within each array and independent between arrays and runs. Train all layers by one simultaneous half-squared-loss SGD step, with learning-rate multipliers m on a,w and m^2 on B, using independently sampled labels in the two runs. Let L(theta)=E[(f_theta-y)^2/2]. For any compatible permutation P define H_m=sup_{0<=t<=1}[L((1-t)theta^A+tP theta^B)-(1-t)L(theta^A)-tL(theta^B)]_+. Then E inf_P H_m>=eta^2/160000000. All arrays remain constant within a run, so every permutation fixes the endpoints. The width-independent scalar reduction F=a sigma(b sigma(w)) has f0=17/18500 and grad F=(78625,78591,69345)/21390625 at (1/4,1/4,1/4). Along the sampled-update segment, its population risk has second derivative <=-1/10000000; independent labels differ with probability 1/2, giving the bound. The activation and its first two derivatives are globally bounded by 1. This rules out a universal width-only replacement for independent SGD noise in this finite-horizon class. A positive excess above the larger endpoint loss, a prescribed nondegenerate initialization, or low-risk converged endpoints is not established.

[Proposition 2 (Ideal-completion extension) of arXiv:2608.25925, '\textbf{Jump Closure and Limit Uniformization\\in the Ideal Completion of the Turing Degre'] Let $P$ be a poset and let $f:P\to P$ be monotone. Define
\[
\widehat f:\Idl(P)\to\Idl(P)
\]
by
\begin{equation}
\widehat f(I)
=\down f[I]
=\{y\in P:\exists x\in I\ (y\leq f(x))\}.

\end{equation}
Then $\widehat f$ is well defined and Scott-continuous. Moreover,
\begin{equation}
\widehat f(\down x)=\down f(x)

\end{equation}
for every $x\in P$.

Let f be in L^1_loc(R^d). Then for Lebesgue-almost every x, (1/|B(x,r)|) integral_{B(x,r)} |f(y) - f(x)| dy -> 0 as r -> 0; such an x is called a Lebesgue point of f. In particular the averages of f over shrinking balls converge to f(x) for a.e. x. The result persists if balls are replaced by any family of sets U_r shrinking NICELY to x, meaning U_r is contained in B(x,r) and |U_r| >= c |B(x,r)| for a fixed c > 0 (cubes centred at x, for instance). It FAILS for families of arbitrary eccentricity: in R^2 there is an integrable f whose averages over rectangles centred at x with sides parallel to the axes and both side lengths tending to 0 fail to converge at almost every x, because the strong maximal function is not of weak type (1,1). The a.e. exceptional set genuinely depends on f and cannot be taken empty. [standard; e.g. Stein and Shakarchi, Real Analysis, Chapter 3, Corollary 1.5 and Section 1.4]

body: [Theorem 18 (Morse transfer from induced subcomplexes) of arXiv:2609.01882, '\textbf{Coxeter Descents and Parabolic Homotopy Colimits}\\[2mm] \large A Hochster-type de'] For each $D\subseteq S$, the unit matchings in Lemmas~\ref{lem:conereduction} and \ref{lem:descentclosure} give an explicit algebraic Morse reduction of the $D$-relative pair to the suspended augmented chains of $\sd\mathcal K_D$. Consequently any unit acyclic matching on $\sd\mathcal K_D$ may be applied as a second algebraic Morse reduction, shifted one degree upward. If $\mathcal K_D\ne\{\varnothing\}$ and the chosen matching has a critical vertex, the augmentation generator can be cancelled with the suspension of one such vertex; the remaining critical generators represent the shifted reduced Morse complex of $\sd\mathcal K_D$.

[Lemma modifiedEP9.6 of arXiv:2506.10448, 'Hitting probabilities and the Ekstr\"om--Persson conjecture'] Let $\mu$ and $\theta$ be probability measures on a separable metric space $X$, let 
$(V_k)_{k=1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of Borel subsets of $X$ such that $0<\mu(V_k)<1$ for
every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $\underline r$ be a sequence of positive numbers tending to $0$.
Suppose that there exists a number $s>0$ such that 
\begin{equation}
f_{\theta}(\underline{\rho})=s_2(\underline{\rho})
\end{equation}
for every sequence $\underline{\rho}=(\rho_k)_{k=1}^\infty$ of radii with 
$s_2(\underline{\rho})\leq s$. Assume also that
there exists a constant $C$ such that, for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and every $x\in \spt \theta$,
\[
\theta(B(x,2r_k))\leq C\mu_{V_k}(B(x,r_k))
\] 
where $\mu_{V_k}:=\mu(V_k)^{-1}\mu_{|_{V_k}}$.
If there exists $t\in\mathopen]0,s\mathclose[$ such that 
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\mu(V_k)r_k^t=\infty,
\]

[Proposition Bounded-regularizer transfer below the
\texorpdfstring{\(\psi_1\)}{psi1} scale of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:weibull-exact-transfer}
Fix any \(L>0\).  Assume the hypotheses on the disorder array and \(V\)
from (thm:weibull-bulk of the paper), and assume
that \(\widehat{\mathscr C}_{N,L}^J(V)\) is finite and positive for all
sufficiently large \(N\).  Put
\(\Phi=\Phi_p^{\rm bulk}(V)\) and
\[
 \widehat P^{\,c}_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta,R)
 =
 \frac1N\log
 \mathbb E\widehat\mathcal Z_{N,L}^J(V,\varepsilon,f_{\eta,R})
\]
and define
\begin{align*}
 \delta_{L,\mathrm{dr},c}^{J,\mathrm{up}}(V)
 &:=
 \liminf_{R\to\infty}\liminf_{\eta\downarrow0}
 \liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\limsup_N
 [\widehat Q_{N,L}-\widehat P^{\,c}_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta,R)]_+,\\
 \delta_{L,\mathrm{dr},c}^{J,\mathrm{low}}(V)
 &:=
 \liminf_{R\to\infty}\liminf_{\eta\downarrow0}
 \liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\limsup_N
 [\widehat P^{\,c}_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta,R)-\widehat Q_{N,L}]_+.
\end{align*}
Then every conclusion of (thm:conditional-transfer of the paper) holds with
the two uncut defects replaced by these cutoff defects.  In particular,
if both vanish, the exact max identities
(equation eq:exact-upper-defect-formula of the paper)--(equation eq:exact-lower-defect-formula of the paper)
and the necessary-and-sufficient criterion
(equation eq:exact-universality-iff-localized-defect of the paper) remain valid.
This proposition preserves the Weibull transfer route but makes no
uncut determinant or remote-tail claim.

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Hub paths and the largest component of the barely subcritical configuration model (2026). For the configuration model with a degree sequence whose third moment converges, write eps_n = 1 - nu_n with nu_n = sum d_i(d_i - 1)/sum d_i tending to one from below. In his Saint-Flour notes (Open Problem 4.13) van der Hofstad asked to show that in the barely subcritical regime (eps_n -> 0, n eps_n^3 -> infinity) the largest component has order max{d_max/eps_n, eps_n^(-2) log(n eps_n^3)}, and predicted size (d_max/eps_n)(1 + o_P(1)) when eps_n tends to zero slowly enough. The paper shows neither holds in this generality. The degree sequences have vertices of degree one and three and a polynomial number of hubs of a large common degree d that contribute nothing to the third moment in the limit; paths of K hubs joined by direct edges appear, and the component of such a path is a tree with about K d/eps_n vertices. For K = 2, L_1 >= (2 - eta) d_max/eps_n with high probability; for K growing like sqrt(log n), L_1 >= c sqrt(log n) max{d_max/eps_n, eps_n^(-2) log(n eps_n^3)}. The order of L_1 in these examples is not determined. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/hub-paths-barely-subcritical (commit 444515b247a0). Not refereed.
title: Hub paths and the largest component of the barely subcritical configuration model: counterexamples to van der Hofstad's Open Problem 4.13 prediction (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/hub-paths-barely-subcritical)

body:
[Proposition 7 (Fixed-time regularity of functionals of the decoupled flow) of arXiv:2605.03057, 'Uniform-in-time quantitative fluctuations of large scale interacting particle systems'] Let Assumption \ref{ass:flow-smothness} hold. Let $ \varphi \in C_b^7\left( \R^d \right) $.
For $ t \ge 0 $, $ x \in \R^d $, and $ \mu \in \Ptwo $, let $ X_t^{x,\mu} $ be the decoupled flow
associated with the McKean--Vlasov equation, and define
\begin{equation*}
u_t\left( x,\mu \right) = \E\left( \varphi\left( X_t^{x,\mu} \right) \right).
\end{equation*}
Then, for every fixed $ t \ge 0 $, all multi-indices $ \gamma $ and $ \beta $, and
  every integer $ n \ge 0 $ with $1 \le \abs{\gamma} + \abs{\beta} + n
  \le 7$, the mixed derivative
\begin{equation*}
\partial_x^\gamma \partial_v^\beta \partial_\mu^n
u_t\left( x,\mu \right)\left( v_1,\dots,v_n \right)
\end{equation*}
exists and is continuous in $\left( x,\mu,v_1,\dots,v_n \right)$. More precisely, every such derivative is a finite sum of terms of the form
\begin{equation}

\E\left(
\nabla^r \varphi\left( X_t^{x,\mu} \right)
\left[
\partial_x^{\gamma_1} \partial_v^{\beta_1}\partial_\mu^{n_1}
X_t^{x,\mu}\left( \mathbf{v}_1 \right),\dots,
\partial_x^{\gamma_r} \partial_v^{\beta_r}\partial_\mu^{n_r}
X_t^{x,\mu}\left( \mathbf{v}_r \right)
\right]
\right),
\end{equation}
where $ 1 \le r \le 7 $, for each $1 \leq j \leq r$, $\mathbf{v}_j$
denotes an $n_j$-tuple of Lions directions, and each
$\partial_x^{\gamma_j} \partial_v^{\beta_j}\partial_\mu^{n_j}
X_t^{x,\mu}\left( \mathbf{v}_j \right)$
is a mixed derivative of the flow of positive total order $1 \le \abs{\gamma_j} + \abs{\beta_j} + n_j
  \le 7$.

body:
[Theorem 1 (\textsf{Dominant chaos with lower-order perturbations}) of arXiv:2608.12451, '2608.12451'] Fix $\mathsf{S}\in\{{ \mathsf{P}},{\mathsf{R}}\}$, $r\in\N$, and
$\lambda\in(0,\infty)$.  For each $n\in\N$, let\footnote{The sum $\sum_{j=1}^0$ is understood to be empty.}

\noi
\begin{align*}
 F_n\in\cC_{r}^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP),
 \quad
 B_n=\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}B_{n,j},
\AND
 B_{n,j}\in\cC_{j}^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP).
\end{align*} 

\noi
Suppose that $F_n+B_n$ satisfies the lattice condition
\eqref{cond_La} with shift $\theta_n>0$, and define
$X_n:=\theta_n+F_n+B_n$.  Put
$\eps_n:=\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}\norm{B_{n,j}}_4$.
For every $n$ such that $\theta_n>0$, with
$c_{\theta_n}:=(1-e^{-\theta_n})/\theta_n$, define

\noi
\begin{align}
 \mathfrak{R}_{\theta_n}(F_n,\eps_n)
 :=
 c_{\theta_n}\bigg[ 2 \|F_n\|_4\eps_n+\eps_n^2+\frac{\eps_n}{2}
 + 14\bigl(1+ \|F_n\|_4+\eps_n\bigr)^3\eps_n  \bigg]
 +\left(1+\frac{c_{\theta_n}}2\right)\eps_n.
 
\end{align}
Then,

\noi
\begin{align} 
\begin{aligned}
 \dTV\bigl( X_n,  P_{\theta_n}\bigr)  
   & \leq
 c_{\theta_n}\bigg[  | m_2(F_n)-\theta_n|  + \frac{2r-1}{2r}\sqrt{\mathfrak{d}_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)} \\
 &\qquad\qquad\qquad  + \frac23\sqrt{m_2(F_n)\mathfrak d_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)}
 +b_{\mathsf{S}}\mathfrak d_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)  \bigg]  
   +\mathfrak R_{\theta_n}(F_n,\eps_n).
\end{aligned}
\end{align}

\noi
In particular, $\mathfrak R_{\theta_n}(F_n,0)=0$.  Hence, when
$\eps_n=0$, one has $B_n=0$ and \eqref{pert_main_bdd} reduces exactly
to Corollary~\ref{cor_P_quant} if $\mathsf{S}={ \mathsf{P}}$ and to
Corollary~\ref{cor_R_quant} if $\mathsf{S}={\mathsf{R}}$.

If, in addition,
$
 \big(\theta_n,  m_2(F_n), \mathfrak{d}_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)\big)
 \xrightarrow{n\to+\infty}(\lambda, \lambda, 0)$
and
 $\eps_n\to0$,
then
$\dTV(X_n, P_\lambda)\to0$,
the first four moments of $X_n$ converge to those of
$P_\lambda$, and $(X_n^4)_{n\geq1}$ is uniformly integrable.
In the Rademacher case, under $m_2(F_n)\to\lambda$, the condition
$\mathfrak{d}_{\mathsf{R}}(F_n)\to0$ is equivalent to
$\cR(F_n)\to0$ and $\cM(F_n)\to0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \textsf{Dominant chaos with lower-order perturbations}

[Definition 23 of arXiv:2609.02850, 'Canonical-row Chern flow on Bott--Samelson towers:\\ realizable-volume models for Schubert'] Let $\mathbf i=(i_1,\ldots,i_\ell)$ be a word in
$\{1,\ldots,n-1\}$, let
$\epsilon=(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_\ell)\in\{0,1\}^\ell$, and let
$\mathbf d=(d_1,\ldots,d_n)\in\NN^n$.  For $1\le j\le n$, put
\begin{equation}
 T_j=\{0\}\cup\{t\in[\ell]:i_t=j\},
 \qquad
 \tau_j(t)=\max\bigl(T_j\cap\{0,1,\ldots,t\}\bigr),
 \qquad
 \lambda_j=\tau_j(\ell).
\end{equation}
The vertex $v_{j,r}$, for $r\in T_j$, is the rank-$j$ state created at
time $r$; in particular, $v_{j,0}$ is the initial state.  At stage $t$ the
current rank-$j$ state is $v_{j,\tau_j(t)}$.  There is deliberately no
separate vertex for a passive pullback at a time not belonging to $T_j$.

The rooted directed multigraph
$\mathfrak C(\mathbf i,\epsilon,\mathbf d)$ has vertex set
\[
 \{0\}\sqcup\{v_{j,r}:1\le j\le n,\ r\in T_j\}.
\]
For every $t$ with $\epsilon_t=1$, it has one ordinary edge
\begin{equation}
 e_t:v_{i_t,t}\longrightarrow
 v_{i_t+1,\tau_{i_t+1}(t-1)}.
\end{equation}
For every $j$ it has $d_j$ root edges
\begin{equation}
 e_{j,a}:0\longrightarrow v_{j,\lambda_j}
 \qquad(1\le a\le d_j).
\end{equation}
Degrees are counted with edge multiplicity.
title: Definition 23 of arXiv:2609.02850

body:
[Theorem thm:CO of arXiv:2601.09976, 'Stochastic Calculus as Operator Factorization:\\ An Operator--Covariant Derivative and Uni'] Let $X$ be a square-integrable process with natural filtration $(\mathcal{F}_t^X)_{t \in [0,T]}$, energy space~$\mathcal{H}_X$, stochastic integral~$\delta_X$, predictable projection~$\Pi_X$, and operator--covariant derivative $D_X = \delta_X^*$. Assume:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \textup{Centered integrals:} $\mathbb{E}[\delta_X(u)] = 0$ for all $u \in \mathcal{H}_X$.
\item \textup{Isometry on predictable processes:} $\mathbb{E}[|\delta_X(u)|^2] = \|u\|_{\mathcal{H}_X}^2$ for predictable $u \in \mathcal{H}_X$.
\item \textup{Representation property:} Every $\mathcal{F}_T^X$-measurable $\tilde{F} \in L^2(\Omega)$ with $\mathbb{E}[\tilde{F}] = 0$ can be written as $\tilde{F} = \delta_X(v)$ for some predictable $v \in \mathcal{H}_X$.
\end{enumerate}
Then for all $\mathcal{F}_T^X$-measurable $F \in L^2(\Omega)$:
\begin{equation}
F \;=\; \mathbb{E}[F] + \delta_X(\Pi_X D_X F) \;=\; \mathbb{E}[F] + \int_0^T (\Pi_X D_X F)_t\, dX_t.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the operator identity $(\mathrm{Id} - \mathbb{E}) = \delta_X \circ \Pi_X \circ D_X$ holds on $L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_T^X, P)$.

[Lem 85 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] Assume that~\eqref{eq:traces-fast} holds, and let $\pi$ be a separable unital representation of $\A$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[a.] If $\phi:\A\to\rmM_k$ is approximately associated to $\l^{\oplus \infty}$, and $O$ is a neighbourhood of $\phi$ in $\B(\A,\rmM_k)_+$, then
\[\bbP(\X(\pi_n,O) \ne \emptyset) \to 1.\]
If $\pi \lesssim_{\rm{a}} \l^{\oplus \infty}$, then $\rmh_{\bspi}^0(\pi) = \ul{\rmh}_{\bspi}^0(\pi) = 0$.
\item[b.] In general, let $\pi^M$ be the subrepresentation such that $\pi^M \lesssim \l^{\oplus \infty}$ and $\pi^{M^\perp} \spoon \l$ (see Proposition~\ref{prop:Leb-reps}).  Then $\rmh_{\bspi}^0(\pi) = \rmh_{\bspi}^0(\pi^{M^\perp})$ and $\ul{\rmh}_{\bspi}^0(\pi) = \ul{\rmh}_{\bspi}^0(\pi^{M^\perp})$.
\end{enumerate}

For any two probability distributions P and Q on the same discrete finite or countable set X, with pmfs p and q, the Kullback-Leibler divergence satisfies D(P||Q) = sum_{x} p(x) * log(p(x)/q(x)) >= 0, with equality if and only if p(x) = q(x) for every x, i.e. P = Q. This fact is also known as Gibbs' inequality.

[Theorem 1 (Sufficient Maximum Principle) of arXiv:2604.00937, 'Infinite Horizon Optimal Control of Forward-Backward Stochastic Volterra Equations with De'] Let $\hat{u} \in \mathcal{U}$ with corresponding solutions $\hat{X}(t)$, $(\hat{Y}(t), \hat{Z}(t,\cdot), \hat{K}(t,\cdot,\cdot))$, $(\hat{p}(t), \hat{q}(t,\cdot), \hat{r}(t,\cdot,\cdot))$ and $\hat{\lambda}(t)$ of equations (\ref{b1}), (\ref{b2}), (\ref{eq3.2}) and (\ref{p}) respectively. Suppose that:

\begin{description}
\item[Concavity] The function $x \mapsto h(x)$ and the Hamiltonian
\[
(x,x_1,y,z,k(\cdot),u) \mapsto H(t,x,x_1,y,z,k,u,\hat{\lambda}(t),\hat{p}(t),\hat{q}(t,\cdot),\hat{r}(t,\cdot,\cdot))
\]
are concave for all $t \geq 0$.

\item[Conditional Maximum Principle]
\begin{align*}
& \max_{v \in \mathcal{U}} \mathbb{E}\left[ H(t,\hat{X}(t),\hat{X}_1(t),\hat{Y}(t),\hat{Z}(t,\cdot),\hat{K}(t,\cdot,\cdot),v,\hat{\lambda}(t),\hat{p}(t),\hat{q}(t,\cdot),\hat{r}(t,\cdot,\cdot)) \mid \mathcal{G}_t \right] \\
& = \mathbb{E}\left[ H(t,\hat{X}(t),\hat{X}_1(t),\hat{Y}(t),\hat{Z}(t,\cdot),\hat{K}(t,\cdot,\cdot),\hat{u},\hat{\lambda}(t),\hat{p}(t),\hat{q}(t,\cdot),\hat{r}(t,\cdot,\cdot)) \mid \mathcal{G}_t \right].
\end{align*}

\item[Transversality Conditions]
\[
\varlimsup_{T \to \infty} \mathbb{E}[\hat{\lambda}(T)(\hat{Y}(T) - Y(T))] \geq 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \varlimsup_{T \to \infty} \mathbb{E}[\hat{p}(T)(\hat{X}(T) - X(T))] \leq 0.
\]
\end{description}

Then, $\hat{u}$ is an optimal control for our problem.

Method: Test the linear bound on finite cyclic groups with non-commuting equivariant... note that on an abelian group all equivariant operators commute, so non-commuting examples need a non-abelian group; try S_3. Result: Observation that sharpens the question: on any abelian Gamma, equivariant operators are convolution operators and commute, so the linear bound is already known there; the first non-trivial case is a non-abelian finite group, e.g. S_3 acting on itself, where an equivariant Q is right-convolution by an element of the group algebra and two such operators commute iff their group-algebra elements do. d-bar on a finite group is the optimal coupling cost for the normalised Hamming distance under invariant couplings, which is an LP of size 2^6 x 2^6 = 4096 variables for S_3, feasible to compute exactly. I set up the test but did not run it in this batch (time); it is the concrete next experiment: sample Q, Q' as positive contractions in the group algebra of S_3 that do not commute, compute d-bar by the invariant-coupling LP and compare with ||Q - Q'||_1. [Corollary cor:sharp-angular-threshold of arXiv:2609.03264, 'Certified Spherical MUSIC for 3D Localization under Adversarial Subspace Perturbations'] Suppose
\[
    0<A_\gamma\leq1
\]
and that
\[
    q({\bm z})\geq A_\gamma,\qquad \forall {\bm z}\in B_1(0)\setminus\bigcup_{\ell=1}^s B_\rho(\bm{x}_\ell).
\]
Set
\[
    \alpha_\gamma:=\arcsin\sqrt{A_\gamma},
    \qquad
    \theta:=\arcsin\varepsilon_{\rm sub}.
\]
Let \[
    \tau_0:=\varepsilon_{\rm sub}^2
\]
and
\[
    \tau_1
    :=
    \sin^2\left(
        \left(
            \alpha_\gamma-\theta
        \right)_+
    \right).
\]
A strict threshold gap
\[
    \tau_0<\tau_1
\]
holds if and only if
\begin{equation}

\varepsilon_{\rm sub}
    <
    \sin\left(
        \frac12\arcsin\sqrt{A_\gamma}
    \right).
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}
 
   \varepsilon_{\rm sub} < \frac{\sqrt{1-\sqrt{1-A_\gamma}}}{\sqrt 2} .
\end{equation}

DRAFT checked counting reduction; integration referee for the newest fixed-length packet is pending. For nested forbidden edge sets A subset B, every length-n path avoiding A but using B has a unique first B edge(v,w), after k edges. Its prefix avoids B and its suffix avoids A with length n-k-1. Consequently its total count is at most sum over k=0,...,n-1 and oriented(v,w) in B minus A of c_k^B(0,v)*C_(n-k-1)^A(w). Unit edge weights are assumed; include the first-edge weight for a weighted version. Dropping mutual prefix/suffix avoidance increases the count and supplies no scale-uniform collar decay.

[Lemma 44 of arXiv:2608.27372, 'Universality and sharp thresholds for ellipsoid fitting'] Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\R$ with finite second moment,
	let $c>-1$, and let $\zeta\in\R$.  Define
	$$
	m_\mu(\omega):=\int(x-\omega)_+\,d\mu(x),
	\qquad
	s_\mu(\omega):=\int(x-\omega)_+^2\,d\mu(x).
	$$
	There is a unique solution $\omega$ of
	$\omega+\zeta=c\,m_\mu(\omega)$.  For this solution,
	$$
	\sup_{\substack{f\in L^2(\mu),\ f\ge0\\f\not\equiv0}}
	\frac{\left(\int(x+\zeta)f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right)_+^2}
	{\int f(x)^2\,d\mu(x)
		+c\left(\int f\,d\mu\right)^2}
	=
	s_\mu(\omega)+c\,m_\mu(\omega)^2.
	$$
	If the right-hand side is positive, the supremum is attained by every
	positive multiple of $f(x)=(x-\omega)_+$.

body:
[Prop 8 (Fourier transforms of radial homogeneous distributions) of arXiv:2609.01403, '2609.01403'] Under the normalization \eqref{eq:fourier-normalization}, the following
statements hold.

\begin{enumerate}

\item For \(0<\alpha<n\),
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal F^{-1}(|\xi|^{-\alpha})(x)
    =
    \kappa_{n,\alpha}|x|^{\alpha-n}.
    
\end{equation}
The family \(|\xi|^{-\alpha}\), initially defined as a tempered
distribution for \(\Re\alpha<n\), admits a meromorphic continuation
to \(\alpha\in\mathbb C\), with possible poles at
$\alpha=n,n+2,n+4,\cdots$.
The identity \eqref{eq:riesz-kernel-formula} extends accordingly by
meromorphic continuation. Away from the origin, this continuation is
represented by
$\kappa_{n,\alpha}|x|^{\alpha-n}$.
In particular, if \(\alpha=-2k\), \(k\in\mathbb N_0\), then
\[
    \mathcal F^{-1}(|\xi|^{-\alpha})
    =
    (-\Delta)^k\delta_0.
\]

\item Define
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
    \left\langle\operatorname{Fp}|\xi|^{-n},\varphi\right\rangle
    &=
    \int_{|\xi|<1}
    \frac{\varphi(\xi)-\varphi(0)}{|\xi|^n}\,\mathrm{d}\xi\\
    &\quad+
    \int_{|\xi|>1}
    \frac{\varphi(\xi)}{|\xi|^n}\,\mathrm{d}\xi,
    \qquad
    \varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
Then
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal F^{-1}
    \bigl(\operatorname{Fp}|\xi|^{-n}\bigr)
    =
    c_n\log\frac1{|x|}
    +
    c_n\left(
        \log2+\frac12\psi\!\left(\frac n2\right)
        -\frac{\gamma}{2}
    \right)
    \quad\text{in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n),
    
\end{equation}
where
\[
    c_n
    =
    \frac{2^{1-n}}{\pi^{n/2}\Gamma(n/2)},
\]
\(\gamma\) is Euler's constant, and
\(\psi=\Gamma'/\Gamma\).

\end{enumerate}

[Proposition 4 of arXiv:2506.10856, 'The space of multifurcating ranked tree shapes: enumeration, lattice structure, and Markov'] The number of multifurcating ranked tree shapes with $N$ tips and ordered vector $t$ of the string representation of size $K$ is 
\[\binom{N-2K_0(t) - K_1(t) + K-1}{K-1}.\] 
The number of multifurcating ranked tree shapes with $N$ tips and $K$ internal nodes is \[ G(N,K)= \sum_{\substack{t \in \mathbb{N}^K: \; t_1=0, \\ t_i \in [i-1] \text{ for } i=2,3,\ldots,K}} \binom{N-2K_0(t) - K_1(t) + K-1}{K-1} \] where $[i]=\{1,2,\ldots,i\}$.

[Lemma 10 (Log-Hessian bound under Gaussian smoothing) of arXiv:2607.25685, 'Mimicking diffusion processes with differential equations'] Let $q_0$ be a probability density with $-\beta I\preceq\nabla^2\log q_0\preceq-\alpha I$,
$0<\alpha\le\beta<\infty$, and $q:=q_0*\mathcal N(0,\varsigma^2I)$. Then
\[
  -\frac{\beta}{1+\beta\varsigma^2}I\preceq\nabla^2\log q\preceq-\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha\varsigma^2}I,
\]
so $\opnorm{\nabla^2\log q}\le\beta$ uniformly in $\varsigma>0$ and $|\Delta\log q|\le d\beta$.
title: Log-Hessian bound under Gaussian smoothing

[Prop examplestable of arXiv:2605.06488, 'Continuous-state branching processes with L\'evy-Khintchine drift-interaction: Laplace dua'] Assume $\negHone$, $\negHhattwo$, $\hatHone$  and $\Htwo$. Let $X^{\mathrm{e}\infty}$ and $Y^{\mathrm{e}0}$ be the extended $\mathrm{CBDI}s$ respectively at $\infty$ and $0$ with mechanisms $(\Psi,\hat\Psi)$ and $(\hat\Psi,\Psi)$ satisfying
\[\Phi(y)\underset{y\to 0}{\sim} cy^{\alpha} \text{ and } \hat\Sigma(x)\underset{x\to \infty}{\sim} \hat Cx^{\hat\beta+1},\]
with $c\in (0,\infty), \ \alpha\in (0,1)$ and $\hat C\in (0,\infty), \ \hat\beta\in (0,1)$.
      \begin{enumerate}
            \item If $\hat\beta<1-\alpha$, then $\underline{\theta}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\Phi,\hat{\Sigma}}=\infty$, $\overline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\hat\Sigma,\Phi}=0$, and 
        $X^{\mathrm{e}\infty}$ has $\infty$ exit, $Y^{\mathrm{e}0}$ has $0$ entrance.
            \item If $\hat\beta>1-\alpha$, then $\underline{\theta}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\Phi,\hat{\Sigma}}=0$, $\overline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\hat\Sigma,\Phi}=\infty$ and $X^{\mathrm{e}\infty}$ has $\infty$ entrance, $Y^{\mathrm{e}0}$ has $0$ exit.
            \item If $\hat\beta=1-\alpha$, then $\overline{\theta}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\Phi,\hat{\Sigma}}=\underline{\theta}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\Phi,\hat{\Sigma}}=\dfrac{c}{\hat{C}\Gamma(2-\alpha)}$ and $\overline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\hat\Sigma,\Phi}
=\underline{\varrho}_{\,\scriptscriptstyle\hat\Sigma,\Phi}=\dfrac{\hat{C}}{c\Gamma(\alpha)}$. Thus,
            \begin{itemize}
                \item if 
                $c/\hat C>\Gamma(2-\alpha)$, $X^{\mathrm{e}\infty}$ has $\infty$ exit, $Y^{\mathrm{e}0}$ has $0$ entrance,
                \item if $1/\Gamma(\alpha)<c/\hat C<\Gamma(2-\alpha)$, then $X^{\mathrm{e}\infty}$ and $Y^{\mathrm{e}0}$ have respectively $\infty$ and $0$ regular,
                \item if $c/\hat C<1/\Gamma(\alpha)$,  then $X^{\mathrm{e}\infty}$ has $\infty$ entrance, $Y^{\mathrm{e}0}$ has $0$ exit.
       
            \end{itemize}
        \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Definition def:shift-stable-chart of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix an integer $d\geq1$ and $0<\gamma<1$.  A \emph{shift-stable $d$-chart
of depth $\gamma h$} is a family
$(B_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta_h}$, indexed by all sufficiently large integers
$h$ with $\Theta_h\ne\varnothing$, of primitive
$(d+1)$-subsets of $\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$ containing zero for which there are
fixed integers $s\geq1$ and $c_1,\ldots,c_s$, and integer residuals
$x_\nu(\theta,h)$, such that, uniformly for $\theta\in\Theta_h$ and
$J\in\mathbb Z$ with $0\leq J\leq\gamma h$,
\begin{equation}
 |(h-J)B_\theta|
 =\sum_{\nu=1}^{s}c_\nu
  \binom{x_\nu(\theta,h)-J+d}{d},
 \qquad x_\nu(\theta,h)-J\geq0.
\end{equation}
Terms for which $x_\nu(\theta,h)-J<0$ throughout the shift window are
omitted.  This condition is satisfied, in particular, when the family
remains in one finite Hilbert-numerator chamber throughout the window.
Here $d=|B_\theta|-1$ is the dimension of the ambient simplex and the degree
of the binomial coefficient as a polynomial in its upper index; it is not
the dimension of the associated projective curve.
title: Shift-stable binomial chart

[Theo 9 of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] Let $d\ge 1$. 
Let $X=(X_i)_{i\in\Zd}$ be an i.i.d.\ $A$-valued random field, where $A$ is a standard Borel space, 
and let $Y=\varphi(X)$ for some finitary coding $\varphi:A^{\Zd}\to B^{\Zd}$. 
Assume the coding volume has a finite second moment, i.e.
\begin{equation}
\E\left[\,|B_\infty(0,r\!_\varphi(X))|^2\,\right] < \infty\,.

\end{equation}
Then, for every local and continuous $f:B^{\Zd}\to\R$ with the bounded-difference property,

\[
\log \E\big[\exp\{\lambda(f(Y)-\E f(Y))\}\big]
\;\le\;
2^{d}\lambda^2\, \E\big[ (2r\!_\varphi(X)+1)^{2d}\,\big]\,
\|\delta f\|_2^2\,,
\qquad \forall\, \lambda>0.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theo 9 of arXiv:2602.14618

For a finite connected U containing 0 in a uniformly elliptic nearest-neighbor environment, G_U(0,x)=h/(sum_e omega(x,e) r_e), where h is the probability of hitting x before exit (h=1 for x=0) and r_e is the probability of exit before hitting x from x+e, equal to 1 outside U. Conditioned off the outgoing row at x, h and r do not use that row. Consequently spatial iid permits single-site integration but does not make G_U(0,x) independent of omega(x,.). The auxiliary row is E[G_U(0,x)omega(x,e)]/E[G_U(0,x)].

body:
[Thm conformal invariance of Coulomb gas integral of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Let $\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sigma_i \cdot z_i + \sum_{j=1}^{m} \tau_j \cdot \xi_j$ be a divisor on the Riemann sphere $\hat{\mathbb{C}}$, where each screening charge $\tau_j \in \{-2a,\, 2(a + b)\}$ is chosen so that its conformal dimension satisfies $\lambda_b(\tau_j) = 1$. Let $h: \hat{\mathbb{C}} \to \hat{\mathbb{C}}$ be a Möbius transformation, and define
\[
\zeta_j := h(\xi_j), \quad h(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) := \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sigma_i \cdot h(z_i) + \sum_{j=1}^{m} \tau_j \cdot \zeta_j.
\]

Then the Coulomb gas integral transforms covariantly under $h$ as
\begin{equation} 
\left( \prod_{i=1}^{n} h'(z_i)^{\lambda_b(\sigma_i)} \right) 
\oint_{h(\Gamma)} C_{(b)}[h(\boldsymbol{\sigma})] \, d\zeta_1 \cdots d\zeta_m
=
\oint_{\Gamma} C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}] \, d\xi_1 \cdots d\xi_m,
\end{equation}
where $h(\Gamma)$ denotes the image of the integration contour $\Gamma$ under $h$.

Each differential $d\zeta_j$ transforms as $d\zeta_j = h'(\xi_j) \, d\xi_j$, and since $\lambda_b(\tau_j) = 1$, the integrand $C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]\, d\xi_1 \cdots d\xi_m$ is invariant under pullback by $h$, up to the multiplicative factor $\prod_{i} h'(z_i)^{\lambda_b(\sigma_i)}$ determined by the insertion points.
title: Conformal Invariance of the Coulomb Gas Integral

body: A function f: [a,b] -> R is absolutely continuous if for every epsilon > 0 there exists delta > 0 such that, for every finite collection of pairwise disjoint subintervals (a_1,b_1), ..., (a_k,b_k) of [a,b] with sum_{i=1}^k (b_i - a_i) < delta, we have sum_{i=1}^k |f(b_i) - f(a_i)| < epsilon. Every absolutely continuous function is uniformly continuous and of bounded variation, and f is absolutely continuous if and only if f is differentiable Lebesgue-almost everywhere, f' is Lebesgue integrable, and f(x) = f(a) + integral from a to x of f'(t) dt for every x in [a,b]. [standard, e.g. Royden and Fitzpatrick, Real Analysis]
title: Absolutely Continuous Function on a Real Interval

[Corollary 15 (Examples: pointwise macroscopic-loop bounds) of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Fix \(u\in[0,1]\) and \(\theta\in\mathbb N\) with \(\theta>1\).

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
    \item \textbf{Random regular graphs.}
    Let \(G_n\) be the random \(d\)-regular graph on \([n]\).
    If $d>2c_{\theta,u}$, then for every \(\delta>0\) there exist \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that for every $t\ge T_{\theta,u}(d)+\delta$, one has
    \[
    p_{d,n}\!\left(
    \Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Sparse Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi graphs.}
    Let \(G_n\sim G(n,\lambda/n)\). If $\lambda>2c_{\theta,u}$, then for every \(\delta>0\) there exist \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that for every $t\ge T_{\theta,u}(\lambda)+\delta$, one has
    \[
    \Pbb\!\left(
    \Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Simple bounded-degree configuration model.}
    Let \(G_n\) be the simple graph obtained from the configuration model with
    degree sequence \((d_i^{(n)})_{i=1}^n\). Assume that
    \[
    1\le d_i^{(n)}\le \Delta
    \qquad\text{for all }i,n,
    \]
    and $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^{(n)}\to \rho$. If $\rho>2c_{\theta,u}$,
    then for every \(\delta>0\) there exist \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that for every  $t\ge T_{\theta,u}(\rho)+\delta$,
    one has
    \[
    \Pbb\!\left(
    \Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Examples: pointwise macroscopic-loop bounds

[Theorem 38 of arXiv:2608.20252, '2608.20252'] There exists a semigroup $P_t$ on $\L$, which has specification $P_tf(\eta) = E^\eta[f(\eta_t)]$ for $f\in \L$ and finite configurations $\eta$ in terms of the countable-state process.

Moreover, for $\eta, \zeta\in \Omega'$ and $f\in \L$, the semigroup satisfies
$$\big|P_tf(\eta) - P_tf(\zeta)\big| \ \leq \ c(f)e^{4a_0t} \|\eta-\zeta\|$$
and $c(P_t f) \leq c(f)e^{4a_0t}$.
Also,
$$P_tf(\eta) \ = \ f(\eta) + \int_0^t LP_sf(\eta)ds.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 38 of arXiv:2608.20252

The obstruction is exactly the missing large-deviation-level Gaussian approximation. [Lemma coprod-well-based of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $G$ and ${\mathcal{F}}$ be as before. Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be a small collection of based $G$-spaces, such that for every $i\in I$ the object $X_i$ is well-based. Then the maps $X_j\to\bigvee_{i\in I}X_i$ exhibit $\bigvee_{i\in I}X_i$ as a coproduct in the underlying $\infty$-category. 

    Moreover, the analogous statement for orthogonal $G$-spaces holds.
    \begin{proof}
        We will prove the equivariant statement, the proof of the global one being analogous. 
        
        Pick for every $i\in I$ a cofibrant replacement $X'_i\to X_i$. The claim amounts to saying that the induced map $\bigvee_{i\in I}X_i'\to\bigvee_{i\in I}X_i$ is an ${\mathcal{F}}$-weak equivalence, which can be checked after forgetting the basepoint. The map in question is then the induced map on pushouts
        \[
            \begin{tikzcd}
                1\arrow[d,"="'] & \arrow[l] \coprod_{i\in I}1\arrow[d,"="{description}]\arrow[r] & \coprod_{i\in I} X_i'\arrow[d]\\
                1 &\arrow[l]\coprod_{i\in I} 1\arrow[r]& \coprod_{i\in I} X_i\rlap.
            \end{tikzcd}
        \]       
        By assumption the bottom right horizontal map is a coproduct of h-cofibrations, hence itself an h-cofibration; thus, the previous lemma shows that the pushout of the bottom row computes the homotopy pushout. Similarly, the pushout of the top row computes the homotopy pushout as the top right map is a cofibration. The claim follows as $\coprod_{i\in I}X_i'\to\coprod_{i\in I}X_i$ is an ${\mathcal{F}}$-weak equivalence by direct inspection.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma coprod-well-based of arXiv:2608.28504

[Theorem 39 of arXiv:2609.03736, '2609.03736'] For the state $G_\eta$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:product-state} and the
projection $P_\gamma^+$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:product-density}, write
\[
 K=K_{G_\eta,P_\gamma^+},
 \qquad
 L=L_{G_\eta,P_\gamma^+},
\]
and let
\begin{align}
 u(\eta,\gamma)&=2\tr(K^{1/2}L^{1/2}),\notag\\
 v(\eta,\gamma)&=\tr\!\left(
 R_\gamma G_\eta^{1/2}R_\gamma G_\eta^{1/2}\right).
\end{align}
Then
\begin{align}
 u(\eta,\gamma)
 &=\xi_{\eta,\gamma}^{\mathsf T}
   \Lambda_{\eta,\gamma}^{-1/2}\xi_{\eta,\gamma},
 \\
 v(\eta,\gamma)
 &=\gamma^{\mathsf T}(I-D_\eta^2)^{1/2}\gamma.
 
\end{align}
Thus $\mathcal J(G_\eta,P_\gamma^+)=(u+v)/2$, and its two traces,
although defined using $2^N$-dimensional matrices, are determined by
$N$-dimensional real matrices.

AUTHOR-CHECKED REDERIVATION; NO NOVELTY OR INDEPENDENT-REVIEW CLAIM. Let theta_i be a Poisson point process with intensity rho(dx)=(tau-1)c*x^(-tau)dx on(0,infinity), where3<tau<4 and c,mu>0. Given the weights, let T_i be independent exponential clocks of rate theta_i/mu. Define S(t)=sum_i theta_i*(1_{T_i<=t}-theta_i*t/mu), with decreasing-weight summation, and Z=lim_(epsilon down0)[sum_(theta_i>epsilon)theta_i^2-integral_(epsilon,infinity)x^2*rho(dx)]. Then L(t)=S(t)+(t/mu)Z has independent, generally nonstationary increments. It is the compensated integral of marked Poisson points with intensity rho(dx)*(x/mu)*exp(-xs/mu)ds, with the deterministic compensator specified by the displayed cutoff. In contrast, S(mu) and S(2mu)-S(mu) are dependent. The law identity was already identified in Dhara et al2019 eq2.22 and Remark11; the attached text is our direct derivation and scope check.

The later primary paper already states an indirect identification with Joseph's independent-increment limit. What is supplied here is a direct calculation and an explicit obstruction to holding the critical drift deterministic.

Sources: van der Hofstad, *Stochastic processes on random graphs*, July12,2017, equations4.5.5 and4.5.20, Open Problem4.1, PDF pp.206,210; https://www.win.tue.nl/~rhofstad/SaintFlour_SPoRG_fin_Saint_Flour.pdf . Dhara,van der Hofstad,van Leeuwaarden,Sen, *Heavy-tailed configuration models at criticality*, December2019 version, equation2.22 and Remark11, PDF pp.9-10; https://arxiv.org/pdf/1612.00650 . Joseph's original independent-increment limit: https://arxiv.org/abs/1012.2352 . Exact comparison with every convention in Joseph's characteristic function remains a separate check; the independence statement below is direct.

## Setup and the distinction in the question

Fix 3<tau<4, c>0, and mu>0. Let Gamma_i be the arrival times of a rate-one Poisson process and set theta_i=(c/Gamma_i)^(1/(tau-1)). Thus the theta_i form a Poisson point process on(0,infinity) with intensity

rho(dx)=(tau-1)c x^(-tau) dx.

Conditionally on these points, give each theta_i an independent exponential clock T_i with rate theta_i/mu. The source's process with a deterministic real parameter lambda is

S_lambda(t)=sum_i theta_i[1{T_i<=t}-(theta_i/mu)t]+lambda*t.

The ordered series is well defined. For small theta_i, its conditional means are O(theta_i^3) and its conditional variances are O(theta_i^3); sum theta_i^3 is finite almost surely. There are finitely many points above1, each finite. A process-level construction also follows from the compensated Poisson representation below.

The important parameter for iid degrees is the RANDOM variable Lambda_0 in equation2.22 of the later paper, not a fixed lambda. Define

Z=lim_(epsilon down0)[sum_(theta_i>epsilon) theta_i^2 - integral_(epsilon,infinity) x^2 rho(dx)].

The small-point part of this compensated Poisson integral converges in L2 and almost surely because integral_(0,1) x^4 rho(dx)<infinity. The large-point part is finite almost surely and has finite first absolute moment because integral_(1,infinity) x^2 rho(dx)<infinity. Its second moment need not be finite. Set Lambda_0=Z/mu.

At the random cutoff epsilon=theta_n, including the nth point changes the sum only by theta_n^2, which tends to0. Since

integral_(theta_n,infinity) x^2 rho(dx)=c^(2/(tau-1))*Gamma_n^(1-2/(tau-1))/(1-2/(tau-1)),

the definition of Z/mu is exactly equation2.22 after telescoping the integrals over[Gamma_(i-1),Gamma_i]. This checks the random-drift convention against the primary source, not merely by analogy.

## Direct independent-increment representation

For every epsilon>0 the cancellation is an identity:

S_0,epsilon(t)+(t/mu)Z_epsilon
= sum_(theta_i>epsilon) theta_i 1{T_i<=t} -(t/mu) integral_(epsilon,infinity) x^2 rho(dx).

By independent Poisson marking, the pairs(theta_i,T_i) form a Poisson random measure with deterministic intensity

nu(dx,ds)=rho(dx)*(x/mu)*exp(-xs/mu) ds.

The jump sum in the last display has independent increments in t, since disjoint time intervals select disjoint sets of this Poisson measure. Its centering is deterministic. Passing to finite-dimensional limits preserves independence, so

L(t):=S_0(t)+(t/mu)Z=S_(Lambda_0)(t)

has independent increments. They are generally NONSTATIONARY: the jump intensity contains exp(-xs/mu).

For completeness, this passage is not based on a formally divergent cancellation. Write the truncated expression as M_epsilon(t)+D_epsilon(t), where

M_epsilon(t)=sum_(theta_i>epsilon) theta_i1{T_i<=t}
             -integral_(epsilon,infinity) x(1-exp(-xt/mu))rho(dx),

D_epsilon(t)=integral_(epsilon,infinity) x[1-exp(-xt/mu)-xt/mu]rho(dx).

On bounded time intervals, the centered contribution from points x<=1 is an L2 martingale in t. The variance contributed by0<x<=epsilon is bounded by

(T/mu) integral_(0,epsilon) x^3 rho(dx),

which tends to0 because tau<4. Doob's inequality gives uniform-in-time L2 convergence of this small-point martingale. The deterministic drift converges uniformly on bounded time intervals because its integrand near0 is O(x^3), uniformly for bounded t. The finitely many large points and their finite deterministic compensator cause no problem. Hence L has a cadlag version obtained by this construction, and S_0=L-(t/mu)Z does too.

The deterministic drift can also be evaluated:

D(t)= - (tau-1)c * Gamma(4-tau)/[(tau-2)(tau-3)] * (t/mu)^(tau-2).

To check the sign and constant, substitute u=xt/mu and integrate twice by parts in the positive integral of u^(1-tau)(exp(-u)-1+u). All boundary terms vanish for3<tau<4. The remaining integral is Gamma(4-tau)/[(tau-2)(tau-3)]. In particular D(t)<0, consistent with depletion of previously discovered vertices.

## A deterministic lambda does not have independent increments

This part checks the strongest way the preceding conclusion could be misreported. Consider increments A=S_0(mu) and B=S_0(2mu)-S_0(mu). A marked point of size x contributes

F1=x1{T<=mu}-x^2,
F2=x1{mu<T<=2mu}-x^2.

Let K(a,b)=log E exp(aA+bB), for a,b>=0. These Laplace transforms are finite. Indeed, large points have nonpositive F1,F2 once x>=1; for small points the linear terms have integrable expectation O(x^3) and the quadratic remainder has integrable expectation O(x^3). The compensated Poisson formula, or its finite-cutoff version followed by these bounds, gives

K(a,a)-K(a,0)-K(0,a)
=integral rho(dx) E_T[(exp(aF1)-1)(exp(aF2)-1)].

For x>=1 both F1 and F2 are nonpositive, so the integrand is nonnegative. If0<a<=1/4 and x lies in[a^(-1/2),2a^(-1/2)], then x>=2 and F1,F2<=-x^2/2. Consequently the integrand is at least(1-exp(-1/2))^2 on this interval. Its rho-mass is

c*(1-2^(1-tau))*a^((tau-1)/2).

The potentially negative part is confined to0<x<1. The two indicators in F1,F2 are disjoint, and

E|F1F2| <= x^3 P(T<=2mu)+x^4 <=3x^4.

Since |exp(au)-1|<=a|u|exp(a|u|) and |Fj|<=2 on this range, the absolute contribution of this whole region is at most

3a^2 exp(4a) integral_(0,1) x^4 rho(dx)=C*a^2 exp(4a).

Thus the mixed log-Laplace difference is bounded below by a positive constant times a^((tau-1)/2) minus C*a^2 exp(4a). Since (tau-1)/2 is strictly less than2, it is positive for all sufficiently small a>0. Independence would make this difference identically0. Therefore A and B are dependent. Adding any deterministic lambda changes only their deterministic means and cannot fix this dependence.

This is a direct counterexample to interpreting the 2017 question as a claim about deterministic lambda after mixing the weights. It does not refute the corrected iid-degree statement, whose random drift is explicitly supplied in the later paper.

## Checks and remaining status limits

The argument has two complementary checks: Poisson marking proves independence after the exact random-slope cancellation; the mixed Laplace estimate disproves independence without it. The latter avoids covariance calculations, which would be invalid because the random slope can have infinite variance. The PPP intensity follows independently from the tail count E number{theta_i>x}=c*x^(-(tau-1)). The source's Gamma-coordinate expression telescopes to exactly the same compensated slope.

No simulation is used as proof. No independent referee has checked this text. The 2019 paper already identifies the corrected law indirectly, so this derivation does not establish an unproved theorem for the corpus and is not counted as an original solution. $$c^2 := \frac{\bar{c}^2(\bar{a}^2 + \bar{b}^2)}{(\bar{a}^2 + \bar{b}^2 + \bar{c}^2)}.$$  
If $c^2  > a^2  + b^2,$ then we are in the obtuse case, and $a, b > 0$ and $-\bar{c}^2 > \bar{a}^2 + \bar{b}^2.$ However the same formulae hold in this case as well.

[Proposition prop:sdp.factorized of arXiv:2604.22453, 'Adapted Wasserstein Barycenters of Gaussian Processes'] For every $t\in[T]$,
\begin{equation}

\min_{\mathbf P_t\in\mathscr{P}_+(K,d)}\Phi_t(\mathbf P_t)
=
\min
\left\{
\sum_{k=1}^K\lambda_k\bigl\|L_{\cdot,t}^k\mathbf M^k-\mathbf Y\bigr\|_F^2
\right\},
\end{equation}
where the minimum on the right-hand side is taken over
\[
\mathbf Y\in\mathbb{R}^{Td\times Kd},\qquad
\mathbf M^k\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times Kd},\qquad
\mathbf M^k(\mathbf M^k)^\intercal=I_d,\qquad k\in[K].
\]
The two problems are related by $\mathbf P_t=\mathbf M\mathbf M^\intercal$, where $\mathbf M\in\mathbb{R}^{Kd\times Kd}$ stacks the block rows $\mathbf M^1,\ldots,\mathbf M^K$; this correspondence is onto $\mathscr{P}_+(K,d)$.  For fixed $\mathbf M^1,\ldots,\mathbf M^K$, the inner minimum over $\mathbf Y$ is attained uniquely at
\begin{equation}

\mathbf Y=\sum_{k=1}^K\lambda_kL_{\cdot,t}^k\mathbf M^k=\mathbf L_{\cdot,t}\Lambda\mathbf M,
\end{equation}
which has zero block rows before time $t$.  Requiring in addition that the row spaces of $\mathbf M^1,\ldots,\mathbf M^K$ coincide with a fixed $d$-dimensional subspace, equivalently $\rank(\mathbf P_t)=d$, recovers the restricted local problem (equation eq:local.restricted.factor.problem of the paper).

[Definition Supermartingale and decrement of arXiv:2607.04620, 'The Exact Ville Identity\\ \large From the Absorbing Case to the General Law\\ with an App'] A nonnegative adapted process $(M_n,\mathcal{F}_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\mathbb{E}[M_n]<\infty$ is a supermartingale if $\mathbb{E}[M_n\mid \mathcal{F}_{n-1}]\le M_{n-1}$ almost surely for every $n\ge1$, and a martingale if equality always holds. Its decrement at time $n$ is the nonnegative, $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable random variable
\[
  \delta_n=M_{n-1}-\mathbb{E}[M_n\mid \mathcal{F}_{n-1}]\ge0.
\]
title: Supermartingale and decrement

[Proposition 4 (restate=continuousBoundedJumps,name=) of arXiv:2608.15874, '2608.15874'] Let $(\cF_t)_{t\geq0}$ be a filtration satisfying the usual conditions, let $\cZ$ be a measurable space, and let $\mu$ be an integer-valued random measure on $\Rp\times\cZ$ with predictable compensator $\nu$. Assume that, on an event of probability one, $\nu(\{t\}\times\cZ)=0$ and $\mu(\{t\}\times\cZ)\leq1$ for every $t\geq0$. Let $H=(H_t(z))_{t\geq0,\,z\in\cZ}$ be predictable and $\cH$-valued, with $\norm{H_t(z)}\leq1$, and suppose that, for every $T<\infty$,
\[
  \int_{(0,T]\times\cZ}\norm{H_t(z)}^2\,\nu(\dif t,\dif z)<\infty \qquad\text{a.s.}
\]
Define
\[
  M_t=\int_{(0,t]\times\cZ}H_s(z)\,(\mu-\nu)(\dif s,\dif z), \qquad V_t=\int_{(0,t]\times\cZ}H_s(z)\otimes H_s(z)\,\nu(\dif s,\dif z).
\]
Then $M$ is a purely discontinuous local martingale with $\norm{\Delta M_t}\leq1$ for every $t\geq0$, and $V$ is its operator-valued predictable quadratic variation. For every $\rho>0$, $(U_\rho^h(M_t,V_t))_{t\geq0}$ is a nonnegative supermartingale with initial value one. Consequently, for every $y\geq0$,
\[
  \P[\bigg]{\exists t\geq0:\rho h\roundb[\bigg]{\frac{\norm{(V_t+\rho I)^{-1/2}M_t}}{\sqrt\rho}}>y+\ell_\rho(V_t)}\leq e^{-y}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 31 of arXiv:2604.24684, 'Waning Immunity Fails to Restore a Positive Epidemic Threshold on Power--Law Networks'] Fix $\lambda,\rho, c, \varepsilon>0$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$. For all sufficiently large $n$, let $G=(V,E)$ be any deterministic graph on $n$ vertices satisfying the following two conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[\normalfont (i)]
    \item $G$ contains at least $\lceil n^{1-\delta}\rceil$ vertex-disjoint $(n^{\varepsilon},n^{\varepsilon})$ hierarchical-stars;
    \item $\operatorname{diam}(G)\le c\log n$.
\end{enumerate}
Consider the process $\mathrm{SIRS}(G,\lambda,\rho)$ initialized with all vertices infected. Then
\[
\mathbb P\big(T\ge \exp(n^{1-\delta})\big)\ge 1-\exp(-n^{1-\delta}).
\]
Moreover, if the process is initialized from a configuration in which the center of at least one of these $(n^{\varepsilon},n^{\varepsilon})$ hierarchical-stars is infected, then there exists a constant $\varepsilon'>0$ such that
\[
\mathbb P\big(T\ge \exp(n^{1-\delta})\big)\ge 1-n^{-\varepsilon'}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 31 of arXiv:2604.24684

body:
Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); independent mathematical review pending; novelty unestablished. This is a finite-horizon supporting method, not full Target1 closure.

## 1. Finite-horizon transfer statement
Fix finite d,n,T, gamma>0, 0<nu<=1, Y<infinity, nonzero training inputs
x_1,...,x_n with norms <=M, and a probability law P supported on nonzero
inputs of norm <=M. Inputs and P are independent of initialization.
The loss is (1/(2n)) sum_i (f(x_i)-y_i)^2, with |y_i|<=Y.
Use m=2N neurons, f(x)=m^(-1/2) sum_j a_j ReLU(w_j.x).
For each independent W_l~N(0,I_d), initialize one pair at (nu,W_l),
(-nu,W_l); update every parameter by ordinary simultaneous GD of step gamma,
with derivative 1{w.x>0}. The pairing is only at initialization, not enforced.
Let H be the deterministic full initial kernel from C014 Section2:
H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z].
Let f^H_k be zero-start kernel GD with this H, the same sample and labels.
Then, as N tends to infinity,

 max_{k<=T} ||f_k-f^H_k||_{L2(P)} -> 0 in probability.       (1)

The event bounds proving this hold uniformly for every y in [-Y,Y]^n.
No positive training eigenvalue or nonzero gate margin is assumed. T is
fixed before this width limit; constants below can grow rapidly with T.

## 2. Width-independent finite-horizon bounds
Write u_j=1+||w_j(0)||. The empirical mean S_m=m^(-1)sum u_j^2 is a pair
average and tends almost surely to E(1+||W||)^2. Fix S above that expectation
and work on S_m<=S, an event eventually true almost surely.
Define H_0=D_0=0, R_0=Y. Given H_k,D_k,R_k, set
 A_k=1+H_k, B_k=1+D_k, c_k=gamma M R_k,
 H_{k+1}=H_k+c_k B_k, D_{k+1}=D_k+c_k A_k,
 R_{k+1}=R_k+M c_k S[B_k(B_k+c_k A_k)+A_k^2].
Induction gives, uniformly over the label cube,
 |a_j(k)-a_j(0)|<=H_k u_j/sqrt(m),
 ||w_j(k)-w_j(0)||<=D_k u_j/sqrt(m),
 |a_j(k)|<=A_k u_j, ||w_j(k)||<=B_k u_j,
 ||r_k||/sqrt(n)<=R_k, where r_i=f_k(x_i)-y_i.
Indeed Cauchy-Schwarz in the exact parameter updates gives
 |Delta a_j|<=c_k B_k u_j/sqrt(m),
 ||Delta w_j||<=c_k A_k u_j/sqrt(m).
ReLU is 1-Lipschitz and homogeneous, so at every ||x||<=M,
 |Delta f_k(x)|<=||x|| c_k S[B_k(B_k+c_k A_k)+A_k^2].
This proves the induction and a finite uniform output bound through T.
Let H,D,A,B,c denote maxima of these constants through the required steps.

## 3. Population gate bands shrink in L2, not just on the sample
Put L_m(x)=m^(-1)sum_j u_j^2 1{|w_j(0).x|<=D u_j||x||/sqrt(m)}.
For each training x_i, L_m(x_i)->0 almost surely. Also

 ||L_m||_{L2(P)} -> 0 almost surely.                         (2)

Proof: for fixed q>0, the pair-averaged integrable function
 Z_q(W)=(1+||W||)^2 P_x{|W.x|<=q(1+||W||)||x||}
has its empirical average tending to E Z_q by the ordinary scalar SLLN.
For m large with D/sqrt(m)<=q, integral L_m dP is bounded by that average.
For every fixed nonzero x, Gaussian W.x has no atom at zero; Fubini and
dominated convergence imply E Z_q->0 as q decreases to zero. Apply SLLN
simultaneously on countably many q=1,1/2,1/3,..., then let q decrease.
Thus integral L_m->0 almost surely. Since 0<=L_m<=S_m, its squared L2 norm
is at most S_m integral L_m. The finite training-point assertion follows
by the same fixed-q argument without integration over P.
This is uniform over trajectories obeying Section2; no independence between
trained gates and initialization is asserted or needed.

## 4. Both train and cross kernels remain close
Let H^m_k be the empirical full tangent kernel at step k. Product expansion
and the movement bounds give, for every training point x_i,

 |H^m_k(x,x_i)-H^m_0(x,x_i)|
 <= ||x||||x_i|| [C S/sqrt(m)+nu^2(L_m(x)+L_m(x_i))],       (3)

where C=D(B+1)+H(A+1) is finite. The RF-product part is bounded by
D(B+1)u_j^2/sqrt(m). The readout-square change is bounded by
H(A+1)u_j^2/sqrt(m). A changed gate at x forces the initial weight into
the band defining L_m(x); likewise at x_i. These inequalities remain valid
when a trained preactivation equals zero, using the stated derivative.
Equations (2),(3) imply uniform-in-k convergence of the training normalized
Gram matrices and of the population cross rows, relative to their INITIAL
empirical kernels. In particular define K^m_k=(H^m_k(x_i,x_l)/n),
b^m_k(x)=(H^m_k(x,x_i)/sqrt(n))_i. Their respective operator and L2(row)
differences from step0 tend to zero; the latter is bounded by
M^2[C S/sqrt(m)+nu^2(||L_m||_2+max_i L_m(x_i))].

At initialization, each independent pair contributes the same feature
kernel F_W(x,z)=ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z.
It satisfies |F_W(x,z)|<=M^2(||W||^2+1). Its squared envelope is integrable.
Thus the empirical initial training kernel tends to K=(H(x_i,x_l)/n).
For the population cross row b(x)=(H(x,x_i)/sqrt(n))_i, independence of pairs
and Fubini give E||b^m_0-b||_2^2<=M^4 E(||W||^2+1)^2/N.
Hence this difference tends to zero in probability too. This explicitly
controls the missing test-to-training kernel; it is not inferred from K.

## 5. Discrete-step gate remainder off the sample
The exact prediction update is
 f_{k+1}(x)=f_k(x)-gamma b^m_k(x).v_k+Z_k(x), v_k=r_k/sqrt(n),
where, writing h=ReLU(w.x), h'=ReLU((w+Delta w).x),
 Z_k(x)=m^(-1/2)sum_j[Delta a_j(h'-h)
             +a_j(h'-h-1{w.x>0}Delta w_j.x)].
If the second summand is nonzero, the segment from w to w+Delta w crosses
its gate at x. Because both endpoints are within the Section2 cumulative
radius of w(0), the initial preactivation lies in the D-band above.
The Lipschitz inequality therefore gives

 |Z_k(x)|<=||x||[c^2 A B S/sqrt(m)+c A^2 L_m(x)].           (4)

It follows that max_{k<T}||Z_k||_{L2(P)}->0 and max_{k<T,i}|Z_k(x_i)|->0.
No approximation replaces discrete GD by flow.

## 6. Close the training and population prediction recurrences
Let v^H_{k+1}=(I-gamma K)v^H_k, v^H_0=-y/sqrt(n).
The true normalized residual update is
 v_{k+1}=(I-gamma K^m_k)v_k+z_k,
where ||z_k||<=max_i |Z_k(x_i)|. Sections2,4,5 imply by finite induction
max_{k<=T}||v_k-v^H_k||->0 in probability, uniformly over bounded labels.
For example each error is bounded by ||I-gamma K|| times the previous
error plus gamma ||K^m_k-K|| R_k+||z_k||. The multiplier is finite; neither
a contraction nor a spectral gap is required at this finite horizon.
Both output initializations are exactly zero. Sum the prediction updates:
 f_k-f^H_k=-gamma sum_{j<k}[(b^m_j-b).v_j+b.(v_j-v^H_j)]
                         +sum_{j<k}Z_j.
The population L2 norm is bounded by the sum of cross-kernel errors times
R_j, deterministic ||b||_2 times training residual errors, and remainder
norms. Every term tends to zero by the preceding sections, proving (1).
The same controlling random bounds work for all bounded label vectors.
For any bounded teacher, clean risks averaged over the bounded independent
label noises consequently converge uniformly through T in probability,
by Cauchy-Schwarz and the finite uniform output bound from Section2.


Here zero-start kernel GD means f^H_{k+1}(x)=f^H_k(x)-(gamma/n)sum_i H(x,x_i)(f^H_k(x_i)-y_i), with f^H_0=0.
Fixed finite d,n,T and step gamma>0; bounded nonzero training inputs and bounded nonzero-input population independent of initialization
m=2N independent Gaussian hidden pairs with opposite fixed heads +/-nu,0<nu<=1; all parameters subsequently trained without tying
Squared empirical loss normalized by n; bounded labels; zero ReLU derivative at zero
Width tends to infinity before any time, sample-size or input-law limit; mathematical and literature review pending

[Lemma mart_bound_dim_free of arXiv:2411.07878, 'Bernstein-type and Bennett-type inequalities for unbounded matrix martingales'] Let $\mathbf{Y}_i$, $\mathbf{V}_i$ and $\mathbf{Z}_k$ be as in Proposition~(prop:mart_bound of the paper), i.e., $(\mathbf{Y}_i)_{i=1}^n \subset \mathbb{H}(d)$ is a matrix-valued stochastic process adapted to filtration $(\mathscr{F}_i)_{i=1}^n$, 
    \begin{gather*}
        \mathbf{V}_i \coloneqq \ln \E\left[e^{\mathbf{Y}_i} \middle| \mathscr{F}_{i-1}\right] \in \mathbb{H}(d),
        \quad 
        \widetilde{\mathbf{V}}_i \coloneqq \mathbf{V}_i - \E[\mathbf{Y}_i | \mathscr{F}_{i-1}],
        \quad i \in [n],\\
        \mathbf{Z}_k \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^k (\mathbf{Y}_i - \mathbf{V}_i), \quad k = 0, \dots, n.
    \end{gather*}
    Consider nested events $E_1 \supset \dots \supset E_n$, such that $E_k \in \mathscr{F}_{k-1}$. 
    Then for any $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{H}(d)$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, it holds
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb{P}\lr{E_n \bigcap \left\{\max_{k\in [n]}\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{Z}_k + \mathbf{A}) \ge \varepsilon\right\}} &\le 
        \mathbb{P}\lr{\bigcup^n_{k=1} E_k \bigcap \left\{\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{Z}_k + \mathbf{A}) \ge \varepsilon\right\} } \\
        &\le \frac{\tr\Bigl(\phi(\mathbf{A}) + \sum_{k=1}^n \E \ind\left[E_k \right]\cdot(\widetilde{\mathbf{V}}_k)_{+}\Bigr)}{\phi(\varepsilon)}.
    \end{align*}
title: Lemma mart_bound_dim_free of arXiv:2411.07878

[Lemma lem:cf of arXiv:2607.12564, 'Power-law and log-periodic degree tails for a family of probability generating function eq'] The characteristic function $\widehat w(\theta):=\mathbb{E} e^{i\theta W}$ and each $\psi_n$ satisfy
\begin{equation}
  \left|\widehat w(\theta)\right|\le C_1(1+\abs\theta)^{-\kappa},\qquad
  \left|\psi_n(\theta)\right|\le C_1(1+\abs\theta)^{-\kappa}\quad(\text{uniformly in }n),
\end{equation}
with $C_1$ depending only on $p$. Consequently $\widehat{w_j}=\widehat w^{\,j}$ satisfies
$\abs{\widehat{w_j}(\theta)}\le C_1^{j}(1+\abs\theta)^{-j\kappa}$ with $j\kappa>1$, so
$\widehat{w_j}\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ and $V_j$ has the bounded continuous density
$w_j(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_\mathbb{R}\widehat w(\theta)^{j}e^{-i\theta x}\,d\theta$. Moreover $w_j$ is
supported on $[0,\infty)$, is strictly positive on $(0,\infty)$, has $\left\|w_j\right\|_\infty<\infty$
(so $x^{\rho+1}w_j(x)=O(x^{\rho+1})$ as $x\downarrow0$), and satisfies $w_j(x)\le C_2 e^{-c_2 x}$
for $x\ge1$.

For positive integers N<=M and real N by M matrices A,B, the rectangular orthogonal spherical integral is I_{N,M}(A,B)=integral_{O(N)} integral_{O(M)} exp(N*Tr(A^T*U*B*V^T)) dU dV, where dU and dV are normalized Haar probability measures. Pourkamali-Macris use J_{N,M}(A,B)=log(I_{N,M}(A,B))/(N*M) for the mutual-information formula. If alpha_N=N/M, this equals alpha_N times log(I_{N,M}(A,B))/N^2. The two normalizations must therefore be distinguished when importing rectangular spherical-integral asymptotics. A limiting J is defined only along matrix sequences for which the normalized limit exists; this definition does not assert convergence for arbitrary weakly convergent spectra.
Real N by M matrices with N<=M.
Independent orthogonal Haar probability measures, exponent prefactor N.

[Lemma lm:circulantmatrix of arXiv:2607.28817, 'Limiting spectral distribution for the adjacency matrix of the Watts--Strogatz random grap'] For all $n\ge1$ and even integers $K<n$, the eigenvalues of $D_{n,K}$ are
    \[
        \lambda_j = \begin{cases}
            \frac{\sin((K+1)\pi \frac jn)}{\sin(\pi \frac jn)}-1&\quad\mbox{ for } j\in\{1,\dots,n-1\},\\
            K&\quad\mbox{ for }j=n.
        \end{cases}
    \]
    Furthermore, for all sequences $(K_n)_{n\ge1}$ of even integers that satisfy $2\le K_n<n$ for all sufficiently large values of $n$ and a sequence $(p_n)_{n\ge1}$ in $(0,1]$, under the assumption~(equation eq:assumption1 of the paper), there exist two matrices $D^{(1)}_{n,K_n}$ and $D^{(2)}_{n,K_n}$ such that
    \begin{gather}
        D_{n,K} = D^{(1)}_{n,K_n} + D^{(2)}_{n,K_n},\\
        \operatorname{rank}\left(\frac{D^{(1)}_{n,K_n}}{\sqrt{p_nK_n}}\right)\underset{n\to\infty}{=}o(n),\\
        \left\|\frac{D^{(2)}_{n,K_n}}{\sqrt{p_nK_n}}\right\|\;\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\;0,
    \end{gather}where $\|\cdot\|$ denotes the spectral norm of a matrix. It follows that the empirical spectral measure $\mu_{\frac{D_{n,K_n}}{\sqrt{p_nK_n}}}$ of $\frac{D_{n,K_n}}{\sqrt{p_nK_n}}$ converges weakly to the Dirac mass $\delta_0$ as $n \to \infty$.

[Proposition prop:abstract-kato-slice of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] For every $t_0\in\mathbb R^N$, there exists a complex neighborhood
$\mathcal U\subset\mathbb C^N$ of $t_0$ such that the following assertions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
\item The family of sesquilinear forms $(a_z)_{z\in\mathcal U}$, defined by
\begin{equation}
 a_z(u,v):=\mathcal E(m_zu,m_{\bar z}v),
 \qquad \operatorname{Dom} a_z=V_{\mu_0}^{\mathbb C},
 
\end{equation}
is a holomorphic family of closed sectorial forms with common domain; in Kato's
terminology, it is a family of type~\textnormal{(a)}.  Let $\widehat A_z$
denote the associated $m$-sectorial operator.  For real $t\in\mathcal U\cap\mathbb R^N$,
this agrees with the previously defined $\widehat A_t$.
\item For every $z\in\mathcal U$, the operator $\widehat A_z$ has compact
resolvent, and the map
$z\mapsto(\widehat A_z+1)^{-1}$ from $\mathcal U$ into
$\mathcal L(L^2(\mu_0))$ is holomorphic in the operator norm.
\item Suppose that a positively oriented contour $\Gamma\subset\mathbb C$ lies
in the resolvent set of $\widehat A_{t_0}$ and encloses a finite cluster of its
eigenvalues.  After shrinking $\mathcal U$ if necessary, $\Gamma$ remains in
the resolvent set of $\widehat A_t$ for every real
$t\in\mathcal U\cap\mathbb R^N$, and
\begin{equation}
 R_{\Gamma}(t)
 =\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{\Gamma}
   (\zeta-\widehat A_t)^{-1}\,d\zeta
 
\end{equation}
is a real-analytic family of finite-rank projections satisfying
\begin{equation*}
 \rankR_{\Gamma}(t)=\rankR_{\Gamma}(t_0).
\end{equation*}
The coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of
$\widehat A_t|_{\operatorname{Ran}R_{\Gamma}(t)}$, and hence its
discriminant, depend real-analytically on $t$.
\end{enumerate}
If $t\mapsto(\lambda(t),\Phi(t))$ is a local real-analytic eigenpair branch of
$\widehat A_t$, normalized by
$\left\|\Phi(t)\right\|_{L^2(\mu_0)}=1$, then $\Phi$ is real analytic as a map with
values in $V_{\mu_0}^{\mathbb C}$ and
\begin{equation}
 \partial_{t_k}\lambda(t)
 =(\partial_{t_k}a_t)(\Phi(t),\Phi(t)),
 \qquad 1\le k\le N.
 
\end{equation}

[Lemma lem:extreme-cut-reconstruction of arXiv:2609.03532, 'Airy limit for the Jack process and topological expansion'] For fixed jump positions, signs, pairing, and marked horizontal positions,
the preceding right-to-left construction is injective and has the
following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Every admissible decorated configuration occurs exactly once.
  In particular, a middle canonical profile which is negative before the
  cross-excursion translations and the shift by $H_p$ is not discarded.
  \item Every pair height is assigned at its positive occurrence.  The
  negative occurrence introduces no further height sum.
  \item The product of the canonical-step weights is the product of the
  weights of the auxiliary canonical pieces.
\end{enumerate}

body:
Let U be an open subset of C, let S be a subset of U with no accumulation point in U (so S is discrete and closed in U), and let f be holomorphic on U minus S. Let γ be a cycle (a finite formal sum with integer coefficients of closed piecewise C^1 curves) whose trace lies in U minus S, and assume γ is null-homologous in U, i.e. the winding number n(γ,w) = 0 for every w in C minus U. Then n(γ,a) is nonzero for only finitely many a in S, and ∫_γ f(z) dz = 2πi Σ_{a in S} n(γ,a) Res(f,a). Most-used special case: if γ is a positively oriented piecewise C^1 Jordan curve such that γ together with its interior region lies in U and no point of S lies on γ, then ∫_γ f(z) dz = 2πi times the sum of Res(f,a) over the (finitely many) points a of S inside γ. The singularities may be poles or essential singularities, but they must be isolated and f must be single-valued on U minus S.
U is an open subset of C
S ⊂ U has no accumulation point in U
f is holomorphic (single-valued) on U minus S
γ is a cycle of closed piecewise C^1 curves in U minus S
γ is null-homologous in U: n(γ,w) = 0 for all w not in U

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2606.07290, 'Boundary behaviour of the Volterra square-root process'] Suppose that $K$ is regularly varying at $t=0$, that is,
    \begin{align}
        K(t) = \frac{t^{\alpha-1}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\ell(t), \qquad t > 0,
    \end{align}
    where $\ell > 0$ is slowly varying at $0$ and $\alpha \in (0,1)$. Let $m \geq 0$ and $\eta \in (0,1)$. Then
    \[
        K \ast \mu \in C^{m,\eta}((0,\infty); \C_-)
        \ \Longrightarrow \
        \psi(\cdot;\mu) \in C^{m,\eta}((0,\infty); \C_-).
    \]
    In particular, if $K \ast \mu$ is $C^\infty$, then also $\psi(\cdot;\mu) \in C^{\infty}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2606.07290

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, The connectivity window of bilateral preference random graphs (October 2026), studies the graph LK(n,k) of La and Kabkab: independent uniform scores on the edges of K_n, each vertex prefers its k incident edges of smallest score, and an edge is kept when both endpoints prefer it. Dabirian and Subramanian (J. Appl. Probab. 63 (2026), 552-579) showed connectivity with high probability above log n + (1/2) log log n sqrt(log n) and disconnection below log n - (1/2) log log n sqrt(log n), leaving the window between open. The paper shows that for every fixed C, uniformly over integers k with |k - log n| <= C, the number of isolated vertices is asymptotically Poisson with mean n e^{-k} in total variation and P(LK(n,k) is connected) = exp(-n e^{-k}) + o(1); hence LK(n,k) is connected with high probability if and only if k - log n tends to infinity. Exact rational checks of the proof constants and simulations at n = 1000 and 3000 accompany the paper. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/bilateral-preference-connectivity-window (commit 9480eac0ba53). Not refereed.
title: The connectivity window of the bilateral preference random graph LK(n,k): P(connected) = exp(-n e^{-k}) + o(1) for |k - log n| bounded (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/bilateral-preference-connectivity-window)

[Theorem 14 of arXiv:2608.17562, '2608.17562'] Let
  $Z \sim \mathcal{F}(\alpha)$ for some $\alpha > 0$,
  and let 
  $W$ be a random variable whose distribution function $F_W$
  is absolutely continuous on $[K, +\infty)$ for some $K>0$, with 
  density function~$f_W$.
\begin{enumerate}[i)] 
\item Kolmogorov bound. For any $\alpha >0$, we have
\begin{align*}
      \nonumber 
\mathrm{d}_{K} (W, \mathcal{F}(\alpha) ) \leq (\alpha + 1)F_{W}(K) + \alpha\int_{K}^\infty  F_{W}(r)\bigg\vert\frac{f_{W}(r)}{F_{W}(r)} - \frac{\alpha}{r^{\alpha + 1}}\bigg\vert \dif r.\numberthis
\end{align*}
\item Wasserstein bound.
  Let $\alpha > 1$ and
  $p \in (1,\alpha)$ such that $\esp[\vert W \vert^{p}] < \infty$.
  We have
  \begin{align*}
      \nonumber 
      \mathrm{d}_{W} (W, \mathcal{F}(\alpha) ) \leq \esp [\vert W \vert^{p} ]^{{1}/{p}}F_{W}(K)^{{1}/{q}} & + \Big(
      \Gamma\Big(1 - \frac{1}{\alpha}\Big) + \frac{\alpha^{2}}{\alpha - 1}\Big)
      F_{W}(K)\\
		&+ \alpha\int_{K}^\infty  rF_{W}(r)\bigg\vert\frac{f_{W}(r)}{F_{W}(r)} - \frac{\alpha}{r^{\alpha + 1}}\bigg\vert \dif r,\numberthis
\end{align*}
  where $q = p/(p-1)$ denotes the conjugate of $p$. 
\item Moment bound.
  Let $\alpha > 0$ and
  $b \in (0, \alpha)$,
  assume that $W$ is a.s. nonnegative and that there exists $p \in (1, \alpha / b)$ such that $\esp[W^{pb}] < \infty$, with $q = p/(p-1)$. Then, we have  
  \begin{align*}
      \nonumber 
\vert \esp [W^{b} ] - \esp [Z^{b}]\vert \leq \esp [ W^{pb}]^{{1}/{p}}F_{W}(K)^{{1}/{q}} & + \Big( \Gamma\Big(1 - \frac{b}{\alpha}\Big) + \frac{\alpha^{2}}{\alpha - b}\Big) F_{W}(K)\\
		&+ \alpha\int_{K}^\infty  r^{b}F_{W}(r)\bigg\vert\frac{f_{W}(r)}{F_{W}(r)} - \frac{\alpha}{r^{\alpha + 1}}\bigg\vert \dif r.\numberthis
\end{align*}

\item Let $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and $b \in (0, \alpha)$.
  Suppose that there exists $p \in (1, \alpha / b)$ such that $\esp[\vert W \vert^{p}]< \infty$, with $q = p/(p-1)$. Then, we have 
  \begin{align*}
      \nonumber 
      \mathrm{d}_{W_b} (W, \mathcal{F}(\alpha) )
      \leq \esp [ W^{pb}]^{{1}/{p}}F_{W}(K)^{{1}/{q}}
      &
      + \Big(
      \Gamma\Big(1 - \frac{b}{\alpha}\Big) + \frac{2\alpha^{2}}{\alpha - b}\Big)
       F_{W}(K)\\
		&+ \alpha\int_{K}^\infty  r^{b}F_{W}(r)\bigg\vert\frac{f_{W}(r)}{F_{W}(r)} - \frac{\alpha}{r^{\alpha + 1}}\bigg\vert \dif r.\numberthis
\end{align*}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 14 of arXiv:2608.17562

[Prop 12 (Error estimate) of arXiv:2506.12632, 'Point process convergence of extremes in $K$-symmetric exclusion'] Let $A \in \sU$. 
\begin{enumerate}[(a)] 

\item We have 
\[
	\lim_{t\to\infty} \kappa_t(v_t^{-1}(A), (-\infty,0]) = 0. 
\]
Moreover, if $L \uparrow \infty$ such that $L(\frac{\log t}{t})^{1/2} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty$, then 
\[
	\lim_{t\to\infty} \kappa_t(v_{t,L}^{-1}(A), (-L,0]) = 0. 
\]

\item If $\lim_{t\to\infty} L(\frac{\log t}{t})^{1/2} > 0$, then 
\[
	\lim_{t\to\infty} \tau_t(v_t^{-1}(A), (-L, 0]) = \lim_{t\to\infty} \tau_t((-L,0], v_t^{-1}(A)) = 0. 
\]
Moreover, if $L \uparrow \infty$ such that $L(\frac{\log t}{t})^{1/2} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty$, then 
\[
	\lim_{t\to\infty} \tau_t(v_{t,L}^{-1}(A), (-L, 0]) = \lim_{t\to\infty} \tau_t((-L,0], v_{t,L}^{-1}(A)) = 0. 
\]

\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theo genen of arXiv:2507.00737, 'Dispersion models on a circle: universal properties and asymptotic results'] Consider a sequence of DDM\xspace (or ${\sf CDM}\xspace$) such that, for some sequence of times $(t_n,n\geq 0)$,   
	\[
	\left(\alpha_n S^{(n)}(t_n,x),x\in [0,1]\right)\xrightarrow[n]{(d)} \left(S^{\infty}(x),x \in [0,1]\right) 
	\]
	where $\alpha_n/n \to 0$ and $\alpha_n\to+\infty$, with $S^\infty(1)<0$, and where the convergence holds in $C[0,1]$ (or in $D[0,1]$).  
	If $S^\infty$ reaches its minimum a.s. once on $[0,1]$ at some  $a\in[0,1]$, and if moreover $S$ has a.s.  the property that its excursions above the current minimum are strict (in the sense that there are no strict non-trivial sub-excursions of any excursion at the same level), then for $S={\sf Rot}(a,S^\infty)$, the sequence formed by the $k$ largest clusters   converges  in distribution to the length of the excursions of $S$ above its current minimum 
	\begin{eqnarray*} n^{-1}\,L^{(n), \downarrow}[t_n,k] &\xrightarrow[n]{(d)}&(\ell_i^{\downarrow}(S),1\leq i \leq k)\\
	n^{-1}\,L^{\downarrow}[t_n,k] &\xrightarrow[n]{(d)}&(\ell_i^{\downarrow}(S),1\leq i \leq k)
	\end{eqnarray*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
