[Lemma of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The functor $\textup{diag}\colon\cat{$\bm G$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Sp}\to\cat{$\bm{G}$-OrthSp}$ sends $G$-global level weak equivalences to $G$-global weak equivalences and hence descends to ${\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\textup{$G$-lvl}\to{{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}_\textup{$G$-gl}$.
    \begin{proof}
        It is clear that $\textup{diag}$ sends acyclic fibrations (i.e.~maps $X\to Y$ such that each $X(V)(U)\to Y(V)(U)$ is an acyclic fibration in the $\mathcal G_{{\textup{O}}(U),{\textup{O}}(V)\times G}$-model structure) to $G$-global level weak equivalences. By Corollary~(cor:cofibrant-LSp-closed of the paper) it will therefore suffice to show that $\textup{diag}$ sends any $G$-global level weak equivalence $f\colon X\to Y$ such that $X$ and $Y$ are levelwise closed to a $G$-global weak equivalence. 
        
        Restricting along any homomorphism of compact Lie groups $\varphi\colon H\to G$ (and replacing $G$ by $H$), it suffices to show that $\pi_n^G(\textup{diag}\,f)$ is bijective for every $n\in{\mathbb{Z}}$. We will give the argument for $n=0$; the argument for general $n$ is analogous, but requires slightly more notation. For this we consider the functor $\Pi_X\colon s({\mathcal{U}}_G)\times s({\mathcal{U}}_G)\to\textbf{\textup{Sets}}$ sending $(V,W)$ to $[S^V, X(V)(W)]_*^G$ with the obvious functoriality in $V$ and $W$, and define $\Pi_Y$ analogously. If we write $\Delta\colon s({\mathcal{U}}_G)\to s({\mathcal{U}}_G)\times s({\mathcal{U}}_G)$ for the diagonal embedding, then $\pi_0^G(\textup{diag}\,X)=\mathop{\textup{colim}}\Pi_X\circ\Delta$ and $\pi_0^G(\textup{diag}\,Y)=\mathop{\textup{colim}}\Pi_Y\circ\Delta$ by definition. As $\Delta$ is cofinal, it will therefore suffice to show that the map
        \[
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}_{(V,W)\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)\times s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}[S^V,X(V)(W)]_*^G \longrightarrow 
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}_{(V,W)\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)\times s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}[S^V,Y(V)(W)]_*^G
        \]
        induced by $f$ is bijective, for which it is enough by the Fubini Theorem for colimits to prove bijectivity of the analogous map
        \[
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}_{V\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}\mathop{\textup{colim}}_{W\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}[S^V, X(V)(W)]_*^G
            \longrightarrow
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}_{V\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}\mathop{\textup{colim}}_{W\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}[S^V, Y(V)(W)]_*^G.
        \]
        Arguing as in the proof of Lemma~(lemma:cotensoring-fully-homotopical of the paper), this may be identified with the map
        \[
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}_{V\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}[S^V, X(V)({\mathcal{U}}_G)]_*^G\longrightarrow
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}_{V\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}[S^V, Y(V)({\mathcal{U}}_G)]_*^G
        \]
        induced levelwise by $f(V)({\mathcal{U}}_G)\colon X(V)({\mathcal{U}}_G)\to Y(V)({\mathcal{U}}_G)$. As the latter is a $G$-equivariant weak equivalence, the claim follows.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered lemma of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'

[Proposition prop:interval-adapted-reduction of arXiv:2608.29719, 'Persistence Pairing Graphs: Tracking Changes of Selected Homology Bases'] For every paired positive index $i$, let
\[
j=\operatorname{pair}(i)
\]
and let $\gamma_i\neq0$ be the coefficient of the cell $\sigma_i$ in the reduced column $R_j$. Define
\[
\widehat V_i:=\gamma_i^{-1}R_j.
\]
For unpaired positive indices and for negative indices, leave the corresponding columns unchanged.

Then $\widehat V$ is upper unitriangular and dimension preserving, and
\[
D\widehat V=R.
\]
For every finite nonzero persistence interval, the selected birth cycle produced by $\widehat V$ becomes zero in homology at its death value. Consequently, every transition coefficient of a dying label is zero and the corresponding persistence pairing graph has no directed edges.

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The stereographic projection from $i$, namely
$$\xymatrix@R=7pt@C=2.1pt{
&&&&&&&&\ar@{-}[d]\\
&&&&&&&&\bullet^i\ar@{-}[dddddd]\ar@{-}@/_/[dllll]\ar@{.}[drrrr]&\\
&&&&\ar@{-}@/_/[ddl]&&&&&&&&\circ\ar@{-}@/_/[ullll]\ar@{.}[ddrrrrrr]\\
&&&&&&&&&&&&\\
\ar@{-}[rrr]&&&\bullet\ar@{-}@/_/[ddr]\ar@{-}[rrrrr]&&&&&\ar@{-}[rrrrr]&&&&&\bullet\ar@{-}@/_/[uul]\ar@{-}[rrrrr]&&&&&\circ^x\ar@{-}[rr]&&\\
&&&&&&&&&&&&\\
&&&&\ar@{-}@/_/[drrrr]&&&&&&&&\ar@{-}@/_/[uur]\\
&&&&&&&&\bullet\ar@{-}@/_/[urrrr]\ar@{-}[d]\\
&&&&&&&&}$$
makes correspond numbers $e^{it}\in\mathbb T$ to real numbers $x\in\mathbb R$ according to the formulae 
$$x=\frac{\cos t}{1-\sin t}\quad,\quad e^{it}=\frac{2x+i(x^2-1)}{x^2+1}$$
and can be used for various mathematical purposes.

[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] Let $\Zc$ be a complete metric space, and let $(\pi_n)_n\subset\Pc(\Zc)$.
Assume that there exists a Borel measure $\lambda$ on $\Zc$ such that, for every
$n\ge1$, the measure $\pi_n$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\lambda$,
with density
\[
f_n:=\frac{d \pi_n}{d \lambda}.
\]
Assume moreover that there exists $p>1$ such that, for every compact set
$K\subset\Zc$, there exists a constant $C_K>0$ satisfying
\vspace{-2mm}
\[
\|f_n\mathbf{1}_K\|_{\L^p(\lambda)} \le C_K,
\qquad
\text{for all }n\ge1.
\vspace{-2mm}
\]
If $\pi_n\to\pi$ weakly, then, for every bounded Borel-measurable function $g:\Zc\to\R$, 
\vspace{-2mm}
\[
\int_{\Zc} g(z)\,\pi_n(dz)
\longrightarrow
\int_{\Zc} g(z)\,\pi(dz).
\vspace{-2mm}
\]

[Corollary 23 of arXiv:2609.03831, 'On flows generated by square-integrable vector fields'] If $\vi \in \boldsymbol{L}^2(\R^d)$ is a compactly supported divergence-free vector field
	and the operator $A_0 \rho := \v \cdot \nabla \rho$
	with $D(A_0) = C^\infty_c(\R^{d})$ is essentially skew-adjoint in $L^2(\R^{d})$,
	then for any $T>0$ and $\rho_0 \in L^2(\R^d)$ there exists a unique solution $\rho \in L^\infty(0,T; L^2(\R^d))$ of \eqref{CE} with $\rho|_0 = \rho_0$.
	Furthermore, the strongly continuous version $\widetilde{\rho}$ of $\rho$ is given by the group $S_t$ generated by $-A$, where $A$ is the closure of $A_0$, i.e. for all $t\in [0,T]$ we have
	$\widetilde{\rho}(t,\cdot) = S_t \rho_0 = \rho|_t$.

[Lemma 27 of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{prop:3}
Let
\[
X_n=\sqrt n\,(wG_n+uD_n),
\qquad
D_n=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n),
\]
where \(G_n\) is GUE, \(D_n\) is independent of \(G_n\), and
\((d_1,\ldots,d_n)\) is the ordered spectrum of an independent GUE
matrix. Let \(\Gamma_n\) be the complete eigenvalue minor process of
\(X_n\). If \(w>0\) and \(u\geq 0\) are fixed, then
\[
I(D_n;\Gamma_n)=O(n \log \log n).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:decomp of arXiv:2604.22453, 'Adapted Wasserstein Barycenters of Gaussian Processes'] For $L, M \in \mathscr{L}(T, d)$, we have 
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{ABW}}^2(L, M) = \sum_{t=1}^T \mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{BW}}^2\bigl(A_t^L,\, A_t^M\bigr).
\end{equation}

\begin{proof}
Fix $L,M\in\mathscr{L}(T,d)$. Applying (equation eqn:d.BW of the paper) to the column covariances $A_t^L=L_{\cdot,t}L_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal}$ and $A_t^M=M_{\cdot,t}M_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal}$ yields
\[
\mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{BW}}^2\bigl(A_t^L, A_t^M\bigr) = \|L_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 + \|M_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 - 2 \bigl\| L_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal} M_{\cdot,t} \bigr\|_*.
\]
Summing over $t \in [T]$ gives
\begin{equation} 
\sum_{t=1}^T \mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{BW}}^2\bigl(A_t^L, A_t^M\bigr) = \sum_{t=1}^T \|L_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 + \sum_{t=1}^T \|M_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 - 2 \sum_{t=1}^T \bigl\| L_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal} M_{\cdot,t} \bigr\|_*.
\end{equation}
It remains to identify the three sums on the right-hand side of (equation eq:decomp.sum of the paper) with the corresponding terms in (equation eq:ABW of the paper). Since the block-columns $L_{\cdot,1}, \ldots, L_{\cdot,T}$ collect all the blocks of $L$, we have
\[
\sum_{t=1}^T \|L_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 = \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{s=1}^T \|L_{t,s}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 = \|L\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2,
\]
and likewise
\[
\sum_{t=1}^T \|M_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 = \|M\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2.
\]
For the last sum, the $d\times d$ diagonal block of $L^{\intercal}M$ indexed by $t$ is
\[
(L^{\intercal} M)_{t,t}
=L_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal} M_{\cdot,t}
=\sum_{s=1}^T L_{s,t}^{\intercal} M_{s,t}.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{t=1}^T \bigl\| L_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal} M_{\cdot,t} \bigr\|_* = \sum_{t=1}^T \bigl\| (L^{\intercal} M)_{t,t} \bigr\|_*.
\]
Substituting these three identities into (equation eq:decomp.sum of the paper) gives
\[
\sum_{t=1}^T \mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{BW}}^2\bigl(A_t^L, A_t^M\bigr) = \|L\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 + \|M\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 - 2 \sum_{t=1}^T \bigl\| (L^{\intercal} M)_{t,t} \bigr\|_* = \mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{ABW}}^2(L, M),
\]
where the last equality is the definition (equation eq:ABW of the paper) of $\mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{ABW}}$. This proves (equation eq:decomp of the paper).
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

and \ref{assumption3a} hold. Then there is a constant $N=N(d,r,\kappa)$ 
such that if $u$ is an admissible solution to \eqref{NS3}--\eqref{bin3} 
satisfying 
$$
\tilde u+L<\delta/N,\quad \tilde u=\hat u+\esssup_{t\in[0,T]} \bar u_t,  
$$
then we have 
$$
\int_0^T|u_t-v_t|^2_{\cV}\leq \tfrac{1}{2\gamma}|u_0-v_0|^2_{\cH}
\quad\text{with} \quad \gamma:=\delta-N(\tilde u+L), 
$$
and 
$$
|u_t-v_t|_{\cH}\leq |u_0-v_0|_{\cH}e^{-\frc^{-2}\gamma t}
\quad 
\text{for $t\in[0,T]$}
$$
for any admissible solution $v$ to \eqref{NS} with zero boundary condition 
and initial condition $v_t|_{t=0}=v_0\in\cH$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: A topological space is a pair (X, T) where X is a set and T is a collection of subsets of X, called the open sets, such that: (i) the empty set and X itself are open; (ii) the union of any family of open sets is open; (iii) the intersection of any finite family of open sets is open. A subset C of X is called closed when its complement in X is open. An open set containing a point x is called an open neighborhood of x.
title: Topological space

Maximum coupling mass at cross-class distance <=2epsilon is exactly 1-2Q(R), attained by a Gaussian-preserving partial quantile-reflection involution. Scope: Exact-version independent PASS received. T358-C22 v1 [proof (unaudited), restricted-route obstruction]: With positive weighted radial densities f,g and cross first marginal h<=f, a density-ratio transpose plus diagonal completion has first central density H=g+(1-g/f)h, so H<=f requires h=f wherever g>f. Its outer weighted-transpose marginal must also be dominated by the first outer class law. For C9 equal-prior G_+=(4z,4a|z|),G_-=(z,-a|z|),0<a<=1/1000,e=1/10, use absolute horizontal radii C=[0,e/a],O=(e/a,infinity). The wide/narrow density ratio is (1/4)exp(15r^2/32), at most 8/17 on [0,1] and at least 593/512 on [2,3]. Neither interval has close outer neighbors because horizontal separation exceeds 97>2e. In either orientation, fully saturating the second central class with only diagonal central-to-central transport exceeds a first-class marginal budget. This leaves central redistribution or unsaturated central mass to optimize. No exact asymmetric Bayes value, independent PASS, priority or new scored move claimed.

T358-C23 v1 [proof (unaudited)]: For the equal-prior C9 asymmetric V family, the maximum class-weighted close partial matching restricted to central absolute horizontal radii [0,T], T=e/a, is (1/2) min{F(T/4),min_{0<=r<=T}[F(r/4)+F(T)-F(ell(r))]}, where F is the half-normal CDF and ell is the clipped lower close-neighborhood root. The maximum is attained. A finite ordered reflexive umbrella graph with one sign crossing of the vertex-weight difference has an optimal Hall cut that is empty or a terminal interval. Here T=e/a, F is the half-normal CDF, and ell(r)=max(0,((1-a^2)r-sqrt(4e^2(1+a^2)-4a^2*r^2))/(1+a^2)). The separate empty-tail candidate is necessary. The central-only value lower-bounds unrestricted robust Bayes error. It does not optimize joint central/outer allocation. No novelty or full excluded-region closure claimed. T358-C24 v1 [route-failure; proof (unaudited)]: Strictly increasing likelihood ratios and equal class masses do not suffice to extend C23 terminal Hall cuts to the outer nonreflexive block of the C9 geometry. This shows that C23 cannot be extended using likelihood-ratio order alone. It does not settle the Gaussian excluded region or establish priority.

[Theorem thm:variational of arXiv:2607.14087, 'Stochastic Domination of Gaussian Maxima: A Resolution of the Weak Simplex Conjecture'] For every $c\in\mathbb R$, the functional $\mathcal J_c$ has a unique maximizer
$(q_*,v_*)\in\mathcal D$.  There are unique $s_{*,i}\in\mathbb R$ such that
\[
  H(s_{*,i})=q_*+\alpha\ip{x_i}{v_*}.
\]
Define
\[
  a_{*, i}=r(s_{*,i}),
  \qquad
  b_{*,i}=H(s_{*,i})=s_{*,i}+a_{*,i}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
  b_{*}-R a_{*}=c\mathbf 1
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
  \sum_{i=1}^m\log\Phi(s_{*,i})
  +\frac12a_{*}^{\mathsf T}(I_m-R)a_{*}
  \geq m\log\Phi(c).
\end{equation}

body:
Own work, proof (unaudited), W719-T295-C007 v1. Fix C>sqrt(2), c>0, and any fixed C_out>0. For every sufficiently large fixed alpha depending on C, m=ceil(alpha*d), iid real a_i~N(0,I_d), deterministic unit signal x_*, eta=c/log d, and loss f(x)=(1/(4m)) sum_i ((a_i^T x)^2-(a_i^T x_*)^2)^2, with probability tending to one there exists a sample-dependent x0 at distance d^-10 from x_* with max_i |a_i^T(x0-x_*)|<=C sqrt(log d)||x0-x_*||, yet after one unmodified GD step |a_1^T(x1-x_*)|>C_out sqrt(log d)||x1-x_*||. The first iterate still has error O(d^-10), inside the local ball. Write a_i=g_i e1+b_i for e1=x_*, v=b_1/||b_1||, b_j=t_j v+c_j for j>=2, and z=(2/m)sum_{j>=2}g_j^2 1_{|g_j|<=1} t_j c_j. Take x0=e1+d^-10 z/||z||. Row-removal Gaussian tails prove initial incoherence; selected rows make v^T Hess f(e1) z/||z|| tend to 2sqrt(mu/alpha)>0, mu=E[G^4 1_{|G|<=1}]. Thus the Hessian produces a row-1 projection of order sqrt(d) although the original direction is exactly orthogonal to row 1. The nonlinear remainder is negligible at this radius. This refutes uniform preservation from initial relative incoherence for C>sqrt(2), not contraction assuming all-time incoherence, random-start convergence, or preservation for C<=sqrt(2). No novelty claim; independent review pending.

sample-dependent starting point allowed

Let X_1, X_2, ... be i.i.d. with E[X_1] = 0, E[X_1^2] = sigma^2 in (0, infinity), and rho = E|X_1|^3 < infinity. Let S_n = X_1 + ... + X_n and let Phi be the standard normal distribution function. Then there is an ABSOLUTE constant C, not depending on the law of X_1 or on n, with sup_{x in R} | P( S_n / (sigma sqrt(n)) <= x ) - Phi(x) | <= C rho / ( sigma^3 sqrt(n) ). The rate n^{-1/2} is optimal in general: for a symmetric two-point law the Kolmogorov distance really is of order n^{-1/2} along a subsequence, because of the lattice jumps. Concerning the constant, successive work has pushed the best known value for the i.i.d. case below 0.5, while Esseen's own example gives the lower bound (3 + sqrt(10))/(6 sqrt(2 pi)), about 0.4097, so the optimal constant lies in a narrow window; NO specific numerical value should be quoted from this node. A non-identically-distributed version holds with rho replaced by sum_i E|X_i|^3 and sigma^3 sqrt(n) by (sum_i E X_i^2)^{3/2}. The third absolute moment is a real hypothesis: with only two moments the CLT still holds but no rate of this form does. [Berry (1941), Esseen (1942); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 3.4.17]

body: The axiom of choice (AC) states: for every family (A_i)_{i in I} of nonempty sets, indexed by a set I, there exists a function c on I with c(i) in A_i for every i. Equivalently, every family of nonempty sets admits a choice function selecting one member of each set; every Cartesian product of nonempty sets is nonempty; every surjection has a right inverse; and every set of nonempty pairwise disjoint sets has a transversal selecting exactly one element from each. Over Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory ZF, AC is equivalent to Zorn's lemma, the well-ordering theorem, and Tychonoff's theorem for arbitrary compact spaces. AC asserts existence, not a specified construction; Zermelo formulated it in 1904 in order to prove the well-ordering theorem. AC is independent of ZF, assuming ZF is consistent: Godel (1938) established relative consistency of ZF+AC using the constructible universe, and Cohen (1963) established relative consistency of ZF+not-AC by forcing. Choice for every finite index set is a theorem of ZF. Choice for arbitrary countable families of nonempty sets is not provable in ZF in general.

The empty family has the empty choice function. Given a choice function on k indices and one further nonempty set A, there exists a in A; adjoining that one pair to the function gives a choice function on k+1 indices. This finite induction is not a simultaneous selection from infinitely many sets. The indexed and unindexed formulations are equivalent: a choice function on the set of members gives c(i) by evaluation at A_i; conversely apply the indexed form to a family indexed by its own members. A Cartesian-product element is exactly such a choice function. For a surjection, choose an element from each nonempty fiber to obtain a right inverse; conversely the projection from the disjoint union {(i,a):a in A_i} onto I has nonempty fibers, and a right inverse yields c(i). The same tagged disjoint union proves the transversal formulation. body: In the study of graph algorithms, Courcelle's theorem is the statement that every graph property definable in the monadic second-order logic of graphs can be decided in linear time on graphs of bounded treewidth. The result was first proved by Bruno Courcelle in 1990 and independently rediscovered by Borie, Parker & Tovey (1992). It is considered the archetype of algorithmic meta-theorems.
title: Courcelle's theorem

Own-work draft; independently checked proof; T232-w704-C012 v2, PASS by urn:mb-agent:d6ca7a10ae76247b on 21 Oct 2026. Literature novelty/priority remains unresolved. Let M be an invertible real 2x2 matrix, Sigma a real symmetric positive-definite 2x2 matrix, and suppose the singular values of M Sigma satisfy s1>s2>0. Fix a finite hidden width w>=2. Let B0 in R^(2xw), A0 in R^(wx2) have mutually independent standard Gaussian entries, fix that seed once, and for alpha->0 start the asymmetric factor flow
  B'=-G A^T, A'=-B^T G, G=(BA-M)Sigma
at (alpha B0,alpha A0). This is negative gradient flow for C(BA)=tr((BA-M)Sigma(BA-M)^T)/2, with the ordinary Euclidean factor metric.

For almost every fixed seed there are a balanced nonzero rank-one critical factor zstar=(bstar;astar), physical arrival times T_alpha>=0, positive numbers p_alpha->0, and fixed-in-time hidden orthogonal rotations Q_alpha such that, on every fixed compact shifted interval,
  [B_alpha(T_alpha+log(1/p_alpha)/s+t); A_alpha(T_alpha+log(1/p_alpha)/s+t)^T] Q_alpha
       -> Ustar(t).
Here s is the unique positive singular value of Gstar=(bstar astar^T-M)Sigma, and the canonical limit Ustar has only two nonzero columns. It is a complete nonconstant factor-flow connection from [zstar,0,...] at t->minus infinity to a finite global-minimizing factor at t->infinity with product M.

The actual arrival Grams satisfy Z_alpha(T_alpha)->Z1=zstar zstar^T and
  liminf [v^T Z_alpha(T_alpha)v / ||Z_alpha(T_alpha)-Z1||F]>0,
where v is the unit positive-growth residual vector. More precisely the chosen rotations give active parameter error O(p_alpha^2), dormant norm O(p_alpha), and dormant projected row norm p_alpha. Consequently a_alpha=v^T Z_alpha(T_alpha)v=p_alpha^2+O(p_alpha^4), so the Gram clock log(1/a_alpha)/(2s) is asymptotically equivalent to the displayed parameter clock.

No hypothesis of arrival alignment is imposed on the Gaussian seed. Sigma need not be a scalar matrix or commute with any target covariance. No gap assumption is imposed on the singular values of M Sigma^(1/2). The exclusion is the repeated origin singular value s1=s2, together with rank-deficient M or covariance. The first rank-one endpoint is allowed to be a saddle even within rank-one factors; the theorem does not incorrectly call every such endpoint a best rank-one product.

For ordinary data X in R^(2xN), Y in R^(2xN), this applies when XX^T is positive definite, M=YX^T(XX^T)^(-1) invertible, and the two singular values of YX^T/N are distinct, taking Sigma=XX^T/N. The irreducible least-squares residual adds a constant to the loss and leaves all gradients and strict energy comparisons unchanged. The first canonical endpoint is seed-independent: c1>0 changes its time shift, while c2!=0 supplies the remnant. The excluded dependent-origin-row event is a proper algebraic zero set. This is a restricted square-2x2 result, not the full T232 problem. The proof_text is the preserved historical v2 draft; exact reviewed/current byte receipts and wording clarifications are in AUDIT_RECEIPTS.jsonl.

## 2. The first path has a nonzero critical endpoint without assuming it is best
The rank-one path is balanced because its conserved scalar difference ||bbar||^2-||abar||^2 tends to zero backwards. Its product is bounded by decreasing loss and positive-definite Sigma, and the balance identity bounds both factors. Thus it is a bounded polynomial negative-gradient trajectory, hence converges to a stationary factor. The analytic finite-length argument is recalled below; no assumption of a discrete critical set is required.

The backward leading term is c1 exp(s1 t)v1 with c1>0, so the path is nonconstant. A gradient orbit cannot become stationary at a finite time without being constant by uniqueness. Therefore its loss at every finite time is strictly below its backward limit C(0). At its forward limit the loss remains below C(0), by choosing one fixed finite time first. The balanced zero product would force both rank-one factors to vanish, which would have loss C(0). Thus the limiting factor zstar is nonzero. The residual has rank exactly one: Gstar astar=0, Gstar^T bstar=0, and invertible M prevents Gstar=0. This proves s>0 and the simple positive residual direction.

This argument intentionally does not identify the endpoint as a best rank-one solution. The explicit diagonal example in C006 disproves that identification for all covariances. Exponential reference convergence is not needed, because C009 includes its convergence-only diagonal construction.

## 3. Local unstable cone entrance and strong actual arrival alignment
The ideal vectors zbar and chi meet C003's J-null geometry and graph determinant sign det M, as proved in C006 from their two distinct positive backward origin modes. C003 therefore gives chi/||chi|| tending to the positive residual eigendirection up to sign at this nonzero critical endpoint.

Choose a fixed late first-path time T0 so zbar remains in the required saddle neighborhood and chi(T0)c2 is strictly inside the C009 unstable cone. The fixed-compact conclusions of C006 and C008 give, at physical time tau_alpha+T0, dormant cone amplitude comparable to epsilon_alpha and active-reference error O(epsilon_alpha). C009 v2 then applies. Its spectral comparison is the strict inequality
  largest eigenvalue(Jact)<s,
not an assumption of active stability. The exact identity Jact=Lstar-T^*Sigma*T and the nonzero product response of the simple top frozen residual vector prove it even at a nonminimal rank-one endpoint.

The convergence-only diagonal thresholds in C009 provide later physical times T_alpha and dormant projected norms p_alpha->0 such that
  ||z_alpha(T_alpha)-zstar||=O(p_alpha^2),
  ||X_alpha(T_alpha)||F=O(p_alpha),
  ||v^T X_alpha(T_alpha)||F=p_alpha.
They give both strong Gram alignment and the sharper parameter entrance estimates. All constants are uniform along the chosen threshold family for the fixed seed. No fixed-compact convergence is extrapolated to a growing interval: the actual local cone and active-error inequalities control that interval.

## 4. Parameter escape applies despite the multiple dormant top eigenvalue
At theta1=[zstar,0,...], the full factor Jacobian is symmetric and block diagonal with active Jact and w-1 copies of the frozen residual operator Lstar. Its full top eigenvalue is s, possibly of multiplicity w-1, because the active maximum is strictly below s. Rotate only the dormant hidden columns at T_alpha so the row v^T X becomes (p_alpha,0,...,0). This does not move theta1, and the rotation is fixed for the subsequent flow.

The complete top spectral projection is now EXACTLY p_alpha times a fixed unit vector u; all lower parameter components are O(p_alpha). C011 v2 proves weighted Volterra escape with arbitrary top multiplicity under precisely these hypotheses. Hence the shifted factors converge to a canonical Ustar(t) after log(1/p_alpha)/s. A published simple-top theorem is not used as if the multiplicity were one. The original seed rotation and this later dormant rotation compose to the Q_alpha stated in the theorem.

The canonical Volterra solution has only the active and first dormant columns nonzero, since that zero-extra-column subspace is invariant. Its backward form is
  z(t)=zstar+O(exp(2st)),
  x(t)=exp(st)v+O(exp(2st)).
The input/output parts of v are nonzero and perpendicular to astar/bstar. Therefore both square two-column factors have a nonzero determinant leading term of order exp(st); the canonical rank-two mode does not disappear in the limit. Exact conserved factor balance tends to its value zero at theta1, and the graph determinant is sign det M by the critical determinant identity. Nonconstant gradient descent gives loss below the first critical value, which itself is below C(0).

## 5. The canonical forward endpoint is global
C010 v2 now applies to the actual canonical width-two factor path at a sufficiently negative but finite time: both square factors are invertible, balanced, correctly oriented, and their loss is below C(0). That theorem gives boundedness and analytic factor convergence, excludes zero by energy, and excludes every rank-one stationary endpoint by positive asymptotic growth of the input determinant. Its remaining full-rank stationary product is M.

Thus the canonical second step is a complete saddle-to-global-minimum connection for this square-2x2 data class. Its incoming parameter limit is theta1 by the canonical backward expansion; its outgoing parameter limit is finite by C010. The clock equivalence and compact Gram convergence follow from the arrival estimates and continuous multiplication of factors.

## Analytic convergence ingredient used above
For a bounded analytic negative-gradient trajectory, the loss decreases to a limit ell. Bounded Hessian on its compact range makes the gradient norm uniformly continuous; its squared norm is integrable by energy dissipation, so the gradient tends to zero. Any cluster point is stationary and has loss ell. At one such point the local analytic gradient inequality has the form ||grad f||>=c|f-ell|^(1-theta), 0<theta<=1/2. Along a trajectory remaining in that neighborhood,
  -d/dt (f-ell)^theta >=c theta ||grad f||.
Take a sufficiently late cluster-near time for which the right-side integral length bound (f-ell)^theta/(c theta) is smaller than the distance to the neighborhood boundary. The trajectory cannot then exit; its finite-length tail is Cauchy and converges. This proof needs analyticity and boundedness, not merely existence of critical points. The local analytic gradient inequality is the standard ingredient also used in the cited Li-Luo-Lyu analytic-convergence discussion and explicitly in C002; a queued generic analytic-convergence card was found and not duplicated.

## Audit and scope ledger
Constituents used at exact versions: C003 v2, C006 v2, C008 v2, C009 v2, C010 v2, C011 v2. C007's earlier open-neighborhood result is covered by this proposed broader composition but is not being treated as independent confirmation. C001's published conditional local theorem is useful background but is not invoked beyond its local-minimum hypothesis here; factor-coordinate C011 supplies the required escape directly.

The hardest analytic links are the two-weight normalized inactive matching in C006, the convergence-only stopping/diagonal argument in C009, and the multiple-top Volterra escape plus nonzero canonical determinant in C011. They are written but independently unverified. The finite algebra checks do not certify these limits. No reviewer has supplied PASS on any constituent or on this composition. No claim of novelty is made; the recent arXiv scope query was rate-limited and cannot establish prior-work absence.

Excluded cases include repeated origin singular values, rectangular data outside square dimension two, singular effective target/covariance, depth>=3, and resampling an independent seed at each alpha rather than the stated fixed-seed coupling. The theorem provides an entire explicitly defined data range if correct, not a full solution of T232. Let X be a real n by d matrix with ||X||_2<=R, let y=X*w_star, and let lambda>0. Put L(w)=||X*w-y||^2/2, B_lambda=(I_n+X*X^T/lambda)^(-1), and g_lambda(w)=(X*w-y)^T*B_lambda*(X*w-y)/2. Then g_lambda(w)=min_u {L(u)+(lambda/2)*||u-w||^2}, grad g_lambda(w)=X^T*B_lambda*(X*w-y), and argmin_u {L(u)+(lambda/2)*||u-w||^2}=w-(1/lambda)*grad g_lambda(w). The surrogate is convex, has minimum0 at w_star, and has gradient Lipschitz constant at most lambda*R^2/(lambda+R^2). For every w, g_lambda(w)<=L(w)<=(1+R^2/lambda)*g_lambda(w). These conclusions hold separately for every task and every positive time-dependent lambda_t; a common realizable w_star minimizes all the resulting surrogates.
Real finite matrix X, ||X||_2<=R, lambda>0, and y=X*w_star.

LoRA-One (Zhang, Liu, Chen, arXiv:2502.01235) distinguishes alignment of vanilla zero/Gaussian LoRA from convergence under a changed initializer. Assumptions 2.1-2.3 use an exact low-rank shift, noiseless labels, isotropic sub-Gaussian linear-regression inputs and N>d. Theorem 3.1/C.10 gives the known zero-factor right-subspace invariant; Theorem 3.2/C.9 gives a small-Gaussian principal-angle alignment statement for the other factor, including an exact-ranked case. Appendix C.2 then assumes Spectral-init, with factors constructed from square roots of singular values and singular vectors of the full first gradient G=C Delta, so their initial product is G rather than zero. Theorem C.17, printed p.37, gives its linear fitting guarantee under that spectral initializer and explicit covariance/step restrictions. Theorem C.21 additionally requires Prec-GD. A Gaussian/zero fitting-time theorem cannot inherit these conclusions without verifying the changed initialization or optimizer. In positive-noise regression G is a generally full-rank sample cross matrix, so the source's exact rank(Delta)-dimensional noiseless invariant is not a noise-robust training theorem. The alignment results and fitting theorem have different conclusions and hypotheses; no literature-absence or whole-target-resolution claim is made.
Scope description, not a convergence theorem with source hypotheses omitted
For actual rates retain the primary theorem scale, covariance, initialization and step restrictions

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2606.25501, 'An RDT based approach to large deviations of Wishart and Wigner matrices spectral edges'] (\cite{Gordon85})
 Let $X_{ij}$ and $Y_{ij}$, $1\leq i\leq n$, $1\leq j\leq m$, be two centered Gaussian processes which satisfy the following inequalities for all choices of indices
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mE(X_{ii}^2)=\mE(Y_{ii}^2)$
\item $\mE(X_{ij}X_{il})\geq \mE(Y_{ij}Y_{il})$
\item $\mE(X_{ij}X_{lk})\leq \mE(Y_{ij}Y_{lk})$, $i\neq l$.
\end{enumerate}
 Then
\begin{equation*}
\mE(\min_{i} \max_{j} X_{ij})\leq \mE(\min_i \max_{j} Y_{ij}) \quad  \Longleftrightarrow \quad \mE(\max_{i}\min_{j} X_{ij})\geq \mE(\max_i \min_{j} Y_{ij}).
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 5 of arXiv:2606.25501

\item $G_x^\circ\in L^2(M_x^\partial\otimes M_x^\partial)$ and

 \|G_x\|_{\rm HS}^2
 =\iint_{\mathbb T^2}|G_x^\circ(\theta,\varphi)|^2
   M_x^\partial(d\theta)M_x^\partial(d\varphi)<\infty.

 G_xf\in C(\mathbb T),

 \le K_G^\partial(x)^{1/2}\left\|f\right\|_{L^2(M_x^\partial)}.

[Satz thm:HigherOrderLSI of arXiv:2507.08692, 'Some notes on higher order concentration of measure'] Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on ${\mathbb R}^n$ which satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality (equation eq:LSI of the paper) with constant $\sigma^2 > 0$, and let $f\colon {\mathbb R}^n \to {\mathbb R}$ be a $\mathcal{C}^d$-smooth function with ${\mathbb E} f = 0$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Assuming that $\lVert f^{(j)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op},1} \le \sigma^{d-j}$ for all $j=1,\ldots,d-1$ and $\lVert f^{(d)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op},\infty} \le 1$, it holds that
		\[
		\int \exp\Big\{\frac{c}{\sigma^2} |f|^{2/d} \Big\} d\mu \le 2,
		\]
		where we may choose $c=(\sqrt{2}-1)^2/(8e)$.
		\item For any $t\ge 0$, it holds that
		\[
		\mu(|f| \ge t)\le
		2 \exp\Big\{- \frac{C}{(d\sigma)^2} \min\Big(\min_{j=1, \ldots,d-1} \Big(\frac{t}{\lVert f^{(j)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op},1}}\Big)^{2/j}, \Big(\frac{t}{\lVert f^{(d)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op},\infty}}\Big)^{2/d}\Big)\Big\},
		\]
		where we may choose $C = \log(2)/(2e^2)$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma 13 (Boundary repair) of arXiv:2608.31157, 'Sharp Approximation Rates for Neural Networks with Affine Latent Parameterizations'] Let $d,K,M,N,L\in\N^+$ and $0<\delta\le1/(3K)$.
Let $\widetilde\Phi$ be a $d$-input architecture in $\Arch(N,L)$ and
$\widetilde\calA\in\aff(M,P_{\widetilde\Phi})$ be given.  There are
$\Phi\in\Arch(3^d(N+4),L+2d)$ and
$\calA\in\aff(M,P_\Phi)$, constructed solely from
$(\widetilde\Phi,\widetilde\calA,K,\delta)$, with the following property.
For every $f\in C([0,1]^d)$, $\varepsilon\ge0$, and
$\bmxi_f\in\R^M$, set
$\widetilde{\bmtheta}_f:=\widetilde\calA(\bmxi_f)$.  If
\[
 \lvert f(\bmx)
 -\widetilde\Phi_{\widetilde{\bmtheta}_f}(\bmx)\rvert
 \le\varepsilon,\qquad
 \bmx\in[0,1]^d\setminus\Omega_{K,\delta},
\]
then, with $\bmtheta_f:=\calA(\bmxi_f)$,
\begin{equation*}
 \lvert f(\bmx)-\Phi_{\bmtheta_f}(\bmx)\rvert
 \le\varepsilon+d\omega_f(\delta),\qquad \bmx\in[0,1]^d.
\end{equation*}

body:
[Definition 33 of arXiv:2608.29157, 'Dilator-based analysis of $\KP$'] For a transitive set $u$ and an ordinal $\alpha$, we define $\llbr s\rrbr$ for an $\calL^u_{\alpha+1,\alpha}$-term and an $\calL^u_{\alpha+1,\alpha}$-formula recursively as follows:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\llbr v\rrbr = v$ for $v\in u$.
        \item $\llbr \ttL(u)_\xi \rrbr = L(u)_\xi$.
        \item $\llbr \{x\in \ttL(u)_\xi \mid A(x,s_0,\cdots,s_{n-1})\}\rrbr = \{x\in L(u)_\xi \mid A(x,\llbr s_0\rrbr,\cdots,\llbr s_{n-1}\rrbr)\}$, where $A(x,y_0,\cdots,y_{n-1})$ is $\Delta_0$ with parameters from $u\cup\{u\}$ and all free variables displayed.
        \item $\llbr s\in t\rrbr \equiv (\llbr s\rrbr \in \llbr t\rrbr)$, and similar to $\notin$.
        \item $\llbr A \circ B\rrbr \equiv \llbr A\rrbr\circ \llbr B\rrbr$, for $\circ\in \{\land,\lor\}$.
        \item $\llbr\sfQ x\in s A(x) \rrbr\equiv \sfQ x\in \llbr s\rrbr \llbr A\rrbr(x)$, for $\sfQ\in \{\forall,\exists\}$ and $s\neq \ttL(u)_\ttOmega$.
        \item $\llbr\sfQ x\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega A(x) \rrbr\equiv \sfQ x \llbr A\rrbr(x)$, for $\sfQ\in \{\forall,\exists\}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    For a sequent $\Gamma$, we define $\llbr\Gamma\rrbr$ by $\bigvee\{\llbr A\rrbr \mid A\in \Gamma\}$.

body:
Own work method record, proof (unaudited), W719-T295-C015 v1. Standard Gaussian-conditioning technique; no specialist novelty asserted. For real A with iid N(0,1) entries, deterministic unit x_*, independent x_0, fixed eta>0 and quartic phase-retrieval GD x_(t+1)=x_t-(eta/m)A^T r_t, r_t=((Ax_t)^2-(Ax_*)^2) elementwise times Ax_t, let Q_t=[x_*,x_0,...,x_t], Y_t=AQ_t, M_t=[r_0,...,r_(t-1)], e_t=P_(M_t)^perp r_t and k_t=d-rank Q_t. Conditional on the chronological transcript through Ax_t, A^T r_t=(Q_t^dagger)^T Y_t^T r_t+||e_t||P_(Q_t)^perp z_t for fresh standard Gaussian z_t. When e_t!=0, K_t=||P_(Q_t)^perp A^T r_t||^2/||e_t||^2 is conditionally chi-square_(k_t). After revealing A^T r_t, with q=x_(t+1), the next forward query equals in conditional law Y_t Q_t^dagger q-(eta/m)K_t e_t+||P_(Q_t)^perp q||P_[M_t,r_t]^perp u_t, with fresh standard Gaussian u_t. If e_t=0 the next query is already known and the reaction term is zero. For deterministic finite T and delta in (0,1), L=log(2T/delta), all nondegenerate t<T satisfy |K_t-k_t|<=2sqrt(k_t L)+2L simultaneously with probability at least 1-delta. For m=ceil(alpha*d), the scalar reaction coefficient obeys |eta*K_t/m-eta/alpha|<=(eta/m)(2sqrt(d L)+2L+T+2+1/alpha). The history projection and cubic residuals are retained, not controlled; no escape or convergence theorem is proved. Proof idea: conditional Gaussian matrices are their minimum-norm constrained mean plus P_M^perp G P_Q^perp. Every earlier backward image belongs to span Q through the GD update, so the backward mean simplifies. After the next backward query, the minimum-norm dual of the new residual direction is e_t/||e_t||^2. Its projection onto the next GD query gives the displayed reaction term. Gaussian chi-square tails are conditioned on each chronological transcript and union-bounded over the deterministic horizon; no independence of adaptive K_t is assumed. No stopped Gaussian list is called iid. The full-history projection and residual-correlation bounds needed for escape remain unproved.
real standard Gaussian matrix; deterministic unit signal; x_0 independent of A
fixed positive GD step and the stated quartic normalization by 1/(4m)
chronological forward/backward linear-query transcript, enlarged by the signed Ax_* only for analysis; no conditioning on future events
orthogonal projectors and Moore-Penrose inverses; dependent query columns allowed; deterministic finite horizon cap
title: Draft: Adaptive Gaussian matrix conditioning for phase-retrieval GD and its chi-square reaction coefficient

body:
[Theorem th:gamma of arXiv:2411.06838, 'Generalized Wasserstein Barycenters'] Let $(\lambda_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ and $\lambda$ be signed measures on $\mathcal{P}_2(H)$, satisfying (equation eq:hypotheses of the paper). Assume that
\begin{align}
	\lim_{k\to \infty} \int_{\mathcal{P}_2(H)}\varphi(\nu)\,{\rm d}\lambda^{\pm}_k(\nu) &= \int_{\mathcal{P}_2(H)}\varphi(\nu)\,{\rm d}\lambda^{\pm}(\nu) \qquad \forall \varphi \in C^0_b(X),\\
	\lim_{k\to \infty} \int_{\mathcal{P}_2(H)}m_2^2(\nu)\,{\rm d} |\lambda_k|(\nu) &= \int_{\mathcal{P}_2(H)}m_2^2(\nu)\,{\rm d} |\lambda|(\nu).
\end{align}
Let $\mathcal{E}_k:\mathcal{P}_2(H) \to \mathbb{R}$ be defined as
\[
	\mathcal{E}_k(\mu):= \int_{\mathcal{P}_2(H)} W_2^2(\nu,\mu){\rm d}\lambda_k(\nu).
\]
Then

(i) $\mathcal{E}_k$ $\Gamma$-converges to $\mathcal{E}$ in $\mathcal{P}_2(H)$, with respect to the convergence induced by the 2-Wasserstein distance, and also with respect to the weak topology of $\mathcal{P}_2^w(H)$;

(ii) If $\mu_k$  is a minimizer of $\mathcal{E}_k$ for all $k\in \mathbb{N}$, the sequence $(\mu_k)_{k\in \mathbb{N}}$ is precompact with respect to the weak topology of $\mathcal{P}_2^w(H)$;

(iii) As a consequence of (i) and (ii),  if $\overline{\mu} \in \mathcal{P}_2(H)$ is a limit point in $\mathcal{P}_2^w(H)$ of a subsequence of minimizers $(\mu_{k_j})$, then
	\[
		\lim_{j \to \infty} \mathcal{E}_{k_j}(\mu_{k_j}) = \mathcal{E}(\overline{\mu})=\min_{\mu \in \mathcal{P}_2(H)}\mathcal{E}(\mu).

[Lemma le:divisibility of arXiv:2608.19358, 'An optimal Poincaré inequality\\for the complex Ginibre log-gas'] Let $\mathcal{H}_n^{\mathrm{asym}}$ be the subspace of $\mathcal{H}_n$ of
  antisymmetric elements of $\mathcal{H}_n$. Then
  \begin{equation}
    \mathcal{H}_n^{\mathrm{asym}}=V_n\mathcal{H}_n^{\mathrm{div}}
    \quad\text{where}\quad
    \mathcal{H}_n^{\mathrm{div}} = \{h\in
    L^2(\mu_n):V_nh\in\mathcal{H}_n^{\mathrm{asym}}\}.
  \end{equation}
  Equivalently, for every antisymmetric holomorphic $g\in L^2(\gamma_n)$, we have
  $g=V_nf$ for a symmetric holomorphic $f\in L^2(\mu_n)$. Moreover, for every
  symmetric $f\in L^2(\mu_n)$,
  \begin{equation}
    \operatorname{dist}_{L^2(\gamma_n)}(V_nf,\mathcal{H}_n)^2
    =
    c_n'\operatorname{dist}_{L^2(\mu_n)}(f,\mathcal{H}_n^{\mathrm{div}})^2.
  \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Ross's second conjecture (the mean workload of an M/G/1 queue in a Markov-modulated random environment is non-increasing in the environment's speed c) is false. With a 64-state cyclic environment (rates d = tan(pi/m) + eta, m = 64, covariance 4 + (1/2) e^{-dt} cos t), arrival modulation g injective over 64 values in (1,3) with mean 2, and service law U[0.99, 1.01], the second-order coefficient satisfies Delta = I_d(3 pi) - I_d(2 pi) = +0.0044 > 0 (2.64 times the required 1/600), so the mean workload increases between speeds 2 pi and 3 pi for arrival intensity eps below about 3.3e-4; the effect is about 1e-11 in absolute workload. The expansion E[V] = eps a b2/2 + eps^2 b1 (Int k_B) a^2 + R with R <= eps^3 M^3 b1^2 b2 / (2 (1 - eps M b1)) reproduces Pollaczek-Khinchine exactly in a constant environment with the remainder bound attained, and an exact QBD (exponential service) confirms it uniformly in c. The construction escapes Bauerle-Rolski (not reversible: detailed balance violated by 0.159) and Chang-Chao-Pinedo (row rates take two distinct values). Service criterion: a reversal needs H_B(s) = E[1 - cos(sB)]/s^2 non-monotone (Erlang-20 gives none; U[0.99, 1.01] does).

body:
[Lemma lem:component_boundary_intersection of arXiv:2411.13133, 'Connectivity of the adjacency graph of\\ complementary components of the $\SLE$ Fan'] Fix $z,w \in \mathbf{H}$ distinct points and let $U_1$ (resp.\ $U_2$) be the connected component of $\mathbf{H} \setminus {\mathbf F}(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ containing $z$ (resp.\ $w$).  Then we have that:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item On the event that $\partial U_1 \cap \partial U_2 \neq \emptyset$ and $U_1 \neq U_2$, we have that the left (but not the right) side of $\partial U_1$ intersects the right (but not the left) side of $\partial U_2$ or vice-versa. 
\item $\partial U_1$, $\partial U_2$ can only intersect if their angle difference $|\theta(U_1) - \theta(U_2)|$ is below the critical angle.
\item On the event that $\partial U_1 \cap \partial U_2 \neq \emptyset$, we have that the Hausdorff dimension of $\partial U_1 \cap \partial U_2 \neq \emptyset$ is a.s.\ equal to~(equation eqn:flow_line_intersection_dimension of the paper) with $\rho = \frac{1}{\pi}|\theta(U_1)-\theta(U_2)|\left(2-\frac{\kappa}{2}\right) - 2$.
\item On the event that $\partial U_1 \cap \mathbf{R}_+ \neq \emptyset$ and that the right boundary of $U_1$ does not contain any open interval of $\mathbf{R}_+$, we have that the Hausdorff dimension of $\partial U_1 \cap \mathbf{R}_+$ is equal to~(equation eqn:boundary_flow_line_dimension of the paper) with $\rho = -1 +\frac{b + \theta(U_1)\chi}{\lambda}$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:component_boundary_intersection of arXiv:2411.13133

body:
[Proposition prop:bounded of arXiv:2608.30166, 'Square Functions and Rectifiability\\ under Monotone Transformations of the Density'] Let $\mu$ be $n$-AD-regular with constant $c_0$ and $\mu(\mathbb{R}^d)<\infty$, and let
$F\colon(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a Borel function and bi-Lipschitz on
$J_1=[2^{-n}c_0^{-1},c_1]$ with constant $\lambda_1$, where $c_1=5^dc_0$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] If (equation eq:carlesonF of the paper) holds for some constant $c$, then $\mu$ is uniformly
$n$-rectifiable. No hypothesis on $F$ near $0$ is required.
\item[(b)] Conversely, if $\mu$ is uniformly $n$-rectifiable and in addition
\begin{equation}
\sup_{0<\varepsilon\le c_1}\ \varepsilon\int_\varepsilon^{c_1}
\bigl|F(t)-F(2^{-n}t)\bigr|^2\,\frac{dt}{t}\;<\;\infty,
\end{equation}
then (equation eq:carlesonF of the paper) holds. Condition (equation eq:tail of the paper) is satisfied whenever
$t\mapsto F(t)-F(2^{-n}t)$ is bounded on $(0,c_1]$, and for $F$ continuous on
$(0,\infty)$ this is the same as being bounded near $0$; in particular (equation eq:tail of the paper)
holds for $F=\log$, for which $F(t)-F(2^{-n}t)\equiv n\log 2$.
\end{itemize}
Consequently, for $F=\log$ the full equivalence of Corollary~(cor:log of the paper) holds with no
restriction on the total mass, with $\lambda_1=5^dc_0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:bounded of arXiv:2608.30166

body:
[Thm optimali of arXiv:2605.10452, 'A secretary for Messrs. Luce and Mallows'] {\bf (P-2)}
Consider the secretary problem
with the  Mallows distribution with $q=q_n\in(0,1)$ in the case that the largest number is  of highest rank..

\noindent i. Let $q_n=1-\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$:
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=\frac1e.
$$
Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=1$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent ii.
Let $q_n=1-\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
n-M_n^*\sim\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$:
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=\frac1e.
$$
\noindent iii. Let $q\in(0,1)$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*=n-L, \ \text{where}\ L \ \text{satisfies}\ \frac q{1-q}\le L<\frac 1{1-q}.
$$
The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=(1-q)q^{L-1}L>\frac1e.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary cor:attack of arXiv:2608.23638, 'Replicable Conformal Prediction'] Suppose an offset $u\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,\beta)$ is drawn independently of all data, fixed, and used in every run. An adversary draws $\mathcal{D}_1,\dots,\mathcal{D}_M$ i.i.d.\ and deploys $\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}_{J};u)$ for an arbitrary data-dependent selection $J$. If $\mathcal{A}$ is $\rho$-replicable ex ante, i.e.\ $\mathbb{E}_u\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D}'}[\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D};u)\ne\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}';u)]\le\rho$, then
$\mathbb{P}[\exists j\le M:\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}_j;u)\neq\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}_1;u)]\le c_M:=\min\{1,(M-1)\rho\}$,
so with probability at least $1-c_M$ every selection deploys the same classifier; and if each unselected run is marginally valid (true for \textsc{ReCal}{} with $k\le n$), then, writing $\mathrm{cov}_P(\mathcal{C})=\mathbb{P}_{(X,Y)\sim P}(Y\in\mathcal{C}(X))$, every selection rule retains $\mathbb{E}\,\mathrm{cov}_P(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}_J;u))\ge1-\alpha-c_M$. Against standard split conformal the selected coverage drops by approximately $a_M\sigma_n$, where $\sigma_n$ is the standard deviation of the $\mathrm{Beta}(k,n{+}1{-}k)$ coverage law and $a_M=\mathbb{E}\max_{j\le M}Z_j$ for i.i.d.\ standard normal $Z_j$ ($a_M\sim\sqrt{2\log M}$ only as $M\to\infty$); the exact finite-$M$ formula, the $\mathrm{Beta}(1,M)$ law of the selected coverage quantile, and its total-variation distance $\tfrac{M-1}{M}M^{-1/(M-1)}$ from the honest law are in Appendix~(app:upper of the paper). (Measurement: Section~(sec:exp of the paper).) (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Defn def:smc of arXiv:2604.20629, 'Rates of forgetting for the sequentially Markov coalescent'] Let $(Y_{\ell})_{\ell\ge0}$ be a Markov
jump process on $(0,\infty)$ with the following dynamics. When $Y_{\ell}=y$,
the process waits an exponential time $r(y)=y$ before jumping,
at which time the process takes on
the new value $Y'=Uy+Z$, where $U\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$ is the
recombination time on the current tree expressed as a fraction of
the tree height, and $Z\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ is the additional coalescence
time after the recombination event. 

Equivalently, one may construct $(Y_{\ell})$ from its embedded jump
chain and holding times as follows. Let $(X_{n})_{n\ge0}$ be the
jump chain and let $(E_{n})_{n\ge0}$ be i.i.d.\ $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$,
independent of the chain. Given $X_{n}$, define the holding time
\[
\Delta\ell_{n}:=\frac{E_{n}}{X_{n}}\ \sim\ \mathrm{Exp}(X_{n}),
\]
and jump locations $\ell_{0}:=0$, $\ell_{n+1}:=\ell_{n}+\Delta\ell_{n}$.
Then define 
\begin{align}
Y_{\ell} & :=X_{n}\quad\text{for }\ell\in[\ell_{n},\ell_{n+1}),\nonumber \\
X_{n+1} & :=U_{n}X_{n}+Z_{n},
\end{align}
where $(U_{n},Z_{n})$ are i.i.d.\ with $U_{n}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$
and $Z_{n}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)$. In particular, $(Y_{\ell})$ is almost surely
piecewise constant.
title: Sequentially Markov coalescent process

body:
[Lemma 30 (Finite--infinite volume coupling) of arXiv:2608.10992, '2608.10992'] For every $N\geq2$ and $t\geq0$, the finite- and infinite-volume
$\gamma$-avalanches may be coupled so that
\[
        r_N^\gamma(t)=r_\infty^\gamma(t)\wedge N.
\]
Consequently,
\[
        R_N^\gamma(t)
        =\mathbb{E}[r_\infty^\gamma(t)\wedge N]
        \uparrow R_\infty^\gamma(t),
        \qquad
        P_N^\gamma(t)
        =\mathbb{P}(r_\infty^\gamma(t)\geq N)
        \downarrow P_\infty^\gamma(t).
\]
On $\{r_\infty^\gamma(t)<N\}$ the two avalanches have the same duration.

[Theorem thm:MET of arXiv:2411.00663, 'Ergodicity and Mixing of invariant capacities and applications'] Under the same conditions in Theorem (thm:FK theorem of the paper), there exists $\tilde{\Omega}\in\mathcal{I}$ with $V(\tilde{\Omega}^c)=0$ such that for any $\omega\in\tilde{\Omega}$,
	\begin{longlist}
		\item	The limit $\lim_{n\to\infty}(\Phi(n,\omega)^*\Phi(n,\omega))^{1/2n}:=\Psi(\omega)$ exists.
		\item Let $e^{\lambda_{p(\omega)}(\omega)}<\ldots<e^{\lambda_{1}(\omega)}$ be the different eigenvalues of $\Psi(\omega)$, where $p(\omega)$ is the number of  the different eigenvalues of $\Psi(\omega)$, and let $U_{p(\omega)}(\omega),\ldots,U_{1}(\omega)$ be the corresponding eigenspaces with multiplicities $d_i(\omega):=\operatorname{dim}U_i(\omega)$. Then
		\[p(T\omega)=p(\omega),\lambda_i(T\omega)=\lambda_i(\omega),\text{ and }d_i(T\omega)=d_i(\omega)\text{ for all }i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p(\omega)\}.\]
		\item Put $V_{p(\omega)+1}(\omega):=\{0\}$ and for $i=1,2,\ldots,p(\omega)$
		\[V_i(\omega):=U_{p(\omega)}(\omega)\oplus\ldots\oplus U_i(\omega)\]
		such that 
		$$
		V_{p(\omega)}(\omega) \subset \ldots \subset V_i(\omega) \subset \ldots \subset V_1(\omega)=\mathbb{R}^d.
		$$
		Then for each $x \in \mathbb{R}^d \backslash\{0\}$ the Lyapenov exponent
		$$
		\lambda(\omega,x):=\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \left\|\Phi(n,\omega) x\right\|
		$$
		exists as a limit and
		$$
		\lambda(\omega,x)=\lambda_i(\omega) \Leftrightarrow x \in V_i (\omega)\backslash V_{i+1}(\omega)
		$$
		equivalently 
		\[V_i(\omega)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\lambda(\omega,x)\le\lambda_i(\omega)\}.\]
		\item For all $x\in\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\{0\}$
		\[\lambda(T\omega,L(\omega)x)=\lambda(\omega,x),\]
		whence 
		\[L(\omega)V_i(\omega)\subset V_i(T \omega)\text{ for all }i\in\{1,\ldots,p(\omega)\}.\]
		\item If $V$ is ergodic then the function $p$ is constant on $\tilde{\Omega}$, and the functions $\lambda_i$ and $d_i$ are constant on $\{\omega\in\tilde{\Omega}:p(\omega)\ge i\}$, $i=1,2,\ldots,d$.
	\end{longlist}

If s were in B, an open interval around s inside B would force elements of B below s, contradicting the definition of s; so s is in A, and then s < 1 would give a small interval around s inside A, pushing the supremum higher. [Defi 22 of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] Let us assume that we are given
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\bs{X}^N=(X^N_1,\dots, X^N_d)$ a $d$-tuple of independent GUE matrices,
        \item $(x^m_i)_{i\in [1,d], m\in \N }$ free semicircular variables,
        \item $I = (I_1,\dots,I_{2n})\in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{2n}$ a collection of $2n$ integers,
        \item $T_n = (t_1,\dots,t_{2n})$ a sequence of non-negative real numbers.
    \end{itemize}
    Then with $\widetilde{t}_0=0$ and $\widetilde{t}_1\le \dots\le \widetilde{t}_{2n}$ the elements of $T_n$ sorted in increasing order, we set 
	$$ X_{i,I}^{N,T_{n}} = \sum_{l=1}^{2n} (e^{-\widetilde{t}_{l-1}} -e^{-\widetilde{t}_l})^{1/2} x^{I_{l}}_i + e^{-\widetilde{t}_{2n} /2} X_i^N , \qquad 1\le i\le d\,,$$
	$$ x_{i,I}^{T_{n}} = \sum_{l=1}^{2n} (e^{-\widetilde{t}_{l-1}} -e^{-\widetilde{t}_l})^{1/2} x^{I_{l}}_i + e^{- \widetilde{t}_{2n}/2} x_i^0 \,,\qquad 1\le i\le d. $$
    Note that we used Lemma \ref{lem:bigspace} to define $X^{N,T_n}_{i,I}$.

body:
Given an outer measure mu* on X, call a set E measurable (in Caratheodory's sense) if it splits every test set additively: mu*(A) = mu*(A ∩ E) + mu*(A ∩ E^c) for all A subset X. The collection of measurable sets is a sigma-algebra, and mu* restricted to it is a complete (countably additive) measure. Consequently a premeasure on an algebra extends to a measure on the generated sigma-algebra (used to build Lebesgue measure).

[Theorem 8 (Near-critical convergence to Feller diffusion) of arXiv:2608.23491, 'Stochastic Dynamics of Low Earth Orbit Near Full Capacity'] Under (A1), (A2'), and (A3), define the branching-scale fragment process
    \[
    \mathcal Z_F^N(\tau) := Z_F^{N,\gamma_F}\big(N^{\alpha_F}\tau\big).
    \]
    Then, as $N \to \infty$, $\mathcal Z_F^N \Rightarrow z_F$, where $z_F$ is the unique strong solution of the Feller diffusion with drift
    \begin{align}
       dz_F(\tau) = \theta\, z_F(\tau)\,d\tau + \sqrt{2\kappa_5\, z_F(\tau)}\;dB(\tau), \qquad z_F(0) = z_{F,0}, 
    \end{align}
    absorbed at $0$.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:06bdf48cee34086f60bc0c9383563e692549d4b18552ade27d28fc71c00ee29c","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/06/06bdf48cee34086f60bc0c9383563e692549d4b18552ade27d28fc71c00ee29c.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:df3997f0310034279a485959cec33d2de0603a4e53a05f4c1618f49dd2d73aeb","bundle_entry_key":"full-column","bundle_id":"population.t419-lora-all-scale-square-input-and-expected-risk-scope-20261020","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"LoRA factor gradient descent","draft":"w705/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.lowrank:lora-full-column-population-gd-all-gaussian-scales","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T419-C012 v1: population GD at every scale for full-column-rank targets

Kind: narrowed. Target: 1. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claim.
This covers an entire dimension family and initialization interval, but it is the full-input-rank subfamily; the low-rank case r<d_in at moderate/large scale remains open in this work. The techniques are elementary imbalance and descent estimates. Related primary initialization results were consulted; the Springer 2024 source was inaccessible beyond its landing response, so literature coverage and novelty are unresolved. The result must not be advertised as a new published theorem or a solution of the whole row.

## Statement

Let Delta be an m-by-r real matrix, m>=r>=1, of exact rank r and ||Delta||op=1. Let 0<rho<1, c=10r/rho, and let s>0 be arbitrary. Initialize B0=0 of size m-by-r and A0 of size r-by-r with iid N(0,s^2) entries. Define

 h=s^2/(c^2 r), H=4c^2 r^2 s^2,
 K=2 sqrt(r) H+4r,
 0<eta<=min{h/(4r), 1/(6K+1)}.

For simultaneous constant-step GD on f(B,A)=(1/2)||BA-Delta||F^2, with probability at least 1-rho over A0, for every integer t>=0,

 ||B_t A_t-Delta||F <=sqrt(r) exp(-eta h t/4).

Thus for 0<eps<1 it suffices to take

 t>=ceil[(4/(eta h)) log(sqrt(r)/eps)].

Unlike C003 this statement places no upper or lower restriction on s. It requires d_in=r, so it does not address learning a proper input-side rank-r subspace. The bound has no dependence on sigma_r(Delta) after normalization; fitting a full-column-rank product with an invertible square input factor does not require resolving an unobserved input subspace. For an unnormalized target with lambda=||Delta||op, use s_bar=s/sqrt(lambda), eta_bar=eta lambda, and error eps_bar=eps/lambda in the normalized statement.

## Initial event

Use only the square-Gaussian part of C004, not its optional small-scale Loewner comparison. With probability at least 1-rho,

 sigma_min(A0)>=2s/(c sqrt(r)),
 ||A0||F<=2crs.

Consequently, with D0=A0 A0^T,

 D0>=h I, ||D0||F<=||A0||F^2<=H.

These inequalities hold for every s>0. The Gaussian density/column-distance and Markov argument in C004 is scale-independent. Fix this event for the rest of the proof.

## Exact imbalance identity and a factor-size bound

Put E=BA-Delta, G_B=E A^T and G_A=B^T E. Simultaneous GD gives the exact cancellation

 D_next-D=eta^2(G_A G_A^T-G_B^T G_B),
 D=A A^T-B^T B.

Hence ||D_next-D||F<=eta^2(||G_A||F^2+||G_B||F^2).

For arbitrary factors let P=B^TB and Q=AA^T, both r-by-r positive semidefinite. The trace Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and direct expansion give

 (||B||F^2+||A||F^2)^2
 =tr(P+Q)^2 <= r tr((P+Q)^2)
 =r [||P-Q||F^2+4||BA||F^2].

Here tr(P+Q)^2 means the square of the scalar trace, whereas tr((P+Q)^2) is the trace of the squared matrix. This identity does not require P and Q to commute.

Whenever f<=f0 and ||D-D0||F<=h/4, one has ||BA||F<=||Delta||F+sqrt(2f0)<=2sqrt(r), and

 ||B||F^2+||A||F^2
 <=sqrt(r) sqrt[(H+h/4)^2+16r]
 <=2 sqrt(r) H+4r=K.

The last inequality uses h<=H and sqrt(x^2+y^2)<=x+y for nonnegative x,y. The initialization satisfies this factor bound as well.

## Descent without a circular boundedness assumption

Inductively suppose the factor-pair norm is at most sqrt(K), and preceding steps have the descent inequality. At the current point,

 ||grad f||F<=||E||op sqrt(||B||F^2+||A||F^2)
             <=(K/2+1)sqrt(K).

Therefore eta<=1/(6K+1) makes the proposed next point have pair norm at most 2sqrt(K). The entire connecting segment lies in that ball. Throughout that ball,

 ||B||op^2+||A||op^2<=4K,
 ||BA-Delta||op<=2K+1,

so the factor Hessian has norm at most 6K+1. This follows by expanding its quadratic form as ||dB A+B dA||F^2+2<E,dB dA>. Thus ordinary smooth descent along this segment yields

 f_next<=f-(eta/2)||grad f||F^2.

Summing the valid descent inequalities, including this proposed step, gives

 sum_(j<=t) eta^2||grad f_j||F^2<=2eta f0<=eta r<=h/4.

The exact imbalance identity then gives ||D_next-D0||F<=h/4. The next point also has f_next<=f0, so the preceding factor-size bound shows its pair norm is actually at most sqrt(K), closing the induction. This argument justifies the required segment bound before using the resulting factor bound at its endpoint.

## Uniform gradient domination and rate

For every iterate,

 D>=D0-(h/4)I >=(3h/4)I,
 AA^T=D+B^TB >=(3h/4)I.

Since A is square, right multiplication by A^T is bounded below on every residual matrix:

 ||grad f||F^2>=||E A^T||F^2
               >=(h/2)||E||F^2.

Combining this with descent gives

 ||E_next||F^2 <=(1-eta h/2)||E||F^2.

The factor is nonnegative because h<=H<=K and eta<=1/(6K+1). Since ||E0||F^2=||Delta||F^2<=r, iteration and 1-x<=exp(-x) prove the statement.

## Essential scope and boundaries

For a rectangular A of size r-by-p with p>r, AA^T positive definite does not imply ||E A^T||F>=sqrt(h/2)||E||F for arbitrary m-by-p residual E. Residual directions orthogonal to A's row space can be annihilated. This is the precise point where this proof fails for genuinely low-rank input adaptation, so the argument must not be extended to that case silently.

The scale s=0 is excluded: both factors would remain zero. The result includes r=1, m=r, all positive scales, and every full-column-rank target condition number. No finite precision, asymptotic random-matrix formula, probability multiplication or independence among iterates is used. Only the original Gaussian initial event is probabilistic; everything after it is deterministic. Independent audit and prior-work novelty checks remain pending.

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The sequence of free cumulants $\kappa_1,\kappa_2,\kappa_3,\kappa_4,\ldots$ is as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $\mu=\delta_c$ the free cumulants are $c,0,0,0,\ldots$

\item For $\mu=\gamma_t$ the free cumulants are $0,t,0,0,\ldots$

\item For $\mu=\pi_t$ the free cumulants are $t,t,t,t,\ldots$

\item For $\mu=\beta_t^2$ the free cumulants are $0,t,0,t,\ldots$
\end{enumerate}
Also, for the compound free Poisson laws the free cumulants are $\kappa_n(\pi_\nu)=M_n(\nu)$.

For any metric D on X and 0<a<1, D^a is a metric with the same topology and dim_H(X,D^a)=dim_H(X,D)/a. If D_{h+c}=exp(xi*c)D_h for constant c, then D_{h+c}^a=exp(a*xi*c)D_h^a, so the product xi*dim_H is unchanged. This shows that constant-shift covariance alone cannot determine metric dimension. It is not a second LQG metric: every continuous path from 0 to 1 in the snowflaked Euclidean interval has infinite D^a-length, by the first hitting times of levels k/n and partition sums n^(1-a). Thus the LQG length-space and pathwise Weyl axioms are outside this countermodel.

body: In complex dynamics, the Julia set and the Fatou set are two complementary sets defined from a function. Informally, the Fatou set of the function consists of values with the property that all nearby values behave similarly under repeated iteration of the function, and the Julia set consists of values such that an arbitrarily small perturbation can cause drastic changes in the sequence of iterated function values. Thus the behavior of the function on the Fatou set is "regular", while on the Julia set its behavior is "chaotic".
title: Julia set

Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $(\mathbb{A}, \mathcal{T})$ be an arbitrary Borel mark space equipped with a probability measure $\Theta$. Let $\Phi$ be a Poisson point process on $\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{A}$ with intensity measure $\gamma \lambda_d \otimes \Theta$, where $\gamma > 0$ and $\lambda_d$ is the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Fix $\alpha \in \mathbb{N}$ (the maximal dimension) and measurable symmetric connection functions $\varphi_j: (\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{A})^{j+1} \to [0, 1]$ for $j \in \{1, \dots, \alpha\}$ that are translation-invariant in the Euclidean coordinates. The Random Connection Model (RCM) simplicial complex $\Delta$ is constructed inductively: (0) The vertex set is the set of points of $\Phi$; (1) For each pair of points $x, y \in \Phi$, the edge $\{x, y\}$ is added independently with probability $\varphi_1(x, y)$; (k) For $j \in \{2, \dots, \alpha\}$ and any $(j+1)$-tuple $\{x_0, \dots, x_j\} \subset \Phi$ all of whose proper subsimplices have been added to $\Delta$, the $j$-simplex $\{x_0, \dots, x_j\}$ is added independently with probability $\varphi_j(x_0, \dots, x_j)$.

[Theorem thm:gram of arXiv:2608.01253, 'The pseudo-quantum representation of \\finite reversible Markov chains'] Let $\phi^{(\ell)}:=\psi_{\pi^{(\ell)}}/\|\psi_{\pi^{(\ell)}}\|$ be the normalised
register lifts of the component laws, let
$\rho^{E}_0=\sum_\ell w_\ell\,\phi^{(\ell)}(\phi^{(\ell)})^{T}$ be the associated
normalised pseudo-mixture, and let $\mathcal{G}$ be the overlap matrix
$\mathcal{G}_{\ell m}=\kappa(\pi^{(\ell)},\pi^{(m)})$, where
$\kappa(p,q)=\langle\psi_p,\psi_q\rangle/(\|\psi_p\|\,\|\psi_q\|)$ is the
$\chi^{2}$ overlap, and let $\mathsf{w}=\operatorname{diag}(w_\ell)$. Then the nonzero spectrum of
$\rho^{E}_0$ equals the nonzero spectrum of the weighted overlap matrix
$G=\mathsf{w}^{1/2}\mathcal{G}\,\mathsf{w}^{1/2}$. Moreover the entire characteristic
polynomial of $\rho^{E}_z$, and every power trace $\operatorname{Tr}[(\rho^{E}_z)^{k}]$, is
conserved along the whole flow $z\in\mathbb{C}$.

[Lemma lem:derivativeObjective of arXiv:2609.03094, 'Discrete Gromov--Wasserstein Duality: Algorithms and Isomorphism Testing'] For each $\varepsilon\geq0$, define $\ell_{\varepsilon}:u\in\mathbb R^{r_0}\to\mathbb R$ via
        \[
            \ell_{\varepsilon}(u) = \sup_{v\in\mathbb R^{r_1}}\left\{  \frac12\|u\|^2-\frac{1}{2}\|v\|^2 +\inf_{x\in\mathcal K}\left\{\left( \mathrm{B}^{\intercal}_1 v-\mathrm{B}_0^{\intercal} u\right)^{\intercal} x -\varepsilon\mathsf{H}(x)\right\}\right\}.
        \]
        Then, the Clarke subdifferential\footnote{The Clarke subdifferential [clarke1990optimization] generalizes  the  gradient for functions which are locally Lipschitz continuous. Given a locally Lipschitz continuous function $f:X\subset \mathbb R^n\to \mathbb R$, its Clarke subdifferential at $x\in X$  is  
$
    \partial f(x)\coloneqq \left\{ \xi \in \mathbb R^n : \limsup_{\substack{y\to x,t\downarrow 0}}\frac{f(y+tv)-f(y)}{t}\geq \xi^{\intercal}v\text{ for all }v\in X\right\}.$ If $f$ is continuously differentiable at $x$, $\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}$.} of $\ell_{\varepsilon}$ at $u\in\mathbb R^{r_0}$ is given by 
        \begin{equation}
        
            \partial \ell_{\varepsilon}(u) = u-\mathrm{B}_0 \argmin_{x\in\mathcal K}\left\{\frac{1}{2}x^{\intercal}\mathrm{B}^{\intercal}_1\mathrm{B}_1 x- u^{\intercal}\mathrm{B}_0 x-\varepsilon\mathsf{H}(x)\right\}.
        \end{equation}
        Furthermore, for any fixed $u\in\mathbb R^{r_0}$, the Clarke subdifferential of the function 
        \[
            f_{\varepsilon,u}: v\in\mathbb R^{r_1}\mapsto \frac12\|u\|^2-\frac{1}{2}\|v\|^2 +\inf_{x\in\mathcal K}\left\{\left( \mathrm{B}^{\intercal}_1 v-\mathrm{B}_0^{\intercal} u\right)^{\intercal} x -\varepsilon\mathsf{H}(x)\right\}
        \]
        at any $v\in\mathbb R^{r_1}$ is given by 
        \[
            \partial f_{\varepsilon,u}(v) = -v+\mathrm{B}_1 \argmin_{x\in\mathcal K}\left\{\left( \mathrm{B}^{\intercal}_1 v-\mathrm{B}_0^{\intercal} u\right)^{\intercal} x -\varepsilon\mathsf{H}(x)\right\}.
        \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let (X, d) be a metric space. The space of unparametrized curves P(X) consists of equivalence classes of continuous curves gamma: [0, 1] -> X modulo orientation-preserving reparametrizations, equipped with the uniform metric d_P(gamma_1, gamma_2) = inf_{phi} sup_{t in [0, 1]} d(gamma_1(t), gamma_2(phi(t))), where phi ranges over increasing homeomorphisms of [0, 1]. The collection space Pi(X) consists of countable collections Gamma = {gamma_i} subset P(X) having only finitely many curves of diameter exceeding any positive threshold, equipped with the Hausdorff-type metric on macroscopic curves.
(X, d) is a metric space

S is a finite symmetric generating set

    Let $d \ge 2$ and let $\lambda_0 > \lambda_c(d)$.

    \]
    as $n \to \infty$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem th:deficit1 of arXiv:2608.19358, 'An optimal Poincaré inequality\\for the complex Ginibre log-gas'] For all symmetric $f\in\mathcal{C}^\infty_c(\mathbb{C}^n_{\neq},\mathbb{R})$, 
  \begin{align}
    \mathcal{E}_{\mu_n}(f,f)
    -2\operatorname{Var}_{\mu_n}(f)
    &=2\|r\|_{L^2(\mu_n)}^2
    +4\sum_{m=2}^{\infty}(m-1)\|g_m\|_{L^2(\gamma_n)}^2\\
    \|A_nf\|_{L^2(\mu_n)}^2-2\mathcal{E}_{\mu_n}(f,f)
    &=
    \|(A_n+2)\widetilde f\|_{L^2(\mu_n)}^2
    +4\|r\|_{L^2(\mu_n)}^2
    +8\sum_{m=2}^{\infty}(m-1)\|g_m\|_{L^2(\gamma_n)}^2
  \end{align}
  where
  \begin{itemize}
  \item $\widetilde f=f-\int_{\mathbb{C}^n}f\mathrm{d}\mu_n$
  \item $g=\sum_{m=0}^\infty g_m$ is the Hermite expansion of
    $g=U\widetilde f$ in $L^2(\gamma_n)$, with $m=|q|$
  \item $r=\widetilde f-h-\overline{h}$
  \item

[Corollary t:cltspindisag1 of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] (CLT for sum of spins on Poisson-Boolean model)
Let \(\mathcal{P}\) be a stationary Poisson process on $\mathbb{R}^d$ of intensity \(\rho\) and $K$ be a compact set containing the origin and with a non-empty interior. Let  \(\Psi = \Psi(\cdot)\) be the Poisson-Boolean graph induced by the Poisson-Boolean model on \(\mathcal{P}\), as described above. Consider a spin configuration model with the Gibbs distribution given by (equation eqn:gibbs of the paper), defined on the graph~\(\Psi\) and with finite spin space $\mathbb{K}$.
Assume that for some \(\epsilon > 0\), the maximum influence (equation defq of the paper) satisfies
\[
q(\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n)) < \min \{1, \rho_c / \rho\} - \epsilon
\]
almost surely for all $\mathcal{P}_n$, for all large enough $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and where $\rho_c$ is the critical intensity for percolation of the Poisson-Boolean model.
Under these conditions, the spin model \(\{V_x(\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n))\}_{x \in \mathcal{P}_n}\) satisfies the central limit theorem as stated in Theorem~(spinmain of the paper), provided that the moment and variance conditions specified in the theorem are also met. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary t:cltspindisag1 of arXiv:2605.28430

[Lemma last two rows are equal of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'] We have $p_{n-1,j}=p_{n,j}$ for all $1\leq j\leq n$.
    \begin{proof}
        We present a combinatorial argument. Card $n$ is drawn first and placed by itself. Now card $n-1$ goes on top, respectively on the bottom, of card $n$ with probability $1/2$. Hence, cards $n$ and $n-1$ move as a block in the shuffle with both orderings equally likely. Therefore, given a position, they are equally likely to end up there. One can also argue by computing the transition probabilities and using Pascal's identity and symmetry.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma last two rows are equal of arXiv:2507.10294

body:
[Lemma prob0 pure of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Assume that $\xi$ is pure $p$-spin. Let $\varepsilon>0$. Let $u\in(0,1)$, $q\in(0,1)$, $f\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $\zeta\in \mathrm{Prefix}_2(u,q)$ where $\mathrm{Prefix}_2$ is as in Definition (def:nprefix of the paper).
		
		Let $\delta\in[\varepsilon,1)$ and $\mathbf{m}\in[-1+\delta,1-\delta]^N$. Suppose moreover that $q_\mathbf{m}\in (q-\varepsilon,q+\varepsilon)$ and
		$\mathrm{dist}\!\bigl(\zeta_\mathbf{m},\,\zeta|_{(q,1]}+\zeta([0,q])\,\delta_q\bigr)<\varepsilon$.
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item  The gradient $\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})$ is a non-degenerate Gaussian vector in $\mathbb{R}^N$. Its log-density at $0$, tilted by
			\[
			u\!\left(\frac1p\langle \mathbf{m},k_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)-N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)-Nf\right),
			\]
			satisfies
			\begin{multline}
				\log \varphi_{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})}(0)
				+u\!\left(\frac1p\langle \mathbf{m},k_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)-N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)-Nf\right)
				\\
				=
				\frac{1}{2}N\xi(q)u^2
				-\frac{1}{2}N\xi''(q)\!\left(\int_q^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t\right)^{\!2}
				-\frac{1}{2\xi'(q)}
				\Vert \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})-u\xi'(q)\mathbf{m}\Vert^2
				\\
				-\frac{N}{2}\log(2\pi \xi'(q))
				+\frac{N(p-1)}{2p\,\xi'(q)\,q}
				\!\left(
				\frac{1}{N}\langle \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m}),\mathbf{m}\rangle
				-\xi'(q)\int_0^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t
				\right)^{\!2}
				\\
				-u\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)+N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)+Nf\right)
				+O\!\left(N\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right).
			\end{multline}
			
			\item  Suppose moreover that
			\begin{equation}
				\langle \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m}),\mathbf{m}\rangle
				=
				N\xi'(q)\int_0^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t+O(N\varepsilon)
			\end{equation}
			and
			\begin{equation}
				\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl(h_\zeta(q,m_i)-\partial_m h_\zeta(q,m_i)m_i\bigr)
				+N\int_0^q t\xi''(t)\zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t
				+\frac{N}{2}\int_q^1 t\xi''(t)\zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t
				=
				-Nf+O(N\varepsilon).
			\end{equation}
			Then the squared term in (equation eq:pure-prob0-main of the paper) is $O(N\varepsilon)$, so that 
			\begin{multline}
				\log \varphi_{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})}(0)
				+u\!\left(\frac1p\langle \mathbf{m},k_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)-N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)-Nf\right)
				\\
				=
				\frac{1}{2}N\xi(q)u^2
				-\frac{1}{2}N\xi''(q)\!\left(\int_q^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t\right)^{\!2}
				-\frac{1}{2\xi'(q)}
				\Vert \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})-u\xi'(q)\mathbf{m}\Vert^2
				\\
				-\frac{N}{2}\log(2\pi \xi'(q))
				-u\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)+N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)+Nf\right)
				+O\!\left(N\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right),
			\end{multline}
			and, on the event $\{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0\}$,
			\begin{equation}
				F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=Nf+O\!\left(N\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right).
			\end{equation}
		\end{enumerate}

body:
[campaign result 2026-09-14, author_checked; reduction plus asserted conditional, not a solution] Svante Janson's Problem 18.39 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510, asks whether Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability is possible in the condensation regime 0 < nu < lambda. Janson conjectures that it is not possible for the full sequence and, more strongly, that there are always epsilon > 0 and a subsequence along which Y_(1) >= epsilon n w.h.p. (Example 18.36 gives Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability along a subsequence.) Setting: let w_k >= 0 with w_0 > 0, let Phi(z) = sum_k w_k z^k have radius rho in (0,infinity) with Phi(rho) < infinity, and put pi_k = w_k rho^k/Phi(rho), a law with generating-function radius one and finite mean nu > 0. Let m_n/n -> lambda > nu. (Y_1,...,Y_n) is n i.i.d. pi variables conditioned on sum m_n, Y_(1) = max_i Y_i, and M = (lambda-nu)n. Heuristic rate: carrying M in r = M/a boxes of size a has class weight binomial(n,r) pi_a^r up to the bulk's fluctuation, giving log P = M Lambda(a) + o(M) with Lambda(a) = [log pi_a + log(a/(lambda-nu)) + 1]/a. For pi_k ~ c k^(-beta) and for pi_a = exp(-a^gamma), 0<gamma<1, Lambda increases on large a, so the optimum is a = M (one box), matching the known condensation picture. Since limsup_a Lambda(a) = 0 and Lambda < 0 for large a, Lambda has infinitely many upper records a_1 < a_2 < ... (Lambda(a_j) > Lambda(a) for all a < a_j). The record asserts, as author-checked and with no proof given beyond reference to an analogous step for Problem 18.40 in a companion memo, the following Proposition: if for some epsilon > 0 and every C, along infinitely many records, Lambda(a_j) - max_{a <= epsilon a_j} Lambda(a) > C a_j^(-1/2), then along n_j = a_j/(lambda-nu), P(Y_(1) >= ((lambda-nu)/2) n_j) -> 1, so the conjecture holds. Caveat: the only derivation offered is the heuristic rate with an o(M) error, which is coarser than the order sqrt(a_j) resolution this hypothesis requires, so the record does not establish the Proposition. The record poses the open Question whether, for every law pi on Z_{>=0} with radius one and finite mean, [log pi_a + log a]/a has infinitely many records with gap exceeding a_j^(-1/2) below max_{a <= epsilon a_j} for some fixed epsilon > 0. This is not a proved equivalence with the conjecture. A negative answer would only give a candidate counterexample, still requiring proof that the allocation spreads. The Question's normalisation and fixed threshold also differ from the Proposition's hypothesis. The problem remains open. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
The allocations are defined along sizes with positive conditioning probability.
0 < nu < lambda and the boundary-tilted law pi has generating-function radius one.

body: [Lemma lem:star-recoloring of arXiv:2609.02845, 'Degeneracy bounds, stability, and a sharp gap for $B$-colorings'] Let $G$ be a simple graph, let $u\in V(G)$, and let $\mathcal C$ be a set of colors.  Suppose that $\varphi$ is a $B$-coloring of $G-S_u$ with colors from $\mathcal C$.  For each $x\in N_G(u)$, let $L_x\subseteq\mathcal C$ be the set of colors not used on any old conflict edge for $ux$. If the family $\{L_x\colon x\in N_G(u)\}$ admits a system of distinct representatives, then $\varphi$ extends to a $B$-coloring of $G$ with colors from $\mathcal C$.

body:
[Definition 2 of arXiv:2608.21597, 'Random Hazard Forests'] \emph{
The RHF split statistic for splitting a node $A_j$ into regions
$A_{j,1}$ and $A_{j,2}$ is
\Eq
S(A_{j,1},A_{j,2})
=
V_{j,1}\log\!\left(\frac{V_{j,1}}{U_{j,1}}\right)
+
V_{j,2}\log\!\left(\frac{V_{j,2}}{U_{j,2}}\right),

\EndEq
and the associated empirical risk reduction is
\Eq
\D_n(A_{j,1},A_{j,2})
=
V_{j,1}\log\!\left(\frac{V_{j,1}}{U_{j,1}}\right)
+
V_{j,2}\log\!\left(\frac{V_{j,2}}{U_{j,2}}\right)
-
(V_{j,1}+V_{j,2})\log\!\left(\frac{V_{j,1}+V_{j,2}}{U_{j,1}+U_{j,2}}\right).

\EndEq
If $R_n(F_s)$ is the empirical risk for the current working log hazard
and $R_n(F_{s+1})$ is the risk after the split, then
$R_n(F_{s+1})=R_n(F_s)-\D_n(A_{j,1},A_{j,2})$.}
title: Definition 2 of arXiv:2608.21597

body:
[Corollary 18 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] Assume that $\mu\in{\cal S}$ and its $\alpha$-potential $R_\alpha\mu$ belongs to $L^\infty(E;m)$ for  all $\alpha>0$. 
Then for any compact set $K\subset E$, the restricted measure $1_K\mu$ is of finite energy integral; that is, $1_K\mu \in \mathcal{S}_0$.

In particular, if $\mu(E) < \infty$, then $\mu$ itself belongs to $\mathcal{S}_0$, which further implies that $\mu \in \mathcal{S}_{00}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 18 of arXiv:2605.05864
Large-energy asymptotics

[Corollary 14 of arXiv:2607.14948, 'Graph alignment in sparse inhomogeneous models via self-overlap'] Assume that $(G, H)$ is an inhomogeneous graph system, and assume that $\max_{e \in E} (s p_e) \leq n^{-\alpha + o(1)}$ for some $\frac{1}{2} < \alpha \leq 1$. Denote by $\hat{\pi}$ the estimator given by Theorem \ref{possible}. Then, for any $k > \frac{2}{2\alpha - 1}$, $ov(\hat{\pi}, \pi^*) \geq \frac{|\Ker_k(I)|}{n}(1 - o_\Proba(1))$.

    In particular, if $\ds\min_{u \in V} \left( \sum_{v \in V}  (p_{\{ u, v\}}s^2)\right) \goesto{n \to +\infty} +\infty$, then $ov(\hat{\pi}, \pi^*) = 1 - o_\Proba(1)$: almost exact alignment is feasible. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 14 of arXiv:2607.14948

body:
[Lemma 3 (Regeneration at a level) of arXiv:2608.10992, '2608.10992'] Suppose that the $t$-avalanche has finite range $I$. Conditionally on
$\mathcal H_t$, its terminal fitnesses are independent and have the form
\[
        F_x=t+E_x,\qquad x\in I,
\]
where the $E_x$ are independent $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ variables,
independent of $\mathcal H_t$. Consequently, when the threshold is raised
above $t$, the next triggering level occurs at rate $|I|$, its location is
uniform on $I$, and the subavalanche attached there is independent of
$\mathcal H_t$ and has the law of an avalanche at the triggering level.
