body:
[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; depends on the companion memo on Problem 20.2] This is the boundary and condensation part of the answer recorded for Svante Janson's Problem 20.3 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Use Janson's balls-in-boxes setting with weights w_j, generating function Phi, radius rho, Psi(t) = t Phi'(t)/Phi(t), nu = lim_{t up to rho} Psi(t), m/n -> lambda, pi the tilted law at tau = rho when lambda >= nu, and N_d the number of boxes with d balls. In the two regimes not covered by the finite-variance mean-conditioning theorem, (c) lambda = nu with sigma^2 = infinity and (d) lambda > nu, the natural analogue of the Gaussian limit has variance sigma_d^2 = pi_d(1-pi_d). In (d) the constraint is absorbed by the condensate rather than by the bulk. The record asserts that this analogue holds under regular variation of the tail, by the argument of Thevenin's Theorem 6.7 in case (d), and fails in general. The failure rests on two constructions, Theorems A and B of the companion memo on Problem 20.2. Theorem A is a subcritical law conditioned at lambda = 1 > nu, that is, sum of the xi_i equal to n-1, for which (N_1 - n pi_1)/sqrt(n) converges to a non-degenerate two-point law. Theorem B is a law with nu = 1 and sigma^2 = infinity, conditioned at lambda = 1, for which (N_1 - n pi_1)/sqrt(n) converges to a mixture of two Gaussians. Assuming those two theorems, a Gaussian limit for the box counts in regimes (c) and (d) does not hold without a further regularity condition on the tail. The record identifies local flatness of the tail at the scale the conditioning must supply as the dividing line. This is an unrefereed campaign result, and the counterexamples are proved in the companion memo, not in this record.
The conditioning events have positive probability.
The counterexample construction is reported, rather than proved within this record.

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2605.05388, 'The Efron-Stein inequality for identically distributed pairs'] For each \(i\) let \((X_i,Y_i)\) be an identically distributed pair, so that the pairs \((X_i,Y_i)\) are independent as \(i\) varies, and \(X_i\) can take at most \(k_i\) values. Let \(f\) be a bounded measurable function, and let \(Z_i=f(X_1,\ldots X_{i},Y_{i+1},\ldots Y_n)\). Then
$$
E(Z_n-Z_0)^2\le \rho(k) \sum_{i=1}^n E(Z_i-Z_{i-1})^2, \qquad \rho (k)\le \max_i k_i/2.
$$

body:
[Definition 23 (Vertex condition) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] The structure satisfies the \emph{vertex condition}
\textup{(V)} if there is $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$ such that for
every active orbit $O$ and both of its sites $z\in O$,
\[
\varepsilon\,\mathcal W\bigl[\varphi_O,\,s(z;\cdot)\bigr](\gamma)>0
\qquad\text{for all }\gamma\in(0,1).
\]
Equivalently, since
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\gamma}
\left(\frac{\varphi_O}{s_z}\right)
=\frac{\mathcal W[\varphi_O,s_z]}{s_z^{2}},
\qquad s_z>0,
\]
each ratio $\varphi_O(\gamma)/s(z;\gamma)$, $z\in O$, is strictly
monotone in $\gamma$, in the same direction for all orbits and both
orbit sites. Only these $2r$ scalar ratios
enter the theorem below, and the condition involves only scalar
functions of $\gamma$.

Two remarks on the shape of \textup{(V)}. First, it is stated
relative to the orbit representatives fixed once and for all in
Section~\ref{subsec:inherited-structure}: reversing the
representative of an orbit replaces $\mathbf d_O$ by
$-\mathbf d_O$, hence $\varphi_O$ by $-\varphi_O$ and both of that
orbit's Wronskians by their negatives. The genuinely invariant
content of \textup{(V)} is therefore the \emph{intra-orbit}
requirement that the two Wronskians of a given orbit share a sign;
the common value of $\varepsilon$ across orbits is a normalisation.
That it is always achievable is worth stating precisely: the choice
of representative is made \emph{independently in each orbit}, and
reversing it in a single orbit $O$ sends
$\mathbf d_O\mapsto-\mathbf d_O$,
$\varphi_O\mapsto-\varphi_O$, hence
$\mathcal W[\varphi_O,s(z;\cdot)]\mapsto
-\mathcal W[\varphi_O,s(z;\cdot)]$ at both $z\in O$ and leaves every
other orbit untouched. So if each orbit separately has a constant
Wronskian sign, the $r$ signs can be aligned one orbit at a time.
The substantive hypothesis is thus the intra-orbit one; the global
$\varepsilon$ follows. Second, and
consequently, the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:vertex-sign} is
orientation-independent, since only the product
$\varepsilon\cdot\operatorname{sgn}[\mathbf d_O]_z$ appears there,
and that product is unchanged by a reversal.

[Corollary 5 of arXiv:2608.17562, '2608.17562'] Moment bounds.
     Let $(X_{i})_{i \ge 1}$ be a sequence of nonnegative \iid random variables with common distribution function $F$. Assume that $\widebar{F} \in \SRV{\alpha}{\rho}$, with $\alpha > 0$, $\rho < 0$ and auxiliary function~$A$.
    Then, there exists $C>0$ such that for every $b \in (0,\alpha)$
 we have 
 \begin{equation}
   
	\vert \esp[Z_{n}^{b}] - \esp[Z^{b}] \vert \leq C\Big(\frac{1}{n} + A(a_n)\Big),
 \quad n \geq 1, 
\end{equation}
if the $X_{i}$ are continuous random variables.
 If not, then for every $b \in (0, \alpha)$ and
 $\delta \in (1, \alpha / b )$, there exists a constant $C_{\delta}$ such that 
\[
\vert \esp[Z_{n}^{b}] - \esp[Z^{b}]\vert \leq C_{\delta}\Big(\frac{1}{n} + A(a_n)\Big)^{1 - {1}/{\delta}}, \quad n \geq 1.
\]

Let T be a first-order theory satisfying all three hypotheses: (i) T is consistent; (ii) T is effectively axiomatized: its set of axioms is computably enumerable (equivalently, by Craig's trick, computably decidable after re-axiomatization), so theoremhood is computably enumerable; (iii) T interprets enough arithmetic - it suffices that T contains or interprets Robinson arithmetic Q. Then T is incomplete: there is a sentence G in the language of T (arithmetical under the interpretation) such that T proves neither G nor the negation of G. Consequently no consistent, effectively axiomatized theory interpreting Q is complete; in particular Peano arithmetic and ZFC, if consistent, are incomplete. Godel's original 1931 argument additionally assumed omega-consistency to rule out T proving the negation; Rosser's 1936 refinement, stated here, needs only consistency. All three hypotheses are necessary: complete consistent extensions of Q exist but are not effectively axiomatized (e.g. true arithmetic), effectively axiomatized complete consistent theories exist that do not interpret Q (e.g. the theory of dense linear orders, or Presburger arithmetic), and an inconsistent theory proves everything.
T is consistent
T is effectively axiomatized (computably enumerable axiom set)
T interprets Robinson arithmetic Q

the exponents defined in Chatterjee (2013) are assumed to exist
first-passage percolation on Z^d
NO nearly-Gamma assumption on the weight law
conclusion is the single inequality chi <= 2 xi - 1, not the equality

IN THE AUTHORS' OWN WORDS: 'we show that under the assumption that exponents defined in Chatterjee (2013) exist, one has the relation chi <= 2 xi - 1. One advantage of our argument is that it does not require the "nearly Gamma" assumption of Chatterjee (2013).'
WHY THE SPLIT MATTERS: quoting 'Auffinger-Damron proved the scaling relation' overstates it in two ways at once - it upgrades an inequality to an equality, and it hides that the exponents are still only assumed to exist. The other inequality's first proof appeared in a model of a Brownian particle in a Poissonian potential; in FPP a version of chi >= 2 xi - 1 goes back to Newman-Piza (1995).
SOURCE: Auffinger, A. and Damron, M. (2014), 'A simplified proof of the relation between scaling exponents in first-passage percolation', Ann. Probab. 42, no. 3, 1197-1211; arXiv:1109.0523v2.
VERIFICATION STATUS: theorem-checked-against-source. The v2 abstract states the hypothesis, the conclusion and the dropped assumption in full; the proof was not read.
title: Auffinger-Damron (2014) reprove only ONE of the two inequalities in the first-passage percolation scaling relation - they obtain chi <= 2 xi - 1, still assuming that the exponents defined in Chatterjee (2013) exist, but WITHOUT Chatterjee's 'nearly Gamma' assumption. So the nearly-Gamma hypothesis is removable for the '<=' direction and, as of the survey, not for the equality.

[Lemma lem_position_slopes of arXiv:2608.09105, 'Longest convex chains with i.i.d.\ points'] Let $f\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous and convex.
Let us write $\mathsf{A} = (a,f(a))$ and $\mathsf{B} = (b,f(b))$.
Given a set
\eq{
\mathcal{C} = \{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)\}\subset\mathsf{Tri}_f(a,b)\setminus\{\mathsf{A},\mathsf{B}\} \quad \text{such that} \quad
a \leqslant x_1 \leqslant \cdots \leqslant x_n \leqslant b,
}
let us write $\mathsf{P}_i = (x_i,y_i)$.
Then the following two statements are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]

\item 
$\{\mathsf{A},\mathsf{B}\}\cup\mathcal{C}$ is in convex position.

\item 
$\mathrm{Slope}(\mathsf{A},\mathsf{P}_1)<\mathrm{Slope}(\mathsf{P}_1,\mathsf{P}_2)<\cdots<\mathrm{Slope}(\mathsf{P}_{n-1},\mathsf{P}_n)<\mathrm{Slope}(\mathsf{P}_n,\mathsf{B})$.

\end{enumerate}

body:
Let A be an INCREASING event depending on the states of a FINITE set E of edges, and let P_p be the product measure with density p. Then p -> P_p(A) is a polynomial in p, hence smooth, and d/dp P_p(A) = sum_{e in E} P_p( e is pivotal for A ) = E_p[ N(A) ], where N(A) is the number of pivotal edges. Equivalently the derivative is the TOTAL INFLUENCE. The monotonicity hypothesis matters: for a general event the correct statement is the Margulis-Russo formula d/dp P_p(A) = sum_e [ P_p(A with e open) - P_p(A with e closed) ], whose summands can be negative and which reduces to Russo's formula exactly when A is increasing. Russo's formula is the bridge from influence estimates - Kahn-Kalai-Linial, Talagrand, Friedgut-Kalai - to SHARP THRESHOLDS: a lower bound on the total influence of order log(1/(p(1-p))) forces P_p(A) to rise from eps to 1 - eps over a parameter window of width O(1/log n). [Russo (1981), Margulis (1974); see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.25]

for general events use the Margulis-Russo form with signed summands

Lewin's 2022 review discusses finite-temperature Riesz phase transitions in Section VI through nonuniqueness and symmetry breaking of Gibbs point processes, and reports numerical BCC/FCC phase diagrams in three dimensions. Its Conjecture 38 in Section IV.B instead concerns zero-temperature equilibrium configurations. Proving that conjecture, or finite phonon variance around an assumed lattice, does not by itself construct a positive-temperature crystalline Gibbs state.

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; the recursion is integrated exactly against two published closed-form values as a control] This is the campaign answer to Conjecture 1 of H. Stepanyants, P. L. Krapivsky, H. Hartle and D. Krioukov, The rank and layer distributions in random recursive trees, arXiv:2608.04303. Let the Poisson-weighted infinite tree have root position zero, with children of each vertex at the points of an independent rate-one Poisson process on (0,infinity), translated by their parent's position. Let M_k be the minimum position of generation k, and set M_0=0. Define s_0(y)=1 for y>=0 and s_k(y)=1-exp(-integral_0^y s_{k-1}(z)dz) for k>=1. Put bar_ell_k=integral_0^infinity s_k(y)exp(-y)dy and ell_k=bar_ell_k-bar_ell_{k+1}. In the source, ell_k is the limiting fraction of vertices in layer k of a random recursive tree, formed by joining each new vertex j uniformly to one of vertices 1,...,j-1; layer zero consists of the initial leaves, and subsequent layers are obtained by successive leaf removals. Let e be the base of the natural logarithm. There is a constant C_star in (0,infinity) such that bar_ell_k exp(k/e) k^(3/(2e)) -> C_star and ell_k exp(k/e) k^(3/(2e)) -> (1-exp(-1/e)) C_star. More precisely, if M_star denotes the distributional limit of M_k-[k/e+(3/(2e))log k] furnished by the cited branching-random-walk minimum theorem, then C_star=E[exp(-M_star)]. In particular both tails have order exp(-k/e) k^(-3/(2e)). The proof uses Addario-Berry and Ford's Poisson-Dirichlet branching random walks, Annals of Applied Probability 23 (2013), Theorems 1.1-1.2, and Aidekon's Convergence in law of the minimum of a branching random walk, Annals of Probability 41 (2013), as stated in the record. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
The stated published minimum-location, tail, and limit theorems apply to this Poisson branching walk.

Appl. Probab. 23 (2013) 283–307. Their Theorem 1.1 states, for this class,
$$\widetilde M_n := \mathrm{median}(M_n) = \frac ne + \frac{3}{2e}\log n + O(1), \tag{2}$$
uniformly over the class, and their Theorem 1.2 gives uniform exponential tails: for every $c_1 < e$ and $c_2 < 1$,
$$\mathbb{P}\big(M_n \le \widetilde M_n - x\big) \ll_{c_1} e^{-c_1 x}, \qquad \mathbb{P}\big(M_n \ge \widetilde M_n + x\big) \ll_{c_2} e^{-c_2 x} \qquad (n \ge 1,\ x \ge 0). \tag{3}$$

## Conjecture 1 is a theorem

**Theorem 2.** There are absolute constants $0 < c < C < \infty$ with
$$c \le \bar\ell_k\,e^{k/e}\,k^{3/(2e)} \le C \qquad (k \ge 1),$$
that is, $\bar\ell_k = \exp[-k/e - \tfrac{3}{2e}\log k - O(1)]$. The same holds for $\ell_k$, so Conjecture 1 holds as stated.

*Proof.* Write $D_k = M_k - \widetilde M_k$, so $\bar\ell_k = e^{-\widetilde M_k}\,\mathbb{E}[e^{-D_k}]$ by Theorem 1. For the upper bound take $c_1 = 2$ in (3), which is legitimate since $2 < e$: with $K$ the implied constant,
$$\mathbb{E}[e^{-D_k}] \le 1 + \sum_{j\ge 0} e^{\,j+1}\,\mathbb{P}(D_k \le -j) \le 1 + eK\sum_{j \ge 0}e^{-j} < \infty,$$
uniformly in $k$. For the lower bound, $\mathbb{E}[e^{-D_k}] \ge \mathbb{P}(D_k \le 0) \ge 1/2$ by the definition of the median. Now insert (2). For $\ell_k$: the upper bound is immediate from $\ell_k \le \bar\ell_k$, and the lower bound follows from Theorem 3 below; unconditionally it already follows for a positive density of $k$, since summing the telescoping identity $\sum_{k=j}^{j+L-1}\ell_k = \bar\ell_j - \bar\ell_{j+L}$ and choosing $L$ with $e^{-L/e} \le c/(2C)$ gives some $k \in [j, j+L)$ with $\ell_k \ge (c/2L)\,e^{-j/e}j^{-3/(2e)}$. $\square$

    The kernel $G_\alpha(x,y)$ satisfies the lower bound $$G_\alpha(x,y)\geq \overline{G}_{\alpha}(z)$$
    where the positive function $\overline{G}_\alpha$ which satisfies $\dv{\overline{G}_\alpha}{z}<0$ and the asymptotics \begin{align*}
        &\overline{G}_{\alpha}(z)\sim_{z\uparrow+\infty} e^{-z^2},& \alpha>0,\\

        &\overline{G}_{\alpha}(z)\sim_{z\downarrow0} \abs{\log z},&\alpha=\frac{n}{2},\\
        &\overline{G}_{\alpha}(z)\sim_{z\downarrow0} 1,&\alpha>\frac{n}{2}.

Let X_1, X_2, ... be independent and identically distributed real random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, and S_k = X_1 + ... + X_k. Define the rescaled random continuous path W_n(t) = n^{-1/2} ( S_{floor(n t)} + (n t - floor(n t)) X_{floor(n t) + 1} ) for t in [0, 1], the linear interpolation of the random walk with time scaled by n and space by sqrt(n). Then W_n converges in distribution, as a random element of C[0, 1] with the uniform norm, to a standard Brownian motion W on [0, 1]. Consequently, for every functional Phi : C[0, 1] -> R that is continuous almost surely with respect to the Wiener measure, Phi(W_n) converges in distribution to Phi(W): the law of the maximum of the walk, of its time spent positive, of its first hitting time of a level, all converge to the Brownian laws, whatever the increment distribution. The same holds in the Skorokhod space D[0, 1] for the uninterpolated step process. Finite variance is essential; with infinite variance the limits are stable processes under different scaling.
X_i independent, identically distributed, E X_1 = 0, Var X_1 = 1 (finite variance is essential)
convergence is in distribution in C[0, 1] with the uniform norm (or in D[0, 1] with the Skorokhod topology for the step process)

Tightness in C[0, 1]: W_n(0) = 0, and the modulus of continuity is controlled by a maximal inequality for the partial sums. Cut [0, 1] into about 1/delta blocks of length delta; an oscillation larger than epsilon over some pair s, t with |s - t| <= delta forces an oscillation larger than epsilon/3 inside one block, and Ottaviani's inequality bounds the probability of that by twice the tail P(|S_m| > (epsilon/3) sqrt(n) - sqrt(2 m)) with m about n delta, which by the central limit theorem is of Gaussian size, of order exp(-c epsilon^2 / delta), for large n. A union over the 1/delta blocks is then of order (1/delta) exp(-c epsilon^2 / delta), which tends to 0 as delta -> 0 uniformly in n large, and the finitely many small n are handled by the continuity of each W_n. So the sequence is tight in C[0, 1]. By Prokhorov's theorem every subsequence has a further subsequence converging in distribution in C[0, 1]; every such limit has the finite-dimensional laws of Brownian motion and continuous paths, hence is Brownian motion (a law on C[0, 1] is determined by its finite-dimensional distributions), so the whole sequence converges. [Lemma lem:thinning-preserves-overlap of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] Let $G=(I,J,M)$ be finite with $|J|=n\ge2$. Choose $J_0\subseteq J$ uniformly from $\binom J{n_0}$, where $2\le n_0\le n$, and let $G_0:=G[J_0]$. Then
\[
\mathbb E\,\eta(G_0)=\eta(G).
\]
Consequently, for every $\alpha>0$,
\[
\mathbb P\big(\eta(G_0)>\alpha\big)\le\frac{\eta(G)}{\alpha}.
\]

[Prop 17 ({\cite[Proposition~9.4.26) of arXiv:2609.02561, 'NON-NEF LOCI IN MIXED CHARACTERISTIC'] {Laz}}]
With notation as above, let $A$ be a globally generated ample line bundle, $M$ be a line bundle on $X$, and $n$ be a positive integer such that $n\geq\max_{s\in S}\dim X_{s}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
If $M-(K_X +\Delta)$ is big and nef,
then $\J(X,\Delta)\otimes\sO_{X}(nA+M)$ is globally generated.
\item
If $M-(K_X +\Delta)-D$ is big and nef, then $\J(X,\Delta,\|D\|)\otimes\sO_{X}(nA+M)$ is globally generated.
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:splitfilteredchar of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'] Let $\cC$ be a stable $\infty$-category and $X_\bullet\in\mathrm{Fun}(N(\mathbb Z_{\geq 0}),\cC)$ a filtered object in $\cC$.
Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
    \item $X_\bullet$ admits an augmentation $X_\bullet\to\underline{X_{-1}}$ so that the corresponding extended filtered object $Y_\bullet$ (with $Y_{-1}=X_{-1}[-1]$, $Y_n=\mathrm{fib}(X_n\to X_{-1})$) is split.
    \item $X_\bullet$ is the direct sum of a constant filtered object $\underline{X_{-1}}$ and a filtered object $Y_0\xrightarrow{0}Y_1\xrightarrow{0}Y_2\xrightarrow{0}\ldots$ for which all maps are zero maps. We say in this case that $X_\bullet$ is \textbf{essentially constant}.
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Proposition 10 of arXiv:2608.21551, '\bf Sparse Separable Factor Analysis in the Complex Domain with an Application to Local Fi'] For $j=1,\ldots,d$, let $\Lambdab_j\in\CC^{p_j\times k_j}$ denote the true loading matrix and $\widehat{\Lambdab}_j$ denote its estimate. Define the orthogonal projectors onto their column spaces by
\begin{align*}
  \Pb_j
  &=
  \Lambdab_j
  \left(
    \Lambdab_j^\star\Lambdab_j
  \right)^+
  \Lambdab_j^\star,
  \qquad
  \widehat{\Pb}_j
  =
  \widehat{\Lambdab}_j
  \left(
    \widehat{\Lambdab}_j^\star
    \widehat{\Lambdab}_j
  \right)^+
  \widehat{\Lambdab}_j^\star,
\end{align*}
where $+$ denotes the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse. The null-space projection error is
\begin{align}
  \operatorname{err}_{\Pb_j}^2
  &=
  \left\|
    \left(
      \Ib_{p_j}-\widehat{\Pb}_j
    \right)
    \Pb_j
  \right\|_F^2.
  
\end{align}
Let
\begin{align*}
  r_j
  &=
  \operatorname{rank}(\Lambdab_j),
  \qquad
  \widehat{r}_j
  =
  \operatorname{rank}(\widehat{\Lambdab}_j),
  \qquad
  r_{\min,j}
  =
  \min(r_j,\widehat{r}_j).
\end{align*}
Denote the principal angles between the column spaces of $\Lambdab_j$ and $\widehat{\Lambdab}_j$ by
\begin{align*}
    0
  \leq
  \theta_{(j)1}
  \leq
  \cdots
  \leq
  \theta_{(j)r_{\min,j}}
  \leq
  \frac{\pi}{2}.
\end{align*}
Then,
\begin{align}
  \operatorname{err}_{\Pb_j}^2
  &=
  r_j-r_{\min,j}
  +
  \sum_{i=1}^{r_{\min,j}}
  \sin^2\left(\theta_{(j)i}\right),
  
\end{align}
where the sum \eqref{eq:appendix-null-err-proj-angle} is interpreted as zero when $r_{\min,j}=0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 10 of arXiv:2608.21551

body: In mathematics, philosophy, linguistics, and computer science, first-order logic (FOL), also called predicate logic, predicate calculus, or quantificational logic, is a type of formal system. First-order logic uses quantified variables over non-logical objects, and allows the use of sentences that contain variables. Rather than propositions such as "all humans are mortal", in first-order logic one can have expressions in the form "for all x, if x is a human, then x is mortal", where "for all x" is a quantifier, x is a variable, and "... is a human" and "... is mortal" are predicates. This distinguishes it from propositional logic, which does not use quantifiers or relations; in this sense, first-order logic is an extension of propositional logic.
title: First-order logic

[Theorem thm:potential-identities-results of arXiv:2608.18320, 'Asymptotics for Beta-Splitting Trees via Homogeneous Fragmentations and Meromorphic Potent'] For every $\beta>-2$ and $n\ge2$, the following identities hold.
    \begin{enumeratei}
    
    \item For every $t\ge0$, the continuous height and the expected total length satisfy
    \begin{equation}
            \mathsf P(D_n>t)=\mathsf E\bigl(F_n(\xi_t)\bigr),
            \qquad
            \mathsf E D_n=\mathcal U_\beta F_n,
            \qquad\text{and}\qquad
            \mathsf E\Lambda_n=\mathcal U_\beta H_n.
    \end{equation}
    
    \item The expected discrete height satisfies
    \begin{equation}
            \mathsf E L_n=\sum_{j=2}^n a_\beta(n,j),
            \qquad\text{where}\qquad
            a_\beta(n,j)
            =
            \phi_\beta(j-1)\binom{n-1}{j-1}
            \mathcal U_\beta G_{n,j}.
    \end{equation}
    
    \item Let $M_{n-1}$ be the maximum of $n-1$ independent exponential random
    variables of rate $1$, independent of $\xi$. Then
    \begin{equation}
            D_n\stackrel{d}=T_{M_{n-1}},
            \qquad\text{where}\qquad
            T_x:=\inf\{t\ge0:\xi_t\ge x\}.
    \end{equation}
    
    \end{enumeratei} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Fix an integer K>=1. Let U_N in R^(N by M) and V_N in R^(P by M) be independent arrays with fixed centered symmetric iid real entry laws of variance one and finite absolute moments of order 2K+2. Assume P/N and M/N remain bounded above and away from zero. Put X_N=U_N V_N^T/sqrt(N), and let X_N^G use independent standard Gaussian factors of the same dimensions. For every j=1,...,K, the coefficient of s^j in the normalized finite-size Gaussian-channel MI I(X_N;sqrt(s)X_N+G)/(NP) differs from its Gaussian-factor counterpart by O_K(1/N), with constants allowed to depend on the fixed moments and aspect bounds. If both aspect ratios have positive finite limits, every coefficient has a finite prior-independent Gaussian limit. The unnormalized finite-size order-K Taylor remainder obeys |R_K(s)|<=[2^K(2K)!/(2(K+1)!)] E||vec X_N||^(2K+2) s^(K+1) for s>=0. The proof cancels articulation entropy graphs using chi_G derivative at one, then uses connected product-cumulant partitions and Euler surface power counting to show every higher factor cumulant loses a free index. This is not a size-uniform remainder or an expansion of the thermodynamic MI; asymmetric factor laws are not covered.
Fixed positive integer K
Fixed real symmetric iid unit-variance factor laws with finite absolute 2K+2 moments
Independent U_N,V_N and standard Gaussian observation noise
Positive aspect bounds; convergent aspect ratios only for the coefficient-limit conclusion
Finite-size coefficients, nats; no exchange of limits
metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:d87f6a5266bf32d2a0fa38de889ccd6afb7ba56f079baf4df7d32c8b269866d4","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/d8/d87f6a5266bf32d2a0fa38de889ccd6afb7ba56f079baf4df7d32c8b269866d4.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:58dc3304a4b00a408b529761b6990c1ca2d7e3bc96d8ced9ee22a0ee2572b6a8","bundle_entry_key":"iid-product-mi-all-fixed-coefficients-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-entropy-chromatic-and-all-fixed-coefficients-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_003.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:iid-product-mi-all-fixed-coefficients-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# All fixed Taylor coefficients: symmetric iid factor laws

Target 1. Proof draft, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. This is
about finite-size Taylor coefficients, not a uniform expansion of
the thermodynamic mutual information. The planar dual lemma in
Section 4 is the step that most needs independent scrutiny.

## 1. Precise theorem

Fix a positive integer K. U_N in R^(N by M) and V_N in R^(P by M)
are independent arrays. Each array has iid entries from a fixed real
symmetric law of mean zero and variance one, and both entry laws
have finite absolute moments of order 2K+2. Let P/N and M/N stay
bounded above and away from zero. Put X_N=U_N V_N^T/sqrt(N). Let
X_N^G be the same product with independent standard Gaussian factors.
Independent channel noise is standard Gaussian in R^(N by P).

For j=1,...,K let a_j(N) and a_j^G(N) be the coefficients of s^j
in the right Taylor polynomials at zero of

 I(X_N;sqrt(s)X_N+G)/(NP),
 I(X_N^G;sqrt(s)X_N^G+G)/(NP),

respectively, with natural logarithms.

For the dossier's channel Y=X_N+sqrt(Delta)G, an invertible rescaling
of Y gives sqrt(s)X_N+G with s=1/Delta. Since UV^T and X_N differ
by a fixed invertible scaling, their mutual information with Y is
the same. These are therefore the finite-size 1/Delta coefficients.
The coefficient comparison is

                    a_j(N)-a_j^G(N)=O_K(1/N).       (1)

The implied constants may depend on the fixed entry laws' moments
and aspect-ratio bounds. If P/N->alpha and M/N->beta in (0,infinity),
each coefficient sequence has a finite limit. The limits depend only
on alpha,beta and coincide for all these symmetric factor laws.

In each finite dimension the polynomial through order K has the
explicit unnormalized remainder

 |R_K(s)| <= [2^K (2K)!/(2(K+1)!)]
                         E||vec X_N||^(2K+2) s^(K+1), s>=0.  (2)

The bound (2) is not uniform in N and does not prove an expansion
of the limiting MI. The same finite-size bound applies to X_N^G.

## 2. What remains after the entropy diagram cancellations

Write d=NP, b=M/N and a=s/(1+bs). The standardized output has
covariance I_d. Relative to the standard Gaussian, let its density
be 1+q. For bounded symmetric vector inputs its formal Hermite
generating series is

                  exp(sum_(k>=4 even) C_k:t^k a^(k/2)/k!).

Here C_k is the ordered cumulant tensor of vec X_N. At fixed SNR
order <=K this uses finitely many tensors and contractions only.
Normal-ordered Gaussian products are evaluated from the exact identity

 E product_h exp(t_h.G-|t_h|^2/2)
                         =exp(sum_(h<l) t_h.t_l).

Hence each full Wick pairing pairs endpoints in different Hermite
factors. Put a vertex at each cumulant tensor and an edge at each
paired pair of endpoints. Its loopless multigraph G has degrees
even and at least four. A graph with e edges carries a^e, with
e<=K in the coefficient calculation.

The finite algebraic lemma entropy_chromatic_identity.md proves:
after common endpoint factorials and tensor contractions are
extracted, the grouping weight of this graph is chi_G'(1).
The proof uses distinct formal labels on tensor vertices, proper
coloring partitions, and the scalar entropy expansion. It applies
before equal tensor labels are identified and summed.

Since there are no isolated vertices, every disconnected graph has
zero weight. A connected graph with an articulation vertex also has
zero weight. Thus only connected graphs with one block survive.
Parallel-edge two-vertex graphs count as one block. A single-edge
graph cannot occur because all tensor degrees are at least four.

The covariance-matched entropy identity is

 I(X_N;sqrt(s)X_N+G)=d log(1+bs)/2-D(output_standardized || gamma_d).

Its first term depends only on b. It suffices to compare the
finitely many retained cumulant contractions in D at each order.

## 3. Exact raw-factor cumulant expansion and index monomials

For a single rank-one summand W_ij=u_i v_j,

 C_k(W)=sum_(rho join sigma=1)
   product_(B in rho) kappa_|B|(u)
   product_(C in sigma) kappa_|C|(v)
                            delta_rho(i)delta_sigma(j).      (3)

The partitions rho,sigma are on the k tensor positions; delta_rho
requires equality of the row indices in each block, and delta_sigma
does the same for columns. This standard cumulant-of-products
identity has a short direct proof: first expand moments of the
independent raw u and v families in cumulants. In the outer
moment-to-cumulant inversion, a fixed raw partition pair is allowed
exactly in outer partitions pi above rho join sigma. Its coefficient
is sum_(pi>=rho join sigma) mu(pi,1), which equals one if the join
is 1, and zero otherwise by finite partition-lattice inversion.
That inversion also follows from
sum_l S(m,l)(-1)^(l-1)(l-1)!=1_(m=1), obtained by taking coefficients
in log(exp(x))=x. Thus (3) hides no probabilistic limit theorem.

Centering removes singleton blocks. Symmetry removes all odd blocks.
Every retained block has even size >=2. For each local term in (3),
make a bipartite multigraph H: its vertices are the row and column
blocks, and its k edges are the tensor positions. The join condition
makes H connected, and all vertex degrees are even.

Independence of the M rank-one summands gives

                        C_k(X_N)=(M/N^(k/2)) C_k(W).

Consequently, for a fixed contraction graph with v tensor vertices
and e Wick edges, and a choice of local terms (3), its index sum is
exactly a constant in the fixed raw cumulants times

                         M^v N^(c_i-e) P^(c_j),              (4)

where c_i,c_j are the free row and column equality classes.
Different free classes are allowed to take equal numerical values;
there is no distinct-label exclusion or asymptotic counting shortcut.

## 4. Surface lemma, including the strict loss for a higher cumulant

For every local connected even-degree H choose an Euler circuit.
Pair the two incident edges at every visit to a raw vertex along
that circuit. This refines each raw block into pairs. The refined
row and column pairings together form one cycle on all k positions.
Represent that cycle as a polygon with alternating row and column
corners. Each side is one tensor position, with one row and one
column endpoint.

Glue the two sides paired by each Wick edge, identifying row with
row and column with column. The result is a connected closed surface
map, possibly nonorientable. Locally each side belongs to two
polygons and each vertex link is a cycle: vertex equivalence classes
are generated by the adjacent-corner pairings and side gluings.
Thus this is a surface, not a pinched pseudomanifold. Its faces are
the v polygons, its edges are the e Wick pairs, and its vertices
are the refined equality classes c'_i+c'_j. Its dual adjacency graph
is precisely G. The original raw equalities can only merge refined
classes, so c_i<=c'_i and c_j<=c'_j.

For any connected closed surface map,

                   chi=c'_i+c'_j-e+v<=2.                     (5)

One elementary justification, valid without orientability, is to
choose a primal spanning tree. The dual edges complementary to that
tree are connected: otherwise a nonempty proper set of faces has
all its boundary edges in the primal tree. Around every primal vertex
the selected and unselected faces alternate an even number of times,
so this nonempty boundary is an even-degree subgraph and contains a
cycle. A tree cannot contain that subgraph. Choose a dual spanning
tree in the complement. Contracting the primal tree and then merging
faces along the dual tree leaves one vertex, one face, and
e-[(c'_i+c'_j)-1]-(v-1)=2-chi edges. This number is nonnegative.
If it is zero, the remaining cell is a disk with its whole boundary
collapsed to the single vertex, namely a sphere. Tree contractions
and face mergers preserve the underlying surface. Therefore chi=2
implies the original surface is a sphere.

We also need a planar-map fact with its relevant exceptions exposed:
in a connected sphere map whose dual is loopless and has no
articulation vertex, every primal face boundary is a simple cycle.
Here primal loops are additionally excluded by the row/column colors.
Indeed a primal bridge has the same face on both sides and hence
gives a dual loop, so there are no primal bridges. If the primal
has an articulation vertex, take a leaf block of its block-cut tree.
It contains a cycle because there are no bridges. The rest of the
map also contains a cycle, because it contains another non-bridge
block. The rest meets this leaf block at just its cut vertex and
lies in one face f of that block. The faces internal to the leaf
block communicate in the full dual with faces in the rest only
through f. Both sides contain a face other than f, so f is a dual
articulation, a contradiction. Thus the primal has no articulation.
Finally, a repeated vertex on a face boundary of a bridgeless plane
graph would be an articulation: joining the two boundary visits by
an arc within that face gives a separating Jordan curve through
that vertex, with graph edges on both sides. Deleting that vertex
disconnects the two sides. This proves the asserted simple-boundary
property. It includes a two-vertex parallel-edge block; no simplicity
of the edge graph was assumed.

Suppose now that the original term (3) involves a raw cumulant of
order >=4. At least one raw block was split into at least two visits
on the same polygon. If the refined map has chi<=1, then already

                       c_i+c_j-e+v<=1.

If it has chi=2, it is a sphere. Section 2 guarantees that its dual
G is loopless and has no articulation. Its polygon boundary is
therefore simple by the preceding paragraph. The two distinct visits
split from that raw block are distinct global map vertices.
Reimposing the raw block merges at least these two classes. Again

                       c_i+c_j-e+v<=1.                       (6)

For a pure Gaussian-pairing term only (5) is needed; its exponent
is at most two. This completes the surface power-counting lemma.

## 5. Coefficient comparison and analytic scope

Since P and M are comparable to N, equation (4) has size
O(N^(c_i+c_j-e+v)). Every term with a higher raw cumulant is O(N)
by (6); divided by NP it is O(1/N). At fixed K there are finitely
many contraction graphs, local set partitions and pairing choices,
with finite fixed cumulant coefficients. All pure-pairing terms
are exactly the same for U,V and for their Gaussian replacements.
Expanding a^e=s^e/(1+bs)^e adds only universal powers of b.
This proves (1). Pure-pairing exponents are integers <=2, so their
normalized monomials have finite limits when both aspect ratios
converge. The limits are the same for all the stated symmetric laws.

For bounded vector inputs the finite Hermite coefficient extraction
used above is analytic at each finite order, as in
bounded_prior_expansion.md and sixth_order_coefficients.md: Mehler
estimates and hypercontractivity control each fixed chaos truncation
in the L^p norm needed for its finite entropy expansion.

The posterior-replica streaming bound in finite_moment_expansion.md
gives |F^(K)(s)|<=2^K(2K)! E||X||^(2K+2), where
F(s)=E||E[X|sqrt(s)X+G]||^2. Since I^(K+1)=-F^(K)/2, Taylor's
integral remainder is (2). Symmetric vector truncation and covariance
whitening converge in L^(2K+2); the finite polynomial cumulant
contractions and moment bound converge, and Gaussian output entropy
is continuous. This extends the coefficient formulas and remainder
to the finite-moment inputs in Section 1, without assuming an
unbounded-input analytic series or exponential moments.
The truncated vector need not retain a product-factor representation:
only the general finite-vector coefficient identity is extended by
truncation. Formula (3) is then applied to the actual product input.

The proof establishes neither a uniform-in-N remainder nor a
nonzero radius of analyticity of the thermodynamic MI. It therefore
does not prove the conjectured universal low-SNR phase, and it does
not establish an expansion at the first prior-dependent thermodynamic
order. It shows why searching higher fixed finite-size coefficients
cannot reveal such an order for symmetric factors, if this draft's
finite diagram and surface arguments pass independent review.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:5f137222344a62a63677b52bd9ad3cd8fe51757cc1a2ca0ca661d913ec9b26ff","revision_digest":"sha256:ce3122784ffd46e433a9de1d97d722112f4fa6f5793b4706020c470f229a26fd","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:iid-product-mi-all-fixed-coefficients-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-20 claim w718-T287-011 version 2, proof unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

Let $\alpha\in\mathbb{A}$ be the unique optimizer for $V_{p,\delta}^{\infty}$. Then, there exists $\hat{\alpha} : [0,1]\times{\mathbb R} \to {\mathbb R}$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\alpha(t)=\hat{\alpha}(t,X^\alpha(t))$ for all $t\in[0,1]$ almost surely,
        \item $\hat{\alpha}$ points inwards, i.e., $x\hat{\alpha}(t,x) \le 0$ for all $(t,x)\in[0,1]\times{\mathbb R}$,
        \item $\hat{\alpha}$ is odd, i.e., $\alpha(t,x)=-\alpha(t,-x)$ for all $(t,x)\in[0,1]\times{\mathbb R}$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let Omega in R^n be open. A nondivergence-form operator is Lu = sum_{i,j} a^{ij}(x) D_{ij} u + sum_i b^i(x) D_i u + c(x) u with a^{ij} = a^{ji} real (symmetry is no loss because D_{ij}u is symmetric) and b^i, c real. L is elliptic at x if the matrix (a^{ij}(x)) is positive definite; lambda(x) denotes its smallest eigenvalue. L is uniformly elliptic with constants 0 < lambda <= Lambda if lambda|xi|^2 <= sum a^{ij}(x) xi_i xi_j <= Lambda|xi|^2 for all x (a.e. x for measurable coefficients) and all xi in R^n. Sign convention: here L = +Laplacian when (a^{ij}) = I, b = 0, c = 0, so the maximum principle concerns Lu >= 0 and the favorable sign of the zeroth-order coefficient is c <= 0 (the opposite of the divergence-form convention -div(A grad u) + c u with c >= 0). A classical solution of Lu = f is u in C^2(Omega) with Lu = f pointwise; a strong solution is u in W^{2,p}_loc(Omega) for some 1 <= p <= infinity with Lu = f almost everywhere. If the a^{ij} are C^1 (or Lipschitz), a^{ij} D_{ij} u = D_i(a^{ij} D_j u) - (D_i a^{ij}) D_j u rewrites L in divergence form; for merely measurable a^{ij} the two forms are different theories (De Giorgi-Nash-Moser for divergence form, Krylov-Safonov for nondivergence form).
Omega open in R^n
a^{ij} = a^{ji}, b^i, c real functions on Omega
lambda|xi|^2 <= a^{ij} xi_i xi_j <= Lambda|xi|^2 for uniform ellipticity
title: Uniformly Elliptic Operator in Nondivergence Form and Strong Solutions

A sequence of Borel probability measures (mu_n)_{n in N} in M_1(X) is sequentially tight if for each epsilon > 0 there exists a collection of compact subsets (K_epsilon^delta)_{delta > 0} of X such that: (i) liminf_{n -> infinity} mu_n(B_{K_epsilon^delta}(delta)) >= 1 - epsilon for every delta > 0, where B_A(delta) = {x in X : dist(x, A) < delta}; and (ii) the subspace K_epsilon := overline{bigcup_{delta > 0} K_epsilon^delta} subset X is complete in the metric d.

[Proposition 37 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] The rate function \(J_a\) is real analytic and strictly convex on
\((0,\infty)\). Moreover, there exist \(\varepsilon_a>0\) and a function
\(h_a\), holomorphic on \(\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<\varepsilon_a\}\), such that
\[
        J_a(x)
        =
        J_a(0)+x\log x+h_a(x),
        \qquad 0<x<\varepsilon_a,
\]
and, with the principal branch of the logarithm,
\(z\mapsto J_a(0)+z\log z+h_a(z)\) is holomorphic on
\(\{0<|z|<\varepsilon_a\}\setminus(-\varepsilon_a,0]\). In particular, as
\(x\downarrow0\),
\[
        J_a(x)
        =
        J_a(0)+x\log x+\gamma_a x+O(x^2)
\]
for some real constant \(\gamma_a\).

body: Aldous-Fill Open Problem 4.48(a) is answered in the negative: tau_1 <= tau_0 fails. On the continuous-time birth-and-death chain on {0,1,2} with rate 1 toward 0 and rate eps away from it, tau_0 = 2(1+eps)/(1+eps+eps^2) < 2 while tau_1 -> 2.14619 (the root of e^{-t}(1+t) = 1/e) as eps -> 0: the pair (2,0) separates until the sum of two unit exponentials has arrived. On the path of length k the limiting ratio tau_1/tau_0 is t_k/k with t_k the Gamma(k,1) tail threshold at 1/e (1.0731, 1.0861, 1.0880 at k=4, 1.0868, ...), so sup tau_1/tau_0 lies in [1.0880, 66]. Exact 30-digit check: k=2, eps=0.1 gives tau_0 = 1.981982, tau_1 = 2.010072.

[Lemma l:remainder2case1 of arXiv:2605.22803, 'Persistence of asymptotic variance under transport:\\ from hyperfluctuation to stealthy hy'] Suppose that $\Phi$ is an invariant locally absolutely square-integrable random measure, and that $K$ is an invariant transport kernel. Let $p\geq 0$ and assume that Condition~(c:condition square-integrable general with p of the paper) is satisfied.
Then $K\Phi$ is locally absolutely square-integrable. Further, for $r>0$,
\begin{equation}
    \lim_{r\to\infty} \frac{1}{r^{d-p}} \BE\bigg[\bigg(\int_{B_{2r}^c} |K|(y, B_r) \, |\Phi|(dy) \bigg)^2\bigg] = 0. 
\end{equation}
\begin{proof}
First of all, by Lemma~(l:stronlgy log-dominating modification of the paper), without loss of generality, we can assume that $\rho$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
    \rho(2r) \leq 4 \rho(r), \quad r\geq 0.
\end{equation}
Further, by Lemmas~(l: simplification to lebesgue of the paper) and~(l:condition reduction lebesgue of the paper), there is an invariant nonnegative transport kernel $L$ such that $L(y)$ has support on $\overline{B_1}+y$ for $y\in\R^d$, that $|\Phi|=L\lambda_d$, and that the invariant nonnegative transport kernel $\tilde{K}:=|K|L$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
    \BE\bigg[\bigg(\int \sqrt{\|x\|^{d+p}\rho(\|x\|)+1}\, \tilde{K}_0(dx)\bigg)^2\bigg] < \infty.
\end{equation}
Let $r>2$. Then,
\begin{align*}
    \int_{B_{2r}^c} |K|(y, B_r) \, |\Phi|(dy) &= \iint_{B_{2r}^c} |K|(z, B_r)\, L(y, dz) \, dy\nonumber\\
    &\leq \int_{B_{2r-1}^c}\int |K|(z, B_r) \, L(y, dz) \, dy\nonumber\\
    &= \int_{B_{2r-1}^c} \tilde{K}(y, B_r)\, dy,
\end{align*}
which simplifies the problem. Now this inequality and a two-times application of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality yield
\begin{align}
    \BE\bigg[\bigg(\int_{B_{2r}^c} |K|(y, B_r) \, |\Phi|(dy) \bigg)^2\bigg] &\leq \BE\bigg[\bigg(\int_{B_{2r-1}^c} \tilde{K}(y, B_r) \, dy \bigg)^2\bigg] \nonumber\\
    &= \int_{B_{2r-1}^c}\int_{B_{2r-1}^c} \BE\big[\tilde{K}(y, B_r)\tilde{K}(z, B_r)\big] \,dy\,dz \nonumber\\
    &\leq \int_{B_{2r-1}^c}\int_{B_{2r-1}^c} \sqrt{\BE\big[\tilde{K}(y, B_r)^2\big]\BE\big[\tilde{K}(z, B_r)^2\big]} \,dy\,dz \nonumber\\
    &= \bigg(\int_{B_{2r-1}^c}\sqrt{\BE\big[\tilde{K}(y, B_r)^2\big]} \,dy\bigg)^2\nonumber\\
    &= \Bigg(\int_{B_{2r-1}^c}\frac{\sqrt{(\|y\|^{d+p}\rho(\|y\|)+1)\BE\big[\tilde{K}(y, B_r)^2\big]}}{\sqrt{\|y\|^{d+p}\rho(\|y\|)+1}} \,dy\Bigg)^2 \nonumber\\
    &\leq \int_{B_{2r-1}^c} \frac{1}{\|y\|^{d+p}\rho(\|y\|)+1} \, dy\nonumber\\
    &\quad \ \ \times\int_{B_{2r-1}^c} (\|y\|^{d+p}\rho(\|y\|)+1) \BE\big[\tilde{K}(y, B_r)^2\big] \, dy.
\end{align}
For the first factor, we get
\begin{align*}
    \int_{B_{2r-1}^c}\frac{1}{\|y\|^{d+p}\rho(\|y\|)+1} \, dy &= d\kappa_d \int_{2r-1}^\infty \frac{s^{d-1}}{s^{d+p}\rho(s)+1} \, ds \nonumber\\
    &\leq \frac{d\kappa_d}{2^p r^p} \underbrace{\int_{2r-1}^\infty \frac{1}{s\rho(s)+s^{-(d+p-1)}}\, ds}_{a(r):=}.
\end{align*}
Because $\rho$ is strongly log-dominating, we can derive that $a(r)\to 0$ as $r\to\infty$ by the theorem of dominated convergence.
The second factor can be bounded by
\begin{align*}

[Lemma range_estimates of arXiv:2608.00399, 'The Heavy-tailed Frog Model'] Let $Q \in \mathcal{H}_{\alpha, K}$ for some $\alpha, K > 0$. Fix an arbitrary $\varepsilon \in (0, 1)$.
        Then, there exist positive constants $c_0 = c_0(Q, \varepsilon)$ and $c_1 = c_1(Q)$ such that the following holds:
        for 
        any $r \in \mathbb N^+$ and 
        any subset $D \subseteq B_x(r)$ with $|D| \le (1-\varepsilon) |B_x(r)|$, 
        we have 
        \begin{align} 
        \mathbf P_x \left( \, \left\vert \widetilde{\mathrm{R}}\left(\ell(r)\right) \right\vert \ge c_1 \varepsilon f(r) \, \right) &\ge  c_0,
        \end{align}
        where $\widetilde{\mathrm{R}}(k) := \mathrm{R}(k) \cap B_x(r) \setminus D$ and $f(r)$ and $\ell(r)$ are defined as above.
title: Lemma range_estimates of arXiv:2608.00399

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Test the conjecture's consistency by the boundary values and the contour relations alone. Result: The contour relations plus the known boundary values determine the discrete observable up to a subspace of dimension equal to the number of faces minus the number of independent contour relations, which is of the order of the number of vertices, so the observable is far from determined by what is proved; the conjecture is a statement about the actual random-cluster measure, not derivable from the relations alone. A weaker rigorous consequence that IS available: the contour relations imply that the integral of f_delta along any closed contour vanishes, so any subsequential limit of (2 delta)^{-sigma} f_delta, if tight, is holomorphic (Morera), and its boundary behaviour (modulus fixed on the boundary arcs by the boundary conditions) makes (phi')^sigma the unique candidate if the limit is bounded near a and b. Hence the conjecture reduces to tightness plus a priori bounds near the marked points. This reduction is standard for q = 2 and I confirmed it goes through for all q <= 4 given the contour relations; the a priori bounds are the missing input. Key identity: Contour relations + Morera => any tight subsequential limit is holomorphic with the prescribed boundary modulus; uniqueness then forces (phi')^sigma. Obstruction: Tightness and boundary a priori bounds for the observable are unproved for q not 2.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0050-convergence-of-the-parafermionic-observable-to-phi-sigma-for-q-4
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved
title: Attempt on Convergence of the parafermionic observable to (phi')^sigma for q <= 4

[Theorem 47 of arXiv:2608.18075, '2608.18075'] Fix $T\ge t_*$.  For every $r<\infty$, there are integers
$d_r,R_r<\infty$, and a constant
$C_{T,r}$ such that, for every $w_0\in H^b$ and every unit
$\mathsf p\in H^1$,
\begin{align}
 &\mathbf{E}_{w_0,\mathsf p}
 \left[\log^+\left(
  1+\|J(z,Y_T)\|+\mathsf C_T(z,Y_T)+\mathsf r_T(z,Y_T)^{-1}
 \right)\right]^r \le
 C_{T,r}\left(V_r(w_0)+1+\|\mathsf p\|_{H^1}^{d_r}\right).
 
\end{align}
The orders in $V_r$ and $d_r$ are independent of $T$.  The
estimate is interpreted as $+\infty$ when $[\mathsf p]\notin\PP(H^1)$.
It holds with the same form conditionally after a stopping time.

No fixed a_star in A satisfies {o connects to A,a_star connects to b} subset {o connects to b} for every edge configuration. With each independent edge probability 1/2, P(o connects to b)=7/32, P(o connects to A)=3/4, and min_{a in A}P(a connects to b)=9/32, so product gluing still holds with margin 1/128. Thus only a universal deterministic-witness bridge is refuted, not stochastic gluing.

[Corollary cor:polytope-learning-queries of arXiv:2606.19763, 'Optimal Sparsification of Gaussian Processes'] Let $r\geq1$, let $0<\eps<1/2$, and let $f:\R^n\to\zo$ be an unknown
	Boolean function. 
	There is an algorithm which, given black-box query access to $f$, runs in
	time
	\[
		\poly(n)\cdot
		2^{
			\poly\pbra{
				\log(\alpha(r,\eps/2))/\eps
			}
		}
		= \poly(n)\cdot 2^{\poly(r, 1/\eps)}
	\]
	and, with probability $9/10$, outputs a hypothesis $h:\R^n\to\zo$ satisfying
	\[
		\mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{G}}(f,h)
		\leq
		\mathrm{OPT}_r(f)+\eps\,.
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Agnostic learning with queries

[Proposition 10 of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Let~\(\chi\) be a Navier--Stokes potential and let \(I^\beta\) and \(I^{\beta\gamma}\) be algebraic source terms. Then the system
\bel{eq:pot-general-sources}
\nabla_\alpha T_\chi^{\alpha\beta}=I^\beta,
\qquad
\nabla_\alpha A_\chi^{\alpha\beta\gamma}=I^{\beta\gamma}
\ee
is symmetric hyperbolic in the interior of the state space, and the particle-number current satisfies
\bel{eq:pot-chain-identity}
\nabla_\alpha\vNumb_\chi^\alpha
=-\beta_\beta I^\beta
-\zeta_{\beta\gamma}I^{\beta\gamma}.
\ee
Moreover, let \(n\) be future timelike and set
\be
U^{\alpha A}
\coloneqq
\frac{\del^2\chi}{\del\beta_\alpha\del\Xi_A},
\qquad
Y^A\coloneqq-n_\alpha U^{\alpha A},
\qquad
\eta_n\coloneqq n_\alpha\vNumb_\chi^\alpha,
\qquad
\Xi=(\beta,\zeta).
\ee
Then \(\eta_n\) is strictly convex as a function of the normal conserved variables~\(Y\).
title: Proposition 10 of arXiv:2608.31171

body: [Defn SWG of arXiv:2412.03415, 'Critical first passage percolation on random graphs'] Initialize with ${\sf SWG}_{1}^{v}=\{v\}$. Add the edge and vertex with minimal edge weight connecting $v$ to one of its neighbors. The growth of $({\sf SWG}^{v}_m)_{m\geqslant 1}$ is then defined recursively: given ${\sf SWG}^v_{m}$, we obtain ${\sf SWG}^v_{m+1}$ by adding the edge and the end vertex connected to ${\sf SWG}^v_{m}$ with minimal edge weight (ties broken arbitrarily).
title: Smallest-weight graph

[Definition def:lipschitz of arXiv:2609.03980, 'Decay Rates and Domain Dependence of a Coupled Wave-Heat System with Spatially Dependant H'] \begin{enumerate}
    \item Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a non-empty domain. We call $\Omega$ a (strongly) \textit{Lipschitz domain} if $n=1$ or if for every $x\in \partial\Omega$, there is an open neighborhood $U_x \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ around $x$, an orthogonal matrix $O_x \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ and a Lipschitz function 
    $\phi_x: \mathbb{R}^{n-1}\to \mathbb{R}$ with 
    \begin{align*}
       O_x (U_x\cap \Omega) = \{(\xi,y) \in \mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times \mathbb{R}~|~ y < \phi_x(\xi) \}\cap O_x(U_x).
    \end{align*}

    
    \item Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a non-empty, bounded Lipschitz domain, and let $\Omega_w,\Omega_h\subset \Omega$ be two disjoint, non-empty Lipschitz domains. If 
    $\overline{\Omega}=\overline{\Omega_w\cup \Omega_h}$, we call $(\Omega,\Omega_w,\Omega_h)$ a \textit{Lipschitz interface triple} with interface $\gamma.$ 
    In this case, we set
    $$\Gamma_w  \coloneq  \partial\Omega\backslash\partial\Omega_h, ~~\Gamma_h \coloneq \partial\Omega\backslash\partial\Omega_w,~~ \gamma \coloneq  \partial\Omega_w\backslash\overline{\Gamma_h} = \partial\Omega_h\backslash\overline{\Gamma_w}.$$
    Furthermore, we denote by $\nu_w,\nu_h$ the unit outer normal vectors on $\Gamma_w,\Gamma_h$, which exist almost everywhere due to Rademacher's Theorem for $n\geq 2,$ and trivially everywhere in the case $n=1.$

    
Our assumptions on $(\Omega,\Omega_w,\Omega_h)$ are weaker than the assumptions imposed in  [ines,zuazualongtime].

    \item Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a non-empty Lipschitz domain, and let $\Gamma\subset \partial\Omega$ be a non-empty, relatively open subset of the boundary.
    We call $(\Omega,\Gamma)$ an \textit{admissible} Lipschitz pair, if there exists some domain $\Tilde{\Omega}\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ such that 
    $$(\Omega\cup \Gamma\cup \Tilde{\Omega}, \Omega, \Tilde{\Omega})$$ is a Lipschitz interface triple with interface $\Gamma$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Lipschitz interface triples

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2605.31374, 'Multi-point functions of a full-plane two-state\\ fuzzy $4$-Potts model'] For any $s>1$, the magnetization field $\Phi_\delta$ converges in law to a
random distribution $\Phi_0$ in $\mathcal H^{-s}(\mathbb R^2)$ as $\delta\to0$.
Moreover, the law of $\Phi_0$ is uniquely characterized by the
moment identities $\mathbb E\left[\left(\int \Phi_0 h\right)^n\right] = M_n(h)$ for every $h\in\mathcal H^s_0(\mathbb R^2)$
and every $n\in\N$.
In particular, for each such $h$, the law of $\int\Phi_0h$ is determined by $(M_n(h))_{n\in\N}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Guionnet-Huang Theorem1.1, existence and normalization assertion in the bounded-norm, log-regular case. Let m_n>=n, m_n/n->1+gamma for a finite gamma>=0, and rho=(1+gamma)^(-1). Let A_n,B_n be deterministic real n by m_n matrices with sup_n max(||A_n||_op,||B_n||_op)<=K for a finite K. For C=A,B let nu_hat_Cn=(1/(2n))*sum_{i=1}^n (delta_{s_i(C_n)}+delta_{-s_i(C_n)}) be its symmetrized empirical singular-value probability law. Suppose these laws converge weakly to symmetric probabilities nu_hat_A,nu_hat_B. Assume for both limits finite logarithmic energy Sigma(nu)=integral integral log|x-y| dnu(x)dnu(y)>-infinity and finite logarithmic moment integral log|x| dnu(x)>-infinity. Thus their second moments are bounded, and all the source logarithmic regularity conditions are imposed, including at the square endpoint. With independent normalized Haar U in O(n), V in O(m_n), set I_n,m(A_n,B_n)=integral exp(n*Tr(A_n^T*U*B_n*V^T)) dU dV. Then n^(-2)*log I_n,m_n(A_n,B_n) has a finite limit depending only on gamma and the two limiting symmetrized singular laws. In the notation of source equation1.5 that limit is (1/2)*mathcalI^gamma(nu_hat_A,nu_hat_B); this card extracts the existence and normalization assertion, under the displayed stronger bounded-norm/log-regular hypotheses. Consequently, with N=n,M=m_n and J_N,M(A,B)=log I_N,M(A,B)/(N*M), the limit of J is (rho/2)*mathcalI^gamma(nu_hat_A,nu_hat_B), where gamma=1/rho-1. The factor rho converts the source n^2 normalization to n*m. Here gamma is the source aspect parameter called alpha in Guionnet-Huang; rho is the reciprocal aspect ratio called alpha in the Pourkamali-Macris application. The stated case is real orthogonal Haar and uses the exponent n, without an additional beta factor.
Real rectangular deterministic matrices; m_n/n->1+gamma in [1,infinity); independent normalized orthogonal Haar matrices.
Uniform bounded operator norms and weak convergence of the two symmetrized singular-value empirical laws.
Both limiting measures have finite logarithmic energy and logarithmic moment, explicitly imposed for every gamma.

[Defn Chordal link pattern of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Given $\boldsymbol{z}=\{z_1,z_2,...,z_n\}$ on the real line, a link pattern is a homotopically equivalent class of non-intersecting curves connecting pair of boundary points (links) or connecting boundary points and the infinity (rays). The link patterns with $n$ boundary points and $m$ links are called $(n,m)$-links, denoted by ${\rm LP}(n,m)$.

The number of chordal $(n,m)$-links is given by $|{\rm LP}(n,m)|=C_{n}^{m+1}-C_{n}^{m}$.

[Lemma 5 (\cite{Chen2013}*{Lemma 4}) of arXiv:2608.10515, 'Limiting Law of Local Fields for the Mean Field Ghatak-Sherrington Model'] Let $k\in\N$. Suppose that $V_1,\ldots,V_{2k}:\R^2\to\R$ are twice continuously differentiable and of moderate growth, together with their first and second partial derivatives. Define
\[
  \phi(t)=\E_0\left[\prod_{i=1}^{2k}V_i(u_i(t),r)\right],\qquad 0\le t\le 1.
\]
Then $\phi$ is differentiable on $(0,1)$ and
\begin{align}
\phi'(t)
=&\frac12\sum_{i\le 2k}T_{i,i}\E_0\left[\frac{\partial^2V_i}{\partial x^2}(u_i(t),r)\prod_{\substack{j\le 2k\\ j\ne i}}V_j(u_j(t),r)\right] \notag\\
&+\frac12\sum_{\substack{i,j\le 2k\\ i\ne j}}T_{i,j}\E_0\left[\frac{\partial V_i}{\partial x}(u_i(t),r)\frac{\partial V_j}{\partial x}(u_j(t),r)
\prod_{\substack{h\le 2k\\ h\ne i,j}}V_h(u_h(t),r)\right] \notag\\
&+\frac1{2\sqrt t}\sum_{i\le 2k}T_i\E_0\left[\frac{\partial^2V_i}{\partial x\partial y}(u_i(t),r)\prod_{\substack{j\le 2k\\ j\ne i}}V_j(u_j(t),r)\right] \notag\\
&+\frac1{2\sqrt t}\sum_{\substack{i,j\le 2k\\ i\ne j}}T_i\E_0\left[\frac{\partial V_i}{\partial x}(u_i(t),r)\frac{\partial V_j}{\partial y}(u_j(t),r)
\prod_{\substack{h\le 2k\\ h\ne i,j}}V_h(u_h(t),r)\right].
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \cite{Chen2013}*{Lemma 4}

[Corollary 11 (Conditional first-break law and moments) of arXiv:2605.09641, 'The Ballot Event for Two-Player Coupon Collection: A Renewal--Catalan Asymptotic'] Let $K_d$ be the extended first-break level from
Lemma~\ref{lem:first-break}, and let
\[
        \mathcal B_d:=\{\text{the ultimate winner was never behind}\}.
\]
Then, conditional on $\mathcal E_A$,
\[
        \frac{K_d}{\sqrt d}\Rightarrow X,
        \qquad
        \Prob(X\in \dd x)=2x e^{-x^2}\Ind_{\{x>0\}}\dd x .
\]
The same convergence holds conditional on $\mathcal B_d$.

Moreover, for every fixed $p>0$,
\[
        \E\left[\left(\frac{K_d}{\sqrt d}\right)^p\right]
        \longrightarrow
        \Gamma\left(1+\frac p2\right),
\]
and
\[
        \E\left[
        \left(\frac{K_d}{\sqrt d}\right)^p
        \,\middle|\,\mathcal E_A\right]
        \longrightarrow
        \Gamma\left(1+\frac p2\right).
\]
The same conditional moment convergence holds with $\mathcal E_A$ replaced by
$\mathcal B_d$.  In particular,
\[
        \E K_d\sim \frac{\sqrt\pi}{2}\sqrt d,
        \qquad
        \operatorname{Var}(K_d)\sim
        \left(1-\frac\pi4\right)d,
\]
and the same expectation and variance asymptotics hold conditional on
$\mathcal E_A$ and conditional on $\mathcal B_d$.

Let Q = sum_{r=1}^m lambda_r chi^2_{h_r; delta_r^2}, where the lambda_r are distinct nonzero reals and the chi^2_{h_r; delta_r^2} are independent noncentral chi-square variables with h_r degrees of freedom and noncentrality delta_r^2 (any (x+mu)'A(x+mu) with x Gaussian, nonsingular covariance, reduces to this). Then for every x: P(Q > x) = 1/2 + (1/pi) int_0^infinity sin(theta(u)) / (u rho(u)) du, with theta(u) = (1/2) sum_r [h_r arctan(lambda_r u) + delta_r^2 lambda_r u (1 + lambda_r^2 u^2)^{-1}] - (1/2) x u and rho(u) = prod_r (1 + lambda_r^2 u^2)^{h_r/4} exp{(1/2) sum_r (delta_r lambda_r u)^2 / (1 + lambda_r^2 u^2)}. For central forms with even degrees of freedom there are finite expressions for P(Q > x) and the density.

Assumes: Gaussian inputs; the lambda_r are the distinct nonzero eigenvalues of A Sigma with multiplicities h_r

[Definition 20 ($\AS$) of arXiv:2511.07350, 'Decoupling of clusters in independent sets in a percolated hypercube'] Define the random independent set $\hat{I}$ in $\Qp$ via the following procedure.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Let $\cH$ be $\cE$ or $\cO$, with probabilities $q^\cE$ and $q^\cO$ respectively.
		
		\item Let $\tilde{S}$ denote a subset of $\cH$ constructed by including each $v \in \cH$ independently with probability
		$\fr{\phi_v}{1 + \phi_v}$. In other words, sample $\tilde{S} \sim \pi^\cH$, where $\pi^\cH$ was defined in \eqref{eq:pidef}
		(with the superscript $\cH$ being implicit in that definition).
		
		\item If $\tilde{S} \notin \Sep_{\leq 2}$ (recall this notation from just above \eqref{eq:smallpolymerpfdef}), terminate the algorithm with a result of failure.
		Otherwise, remove all dimers from $\tilde{S}$ and let $S_1$ denote the resulting set of well-separated singletons.
		
		\item Let $S_2$ denote a collection of dimers constructed by including each $\{u,v\} \in \Dim^\cH$ independently with probability
		$\fr{\phi_\fd}{1 + \phi_\fd}$.
		
		\item If $S_1 \cup S_2 \notin \Sep_{\leq 2}$, terminate the algorithm with a result of failure.
		Otherwise, let $\hat{S} = S_1 \cup S_2$.
		
		\item Let $\hat{I}$ denote the independent set with $\hat{I} \cap \cH = \hat{S}$ and with every vertex in $\Q \setminus \cH$
		which does not neighbor $\hat{S}$ included independently with probability $\fr{1}{2}$ each.
		
	\end{enumerate}

DRAFT AUDIT CONCEPT; independent referee pending. For q>=1 and 0<p<1, a finite FK edge conditional, given any subset of the other edges, lies between a=p/(p+q(1-p)) and p. The bounds follow from the open/closed component-count ratio and the tower property. For integer d>=1, in wired boxes [-N,N]^d, integer N>=1, connection of the origin to the boundary is at most 2d*p*((2d-1)*p)^(N-1), by sequential path conditioning and a union bound. At q=3,d=3,p=1/10 all local edge conditionals are at least 1/28, yet the one-arm bound is (3/5)*2^(-(N-1)) and tends to zero. The example is subcritical and does not refute C0048. Local positivity alone cannot supply the uniform critical gap.

[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2608.13677, 'Asymptotically complete free-energy dissipation: \\ a coarse MLSI holds at any positive te'] \label[lemma]{lemma:computation_flip_density}
    Suppose \(\sigma(\mu) < \infty\), or even just \(\mu \ll \mu \circ \mathrm{flip}_0^{-1}\) (or, equivalently, \(\mu \circ \mathrm{flip}_0^{-1} \ll \mu\)).
    Then, for \(\mu\)-a.e. \(\eta\) and all \(x \in \Lambda_n\), we have 
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{\d \mu_{\Lambda_n \vert \Lambda_n^c}(\cdot \vert \eta) }{\d (\mu_{\Lambda_n \vert \Lambda_n^c}(\cdot \vert \eta) \circ \mathrm{flip}_x^{-1})}(\eta_{\Lambda_n})
        = \frac{\mathrm{d}\mu}{\mathrm{d}(\mu \circ \mathrm{flip}_0^{-1})}(\theta_{x}\eta),
    \end{align*} where \(\theta_x\) means translation by \(x\), i.e., \((\theta_x \eta)_y = \eta_{y+x}\) for all \(y \in \Z^d\).

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:f3f089db25a71026dc997a1c17809e04c99da3cae3618b510cb32edcdef6aa48","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/f3/f3f089db25a71026dc997a1c17809e04c99da3cae3618b510cb32edcdef6aa48.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:91acd56335975a932539f4073e0edfa8458a1eb6dee249a431112ed253e3e53b","bundle_entry_key":"weighted-canonical-diameter","bundle_id":"population.probability-critical-moments-two-end-kernels-and-dependence-006","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"codex-probability-1000-20h-20260906/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.markov:known-pak-diameter-squared-weighted-cayley-relaxation-bound","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# P0248: optimized Cayley walk ? known-result rederivation

Status: author-checked rederivation of a literature-resolved historical question. This is excluded from the current-open target and original-solution count. No independent review of this proof is claimed.

Aldous?Fill, Conjecture/Open Problem 7.18, PDF page 253, asks whether a finite Cayley graph admits a symmetric generator distribution with relaxation time at most a universal constant times its squared diameter. Igor Pak, *Using stopping times to bound mixing times*, SODA 1999, Theorem 3.1, explicitly states that it resolves this question. The author-hosted PDF is internally dated October 31, 2004: https://www.math.ucla.edu/~pak/papers/soda4.pdf . The date of the archived copy is distinguished from the 1999 publication date.

## Construction and direct proof

Let the finite group be $G$, with inverse-closed generating set $S$ excluding the identity, and diameter $D$. For every $x\in G$, choose a geodesic word $w_x$ of length $\ell_x$. Randomize the word for $x$ equally between $w_x$ and the reversed, inverted word chosen for $x^{-1}$. Both words represent $x$ and have the same length. Let $N_s(x)$ be the number of occurrences of $s$ in this randomized word. Define

$$a_s=\frac1{|G|}\sum_x \ell_x\,\mathbb E N_s(x),\qquad A=\sum_s a_s=\frac1{|G|}\sum_x\ell_x^2\le D^2.$$

Inversion of words shows $a_s=a_{s^{-1}}$. Each $a_s>0$, because the word representing $s$ has length one. Thus $\mu(s)=a_s/A$ is a symmetric probability measure whose support is exactly $S$.

For a real function $f$ and uniform $\pi$, the independent uniform-pair identity is

$$\operatorname{Var}_\pi f=\frac1{2|G|^2}\sum_{z,x\in G}(f(zx)-f(z))^2.$$

Telescope along the chosen word for $x$ and use Cauchy?Schwarz. For each occurrence of $s$, translating the summation variable $z$ by the preceding prefix leaves the uniform sum unchanged. Therefore

$$\operatorname{Var}_\pi f\le\frac12\sum_s a_s\,\mathbb E_{z\sim\pi}(f(zs)-f(z))^2=A\,\mathcal E_\mu(f,f).$$

The variational characterization of the gap gives $\tau_2\le A\le D^2$. This is the continuous-time/rate-one spectral convention $\tau_2=(1-\lambda_2)^{-1}$; it is not a claim about absolute discrete-time eigenvalues when the graph is bipartite. Adding one-half holding makes aperiodic discrete-time mixing and changes the relaxation bound by a factor two.

## Second check and limits

The Aldous?Fill comparison theorem 7.16, with comparison increments uniform on the whole group, gives $\tau_2\le\max_s a_s/\mu(s)=A$. It independently reproduces the direct Dirichlet-form argument. The inversion randomization is necessary to justify symmetry in a noncommutative group; a deterministically chosen word table need not give symmetric counts.

This derivation was written before the Pak source was found in the campaign's later-literature check. Discovery order does not imply novelty. [Defn Inner product on standard module of arXiv:2506.01306, 'Asymptotic of Coulomb gas integral, Temperley-Lieb type algebras and pure partition functi'] Let $x, y \in V_{n,m}$ be two $(n,m)$-link states and $\delta \in \mathbb{C}$. Define $\langle x, y \rangle_{n,m}$ as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Reflect $x$ across a vertical axis (mirror image).
    \item Glue $x$ to $y$ vertically, forming a closed link diagram.
    \item If all defects pair, and $l(\alpha,\beta)$ closed loops are formed, then
    \[
    \langle x, y \rangle_{n,m} := \delta^{l(\alpha,\beta)}.
    \]
    \item Otherwise, if any defects remain unpaired, then $\langle x, y \rangle_{n,m} := 0$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Inner product on standard module

body:
[Lem 50 of arXiv:2604.03777, 'Equilibrium fluctuations for a multi-species particle system with long jumps'] For $r>1$, let $\phi\in\cC^r$ be a scaling function and $\psi$ the associated mother wavelet. 
Then, there exists a constant $C=C(\phi,\psi)>0$ 
such that for any $p\in\NN$, $p<r$, all $z\in\Lambda_0$, $m\geq 1$, $x\in\Lambda_m$ and $v\in\R$, we have 
\begin{equ}[e:BoundsWavelets]
\|\partial_y^p\phi^z(\cdot-v)\|_{L^2(\R)}\leq C\,,\qquad\text{and}\qquad \|\partial_y^p\psi_m^x(\cdot-v)\|_{L^2(\R)}\leq C 2^{\frac{mp}{2}}\,.
\end{equ}
Let $h$ be a smooth and compactly supported function. Then, for $v\in\R$, 
$\langle h(\cdot-v), \phi_z\rangle_{L^2(\R)}$ and 
$\langle h(\cdot-v), \psi_m^x\rangle_{L^2(\R)}$ are 
non-zero for at most finitely many $z\in\Lambda_0$ and $O(2^m)$ $x\in\Lambda_m$, $m\geq 1$, 
where in both cases the exact number is independent of $v$. 
Furthermore, there exists a constant $C=C(h, \phi,\psi)>0$ such that 
for all $z\in\Lambda_0$, $m\geq 1$, $x\in\Lambda_m$ and $v\in\R$, and any $j\in\NN$, $j<r$, we have 
\begin{equ}[e:BoundSmooth]
\big|\langle h(\cdot-v), \phi^z\rangle_{L^2(\R)}\big|\leq C\,,\qquad \text{and}\qquad \big|\langle h(\cdot-v), \psi_m^x\rangle_{L^2(\R)}\big|\leq C 2^{m-mj}
\end{equ}
title: Lem 50 of arXiv:2604.03777

    \begin{align*}
        \sup_{n\geqslant 1}
        \mathbb{E}\left[
            \left|
                \frac{1}{n^{1/3}}\left(\mathcal{H}^{\xi}_1(0,xn^{2/3};n,yn^{2/3})
                + \frac{n}{24}\right)
            \right|^4
        \right]
        <\infty,
    \end{align*}
    where $\mathcal{H}^\xi$ was defined in (equation e:KPZ-cole-hopf of the paper).

body: In decision theory and estimation theory, Stein's example is the observation that when three or more parameters are estimated simultaneously, there exist combined estimators more accurate on average than any method that handles the parameters separately. It is named after Charles Stein of Stanford University, who discovered the phenomenon in 1955.
title: Stein's example
Corollary 16 of arXiv:2512.02538

body:
[Defn H marginal of arXiv:2505.16093, 'Multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Moser system'] The locally commuting n chordal $\mathrm{SLE}_\kappa$ is a compatible family of measures $\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n\right)}$ on $n$ tuples of continuous non-self-crossing curves $\left(\eta^{(1)}, \eta^{(2)},\ldots,\eta^{(n)}\right)$ for all simply connected domain $\Omega$ with $\left(z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)$, and $\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n\right)$ as above that satisfy additionally the conditions below. 

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Conformal invariance}: If $\varphi: \Omega \rightarrow \Omega^{\prime}$ is a conformal map fixing 0, then the pullback measure
$$
\varphi^* \mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega^{\prime} ; \varphi\left(z_1\right), \varphi\left(z_2\right),\ldots,\varphi\left(z_n),\varphi(u)\right)\right)}^{\left(\varphi\left(U_1\right), \varphi\left(U_2\right),\right)}=\left(\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega ; z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n\right)}\right) .
$$

Therefore, it suffices to describe the measure when $\left(\Omega ; z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)=\left(\mathbb{H}; z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_n,0\right)$.
We can extend our definition to arbitrary simply-connected domain $\Omega$ with a marked interior point $u$ by pulling back via a conformal equivalence $\phi:\Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{D}$ sending $u$ to $0$.

\item
\textbf{Domain Markov property}: Let $\left(\gamma^{(1)}, \gamma^{(2)},\ldots,\gamma^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\mathbb{H} ; x_1, x_2,\ldots,x_n\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots, U_n\right)}$ and we parametrize $\gamma^{(j)}$ by their own capacity in $\mathbb{H}$. Let $\mathbf{t}=\left(t_1, t_2,\ldots,t_n\right)$, such that $t_j$ is a stopping time for $\gamma^{(j)}$ and $\gamma_{\left[0, t_j\right]}^{(j)}$ is contained in the interior of $U_j$. Let
$$
\tilde{U}_j=U_j \backslash \gamma_{\left[0, t_j\right]}^{(j)}, \quad \tilde{\gamma}^{(j)}=\gamma^{(j)} \backslash \gamma_{\left[0, t_j\right]}^{(j)}, \quad j=1,2,\ldots,n; \quad \tilde{\Omega}=\mathbb{H} \backslash\left(\gamma_{\left[0, t_1\right]}^{(1)} \cup \gamma_{\left[0, t_2\right]}^{(2)} \cup \ldots \cup \gamma_{\left[0, t_n\right]}^{(n)}\right) .
$$

Then conditionally on $\gamma_{\left[0, t_1\right]}^{(1)} \cup \gamma_{\left[0, t_2\right]}^{(2)} \cup \ldots \cup  \gamma_{\left[0, t_n\right]}^{(n)}$, we have
$$
\left(\tilde{\gamma}^{(1)}, \tilde{\gamma}^{(2)}, \ldots, \tilde{\gamma}^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\tilde{\Omega} ; \gamma_{t_1}^{(1)}, \gamma_{t_2}^{(2)},\ldots,\gamma_{t_n}^{(n)}\right)}^{\left(\tilde{U}_1, \tilde{U}_2, \ldots,\tilde{U}_n\right)} .
$$

\item \textbf{Absolute continuity with respect to independent SLE($\kappa$)}:
 In $\mathbb{H}$-uniformization, let $\left(\gamma^{(1)}, \gamma^{(2)},\ldots,\gamma^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\mathbb{H} ; x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n,u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n)\right.}$. 

We assume that there exist smooth functions $b_j: \mathfrak{X}^n(\boldsymbol{x},u) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, where the chamber: $$\mathfrak{X}^n(\boldsymbol{x},u)=\left\{(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n,u) \in \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{H} \mid x_1<x_2<\ldots<x_n, u \in \mathbb{H} \right\}$$ 
such that the capacity parametrized Loewner driving function $t \mapsto \theta_t^{(j)}$ of $\gamma^{(j)}$ satisfies
\begin{equation} 
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\mathrm{~d} x_{j}(t)=\sqrt{\kappa} \mathrm{d} B_{j}(t)+b_j\left(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),\ldots,x_{n}(t),u\right) \mathrm{d} t \\
\mathrm{~d} x_{k}(t)=\frac{2}{x_{k}(t)-x_{j}(t)} \mathrm{d} t,  k\neq j
\end{array}\right.
\end{equation}
where $B_{j}$ is one-dimensional standard Brownian motion. 

\end{itemize}
title: Local multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$)

body:
[Lemma l.xi-infnity of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let $\xi :\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K} \times \hat\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a stabilizing marking function satisfying  $R^\xi_\infty(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}})<\infty$ a.s. for all $\tilde{x}\in\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ and consider $\xi_\infty$ as defined in (equation scoreconvergence of the paper). The following statements hold.

\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),  labelindent=0pt]
\item   There exist (finite) random variables $n_0:= n_0(\tilde{x}, \tilde{\mathcal{P}})$  such that for all $k \geq n_0$  we have  $R^{\xi}_{W_k}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_k)=R^\xi_{\infty}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}} )$  and $ \xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_k)=\xi_{\infty}(\tilde{x}, \tilde{\mathcal{P}})$. In particular, a.s. for all $\tilde{x}\in\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$, we have that $\xi_{\infty}(\tilde{x}, \tilde{\mathcal{P}}) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n) \ $ i.e., the equivalence (equation e:xi-to-infty of the paper) holds.
\item   $R^\xi_\infty$ is a.s. an upper bound for the radius of stabilization for $\xi_\infty$ as in Definition~(def.Stab.Radius of the paper), i.e., $R^{\xi_{\infty}}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}) \leq R^\xi_\infty(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}})$ a.s..
\item  If $\xi$  satisfies the $p$-moment condition~(equation e:xinpmom of the paper) on finite windows then ~(equation e:xinpmom of the paper) also holds
  for $\xi_\infty$ (i.e., replacing $\xi_{i,n}$ 
  by  
$\xi_\infty(\tilde x_i,\tilde{\mathcal{P}}))$  with the same moment bound $M_p^\xi$.
For this implication to hold, it is enough that $\xi_{\infty}$ is defined as a limit as in (equation e:xi-to-infty of the paper), without requiring that $R^\xi_\infty(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}})<\infty$.  
\item  If $\xi$ is translation invariant  then is so $R^\xi_\infty$ and hence $\xi_\infty$.
\end{enumerate}

Suppose now that $\xi$ is defined on  $\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K} \times
  \mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}}$ and satisfies stopping set stabilization on $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ ~(equation stab-infinite of the paper)  with $p=1$. Then 
\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),  labelindent=0pt]
\setcounter{enumi}{4}
\item  $R^\xi_\infty(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}})<\infty$ for all $\tilde{x}\in\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$, a.s.. Consequently all properties (i)--(iv) hold  and moreover $R^\xi_\infty=R^\xi$ and $\xi_\infty=\xi$ for all $\tilde{x}\in\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$, a.s. 
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem 18 (Keyl--Werner) of arXiv:2609.03736, '2609.03736'] Let $\tau$ be a density matrix on $\CC^m$ with decreasing eigenvalue list
$s$, and let $\Pi_\lambda^{(N)}$ be the $\mathfrak S_N$-isotypic projection
of shape $\lambda$ in $(\CC^m)^{\otimes N}$.  The numbers
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P_{\tau,N}(\lambda)
 =\tr\bigl(\tau^{\otimes N}\Pi_\lambda^{(N)}\bigr)
 
\end{equation}
form a probability measure on partitions of $N$ with at most $m$ parts.
View $\lambda/N$ as an $m$-vector by appending zero parts.  For every
$\varepsilon>0$,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{\substack{\lambda\vdash N\\
        \|\lambda/N-s\|_1>\varepsilon}}
 \tr\bigl(\tau^{\otimes N}\Pi_\lambda^{(N)}\bigr)
 \longrightarrow0.
 
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the normalized row-length vector $\lambda/N$ converges in
probability to the spectrum $s$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Keyl--Werner

[Lemma lem:lcp-nonlocal-square-identity of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] The square $\phi^2$ belongs to $V_x$ and satisfies
\begin{equation}
 A_0(\phi^2)
 =2\Lambda\phi^2M_x^\partial-\Gamma_J(\phi)m
 \qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb T).
\end{equation}
Both terms on the right are finite Radon measures, and
$\Gamma_J(\phi)m\ll m$.  Equivalently, for every real
$\zeta\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal E(\phi^2,\zeta)
 =2\Lambda\int_{\mathbb T}\zeta\phi^2\,dM_x^\partial
  -\int_{\mathbb T}\zeta\,\Gamma_J(\phi)\,dm.
\end{equation}

[Lemma 14 (Matrix concentration inequalities) of arXiv:2608.22595, 'Sparse Additive Off-Policy Evaluation for Reinforcement Learning with Potentially Limited '] Let \(p_1,p_2\geq1\) and write \(D=p_1+p_2\).

\begin{itemize}
\item
Let \(\{\boldsymbol{Z}_j\}_{j=1}^m\) be independent, mean-zero
random matrices of dimension \(p_1\times p_2\). Suppose that
\(\|\boldsymbol{Z}_j\|_2\leq R\) almost surely, and define
\[
\nu^2
=
\max\left\{
\left\|
\sum_{j=1}^m
\mathbb{E}
\left(
\boldsymbol{Z}_j\boldsymbol{Z}_j^\top
\right)
\right\|_2,
\left\|
\sum_{j=1}^m
\mathbb{E}
\left(
\boldsymbol{Z}_j^\top\boldsymbol{Z}_j
\right)
\right\|_2
\right\}.
\]
Then, for any \(u>0\),
\[
\Pr\left[
\left\|
\sum_{j=1}^m\boldsymbol{Z}_j
\right\|_2
>
\sqrt{2\nu^2\{u+\log D\}}
+
\frac{2R}{3}\{u+\log D\}
\right]
\leq
\exp(-u).
\]
In particular, if \(\nu^2\leq mR^2\), then
\[
\Pr\left[
\left\|
\sum_{j=1}^m\boldsymbol{Z}_j
\right\|_2
>
R\sqrt{2m\{u+\log D\}}
+
\frac{2R}{3}\{u+\log D\}
\right]
\leq
\exp(-u).
\]

\item Let \(\{\boldsymbol{X}_j,\mathcal{F}_j\}_{j=1}^m\) be an adapted
sequence of random matrices of dimension \(p_1\times p_2\) satisfying
\(\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{X}_j\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1})
=\boldsymbol{0}\). Suppose that
\(\|\boldsymbol{X}_j\|_2\leq R_j\) almost surely, where
\(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) are deterministic. Then, for any \(u>0\),
\[
\Pr\left[
\left\|
\sum_{j=1}^m\boldsymbol{X}_j
\right\|_2
>
\sqrt{
8\{u+\log D\}
\sum_{j=1}^m R_j^2
}
\right]
\leq
\exp(-u).
\]
In particular, if \(R_j\leq R\) for all \(j\), then
\[
\Pr\left[
\left\|
\sum_{j=1}^m\boldsymbol{X}_j
\right\|_2
>
R\sqrt{8m\{u+\log D\}}
\right]
\leq
\exp(-u).
\]
\end{itemize}

[Theorem lazyGinf of arXiv:2604.07227, 'Transition probabilities of step-reinforced random walks'] Let $S=(S_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ be an irreducible generalized SRRW on a countably infinite group $G$ with parameter $\alpha \in [0,1)$ and step distribution $\mu$ such that $\mu(e_G)\geq \mu_0$ for some $\mu_0\in (0,1/2]$. Then for any $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, one has
$$
 \max_{x \in G} \mathbb{P}(S_n=x) \leq \varepsilon \quad \text{if } n \geq \frac{C(\mu_0)}{1-\alpha} \int_{4}^{8 / \varepsilon}\frac{1 }{u \Phi^2(u)} d u, 
$$
  where $C(\mu_0)$ is a positive constant that depends only on $\mu_0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lazy chains
